0

There are no flowers that do not wilt, yet some flowers never bloom.

This world is truly unfair.

1

“—You good-for-nothing!”

Professor Kyouichirou hollered and beat Shito with his wooden cane, his voice nearly cracking. Shito didn’t even attempt to move out of the way as one of the blows struck him in the head. The impact sent him crumpling to the floor. Even then, without letting up, Professor Kyouichirou continued pummelling Shito’s curled-up body over and over. The entire time, he kept repeating, “Good-for-nothing! Good-for-nothing! Good-for-nothing!”

We watched it happen.

Unable to say or do anything, we watched it happen.

Shadou Kyouichirou, Koutari Hinayoshi, Neo Furuara, Miyoshi Kokoromi, Kasugai Kasuga, Uze Misachi, Ougaki Shito, Suzunashi Neon, Kunagisa Tomo, and I. The aforementioned ten people were gathered inside the Primary Research Ward’s parlour. That meant, with the exception of her, every person at the research facility was currently accounted for.

“——……”

Over an hour had passed since the incident, but the police still hadn’t arrived. Apparently Misachi filed the police report immediately after the body was discovered, but the downpour that visited us in the middle of night paired with the fact we were so deep in the mountains spelt disaster for our current situation. It’s not like the roads had washed away, but it meant it would still take a little while longer before anyone got here.

A murder.

I suppose that’s what you’d call it.

It didn’t feel real, but there were no other words for it. Only yesterday, Utsurigi Gaisuke had spoken so knowingly, and now he was dead. None of it felt real, but I suppose there’s no denying what happened.

“Damnit… and it was my turn to question him today too…”

I mumbled, the image of Shito’s beating still reflected in my eyes. If everything had played out how it was supposed to, what questions would I have even had for that man? I felt like there was something I was meant to ask, but at the same time I felt like there was nothing. In the end, Utsurigi Gaisuke managed to quit while he was ahead. Whether that was something he’d wanted is a different matter altogether.

“—Please, that’s enough already.”

Misachi clung to the professor’s arm.

“Professor, please calm dow—”

“Silence!”

Professor Kyouichirou tore his arm free, and then, just like he had done to Shito, he brought his cane down on her. Misachi raised her arms to protect her face, but when the blow connected, she let out a tiny yelp and collapsed to the floor.

“You’re nothing but nuisances, each and every one of you—”

He said, burying his foot squarely in Misachi’s back.

“——……”

So easily they crumble.

These things called people.

Seeing this small, old man throw such a tantrum- whatever sense of gravity he once held, whatever air of experience, was long gone. Not a trace of the man I met yesterday remained. In his place was something more akin to a toddler, a child whose favourite toy had been broken and was taking it out on everyone around him. A man of such calibre had been reduced to this so easily. For better or for worse, even Shadou Kyouichirou, who had overwhelmed me with his staggering presence, was no better than this.

That’s why, if someone like me were in his shoes-

“—How unsightly, Professor Shadou.”

As Professor Kyouichirou reeled back to beat Misachi once more, a voice as sharp as an arrow reverberated throughout the room. And so, with his cane still raised high above his head, Professor Kyouichirou froze.

The voice belonged to Suzunashi.

Sitting in a chair with her legs crossed, her chin raised as if looking down on the professor, Suzunashi wore an expression of genuine contempt.

“Goodness— I expected more from someone with as grand a title as The Mad Daemon, but I’m beyond disappointed. Imagine my shock when you turned out to be nothing more than another boring brute. How dull. To think, a man who’s lived for sixty years would fall apart over the death of one man, take it out on women and children, and go completely off the rails without once confirming the situation for himself. Honestly, I can’t bare to look at you—”

“Be quiet! A woman who hasn’t even lived thirty years has no right to talk back to me! You know nothing!”

The professor shouted and threw his cane at her. Suzunashi didn’t bother dodging; she didn’t even blink. The head of the cane shattered against her brow. Even then, Suzunashi just huffed and continued to stare at him with disdain.

That glare, it was as if she were genuinely gazing upon a lowly beast. As someone who’s been on the receiving end of that glare, I was more than able to guess how it made the professor feel. It was a glare that made you feel every bit as small and detestable as you really were.

“You wretch… who do you think you’re looking at—?”

“Professor! Please stop!” Shito called out from the floor where he still lay. “Calm down— please collect yourself!”

“Collect myself!? How could anyone collect themselves at a time like this!? If It’s dead-” Professor Kyouichirou turned back to Shito. “If It’s dead, if It’s all gone, what am I to do!? It’s all over! Everything I’ve built ‘till now is ruined!”

《It》—— Utsurigi Gaisuke.

“…Who did it?” Professor Kyouichirou cast his gaze towards the table where we were all sat, his eyes brimming with hatred. “Who killed It? Who’s the one responsible? Who pulled this stunt, and for what purpose!? It was one of you, wasn’t it!? Have you no shame, you scoundrel!?”

He shouted and slammed both fists on the table. But there was no response. It wasn’t because everyone was too frightened to speak, it was simply that no one had the words with which to answer.

Suzunashi had already averted her gaze as if to say, ‘you’re not even worth looking at.’ Her forehead seemed to be bleeding a little, presumably from the cane. However, Suzunashi paid it no mind. She seemed to be thinking about something else, but perhaps she was thinking about nothing at all.

Beside her was Kunagisa, who had simply watched the scene play out in silence.

“——……what a load of nonsense.”

Here’s how it began— if this even counts as the beginning— Regardless, I’m told that Shito was the first to notice anything was out of the ordinary. This morning, like any other morning, he was scheduled to receive a phone call from Utsurigi, but apparently it never came. If that was all it was, then it’d happened plenty of times already— perhaps he’d overslept or forgotten, or maybe he was doing it just to cause trouble. All of which seemed in character for Utsurigi— and so, thinking nothing of it, Shito tried to contact him from his end, but there was no response.

Shito sensed something was off, so he reported the situation to the professor and Misachi. When the order to ‘go and check on him’ was passed down by the professor, Shito did as he was told. This was around half past six.

That’s when Shito discovered it. Drenched in blood, with every inch of his body cut up and mutilated, was Utsurigi Gaisuke. The aforementioned scoundrel's work of murderous art, on full display.

That means, the first to discover Utsurigi Gaisuke’s corpse was Ougaki Shito.

“…scoundrel, huh…?”

I’m not sure what made the professor settle on a word like that, but he had hit the nail on the head. Our seclusion in the heart of the mountains acted as a kind of enclosed environment. So, for example, if someone were to get murdered, the culprit would undoubtedly be found among those who remained. That’s all there was to it.

That’s the kind of terribly hackneyed situation we found ourselves in.

“—Oh my, let’s keep a level head, everyone.”

Just as a sense of hopelessness began to wash over us— no, just as that sense of hopelessness started to grow stale, Neo cut in. He spread his arms wide, as if he’d just told the punchline to a joke, before settling into a relaxed pose.

“There’s nothing to gain from losing our cool. Isn’t that right, professor? First thing’s first, we need to decide what we’re going to do next.”

“Next?” The professor shot a dejected look in Neo’s direction. “What could you possibly suggest? There is no next. Not anymore.”

“Now, now, you shouldn’t be so quick to throw in the towel. Let’s see, let’s start by making sure the one who pulled this stunt is held responsible. Come, look at how excessive it all was, there’s no way they didn’t leave some kind of evidence behind. When the police get here, they’ll catch our culprit right away. From there, we’ll—”

“Our culprit? It’s one of you, is it not?”

“That’s awfully short-sighted, professor. That’s not like the great Professor Kyouichirou at all. Think about it, didn’t we just have an intruder alert the other day? We shouldn’t discount the idea that this was the work of someone from outside. No, I’m certain it was. No matter how impregnable a castle you claim this place to be, it’s not like it’s actually impossible for an intruder to get inside.”

—Intruder.

I stiffened at the mention of the word, but not enough that anyone would notice.

“We shouldn’t just assume it was an inside job. I won’t say it’s impossible, but that kind of thinking isn’t good. For most of us—the researchers, that is– we’d have no motive for doing something like this, would we? After all, It was our precious, precious research subject.”

“Neo!”

The professor yelled in a tone I’d never heard him use before. But even then, “it’s fine, isn’t it? Not like it matters anymore,” Neo answered, completely nonplussed.

“I’m sure Lady Kunagisa and that sensible young woman have it all figured out already; the lad’s probably got a pretty good idea as well. Why else would they come all the way here? Am I wrong? So why not give it a rest? Let’s put an end to all the deception and trickery. Now’s not the time to start pointing fingers without good reason, is it?”

“…………” “…………”

After he’d finished talking, Neo glanced at the professor and Kunagisa in turn. The professor wore a sour expression but didn’t say anything further. As for Kunagisa, she just ignored him as if she wasn't even listening. “Good grief.” Neo shrugged his shoulders. “Alright fine, moving on. What I’m saying is, none of the faculty would have had reason to kill Utsurigi. That much should be obvious. So where does that leave us? Are we to suspect the professor’s secretary, Miss Uze Misachi? Or what about his assistant, the young Ougaki Shito?”

The two of them, still collapsed at the professor’s feet, both looked up at the same time.

“But that’s no good either. Everyone knows the two of them are completely devoted to the professor. Pardon my bluntness, but Ougaki’s loyalty is particularly unusual. So long as it’d upset the professor, there’s no way the two of them could have done it. So what then? That’s right, we’d have no choice but to suspect our guests, Lady Kunagisa and company, but—”

Neo shifted his gaze to us.

“–once again, no dice. After all, the three of them came here to ‘rescue’ Utsurigi, and while there are some of us who may find that choice of words vexing, they surely didn’t intend to murder him. Isn’t that right?” Neo turned to face the professor once more. “And with that, professor, we’ve run out of suspects. Of course, that includes you.”

“……………”

It’d be hard to call his logic sound, but Neo’s reasoning had certainly shut the professor up. No matter how incensed he was, no matter how erratic, downtrodden, rotten, or exhausted, this was the kind of man Shadou Kyouichirou was, the kind who couldn’t turn a blind eye to reason.

“That’s why I can’t picture it being anyone besides an outsider. Given the performative nature of it, maybe it was the work of one of your competitors, professor. If I were you, I’d be a little suspicious of those folks at the Hariuro Foundation or the Baisar Group.”

“…They’d never make such a spectacle of it.”

“Perhaps. Still, it’s a possibility. That’s why it’s a little early to conclude that the scoundrel is one of us. Right? Thoughts, everyone?”

Neo looked back at us, as if expecting us to weigh in.

“……………”

He was right. While his tone was somewhat irreverent, that might’ve just been his way of breaking through this heavy atmosphere. At the very least, he had succeeded at getting everyone — especially the professor— to think about the situation with as much composure as they could muster.

Naturally, that went for me too.

“—Miss Kokoromi,”

She’d positioned herself as far away from us as possible, so I had to call out to her. With a “hm?” her eyes widened, then a thin, mysterious smile formed on her face. “What’s this?” She turned my way.

“…Ya got something to ask me, kiddo?”

“……Miss, wouldn’t you be able to figure something out just by taking a look at it?” I asked anxiously. “After all, you’re an expert on human anatomy. Maybe you could tell us how he was killed, or the cause of death, or something—”

“Heh-heh, never thought there’d come a time when you’d turn to little-old-me. Life’s a drag, but I reckon it’s little moments like this that make it all worthwhile.” Miss Kokoromi flashed me a horrid smile, one I’d seen many times during my time abroad. “Well, I’ve only had a peek, so I can’t say much.”

“——……”

“Given the amount of bleeding, it was blood loss. Either that or trauma-induced shock. But anyone with eyes coulda toldya that much.” Her words weren’t addressed to me specifically; she was speaking to the whole room. “As for time of death, lessee, it woulda been last night, anytime between midnight and three in the morning.”

“That’s a pretty broad window.”

“I s'ppose. Normally, if you’re fixin’ to pin time of death at a glance, ya go off of rigour mortis and the condition of the eyes, but I ain’t had a chance to fiddle with the body yet, and the eyes ain’t in the best condition.”

Both of Utsurigi’s eyes had been gouged out by a pair of scissors.

“Hate to letcha down, but that’s ‘bout all I can say for now.”

“…Thanks.”

I bowed my head and turned away.

Between midnight and three in the morning… what had I been doing during that time? I remember meeting Kasugai at around one a.m., and then, after that—

“My-my, trying to establish an alibi, are we, lad?” Neo said. “If so, there’s a better way to go about it. Isn’t that right, Uze?”

Having suddenly heard her name, Misachi jolted to attention, “Sorry? —What might that be?”

“The door entry logs. Why don’t you go take a look?”

“………………”

Misachi glanced over at the professor. “Hurry up and go,” having lost his patience, the professor snapped at her.

“……Understood.”

Misachi nodded and swiftly shuffled her way out of the room.

The logs…? Neo’s choice of words made me tilt my head. What did he mean? Unless… Did that mean that every time we had entered one of the research wards, the ironclad security system (opened only by keycard, password, voice recognition, and retinal scan—) had kept records of it on some kind of central computer? I see, in that case, we’d be able to definitively narrow down the time the incident took place. After all, to enter the Seventh Ward, you’d have to—

“…you’d have to—”

My thoughts froze.

That’s right. This wasn’t an issue of whether or not the incident had been recorded or anything like that. In order to enter the seventh ward, you’d have to break through the ironclad security system. Not only would anyone without a key assigned to them have been unable to kill Utsurigi, they wouldn’t have even been able to get inside.

But in that case— I looked at Neo. Had he just not noticed? If he had, then he’d have realized there wasn’t an outsider alive who could’ve set foot in the Seventh Ward.

Take the Red Contractor, Aikawa Jun, for example. She was second to none when it came to the art of vocal mimicry and mind-reading, not to mention lock picking; in fact, the gulf in skill was so extreme that, as of yet, none had managed to come second to her (at least, according to the woman herself). And while you might be better off taking the words of someone narcissistic enough to call themselves something as self-aggrandizing as Humanity’s Strongest with a grain of salt, even someone like her would likely find the task of opening these insulated doors impossible. After all, her opponent would’ve been the locking mechanism. A device designed to follow a strict set of logic.

Neo just sat there as composed as could be, his large body sinking into his chair. Of course he’d noticed. There’s no way he hadn’t spotted the inconsistency in his own argument. Then was this just a means of placating the professor?

——He was one clever bastard.

I had just been reminded of that fact. With that in mind, I relaxed once more.

In other words, that meant it was impossible for the three of us— Kunagisa, Suzunashi, and I— to have committed the crime. Without faculty clearance, there’d have been no way for us to make it past the door; that was the obvious conclusion.

“——……”

By that same logic, I could attest to her innocence as well. That left seven— we could narrow the suspects down to the seven researchers who had been here from the start. They were the only ones capable of infiltrating the research ward, that much was certain. If there were any holes in my logic, they weren’t the kind large enough to worry about.

I glanced around casually. Seven people— Professor Kyouichirou, Neo, Koutari, Kasugai, Miss Kokoromi, and Shito— as well as Misachi, who had already left the room. Seven people. Still, not everything Neo said early had been a means to quell the professor. Among these seven people, I couldn’t think of a single one who’d have cause to murder Utsurigi— especially in such a violent fashion. But just because I couldn’t think of one didn’t mean-

“Still, I suppose we should cover our bases,” Neo said. “Last night, I was in my own research ward— the Fifth Ward, the entire time. How about you, Koutari?”

“Me too,” Koutari replied curtly. “No point in walking around in the middle of the night.”

“That goes for me as well.”

“I stepped outside briefly to walk the dogs. I bumped into that boy on the way. Isn’t that right?”

Kasugai asked. I nodded wordlessly.

“And the professor? What about you?”

“Same here,” seemingly irritated by Neo’s question, the professor gave a brusque answer. “I was in the Primary Ward with Shito and Uze the entire time. You’d know as much if you read the logs.”

“Is that so? And? How about you?” Neo turned his attention to us. “What were you all up to last night?”

“We were in the lodge the entire time. I did go for a short walk right before it started raining, though.”

“Hmm, a walk, huh?” Neo nodded pointedly. “I see, going for a late-night stroll is only human, I suppose. In that case, that means the culprit isn’t one of us after all, right? No one even went near the Seventh ward.” Neo said, likely not believing a single word he was saying. I had gone for a late-night stroll, gotten involved in secret affairs, and then lied about it. As Neo said, I was only human. After all, no one’s completely honest at all times.

“…Hey, Inoji,” Suzunashi whispered so that only I could hear, “it looks like we might be in a spot of trouble.”

“—? You think?” I peered at Kunagisa out of the corner of my eye (her expression was as blank as ever), as I stifled my voice in reply to Suzunashi. “Not to borrow the professor’s catchphrase or anything, but it’s all over… With Utsurigi dead, there was no point in even coming here. We went through all this for nothing.”

No, that’s probably not what Suzunashi was talking about. She was most likely referring to our ensuing trouble with the police. They would probably perform a thorough investigation, and it was possible that, as potential suspects in the case, we wouldn’t be allowed to leave Aichi until it was all over. We might be back in Kyoto a little later than expected. I wasn’t so much worried about an uninvolved university student like myself or an unemployed shut-in like Kunagisa, but Suzunashi had a job to get back to (even if she was only a part-timer). I wondered if that’s what she meant by trouble, but Suzunashi said, “That’s not it. It feels like we’re in the eye of the storm… Honestly, nothing good ever comes from listening to Asano’s requests… and I mean never… But if I know that, then why do I always…”

“Um, Suzunashi?”

It seemed like Suzunashi was wallowing in self-loathing. As I gazed in bewilderment, unsuccessfully trying to understand what she was getting at, Misachi returned. She wore a slightly troubled expression. First, she turned to face us, and then, apprehensively, she walked straight to the professor’s side. She whispered something in his ear.

“……What?” the professor blurted out. “And you’re certain about this?”

“Yes… without question.”

She attested. What exactly she attested to was beyond me, but she nodded all the same. “Hmph.” The professor appeared lost in thought. And like that, he made his way over to the table and took a seat. Leaning on his elbows, he sunk even further into contemplation.

“…………”

……What could Misachi have possibly said?

No, the actual words she chose were of little importance. What concerned me was that, upon hearing those words, the professor regained his composure— or rather, the unfathomable presence the professor had when I first met him once again inhabited his small frame. I had yet to realize what it was that I found so unnerving about that fact, but it unnerved me nonetheless.

In other words, I had a bad feeling about it. And just like the bad feeling I had about my reunion with Miss Kokoromi, it twisted my stomach in knots. What’s more, my premonitions had never once been wrong. Just like that contemptible soothsayer, they had never once been wrong.

“——Hmph.”

The professor gave a slight nod then raised his head. Naturally, all eyes were on him.

“Ladies and Gentleman, it appears there’s been some complications.”

Complications? Hearing that word, I glanced at Suzunashi. Her eyes were closed, almost as if she were sleeping. The bleeding from her forehead had already stopped and dried up. I turned my gaze back to the professor. That crafty, experienced grin of his had worked its way back onto his face.

“—Oi, Uze,” the professor turned to her, “—I want you to contact the security at the gate. When the police arrive, have them turn them away.”

“Huh…?” Misachi was shocked. “But, why…?”

“Never mind the reason. Let’s see, tell them it was a simple miscommunication,” The professor set his sights on Shito, “…or perhaps a child’s tasteless prank.”

“…I see,” Misachi nodded uncertainly. She didn’t seem to have a firm grasp on the situation— no, her expression was that of someone who had no grasp on it at all. “…a miscommunication…?”

“What’s the matter? Off with you.”

“……but why……?”

“Do you need me to explain every goddamned thing to you before you do your job?”

“No, that’s not what I-… Please excuse me, I’ll leave right away.”

Misachi hurriedly bowed her head to the professor before scampering out of the room for the second time.

“…What’s the meaning of this, professor?” Neo said, his eyes, still fixed on the door Misachi had just closed behind her. “Turning the police away? Are you in your right mind? What did Uze say?”

“That’s just it, Neo. That’s the issue,” Professor Kyouichirou sneered. “We’ve found ourselves in quite the predicament.”

“…Of course we have.  But what does that have to do with anything? Does turning the police away somehow help us solve the case?”

“Just listen,”

The professor gently brushed aside Neo’s complaints. Then after a moment’s pause, he continued. “Let’s start from the beginning, Neo. There’s something wrong with everything you’ve been saying. The entrance to Utsurigi’s Seventh Ward was sealed by an airtight security system. No matter who the outsider was, they wouldn’t have been able to get past it. That’s certainly the case for the likes of Hariuro and Baisar, at least,”

The professor punctuated ‘at least’ with a sharp staccato. That action was, once again, accompanied by an unexplainable pressure. What on Earth was this old man trying to say?

After having it pointed out to him by the professor, “Ahh, now that you mention it, you might be on to something. I hadn’t noticed,” Neo said unconvincingly. “But still, we shouldn’t be too hasty in assuming it was an inside job. Professor, we’ve been working on this together since the beginning. I understand that you’re out of sorts after what happened to Utsurigi, but we’re all in the same boat. We shouldn’t immediately start assigning blame…”

“Out of sorts? Mind your manners. I’m nothing of the sort. I’m as calm as could be.”

As if the professor's fury had been nothing more than a collective hallucination, he spoke in a stately fashion.

“Be that as it may, professor…”

“At ease, Neo. You’re not suggesting I’d suspect one of my own without good cause, are you? What Uze told me a moment ago, don’t you want to hear it?”

While each of us might have had something to say about his first statement, the second piqued our interest. We all hung on his every word. The professor puffed out his chest a little and said,

“…Last night, there is no record of the Seventh Ward ever being opened.”

“……No record?” Neo repeated. “So what you’re saying is, we have no evidence anyone even entered the Seventh Ward at all, last night?”

“Exactly. The last ones to open the Seventh Ward were, Shito… Lady Kunagisa, and that young lad over there. We have a clear record of the three of them leaving the ward after their audience with Utsurigi. Of course, under any normal circumstance, there’d be no reason to doubt the accuracy of these logs, isn’t that right, Neo?”

Once again, the professor put clear emphasis on ‘under any normal circumstance’. It’s as if he were implying that there was something particular we were failing to consider. …Could it be? Was the professor saying he already figured out who the culprit… or rather, the scoundrel was? It had only been about an hour since the incident was discovered, but had we already reached the dénouement? I highly doubted it, but like Suzunashi said this morning, this wasn’t a movie; I had no way to tell how much time I had left. I felt like this could be the end of it, but there’s also a chance we were only half-way through. There’s no way of knowing exactly how many pages remained.

My position remained uncertain.

“Then… what are you suggesting?” Neo said dubiously, as if he genuinely had no idea what he meant. His irreverent attitude, crumbling. “That certainly complicates things. That would mean no one was even there. Are you certain it’s not just a mechanical error?”

“That’s impossible. But you know that, don't you?”

“Then…” Neo gave it some thought. “The only possible culprits would be the last ones to enter, Shito, and Kunagisa and company… but that doesn’t line up with Misachi’s estimate for time-of-death. Professor, this is starting to look like an impossible crime.”

“One more thing, Neo.” The professor was overflowing with excitement. “Take a deep breath and listen. Let’s keep a level-head, now. It’s unbecoming for a grown man to lose his composure. While checking the logs for the Seventh ward… Uze took the opportunity to confirm the comings and goings of all the other faculty members, myself included.”

“……? The other– you mean us?”

“Who else?” the professor responded heartily. Over the course of the conversation, the professor’s excitement meter had been steadily rising. However, almost inverse-proportionally, my mood… or perhaps my sense of foreboding, grew ever darker. At least, that’s what it felt like.

I finally understood. I still hadn’t the foggiest idea what the professor was trying to say, but I finally understood where this was all leading. That’s why he was acting so composed. That’s why he had seemed so full-of-himself. Jones’ Law: The man who can smile when things go wrong has thought of someone he can blame.

If so, then—

“Now for the results— since Uze isn’t here at the moment, you’ll have to hear it from me— Last night, at least during the window that Misachi provided, not a single person left their own research ward.”

Our breath caught in our throats.

“With one exception, that is… Kasugai,”

The professor said. Still almost entirely expressionless, Kasugai bristled when she heard her name.

“At around one in the morning, Kasugai left the Fourth Ward for around five minutes. That corresponds with the time she claimed to be walking the dogs. That said, it’s not even worth taking into consideration. It should be obvious, but that kind of spectacle would have been impossible to create in a mere five minutes.”

“……I appreciate it,” Kasugai replied. It seemed like some small part of her also wanted to add, not that I really understand. “Thank you very much.”

“…Wha-? Then, that means…” Neo stammered. “…huh? But, professor, doesn’t that mean there’s even less reason to suspect one of us? None of us stepped foot outside. And even if we did, there’s no record of any of us entering or exiting the scene of the crime. In other words, this is-”

“An impossible crime.”

Miss Kokoromi finished Neo’s sentence.

“Don’tcha think, kiddo?”

“……Something like that. Still……”

Choosing my words carefully, I agreed with Miss Kokoromi. Certainly, if you took everything the professor said at face value, then theoretically— No one had entered the Seventh Ward, and what’s more, no one had even gone outside in the first place. If I had to sum it up in a single phrase, it would have to be this:

A locked room.

In the truest sense.

“If this is an impossible crime—”

If that’s what Professor Kyouichirou was trying to tell us, then why did he feel the need to turn away the police? Wouldn’t this be the perfect time for them to make their entrance? As I wracked my brain, I was reminded of a certain pair of detectives from Kyoto. Naturally, all eyes were aimed at where the professor was seated.

The professor wore an audacious smile.

“Impossible? What a ridiculous notion. There’s nothing that’s impossible in this world. Only things that aren’t possible yet.”

“Wait, hang on, professor. If things have already gotten this out of hand, why would you slam the door in the police’s face?” Neo put my exact concern into words. “It’s completely illogical. That doesn’t sound like the professor I know.”

“Good god, Neo, why don’t you try using that brain of yours a little? If you still can’t piece it together after everything I’ve said, you’ll remain an imbecile until the day you die.”

“An imbecile, am I?” Neo folded his arms. “My point still stands, professor.”

“We aren’t the only ones here, now are we?”

The professor said—

And nodded in our direction. Kunagisa, Suzunashi, and I- everyone turned to look at us. Neo looked shocked, Koutari looked unconcerned, Miss Kokoromi looked unsurprised, Kasugai looked indifferent, and Shito looked wide-eyed.

I gulped. Suzunashi’s eyes remained shut. She might have actually fallen asleep. I peered over at Kunagisa sitting next to her; she just sat there wearing the same blank expression as before, as if she wasn’t even paying attention. She was probably thinking about whether Raja Maharaja and Parapa the Rapper were related, or perhaps not. In any case, it was readily apparent that she wasn’t her usual self. I took stock of our current combat ability (though it was a depressing sight to behold) and turned to face the others.

“I can’t just let that slide, Professor Kyouichirou,” I said firmly. “You make it sound like we’re the ones who killed Utsurigi. There are certain things you just can’t say.”

“Hm? Hold on now, I haven’t said anything yet,” the professor sneered, mocking me. “What’s got you so worked up? Could it be that you’re hiding something?”

“As soon as you’re finished suspecting your own colleagues, you immediately lay the blame on us, huh? How convenient. Sure, the lodge has no security, so we were all free to come and go as we pleased, but when it comes to who could even enter the Seventh Ward, we have a clear advantage. Am I wrong? Whether we left a record or not wouldn’t have mattered; without a registered ID, we wouldn’t have been able to get inside in the first place.”

“Ha-ha! Advantage? I wouldn’t be so sure about that! That word’s utterly meaningless!”

The professor laughed heartily, and then, as if a switch had been flipped, he fixed his eyes on me, sneered, and jabbed a finger in my direction.

“You couldn’t have done it alone, kid. You couldn’t have gotten in or out of the Seventh Ward. But you’re not alone, are you? You’ve got something unthinkable lurking amongst you, isn't that right—?”

He took the finger he was pointing at me and shifted it slightly to the side— aiming it at Kunagisa Tomo.

“Isn’t that right, Lady Kunagisa?”

As expected, Kunagisa didn’t even acknowledge him. As if she didn’t even see him, let alone hear him, she made no reaction whatsoever. That said, everyone other than Kunagisa and Suzunashi could barely contain their shock.

“Wai– Professor, that’s…”

“What’s the matter, Neo? Is it really that surprising? After all, that young lady had the charisma to form Cluster. She’s the ex-leader of the victim, our colleague Utsurigi Gaisuke. She could break through security like that with both hands tied behind her back. Isn’t that right, Lady Kunagisa?”

No response. Predictably, her lack of interest seemed to irritate the professor… or perhaps it was frustration, but the professor promptly straightened himself out and plastered a broad smile on his face, putting on a display of composure.

“What’s the matter? You can’t handle the truth?”

“And just how do you figure that, professor?” I noticed my speech had gotten quicker, but I managed to maintain calm. “What makes you think Kunagisa could bypass such an insane security system…?”

“That’s not all she did. After bypassing it, she deleted the logs too. It would’ve been quite the feat if it hadn’t backfired. She completely failed to consider the logs for the other wards, but that just goes to show she’s just a child after all.”

“That’s absurd. It doesn’t make any sense. Just a child? Who do you think you are? If your only argument is that Kunagisa might have been able to open the lock, then you guys could’ve done it t–”

“I have my reasons,” the professor said. “There’s a reason why Kunagisa was the only one able to bypass that lock. It’s the same reason she’s the only one capable of deleting the logs. That’s because, seven years ago, the one who developed our root programs, the one who built such an ‘insane security system’, the one who laid the foundation for this very research facility at the tender age of twelve-years-old, was none other than Lady Kunagisa herself.”

He continued smoothly, jabbing his finger at Kunagisa once more.

Needless to say, Kunagisa showed no reaction. She hadn’t spoken a word since she saw Utsurigi’s mangled corpse. Still. Could what the professor’s saying be true?

“She’s an unfathomable genius, the likes of which a mediocrity like you could never understand. Naturally, she’s beyond my understanding as well. Nonetheless, Lady Kunagisa, it’s for that very reason…I’m accusing all three of you.”

“Accuse? Accuse!?” I rose from my chair. “You’re out of your mind! Your ridiculous theory doesn’t even make any sense!”

“Take it easy, kiddo,” Miss Kokoromi butt into our argument. She had apparently lit a cigarette at some point, and her left hand gripped a can of cola. Just when did she find the time to- “Don’t get your britches in a twist, it’s ugly. Didn’tcha hear Suzunashi earlier?”

“……Miss.”

“Professor, even if that were the case, there’s still one thing I ain’t clear on.”

She said, pointing her cigarette at the professor. I couldn’t tell what brand it was, but it was quite thin, the kind usually marketed towards women. When she lived abroad, she used to smoke cigars, so her lungs probably weren’t the healthiest.

“And what might that be, Miyoshi?”

“Neo’s right about what he said earlier, ain’t he? The three of them came here to rescue Utsurigi. Don’t that mean they ain’t got no motive? It’s as ya say professor, Miss Kunagisa here’s Utsurigi’s former leader- it wouldn’t make a lick of sense. The three of ‘em are just like us researchers, they’ve got no reason to kill him.”

“You’re as myopic as ever, Miyoshi,” the professor said. “Why don’t you try thinking outside the box? We’re academics, are we not? Then again, you are a biologist, so perhaps it can’t be helped…”

“Bless your heart, it almost sounds like you’re disparaging an entire field of study for no good reason, don’t it? Almost like you’re saying mathematics and engineering are more important just to get a rise outta us. Ain’t that right, Kasugai?”

“Precisely. It’s the kind of thing only a conceited engineer who thinks the whole world revolves around his calculations could say. It’s utterly shameless. Perhaps his brain is fried from looking at nothing but numerals all day.”

Kasugai followed Miss Kokoromi’s lead.

Hm? Did cliques exist even among the sciences? I had thought scientists were all relatively alike, but I suppose that’s what happens when you assume. But this probably wasn’t the right time to be thinking about something so frivolous.

That said, Kasugai was the same as she was last night, cool-headed yet capable of spitting venom like it was nothing. Maybe she was my type after all, another frivolous thought floated through my head. Moving swiftly along-

“That wasn’t my intention…” having earned the ire of the two female academics, the professor wore a strained smile, “…forget I said anything. Regardless, Miyoshi, don’t you find Neo’s assumption that they’re here to save Utsurigi a tad baseless?”

“…baseless?” Miss Kokoromi glanced in our direction. “If I remember correctly… the reason we thought that was…umm…”

“Say for example, Lady Kunagisa came to kill Utsurigi from the very start, what then?”

“To kill…?” Miss Kokoromi’s brows knit together. “But why? I don’t follow.”

“In other words, the reason they even came to our facility in the first place was so that they could murder Utsurigi. If they’ve been planning it all along, then—”

“That’s insane!” I exploded. “You want to talk about baseless, then it doesn’t get much more baseless than that. Why on earth would Kunagisa murder her friend and former TEAMmate? I can’t think of a single goddamn reason—”

“Oi, oi, I’d watch your tongue, boy.”

The professor gave an enigmatic shrug.

“Right now, your fate is in my hands. You should be thanking me for turning the police away. Can’t you see how generous I’m being?”

“All I can see is spite, you Mad Daemon.”

Despite my reproach, the professor just smiled cheerfully.

“Still, the lad has a point, professor,” Neo added. “Don’t you think your theory’s a little too far-fetched? It’s not like I can’t see where you’re coming from, but—”

“A motive, huh?” The professor's smile faded. “Not you too, Neo. You can’t possibly be suggesting that Lady Kunagisa would need a motive to murder Utsurigi, are you?”

“I—” Neo hesitated for a moment, “I am. Even if Lady Kunagisa would’ve been able to get past the security, even if she would’ve been able to delete the logs– I can’t imagine someone from the Kunagisa Syndicate— someone from the very heart of the Kunagisa Syndicate— doing something as thoughtless as murdering Utsurigi—”

“That’s because you don’t understand, Neo.”

The professor glared at Kunagisa.

“Of course you don’t. You don’t understand why Lady Kunagisa might’ve felt compelled to murder Utsurigi Gaisuke. Even I can’t think of a suitable reason. But is something as trivial as that really necessary? It’s not, is it? After all, that young lady—”

The professor said something similar the other day. However, this time-

“— is a ⨯⨯⨯⨯⨯⨯⨯”

Before he could finish, I was already moving. It was by no means unconscious. Consciously and deliberately, I stirred my body to action. And yet, my mind was blank. With my fist clenched, I planted one foot up on the table. As I went to launch myself at the professor, something collided with my right temple. It was a cola can. Out of the corner of my eye, I spotted Miss Kokoromi rushing towards me. I’d thought it strange that she’d whip out a drink at a time like this; had she been expecting this to happen? I only considered that possibility after the fact; in the moment, the stimulus of Miss Kokoromi reflected in my eyes never reached my brain. I saw nothing. I heard nothing. I couldn’t see. I couldn’t hear. Sanguine. Everything was red. The colour of blood. Blood-red eyes. All sight and sound were drenched a deep crimson. Still, Miss Kokoromi’s decisive action had succeeded in stalling my movement for but a moment. When I went to lunge at him once more, suddenly, from behind– from right behind, Suzunashi swept my legs out from under me. My body appeared to be floating mid-air just above the wide table. In that brief moment before I landed, Suzunashi grabbed hold of my head, and with her entire body weight behind it, she slammed my body into the table full-force. The sturdy wooden table groaned. Although there’s a chance it was just my bones creaking. Naturally, I had no time to brace myself, so I felt the shock of impact reverberate throughout my entire body, and yet, I still reached out towards Professor Kyouichirou. Miss Kokoromi pinned my arm to the table. She cursed me out as she slapped the side of my face that the can had ruptured against. Meanwhile, Suzunashi took hold of my other arm. The two of them. They seemed to be saying something, but I couldn’t make it out. Calm down. What am I doing, what am-? No. This feels right-

I think-

At that moment, I probably lost my mind.

The moment before Suzunashi delivered the blow to the back of my neck that knocked me out, I saw something flutter at the edges of my vision. Blue hair set upon a backdrop of scarlet. But then again, I may have just been seeing things.

Psycho Logical (Part Two)

2

When I came to my senses— Rather, when I’d become sensible enough to be called sane, I was in a cell. Bare concrete floors, walls, and ceiling. Iron bars. It was dark and gloomy. The air was stale. An oppressive atmosphere hung in the air. The feeling of despair. I felt sluggish. I wanted to drift a little longer. As if I had just woken from a nightmare. Still, it couldn’t have been any more nightmarish than the reality I woke up to. Such pointless thoughts pooled around my mind.

Enough already. I don’t care anymore. A throbbing pain radiated across the back of my head. Nobody. Not a single person here knows when to pull their punches. Not Suzunashi, and not Miss Kokoromi either. They didn’t bother with useless things like mercy. That reminds me, when I was living abroad, Miss Kokoromi used to hit me a lot too. More than half the time- No, nine times out of ten, it was for her own amusement, but in hindsight, the remaining tenth of the time she was probably in the right. Even though I say, ‘in hindsight’, I have no intention of ruminating about stuff like that all this time later. Having to have it beaten into me, not stopping until it all fell apart. Honestly, I haven’t grown at all since then—

“Ah! Iichan, you up?”

Kunagisa’s voice shook me from my fog.

“Mornin’!”

“………mornin’,” after a slight pause, I returned the greeting, picking myself up off the floor. “……umm.”

I surveyed my surroundings once more.

It was the same as my half-asleep mind had perceived it, some kind of prison. Inside, Kunagisa, Suzunashi, and I all sat directly on the concrete floor.

“Oh? You came to, Inoji? Thank goodness. I was worried I punched you a little too hard and put you out for good.”

“I appreciate the concern…” I felt a faint air of unease between us as I bowed my head. “So… where are we?”

“The Fourth Ward. The one Kasugai uses. This is the basement.”

“…Is that right? But it looks just like a prison…”

“Apparently this is one of the cages she houses her test subjects in,” Kunagisa said while grinning. She seemed to be enjoying herself for some reason. “He-he-he, this is my first time inside a cell, y’know. It’s always fun to try new things.”

“This would be my fifth…” I said, gripping the bars. As you might expect, they didn’t budge an inch. “Umm… I’m a little foggy about the situation… could someone explain to me why we’re in a kennel? Unless it turns out we’ve actually been monkeys the entire time, I have a feeling I’m not going to like the answer.”

“It’s the professor’s orders. Speaking of, Inoji, how much do you remember?”

“Truth be told, not much. I do remember getting clobbered by Suzunashi and Miss Kokoromi, though…”      I answered her question honestly. “Let’s see… after I woke up this morning, Suzunashi came to see me on the roof…”

“You’re kidding. That long ago? It’s gonna be a pain in the ass getting you caught up.”

“Just give me a second… I just need to collect myself. I pressed my back against the concrete wall, sitting up straight. “……after that, I put Kunagisa’s hair up, and then…huh? Oh, right. …okay. I remember.”

“Yeah?” Suzunashi nodded. “That saves me an awful lot of trouble.”

“Hehehe, Iichan’s memory’s as crummy as ever. It wouldn’t be strange to forget a few things after a beating like that, though.”

“…………”

Wait. If she could say all that, does that mean Kunagisa was back to normal? With that in mind, “So? What happened while I was out?” I asked Suzunashi. If Kunagisa was her usual self again, asking her would’ve been pointless.

“In short, we’re the prime suspects,” Suzunashi said, “so they locked us up.”

“……Short and sweet, thanks.”

The Fourth Ward. The one run by Kasugai. The basement… It made me feel like a lab rat. That said, whether it was better than feeling like a convict was a rather delicate question for me. To be locked up here of all places meant the professor was far crueler than I’d imagined.

Hmmm… That reminds me, during a certain murder case, I’d come up with the idea of quarantining the prime suspect. I see, so this was what it felt like to be on the receiving end. It might be too little too late, but I resolved to never make such a suggestion again.

“So, what happens next?”

“Sadly, nothing. The professor said, ‘we’re going to have to ask you to wait here while we figure out what to do with you. Don’t worry, no harm will come to you,’ or something along those lines.”

“Is that so…?” If he didn’t consider imprisoning us a form of harm, I shudder to think what would make the cut. “…Ahh, I just finished remembering…oh man.”

Belatedly, I called out in surprise. I must’ve looked like quite the fool.

Suzunashi looked at me judgmentally. “Well, that’s the short of it,” she said. “I didn’t think there’d be much point in resisting all by myself, so I complied… No, to be honest, I knew from the start that nothing good would come from going anywhere with you, yet here I am. Trouble seems to find you anywhere. Although this time, it seems like you were actively looking for it.”

“It’s not like I expected this to happen either…” Moreover, no matter how I look at it, I don’t think I was even the least bit responsible for what happened. Seeing as I wasn’t the one who killed Utsurigi, Suzunashi was complaining about the wrong guy. “Talk about unexpected… and just when I thought things were looking up…”

“Hehehe, that’s why there’s never a dull moment with Iichan around!” Kunagisa laughed delightedly. “You never have time to be bored. Life sure is fun, huh?”

“……your comrade was the one who was murdered, you know.”

“Hm?” Kunagisa tilted her head. “…sure, but still, there’s no point humming and hawing about things that you can’t change. Humans are meant to live their lives looking forwards, y’know.”

“…I forgot, that’s just the kind of person you are, aren't you?”

That’s right, she was. The Kunagisa that had been here a while ago must’ve been some kind of mistake and nothing more. Yeah. Let’s go with that for now.

“Anyways, first things first… we need to figure out how to get out of this situation.”

“Get out of it, huh…? Lovely goal, that.” Suzunashi rattled the iron bars. “But not even I can get through these. If Asano were here, she might’ve been able to do something about it though…”

“…Miiko can cut through iron?”

“Well, she can cut through konjac, at least… I’ve heard stories of people who can quick-draw fast enough to cut iron though. But I guess there’s no point in talking about someone who’s not even here.”

“You got that right.”

I gazed up at the ceiling. If this were a movie, then this would be the point where I’d spot a conveniently placed ventilation shaft we could escape from, but since this was reality, there was no such thing. Such a lucky break would never actually happen in real life. Good grief, no wonder the air was so stale. Damnit, they could have at least kept us somewhere more humane. Regardless, looking at it realistically, it didn’t seem like there was any way to escape from our cell. It was locked tight, and the three of us had no lock picking skills to speak of.

“Still… that geezer’s full of shit.”

“Oh? It’s not every day Iichan curses in front of others.”

“It’s not every day that something like this happens either. Damnit. They’re not gonna make us sit around until they’re ready to torture us, are they?”

Given that Miss Kokoromi was here, it was certainly a possibility. Putting aside whether she would actually go through with it, doing things that other people hated was her specialty. She didn’t wind up with such a gaudy and eccentric nickname like The Early Reaper for no reason.

“There’s no way, right? After all, that lady stopped you before you did anything, didn’t she? If Iichan hit the professor, we’d be in a lot more trouble. All hell would’ve broken loose. Thinking about it like that, maybe Kokoromi-chan’s a good person after all.”

“A good person, huh…? I suppose there’s a chance.”

Ignorance is bliss. Hmph, while I was unconscious, it seems like Suzunashi had given Kunagisa a lecture on Miss Kokoromi. Since it was Suzunashi, she probably painted a fairly harmless picture of her.

“And by the way, Iichan, nothing the professor said was all that crazy. It makes sense enough.”

“What? In what way? It’s about as absurd as you can get. It’s not even a stretch, it’s like he didn’t bother trying to make sense at all. A grade schooler who hasn’t even memorized their times tables yet could come up with a better theory than that.”

“I can’t multiply either, you know–” Suzunashi butt-in. “I dropped out before we learned how.”

“…………” “…………”

“? Feel free to continue?”

“Oh… uhh, what were we talking about again?” The shock made me forget. “Right, we’re talking about how the professor’s off his rocker. It’s way too far-fetched. Let’s see if I’ve got this right: no one left their research ward, and no one entered the Seventh ward, therefore Kunagisa and crew are the culprits. What kind of logic is that? Even Goldbach’s conjecture makes more sense.”

“Crew, eh?” Kunagisa giggled deviously. It seems she’d taken a liking to my choice of words. “Yup, crew’s perfect. Crew, it has a nice ring to it, hehehe.”

“……well, it’s better than Kunagisa and her band of merry men at least… And stop trying to change the subject. I’ve got enough on my plate already… In what way does the professor’s theory make any sense? Being the former leader of Cluster doesn’t automatically mean Lady Kunagisa could’ve easily cracked a lock as crazy as that. Honestly, what a crock of—”

“I could’ve.” Kunagisa stated plainly.

“——……Come again?”

“I could’ve opened it.” She repeated. “Easily, too.”

“Easily?”  “Easy as pie.”

Kunagisa didn’t leave even the hair’s breadth required to start a new paragraph between my question and her reply; it left me gripping my head.

“…Just what are you trying to say, Lady Kunagisa?”

“The professor already mentioned it, didn’t he? The one who laid the groundwork for that system was me, y’know. To be fair, I also had a little help from Nao-kun and Micchan. I knew exactly what kind of mechanism it was before I even looked at it.”

Micchan— Kasumioka Douji. A good friend of Nao’s, and, to borrow Neo’s phrasing, someone who was once close to ‘the very heart of the Kunagisa Syndicate’. Currently— well, leaving what they’re currently up to aside, back in the day, before I met Kunagisa, Nao, Kasumioka, and Kunagisa were attached at the hip. That said, Nao and Kasumioka were less than amateurs when it came to mechanical engineering. Which means, it’s probably safe to assume Kunagisa had developed the entire system by herself.

“—Still, without your tools, there’s not much you could’ve done. If there were locks that you could open just by knowing how they work, everyone would be a picklock. Even I know how the mechanism on my front door works, but without my key, I’d be out of luck.”

“Yup, you’ve got a point.” Kunagisa nodded. “That’s why, unless you’re someone like Jun-chan, it’d be pretty hopeless. But— let’s see, what about this, Iichan? When we got to the facility, you wrote our names on the visitor registry, right?”

“Huh? Hang on, you were watching? I thought you were completely focused on your game.”

“I wasn’t gaming, I’ll have you know… But do you remember what the security guard said? Something about how the old school method is harder to tamper with than if it was digital?”

“I think so?” It’d been so long that I’d forgotten. “But so what if he did?”

“It means, high-tech systems have high-tech loopholes. Specifically, I could have done it when I went to visit Sacchan at the Seventh Ward. I coulda taken the opportunity to borrow a computer from Sacchan and use it to gain access to some kind of mother computer in the Primary Ward. Then I coulda registered myself as a new faculty member. Using a bootable business card, of course. Finally, after murdering Sacchan, I’d delete it all. I’d even use a tool to scrub the logs; it woulda been like the doors had never opened at all.”

On the face of it, it seemed all too straightforward. However, that’s only because Kunagisa’s explanation had been dumbed down quite a lot; in reality, there would have been plenty of protections, firewalls, safeguard programs, and alarms she would have needed to bypass.

—But this is Kunagisa we’re talking about.

It was certainly possible. Kunagisa Tomo already boasted vast technological know-how, so if she had also known the security’s core systems inside-out, then-

Bafflingly enough, the professor was right.

“When it comes to computer security, there’s this thing called administrator access, y’see. So at the very least, he’s right that I would’ve had a huge advantage over everyone else. Come to think of it, Hiichan was always the best at breaking through security… I was no slouch either, though.”

“Hiichan was Double-Flick, right?”

“Huh? Wowow, I’m shocked! Iichan’s memory’s actually functioning normally? Wait, I guess it’s normal for it not to function at all, so when it works, it’s actually functioning abnormally, I suppose.”

“Don’t say something so rude so innocently. Utsurigi kept mentioning them. Their name came up almost as much as yours and Chee-kun’s.”

“Hmph. I’ll never understand that man.”

To get Kunagisa of all people to say something like that about you, you would have to be beyond help. Still, nothing good ever comes from speaking ill of the dead. Even in the case of oddballs like Utsurigi. Crucified and murdered— No, I’ve got that backwards. Utsurigi Gaisuke was murdered and then crucified. If they heard about what happened here, would Hiichan, or Chee-kun, or Acchan, or any of his former TEAMmates mourn him? Since I didn’t know any of them personally, there was no way for me to know.

“Still, what was up with that message? 《You just watch,『DEAD BLUE』!!》,was it? If you were to put it in Japanese, it’d be something like ‘maa miteiro yo, Shisen no Ao’, right?”

“Who knows? Aren’t they just warning me not to do anything unnecessary? They’re tying up loose ends, right? He-he-he.” As if she found it amusing to refer to herself as a proverbial loose end, Kunagisa giggled to herself. The amount of guts it took to laugh at a play-on-words like that was enough to unnerve even someone like me.

“Anything unnecessary…? Like trying to rescue Utsurigi? But it kinda defeats the point to leave a message like that if they just killed him anyway.”

“We might have no choice but to leave that question for later… If you’ve got time to worry about something like that, then you really oughta focus on why the culprit mercilessly mangled Sacchan’s body like that, or why they stole his arms.”

“If we’re talking about reasons someone might go out of their way to dice someone to pieces, then the first thing that comes to mind is some kind of grudge…”

That said, I couldn’t picture Utsurigi, who hadn’t stepped foot outside that building in over a year, having done something to warrant such a wretched fate. Of course, that only goes for his time at the facility— if we take into account all the terrible things he did during his TEAM days, then perhaps this kind of thing was unavoidable, so I couldn’t dismiss the possibility.

“Still, even if you could get past that lock, you’d still be lacking a reason… or need to kill Utsurigi. Besides, when you were in the Seventh Ward, you were with me or Shito the entire time, weren’t you? You were on your own when talking to Utsurigi, but there’s no computer in that room. Getting access to the mother computer would’ve been impossible, wouldn’t it?”

“Ha-ha, what a blissful thing to say, Inoji,” Suzunashi laughed. “The professor couldn’t care less about little inconsistencies like that.”

“—What’s that supposed to mean?”

“It means even the slightest justification would be more than enough. The professor doesn’t actually believe that Blue is the culprit. Probably. It’s like you said, Inoji. It’s just a matter of how far he can stretch it. That’s why there’s bound to be some time lag.”

“Time lag—?”

“Exactly. Right about now, the professor… along with his entire faculty, is trying to come up with evidence that implicates Kunagisa and crew. Someone– I think it was Kasugai– said, ‘give them five hours and they’ll have figured out what to do with you.’ We were just discussing that before you woke up.”

“…And?”

“Essentially, Iichan,” Kunagisa spoke listlessly, “the professor’s probably trying to make me Sacchan’s replacement.”

I was speechless. Kunagisa—Utsurigi’s replacement? That’s- That would be-

“In exchange for not turning her over to the police, they’ll have her play along with their research— no, their experiments.”

“But… that’s insane.”

“Sure is. But that’s the situation we find ourselves in,” Suzunashi seemed somewhat resigned. “I’m not sure what they have planned for me and Inoji, but… let’s see, they’ll probably use us as hostages to keep Blue in check. That’s what I’d do, anyway.”

“That’s…”

That said, Kunagisa Tomo would make a suitable replacement for Utsurigi Gaisuke. No, she’d be one hell of an upgrade. If Kunagisa was right about what the professor was up to, that is. When it came to guinea pigs, there were none more suitable than Kunagisa Tomo. Utsurigi had been fine enough, but Kunagisa was simply the best.

The Ultimate Human Dogma.

“I… I— won’t let that bastard-”

“Whoa now, don’t blow another gasket. If I have to deal with that alone, I’m not confident I could pull it off without hurting you. It only turned out okay last time because I had Miyoshi helping me. So unless you’re okay with me breaking half your bones, I’d hold off if I were you.”

“…I’m fine. I’m calm,” I said, slamming my fist against the concrete wall. It hurt. “I’m completely calm.”

“Hehehe,” Kunagisa laughed cheerfully (despite the conversation being about her). “This really takes me back. Being in a pinch like this, facing a crisis-like situation, and stuff.”

Crisis-like? What’s that?

“…You’re really enjoying yourself, aren't you?”

“Pretty much. Still, this is nothing compared to what happened the first time I met Iichan. I mean, it’s not like we’re gonna get murdered or anything.”

“…One thing’s for sure, coming here was completely pointless,” I said. “Now then, what do we do now? Any ideas, Suzunashi?”

“There’s nothing we can do,” she said. “When I don’t come back, Asano will probably catch on and take some kind of action… but that wouldn’t be for another couple days.”

“I can’t do anything either, not locked up thirty metres underground, anyways. They took away my cell phone, and I don’t have my PDA either. We’re hopeless, helpless, and weightless.”

“No, we still have that last one.”

I let out a dejected sigh.

“It looks like… there’s no way out of this dire situation after all.”

“—Oh, but there is."

As natural as could be, as if it were simply a matter of course, a voice cut through my despondency. As if it had been waiting its turn, it struck with perfect timing. It wasn’t Suzunashi’s voice, nor was it Kunagisa’s, and it obviously wasn’t mine; it came from beyond the iron bars.

There, with her arms crossed, stood Ishimaru Kouta.

Without so much as a footstep, hint of her presence, or any kind of advanced warning, she was simply there.

Her denim hunting cap, pulled low, with her denim coat and high-laced boots. The sharp gaze that peeked out from behind her glasses peered down at us. She was grinning, as if she found our predicament amusing— just like Kunagisa, she was smiling as if she were enjoying herself from the bottom of her heart.

“—Greetings to those of you with whom I’m not yet acquainted. And to you, my dear friend, a simple hello will do. My name is Ishimaru Kouta.” In the gloom of the basement, I could just barely make out her features; her lips curled as she looked down her nose at us. “Pleasure to make your acquaintance.”

Warily, Suzunashi knit her brows, assuming a guarded stance. Kunagisa’s eyes went wide as she gazed in wonder. And, with my back still pressed against the concrete wall, I stood up.

“…Yo, Kouta. Thanks for last night,” Carefully, carefully, extremely carefully, I chose my next words. “What a coincidence meeting you here.”

“'A ‘serendipitous encounter’ would be more fitting, dear friend.” Her brazen manner and overly-familiar choice of words sounded almost tongue-in-cheek. “Honestly, how cliché.”

“…What happened? What are you doing in a place like this? Don’t tell me you got lost?”

“Heavens, no. Nothing of the sort, dear friend. Nothing of the sort,” Kouta snickered as she tried to stifle her laughter. “I heard they had an exotic animal caged up down here, so I came to see what the fuss was about. Supposedly, this animal lunged at Professor Shadou Kyouichirou.”

“……”

“You don’t laugh, do you?” Kouta said after a pause. She sounded a little bored. “Smiling is a fundamental pillar of communication, don’t you know? How do you expect to maintain a consummate set of relationships without it? Or perhaps you don’t concern yourself with such matters?”

“I thank you for your gracious advice, Ishimaru Kouta. But I’d rather die than laugh for no reason.” I gave a half-hearted nod. “Now then, do you have some business with us? How did you get in here anyhow?”

“A fine question. However, I’ll have to insist we save that bit of fun for later—” Kouta took her eyes off me and gazed over at Kunagisa and Suzunashi. “Oh ho, two ladies in a cage? Now there’s a lovely sight.”

She said it in a way implied the third occupant somehow spoiled the view.

Suzunashi chuckled lightly at Kouta’s abrupt non sequitur.

“You’re pretty popular, huh, Inoji? Who’d’ve thought you had two acquaintances in a remote place like this,” instead of talking to Kouta, she addressed me. “And they’re both women too. You’re basically Ariwara no Narihara.”

“Right…” I didn’t really understand the comparison.

“So, how do you two know each other, you and this lovely lady here?”

“Yesterday, I propositioned this fine gentleman, but I was soundly rejected.”

Before I could get a word in, Kouta answered for me. The nerve.

“Isn’t that right, dear friend?”

“…Yeah. Well, about a tenth of it is true, anyhow.”

“Even ten percent of truth is more than enough, is it not?” Her tone was different somehow. “However, it appears your circumstances have changed. I don’t suppose you might reconsider…?”

“No one likes an overly persistent woman,” Suzunashi said, finally addressing Kouta. “Just ask your dear friend here.”

Unfazed, Kouta simply said, “perhaps.” It was like she had taken all of Suzunashi’s animosity, and deflected it without even trying. While she may have made it seem like nothing, I knew for a fact that it was a monstrous feat.

“Unfortunately, I just don’t know when to give up. …I’d be ever so grateful if you could reign in your hostility a bit. I don’t have to be your enemy. In fact, I bet we’d get along swimmingly… especially you.” She nodded in my direction. “Don’t you agree, dear friend?”

“Earlier you said you heard about us?” Instead of answering Kouta, Suzunashi responded with a question of her own. “You said you heard about us and that’s why you’re here, didn’t you? You know what that tells me? It tells me that someone told you we were locked up down here.”

“—Oh my, did I say that? Oh well, it’s of no importance. You’re as shrewd as you look—Suzunashi, was it?” She grinned even wider than before. “However, I wish you’d focus that shrewdness somewhere else. I said it from the beginning, didn’t I? There’s a way out. Don’t you think that should take precedence right now?”

A way out. A way out of this dire situation.

Predictably, Suzunashi grew quiet. Taking a quick glance at Kunagisa, she was frozen in the same pose as when Kouta first appeared. Her eyes wide, her head tilted. Every once in a while, her brain would freeze like this.

Clap, Kouta clasped her hands together in front of her.

“Essentially, what I’m asking is this: ‘shall I lend you a hand?’”

My expression suddenly stiffened.

I remembered last night.

“——……”

“You don’t trust me, do you? You’re suspicious of me, are you not? I sympathize with your concern. I wouldn’t trust anyone who appeared out of the blue with such an offer either. That’s just common sense. However…”

Kouta reached into her pocket and fished out a knife. The knife was narrow and pointed, almost like an awl, or perhaps the shaft of an arrow. Additionally, the blade was quite short; all in all, it didn’t look like a particularly user-friendly design. That’s right, this blade was never intended to stab people or shred things, but instead, its main purpose was to serve as a type of anti-lock blade—

“Oh my, are you familiar with knives like these? Then I needn’t waste my breath explaining it.” Kouta made a show of twirling the knife, slicing the air. “This knife was a present from a dear friend, so I can’t be too rough with it. That said—”

With that, she inserted the knife into the keyhole of the lock holding the iron bars shut. Rattle rattle, she jimmied the lock two or three times followed by the sound of something coming undone, then the latch on the cell door released. Creaaak, the rusty door slowly swung open.

“—this isn’t a matter of trust or doubt, but pragmatism.”

“…What do you want?”

Hearing my question, Kouta made a wicked expression.

“How uncouth. Didn’t your mother teach you to show gratitude when someone helps you?”

“Unfortunately, I grew up exceptionally spoiled… Because of that, I wound up somewhat distrusting of others.”

“That’s rather consummate, my dear friend.” Kouta smiled elegantly. “‘Tis a trivial matter. It’s certainly not something you need to fret over. Naturally, my proposition is the exact same as the one I made last night, dear friend.”

“…Is that so?”

I nodded tentatively.

The same request as last night. In other words-

“…And what if I were to refuse again?”

“Nothing. That is consummate in its own right. Feel free to refuse to your heart’s content. In that case, we would simply go our separate ways.” Kouta showed me her palms in what seemed like a small act of capitulation. “You see, I was raised to always maintain a certain level of decorum. Not by my parents, mind you… Regardless, ‘If you expect others to show you kindness, you must first offer kindness expecting nothing in return.’ Everything thus far has been a service.”

“…I see.”

Just how far could I trust her?

My lexicon doesn’t contain a word to describe anything as ridiculous as putting ‘faith’ in a stranger you’ve just met, and ‘trust’ was out of the question. And so, this woman— Ishimaru Kouta, didn’t strike me as trustworthy, but as a dangerous individual I needed to treat with the utmost caution. That’s how I felt last night, and I felt that way still.

Moreover, the fact that she had chosen Zerozaki as her fake surname was the most frightening thing of all. I heard it from Red. ‘No one would ever label themselves a Zerozaki,’ and yet, the person standing right in front of me had not only openly worn that label, but had succeeded in infiltrating this facility without even trying to hide. What did that say about her?

But still— how much worse could our situation get?

“Kishimaru, was it?” as I was hesitating over how to answer Kouta’s request, Suzunashi spoke up. “Kishimaru, you see-”

“…The name is Ishimaru,” Kouta replied, somewhat annoyed. “Ishimaru Kouta. Please get it right.”

“Apologies,” Suzunashi gave a slight shrug. “It’s a generous proposal, but I’m afraid we won’t be taking you up on it— I don’t know what it is you want with Inoji, but it’s not going to happen.”

“Oh? And why is that?” Kouta tilted her head in an exaggerated fashion. “Perhaps my proposal is something mind-numbingly simple? Perhaps I need a two-thousand-yen bill, or a coupon?”

“It was never much of a deal in the first place,” Suzunashi said. “We’d never make it out. Or rather, even if we did make it out, it’d be pointless. Even if we left this cage, it’s not like it’d make a difference, right? I’m right, aren’t I, Inoji?”

“…Yeah.”

That’s right. It was just as Suzunashi said. Even if we were to escape this cage, we’d never even make it out of Kasugai’s Fourth Ward. This building had no windows, and the only entrance was— lorded over by that troublesome security lock. If, and this is a pretty big ‘if’, everything Kunagisa had said was true, then we might be able to pull it off. If we were to use one of the many computers bound to be in this ward to access the mother computer and gain administrator access, then we’d be able to disable the lock. With that, we’d probably be able to leave the ward. And from there, it’s even possible we’d be able to figure a way out of the facility. But even then, the Fiat was likely impounded, and the security at the gate would undoubtedly be heightened. Moreover, among the three of us, the only one with the stamina to make it down the mountain on foot would be Suzunashi.

Even if we ignore the countless obstacles ahead of us and make the outrageously optimistic assumption that our escape would be successful, if Professor Kyouichirou contacted the police, we’d just end up arrested anyhow. The professor would likely be more than happy with that outcome as well.

“—That’s why it makes no difference whether we stay here or not, Kouta,”

Suzunashi laughed bitterly.

“We’re boxed in on all sides with enemies on all fronts.”

“No no, you’re merely boxed in on most sides with enemies on most fronts. It helps no one to be pessimistic,” Kouta winked. “That’s precisely why we should make a deal. I have no intention of making a proposition that doesn’t also benefit my compatriots. After all, if my benefit isn’t directly correlated with yours, then we can hardly consider this a true team effort.”

Honestly, what a lovely way of thinking. I even found myself agreeing with her. Everything Kouta said was completely correct. But still, it’s not like that’s all it was.

“So what do you suggest? Is this where we circle back to that way out you mentioned?”

“Precisely, dear friend. I’d expect nothing less from the man who caught my eye… how sharp, how sharp indeed.”

“………”

I kept quiet and waited for Kouta to continue. Suzunashi did the same. I had my doubts about whether Kunagisa had even been listening, but she was silent nonetheless.

“—you need only find the true culprit and prove yourselves innocent.”

Kouta spoke eventually.

“If you do, Professor Kyouichirou will be left without reason to detain you. Am I mistaken?”

“—the true culprit?”

The true culprit behind Utsurigi Gaisuke’s murder and subsequent crucifixion. The one who landed us in this mess in the first place.

“—that’s-”

I brought a hand to my mouth, lost in thought. I turned Kouta’s words over and over again in my mind. That’s it. I’d been careless. When all was said and done, someone had to have done it. Rather than focusing on the absurdity of Professor Kyouichirou’s rambling theory, I should have realized that there was a better solution. That’s right. As long as I could successfully find that solution, then I could bring Professor Kyouichirou’s plan crashing down around his ears.

This was a secluded location. Closed off from the outside. The conditions were severely limiting. In that case, the true culprit– if the true culprit was really one of us then– That– That would certainly–

“That would certainly be…”

“Worth a shot, right?” Suzunashi finished my sentence. “It’s certainly worth trying, but it sounds like a pipe dream. It’s always nice to aim big, but we don’t have nearly enough time. Kasugai said they'll come to a decision in the next five hours. If they do, we’re finished. It’s already been an hour since then, so we’ve only got four hours left. There’s no way we can figure out the culprit in just—”

“Four hours!” Kouta interrupted in a sing-song voice. “Four hours, you say? We may as well have an eternity. In fact, we may even have too much time.” Kouta turned to me excitedly. “—Right? Don’t you agree, dear friend?”

“…With your help, it would seem so, Kouta.”

I nodded begrudgingly.

Suzunashi was right, we were in a tight spot. Miss Kokoromi had also been right about this not being another senseless murder, it was a locked room— a hard-locked room we couldn’t begin to explain. In other words, an impossible crime. The needlessly strict mechanical gatekeeper, the reason Utsurigi was so viciously crucified, and the meaning behind that bloody message. It was a daunting enough challenge on its own, let alone with a time limit.

However,

It was just as Kouta said, this might be our best chance. Even if it meant making the worst choice at the same time.

“So? What shall it be? I shan’t force you to do anything.”

Kouta extended her right hand through the iron bars. Suzunashi didn’t say anything else, neither did Kunagisa.

I steeled my resolve and took her hand.

It felt like I had grasped the hand of a human.

Psycho Logical (Part Two)

3

Suzunashi and Kunagisa stayed behind in the cage while Kouta and I set off to act. It would be an exaggeration to say we split into a reserve force and an advance force, but since there was no way we could meander about as one big group, we all agreed that someone would have to remain in the cell. That said, we couldn’t leave someone on their own (there was no guarantee Kasugai wouldn’t return before the four hours were up, so if our escape was discovered, being alone wouldn’t just be frightening, it would be dangerous), and since we couldn’t leave the intruder, Kouta, behind (I’d suggested as much, but it was flatly rejected. Obviously), that meant, among the three of us— Kunagisa, Suzunashi, and I— only one would be part of the advance force. Suzunashi was the first to decline (“because I’m dumb”), so the choice was between Kunagisa and me. Objectively, Kunagisa was clearly smarter than me, but it didn’t feel right entrusting Kunagisa to a suspicious individual like Kouta, and besides, I couldn’t imagine Kunagisa being able to keep a low profile. She wouldn’t last two seconds outside the cage before being caught. Since professor Kyouichirou’s sole target was Kunagisa, even if worse came to worst, as long as Kunagisa was still locked up, he wouldn’t do anything rash— he wouldn’t. Joining the advance force was my only option.

It was a similar conundrum to the chicken, the fox, and the grain.

I left the cell.

“—what a load of nonsense.”

I muttered my usual line and made my way over to Kouta. Kouta pulled her cap low once again and said, “I’m counting on you, so without further ado, let us begin. We can’t spend all day dawdling in a place like this.”

“—Right. We can’t.” I nodded, then I turned back towards the cage and said, “Well then, Suzunashi, I’ll leave everything here to you… take care of Kunagisa."

“Given the circumstances, I can’t say I’m bursting with confidence. Still, leave it to me,” Suzunashi said. “Inoji, our lives are in your hands.”

I wound up entrusted with something unthinkable.

Counting on, relying on, and entrusting one another.

Hang on, isn’t this-?

It’s almost like we trusted one another.

“Iichan,”

Kunagisa said abruptly.

“If things go bad… if Iichan really thinks he can’t do it, feel free to call Nao-kun.”

“…………”

Call Nao. I knew exactly what that meant. If Kunagisa was ever in direct danger, we were to rely on that man’s power.

“…Understood. I’ll do that then. But only if things go belly up.”

“One more thing, Iichan. Do you remember?” Kunagisa continued, looking up at me from her seated position. “I told you something a long time ago. One of TEAM’s rules was that we promised never to leak information about other members.”

“…Yeah, I think you mentioned it. It sounds familiar at least.”

“I’m breaking that promise,”

Kunagisa said.

“——Yesterday, Sacchan said something like this, ‘it might be time for me to restore my wicked name.’”

Restore his wicked name.

Utsurigi’s name— Malignant Green. A pseudonym he’d earned by committing atrocity after atrocity during his time as TEAM’s ultimate disruptor. And he wanted to live up to a name like that? He wanted to reclaim it? That’s- Why would Utsurigi, condemned to crucifixion and long gone, say something like that? No, still, more importantly-

“Why tell me that now?”

“It didn’t seem fair not to. We’re short on time, so that’s all I can say. I just wanted you to know,” Kunagisa said in an uncharacteristically distant tone of voice. “Hey, Iichan. You wouldn’t abandon me, or hate me or anything, right?”

“Never.”

I answered immediately.

I was able to give an immediate answer.

The one who was most relieved by that fact was likely not Kunagisa, but myself.

“Don’t make me state the obvious. It’s a pain to even have to answer those kinds of questions. Something like this is nothing to us, Tomo.”

“That’s right. Thank goodness,”

And with that, Kunagisa beamed me her usual innocent smile. That was all I needed. I steeled my resolve and said, “Let’s get going, Kouta.” She nodded. “First thing’s first, let’s talk strategy.” We began walking.

“We need a firm grasp on the situation. To that end, we first need to leave this building.”

“Exactly. I think I asked you already, but how did you get inside in the first place, Kouta.”

“I was just about to explain that to you. For the time being, please come with me.”

I shadowed Kouta as she plodded on ahead. We quickly rounded a corner and the cage faded out of sight; I could no longer see Kunagisa or Suzunashi.

That’s when Kouta let out a chuckle.

“—What’s so funny?”

“‘Tis nothing, pay me no mind. Would you call it friendship, love, or perhaps neither? The two of them are plenty alluring, but which one does your heart desire, my dear friend?”

“It’s not like that. Not with Suzunashi, and not with Kunagisa either. My heart belongs to the samurai-like lady who lives next door,” I responded curtly. “Besides, it’s not like that’s any of your business, is it?”

“Oh ho, of course it isn’t. ‘Tis none of my concern. You and I are of no relation, and that’s consummate enough. That said, is it so unusual to want to know more about the partner with whom you are bound in life and death, my dear friend?”
