“I have no intention of committing a lovers’ suicide with you, Kouta,” I tried my best to sound nonchalant about it. “And if you want to go there, it seems like you know an awful lot about us already, but I don’t know the first thing about you. I can’t help feeling a little uneasy about that.”

“Uneasy? Marvellous. Please keep it that way. That would work out best for both of us,” Kouta kept walking at the same brisk pace as she answered. “So long as you keep your promise, you shan’t hear a complaint from me. I’m being sincere when I say, trust isn’t something I want from you.”

“That’s awfully pragmatic.”

“It’s realistic.”

It was an utterly meaningless exchange. Part of me wondered if this was okay, the other part of me preferred it this way. After all, at that moment, I had no choice but to rely on this woman.

“—Over here,”

Kouta gestured to a green iron door. She undid the lock with her awl-shaped knife and pushed the door open. Inside was a stairwell that continued to the upper floors. By the looks of it, it was some kind of emergency staircase.

“—Is this where you came from?”

“Precisely. The elevator is far too loud, you see. If we use it, we shall be detected right away. Now, pick up the pace. We have a time limit, do we not? It would be consummate if you could hurry.”

While I hesitated, Kouta had already begun climbing the stairs. She didn’t show even the slightest hint of indecision. In other words, she had expected things to play out this way from the very start. That I’d put up with her request. That I’d do whatever she told me to. Everything was going according to plan. I lightly shook my head and planted a foot on the first step. The door closed on its own, and I heard the sound of it locking behind me. Apparently, it had a simple automated locking mechanism.

“One slight correction,” Kouta said. “It’s as you say, everything is more or less proceeding according to plan; however, there is one thing that I didn’t account for.”

“……I hadn’t even said anything yet.”

“I was convinced that winning you over would take a little more time,” Kouta ignored my interjection and continued on. “Given your attitude last night, that is. Naturally, this outcome is far more consummate. Still, you didn’t strike me as the particularly understanding sort. Even with your back against the wall, I never expected you to acquiesce so easily. Why did you?”

“I have…an acquaintance.” I let out a sigh and began to answer. “They’re someone like you. No, you’re nothing alike. It’s not like I even begin to understand you, and I definitely don’t understand them, but… taxonomically, I feel like you two would share a classification.”

“…Is that so? Colour me intrigued.”

“Then again, they’re what you might call a jack-of-all-trades, or well, a contractor,” I said. “Not a thief like yourself.”

“—Oh ho, I see. That, too, is consummate… Not to sound like Miss All-black, but you’re surprisingly popular. In any case, it’s splendid that we could settle things so quickly.”

Miss All-Black? Who’s that? Ahh, she must have meant Suzunashi.

Blowing past the door on the first-floor landing, Kouta continued her climb towards the second floor.

“……? We’re still going up? The only way in or out is on the first floor, isn’t it?”

“Isn’t the fact that you can’t use that entrance the reason you’re in this mess to begin with? If the ordinary method is out of the question, then ‘tis only consummate to try something out of the ordinary. Or rather… there’s something more important to consider. How do you want to go about this?”

“How do I-? Are you being vague on purpose?”

“Not at all. It’s just that, this case… how confident are you that you’ll be able to solve it without further incident? I figured I ought to get that question out of the way.”

“Things could hardly get much worse. We got locked up in a kennel… Still, confidence, huh? ……There’s only one thing I can say for certain.” I hadn’t meant to mimic Kouta by giving such a vague answer. “I’ve experienced this pattern countless times already. There wasn’t a case among them that I couldn’t solve.”

“…You’re unexpectedly self-assured. I’m a little surprised.”

“I’m speaking from experience. That’s all. …if anything, this all feels a little lacking.” There was no emotion in my voice. “Compared to the incident that ruined Kunagisa and I, something like this falls woefully short. Kunagisa’s former comrade having his eyes gouged out, throat pierced, chest carved open, bowels gutted, legs skewered, arms removed, and his crucifixion topped off with a sentence scrawled in his own blood, all within a locked room– well, it might score a sixty.”

“‘Tis still a passing grade.”

“Perhaps. …That said, this is my first time with a time limit. Four hours…… maybe less. We need to be back before then.”

“In the unlikely event that you’re unable to solve the case before the four hours are up, what do you plan to do then?” Kouta said. “Despite what I said in front of Miss All-black, it’d be troublesome if you were to rely on me too much. My objective lies elsewhere, and while our alliance may have landed us in the same boat, ‘tis not like we have to be thrilled about it.”

“I’m well aware. And don’t worry, I’m certainly not thrilled. But still… in the event I fail, huh?”

“Would you call that… ‘Nao-kun’ fellow?”

Kouta lowered her voice slightly.

“That’s my last resort. No, if forming a united front with you was the worst choice I could make, then calling Nao would have to be the lowest.”

If I made that choice— If Kunagisa Nao was made aware of the kind of treatment his little sister, Kunagisa Tomo, was subject to– forget four hours, this whole incident would be settled in under four seconds. Nao would use every ounce of power at his disposal to resolve this case— No, without a doubt, he’d quash it. However, that’s– That’s the one thing that I–

“—If at all possible, that’s a measure I’d rather not take.”

“……Hmm? I’m not sure I understand… but I do recognize your apprehension. So, what then? Would you pass the torch to that ‘contractor’ you mentioned earlier?”

“In all honesty… that’s also something I’d rather avoid,” I answered truthfully. “It has nothing to do with whether it’d be a good idea or not, it’s just… let’s see. It’s because I want to be their friend. I want to just be friends. I’d rather avoid any unnecessary give-and-take or debts of gratitude, and the last thing I want is a business relationship,”

I said, but the truth had been that I already owed her a fair deal.

“I wouldn’t have been against asking for their help with something as simple as rescuing Utsurigi, but now that things have escalated like this, it’s already more than I can ask of them.”

“You’re afraid of bothering them because they’re your friend? Is that not backwards? What is a friend if not someone you can turn to in your time of need?”

“To me? All kinds of things.”

That kind of thing was hard to define. Its edges, fuzzy and hard to make out. In order to get a firm grasp on it, I’d have to spend a considerable amount of time ruminating over it, and frankly, I wasn’t willing to put in the effort. Especially given current circumstances.

“To me, living is one big contradiction.” It was a conclusion I’d just reached. “I’m glad I was able to become their friend. I’m glad we can share a meaningless conversation, or a meal, or a room for the night. I’m glad I can get spoiled, teased, hit, or picked on by someone as amazing as that. All in all, I’m glad I get to be their friend. That’s why, one day, I want them to feel glad that they were mine. It may be stupid, but that’s just how it is.”

“—Is that so? …Well, that’s certainly consummate of you.” Some part of what I said must have struck a chord with Kouta because she briefly looked back over her shoulder and flashed me a cheerful expression. Surprisingly, I found her smile quite pleasant. “So what do you have in mind? If it’s starting to look like you won’t solve the case in time, that is. Let me say this now, I don’t think it’s possible to reason with the professor. That Mad Daemon’s hard at work on his nefarious dealings as we speak; you won’t have any luck trying to talk him down.”

“…You were listening to our conversation?”

“Part of it. Something about how he aims to use Kunagisa as Utsurigi’s substitute, or what have you.”

“Is that so? Nothing gets past you, it seems… Let’s see… in that case, I guess it can’t be helped. I’d give up.”

“A lie, no doubt,” came Kouta’s immediate reply. “You don’t strike me as someone who’d give up so easily.”

“Really? Maybe you’re right.”

However, I hadn’t lied to her. It was the honest to goodness truth. My true feelings on the matter. If things did play out that way, I’d give up. I’d stop trying to resolve this cleanly. I’d give up on putting an end to it without having to dirty my hands. Now that things had gotten this dire, I didn’t have the luxury of worrying about the last shreds of normalcy I’ve barely managed to cling onto these past nineteen years. I quietly confirmed that the knife in my jacket pocket hadn’t been taken from me.

“Let’s move on. ‘Tis not consummate to only consider the worst-case scenario. We should set our sights on a brighter future.”

With that, Kouta finished her ascent up the stairs. Wait, finished? In other words, this was— it couldn’t be—

“—The roof?”

“Indeed,” Kouta said, nodding as she unlocked the door with the knife. “The roof.”

Following Kouta, I stepped out onto the rooftop. The roof was tiled, with a clothesline directly in front of us. It must’ve been built for the purpose of drying laundry; however, the clothesline didn’t look like it had ever seen any use. If anything, the place lacked any human presence at all. It was enough to make me question whether anyone had set foot up here since the day of its construction.

A handful of puddles had formed on the tile. No doubt, remnants of last night.

When I lifted my gaze, I was treated to a sweeping view of the surrounding scenery. It was quite stunning. The cedar forest stretched out from beyond the castle wall. There was hardly a man-made object in sight, it was truly picturesque. If anything, the amount of nature on display almost felt unnatural.

But this was no time to soak in the sights.

“I’d ask you not to get too close to the edge. The research wards are without windows, so the chances of getting spotted are slim, but that doesn’t mean you won’t be seen by anybody moving between wards,” Kouta said as she made her own way towards the roof’s edge. Still unsure of what we were doing there, I followed after her.

“Umm, Kouta? You’re not about to suggest we rappel down the building or anything, right?”

“That wouldn’t be an unconsummate idea, but if that were the case, it’d do nothing to explain how I got into the ward in the first place.” Kouta’s feet shuffled to a stop nearly at the edge of the rooftop that faced the Fifth Ward. Once there, she stood tall.

“…Well then, if you would please follow me.”

Not even a moment later, she took a single step back and leapt with all her might. She leapt. In other words, just before the ledge— or rather, directly on it. She planted her foot less than a millimetre away from the small eavestrough that carried the rain water away. Just beyond– lay thin air, and–

The Fifth Ward.

So nimbly that I half expected it to come accompanied by a ‘woosh’ sound effect, Kouta touched down on the other side before turning back to face me. Her two decorative braids, coming to rest across her shoulders a few moments later.

“—Alright, whenever you’re ready.”

“‘Whenever you’re ready,’ she says…” Naturally, I shrunk back. “Ready for what, exactly?”

“It’s nothing to balk at. There’s no way a grown man wouldn’t be able to handle a measly two metre jump. Am I mistaken?”

Two metres. Certainly, the gap between the Fourth Ward and the Fifth Ward was about that wide. The impression I had yesterday was spot on; the buildings at this research facility were constructed suffocatingly close together. However, the distance was not the problem.

Standing over the edge, I peered down. As I thought, the building was four stories tall. That said, since the ceilings were designed to be higher than your average building’s, even a conservative estimate would place us ten metres above the ground. A fall from this height would be more than enough to kill you, even if you landed on your feet.

Of course, something like leaping two metres would’ve been no sweat. However, if failure meant death, then it’s only natural that confidence would turn to apprehension.

“What’s this? Have you caught the jitters? I didn’t think such a thing was possible. I never would’ve guessed my dear friend would be such a chicken.”

“…Would pointing out that I’m still a minor and therefor technically not a grown man get me out of this situation?”

“If you mean to tell me you don’t intend to overcome your predicament, and consequently prove to me you aren’t a chicken, then by all means.”

Hearing that, even I would have no choice but to buckle down. Kouta’s run up had been less than a metre— and that was probably more than enough for me as well— but I took three, no, four steps back, followed by one more. I took a sharp breath in, and then took a final step for good measure.

“…………”

New Genre: Sports-mystery.

“……Honestly, nonsense through and through,”

I mumbled and then began sprinting. I could make the jump without question. If all it took was jumping from the Fourth Ward to the fifth, then it would have been simple. The problem at hand was whether I could take off correctly. If I were to trip over the ledge, it would mean the end of the volume. Fearing that outcome, in the end, I took off a few dozen centimetres before the edge.

After the feeling of having been freed from gravity,

I felt the shock of its return with my whole body.

“—umph.”

I touched down with both legs. In an almost squatting position, I found myself on the roof of the Fifth Ward. At the very least, the story hadn’t ended with me miserably splattered across the ground like a bright red tomato or a split pomegranate.

Clap, clap, clap, the sound of Kouta’s insincere applause. “Exemplary, my dear friend. Three whole metres. To leap that far with that kind of approach, hmm, it appears your athleticism may be consummate, after all.”

“I did well in P.E. and academics, I’ll have you know.” I tried to look unaffected as I gradually calmed my beating heart. There was no need for me to put on airs, and I wasn’t concerned with my pride or my image; I just figured it would be best not to show Kouta too much weakness. “So? Now that we’re at the Fifth ward, what’s next?”

“What’s next, you say?”

“Yeah, as in what’s the plan? The entrance to this building’s under security too; nothing’s changed. Granted, we did manage to get out of the Fourth Ward like you promised, but… that just means we’re more likely to get caught if we’re careless—”

Then, just as I turned to face Kouta-

The door directly ahead of me that lead to the research ward’s interior slowly swung open, and, as if on cue and without any warning, Neo Furuara appeared. With his white lab coat clinging to his rotund body and a cigarette hanging from his lips, he made his way towards us as casually as could be.

In a panic, I began looking for a place to hide– a fool’s errand on this wide-open rooftop– but a moment later I would learn that there was no need to hide in the first place.

Neo smiled cynically.

“Yo, Ishimaru,”

He said.

As for me, who was still supposed to be locked up underground, he only spared me a single glance before turning back to face Kouta, and, face to face with the woman he should have deemed an outsider and intruder, he bowed deeply.

“I had intended to greet you here, but things appear to be advancing much faster than I expected. I ask that you please pardon the late reception.”

“Pay it no mind,” Kouta replied coolly. “More importantly, how about preparing something to drink for my dear friend here?”

It was to be expected.

How had Kouta managed to infiltrate such an impenetrable facility in the first place? What’s more, how come Kouta, who the guards claimed ‘had already fled the facility,’ was still soundly within its walls? There were countless questions raised by Kouta’s presence. All of which could be answered by the existence of a double-agent somewhere within the facility, be it a member of security or otherwise. That much, I had predicted.

However, I never would have expected the double-agent to be one of the researchers.

As I drank the excessively sweet coffee that Neo made for me, I peered over at him. I had meant to do so in secret, but the ever-observant Neo noticed my gaze and chuckled.

“What’s the matter?” Neo said with a condescending smirk. “Are you the type that doesn’t drink coffee? If so, I also have tea. What I’d really like to recommend is some liquor, but well, it’s probably best we don’t dull your wits given what’s coming.”

“…I’m not good with liquor.”

“Ah, Miyoshi did mention that, didn’t she? Something about you being hospitalized after chugging an entire bottle of vodka, and how you haven’t touched a drop of the stuff since.”

My mentor sure loves to run her mouth, doesn’t she?

“…It’s fine, I like coffee. I prefer it black, but I love the sweet, canned stuff too. That said, I don’t think coffee cares much about whether I like it or not.”

“Ha-ha, I know what you mean. It’s rough when they don’t like you back, ain’t it?” Neo replied with a grin. “I can’t stand black coffee. Not one bit. Anything spicy or bitter can disappear for all I care. If I ever start a religion, ‘thou shalt not partake of the coffee bean’ will be one of my ten commandments.”

“……………”

The Fifth Ward’s fourth floor. Neo Furuara’s private quarters. It didn’t really look like the room of an academic, if anything, when taking the appearance of the man himself into consideration, it felt more like the room of a mediaeval aristocrat. A wine cooler, an extravagant sofa, an intricately patterned wooden table, a chandelier hanging from the ceiling, and all four walls plastered with paintings. They weren't just any ordinary paintings either; they were exclusively the kind you could find hanging in a museum. They were re-creations of course, but it gave a glimpse into his refined tastes. “Hm? Have the paintings caught your eye?” Neo said. “I must admit, I’m somewhat ashamed by the lack of theme.”

It was true. The paintings that adorned the walls held little relation to one another. From landscapes, portraits, and abstracts, to impressionism, cubism, and surrealism— there was even some automatism mixed in. There was a bit of everything. If he felt so inclined, he could probably turn this room into a miniature art exhibit.

“Do you like painting?”

“I do, although it seems painting doesn’t care much for me,” Neo said, looking just a little bit pleased. “My talent outstripped my passions, so to speak. That’s a story from back when I was a student, however… a middle school student, no less. But yes, there was a time when I fancied myself a painter.”

“I see.” He probably meant ‘my passions outstripped my talent,’ but I didn’t think there was much point in correcting such a simple mistake. “So, how’d it go?”

“Horrendously. It’s one thing to admire paintings, but actually painting them is a different matter altogether. I was painting what was supposed to be a self-portrait when my art instructor came up and said, ‘deary me, is this what I think it is? It is, isn’t it? An abstract landscape. Well… it’s certainly unique.’”

“………” Having had a similar experience, I couldn’t laugh. “…and that’s why you switched to academia?”

“Ha-ha, no need to glare at me like that. That’s the same glare you gave the professor earlier, isn’t it? Talk about scary. Don’t you get it? I’m an ally. See, I made you a coffee, didn’t I?”

“An ally, huh?”

An ally to whom, exactly? That was the point of contention. At the very least, he wasn’t an ally to the professor. That much was certain, but it would be naïve to conclude that that made him an ally of mine. Even calling him Kouta’s ally would be questionable. Given what I saw of their exchange earlier, it didn’t seem like their relationship was one built on trust. I took a sip of the coffee, savouring the taste for a moment before gulping it down. I felt it warm me up from within.

“Who are you, really?”

“Awfully straightforward, aren’t you…? Heh, here’s how I’d answer,” Neo spread his arms wide and answered in his outdated fashion, “an expert informant! A professional backstabber! A specialist in secrecy! An immoral copycat! That is the man I, Neo Furuara, am!”

“……………”

“Don’t shrink away like that.”

“Too late.” I shrank back almost five kilometres. “So essentially, you and Kouta are co-conspirators sent by a rival organization to spy on the facility?”

“Not quite. Ishimaru and I aren’t exactly partners in crime. I suppose we’re more like accessories after the fact… It’s hard to say.” Neo made a difficult expression. “It’s best if you don’t ask too many questions about me. Knowing too much is liable to shorten your life expectancy, that’s for sure. But well, isn’t it enough that I’m not on the professor's side so I can lend you a hand like this?”

“………I suppose it is."

Neo’s objective was likely very similar to Kouta’s. However, unlike Kouta, who seemed motivated entirely by her own will, Neo seemed to belong to some kind of organization… an organization that stood opposed to this facility and its corporate backer, the Kunagisa House. Thanks to Neo’s meticulous preparation, he had somehow managed to infiltrate the facility as a member of faculty— meaning he was in for the long haul— Whereas Kouta’s lack of meticulous preparation had left her more adaptable. That was the nature of their collaboration.

That said, Neo was right; I was better off pretending I knew nothing. At the very least, given how short I was on time, I didn’t have the luxury of fussing over some company’s research or potential profits.

“—Still… It seems you’ve gone and caught the eye of quite the troublesome individual.”

“Troublesome individual? You mean Kouta?”

“Who else? Dangerous people seem to take a liking to you,” Neo said self-effacingly. “Well, given your circumstances, I suppose there was no avoiding it this time around, but you’re better off not having anything to do with Ishimaru when this is done. I don’t have the slightest clue why Ishimaru is so intent on cooperating with you, but try and take this as a piece of sagely advice. Heh, what’s the matter, you don’t believe me? Sure, I admit it. Compared to how she used to be… compared to how she was when we first met, she’s mellowed out considerably. Still, there was a time when that woman was known as The Seventh Spear…”

Given the way he talked about her, it seemed that this wasn’t the only occasion where Neo and Kouta had worked together. In that case, just as Neo wasn’t some run-of-the-mill informant, Kouta likely wasn’t some run-of-the-mill corporate thief either. That whole mess was something I’d prefer to avoid, but at the same time, I wasn’t sure I could afford to. Not while the possibility remained that it was related to Utsurigi’s case.

“Putting that aside, what do you plan to do next?” In an instant, Neo’s tone reverted to normal. “Frankly, this problem is in a class of its own. The professor’s theory is absurd, but for the time being, it’s the only thing that’s been proposed that’s actually possible. I can’t say it’s the best solution, but it doesn’t look too bad at a glance. I probably don’t need to tell you that the security system’s your biggest roadblock. Key-card. Password. Retina scan. Voice Identification. ID Number. And finally, the logs sent to the mother computer. I’m sure you think it was one of us, but that’s not especially believable either. I still suspect it’s the work of an outsider. But if that’s the case, they probably made their way down the mountain ages ago; solving it in the next four hours is going to be impossible.”

“—It’s unbecoming to try and frighten children.”

By now, there should be no need to clarify whose voice it was. At some point, without either of us noticing, Kouta had appeared behind Neo, clutching a bundle of papers. She really lacked any and all presence. Neo must’ve grown accustomed to it because he didn’t seem at all surprised. “Yo, Ishimaru. How long have you been standing there?” Neo asked without turning around.

“Since the part where you offered your sagely advice. We can take our time hashing out our difference of opinion regarding that later, Neo. But more pressingly, dear friend, take a gander at these,”

First, Kouta sat down next to Neo so she was facing me, then she handed me the bundle of papers she was holding. Written on them, I found lines and lines of mind-numbingly incomprehensible English letters and numbers. No, this wasn’t English. This was programming, or in a broad sense, machine language.

“And these are…?”

“I printed them out on the off chance they prove useful. They’re the logs from the mother computer.” Kouta shot a quick glance at Neo. “…Neo’s personal computer is rather sluggish, so it took more time than I would have liked. …Ah, there they are. These are the records from last night. The four-digit number indicates the time, and the code next to it correlates to the research ward.”

As I listened to Kouta’s explanation, I poured over the logs, but the only thing I ended up discovering was that the professor had been telling the truth. As previously claimed, last night, the only one to leave their research ward was Kasugai, and even in Kasugai’s case, she only stepped outside for five to ten minutes. Going off these records, Professor Kyouichirou and his entire faculty all had alibis. Using the process of elimination, I had to admit that Kunagisa and crew were currently the most suspicious.

Things were looking grim.

Hmph.

Process of elimination, huh…?

“…Is it possible that they were tampered with?”

“Not a chance,” The reply didn’t come from Kouta, but Neo. “None of us have the skill. Not even the professor. Utsurigi might have been able to pull it off, but his area of expertise was different— his specialty was software, not hardware— not to mention he was the one who was murdered. Miyoshi and Kasugai belong to an entirely different field, and if I had to say, Koutari’s more suited to research than any kind of practical application. Ougaki and Uze are out of the question; not because they’re talents are misplaced, but because they lack the level of talent required to begin with.”

“—Even if that’s true for everyone else, the professor could have done it, couldn’t he? He’s The Mad Daemon, after all. If his title isn’t just for show, he should at least be able to manage that much, shouldn’t he?”

“Let me be absolutely clear. Kunagisa Tomo is a genius. Shadou Kyouichirou is not. The difference between the two is much larger than you think, Loverboy.”

“……………”

“That’s right, the professor’s no genius. Of course, for someone of your level… or even mine, it’s hard to see any difference between Lady Kunagisa and the professor at all. The two of them both look like geniuses in our eyes. The people who can actually tell the difference are few and far between. And the professor just so happens to be one of those few. But that’s exactly why– having been forced to realize his own lack of genius– the professor changed course; going from his research on artificial intelligence to this ridiculous experiment is his way of making a statement, don’t you think?”

Ridiculous experiment? That’s exactly what this is. However, if that’s really the case, then even without anything resembling an alibi, the professor would have had no reason to kill Utsurigi. There’s no way he would ruin his own experiment, after all.

“That’s just how people are, they love to look down on others. As we’re all aware, the world isn’t exactly fair, right? No matter who you ask, you’ll get the same answer. I’m sure you’ve heard this thought experiment before, but suppose you asked someone, ‘do you honestly believe that there’s not a single person on Earth who’s worse than you?’ you won’t find a single person who would nod their head.”

Neo seemed to be having fun.

There was no doubt he spoke the truth. There’s just one person on top and countless people beneath them. That’s just how the world works. That said, it wasn’t a particularly nice thing to hear put into words.

“I suppose we’ve gotten off track. Still, that system’s the black-box to end all black-boxes if you ask me. And not just the security, I’m talking about the mother computer as well– One massive black-box. Its contents are known only to its creator, Lady Kunagisa, of course.”

“…That means things are even more grim than I thought,” I tossed the bundle of papers on the table. “…besides, when it comes to computers and the like, I’ve basically already given up. Those kinds of things aren’t exactly my strong suit.”

“Oh?” Neo looked somewhat amused. “Then what is? You’re Miyoshi’s pupil after all, so perhaps anatomy?”

“…I never really cared for anatomy… by the way, Neo,” speaking of anatomy, “Utsurigi’s crucified corpse, what happened to it?”

“Hm? Oh, exactly what you think happened to it. Ougaki and Uze carried it to Miyoshi’s Third Ward… right about now, Kasugai and Miyoshi ought to be in the middle of performing an autopsy. Cause of death, time of death, that sort of thing.”

“Is that so…?”

I gave it some thought. Information regarding Utsurigi’s corpse. I definitely wanted to get my hands on that. I was so shocked by what I saw in that room this morning that I’d be pressed to say that I absorbed any details at all. Besides, it’s not like I had gotten that close a look at it in the first place. And so, it was imperative that I got another look at Utsurigi’s butchered, dismembered body.

One more thing. I absolutely couldn’t ignore the crime scene. I needed to step foot in the room where Utsurigi was crucified once more; I needed to see it for myself. That grizzly scene adorned with that bloody message.

Those two things were absolutely essential, but how would I pull it off?

“First thing’s first, dear friend. Is there not something the two of us have yet to discuss?” I was deep in thought when Kouta called out to me. “With regards to our partnership, is there not something we need to decide?”

“And what’s that?”

“The question of who shall take precedence.” Kouta raised a finger as if lecturing me. “In other words, shall you offer up your information first, or shall I assist you with your search for the truth and rely on your good-will after the fact? The matter of order is also a matter of sincerity.”

“Ahh…” That’s right, isn’t it? “That certainly is a problem…”

Of course, I would have preferred to exchange information after. Not because I was worried about the time limit, but because it was the only trump card I held against Kouta. And Kouta was in the same boat. Even if she were to generously provide her assistance, there was no guarantee I would return the favour. Especially since I’d already shot down her invitation last night. For Kouta to place her full trust in me would have been far too reckless.

Kouta seemed to be thinking something similar as she stared at me in silence.

“How about you flip a coin for it?” Neo suggested. “Every second you waste only worsens your chances, Ishimaru. It doesn’t do the lad any favours either. It’s not like you’re going to find a perfect solution anyhow, so why not settle it with a coin flip? It’s only fair, isn’t it?”

“—Very well. ‘Tis consummate," Kouta said, then she reached into her coat pocket and pulled out something resembling a medal. I knew it wasn’t Japanese yen at least, but at the same time, I couldn’t place its origins. There’s always the off chance that it was a token she’d won at a game centre.

“Well then, dear friend, heads or tails? Please call it.”

“You can hardly call that fair,” I said cautiously. “The one who tosses it controls which face it lands on, don’t they? I’m not saying that I don’t trust you— No, I guess I am– but I’m not leaving everything up to a method that can be rigged by anyone with decent hand-eye coordination…”

“Certainly,” Kouta readily conceded. “Then I’m content with you being the one to toss it, and I being the one to call it. You’d deem that fair, would you not?”

“…Are you sure? Then I’d be the one able to rig it.”

“I have another coin.” Kouta said as she reached into her pocket and procured the second coin. “If I’m holding it in my right hand, then it’s heads. If it’s in my left, then it’s tails. Do you find that agreeable?”

She said, tossing the coin into the air. As both her arms swiftly crossed in front of her, the coin wound up in one of her hands. Which hand that might be, I had no idea.

“…Sounds good to me.”

I lightly tossed the coin. At this point, no strategy remained; it all boiled down to luck. Without catching the coin in my palm, I let it fall onto the table however it may. It bounced a few times, spun, and then finally came to rest facing tails-side up.

Pascal wagers fifty-fifty.

I suppose if I want to be precise, there’s always the chance the coin could’ve landed on its side, so it wasn’t exactly fifty-fifty, but the chances of that happening were ridiculously slim. Besides, the outcome had already been decided. I turned to look at Kouta. She wore a somewhat cynical smile, then she ever-so-slowly opened her left hand. Gripped in her palm– was nothing at all.

“……Very well. This, too, is consummate. You shall take priority.” Kouta lifted herself off the sofa and gazed down at me. “Well then, cases like these need to be resolved step-by-step. Let us acquire the autopsy report and examine the crime scene. Which should come first, Utsurigi’s corpse, or the crime scene? Please come to a decision."

Returning Kouta’s gaze, I gave my answer.

“…Let’s see. For the time being, let’s start with— yeah, let’s start with the corpse. The more time passes, the less information we’ll be able to get from the examination.” I turned to Neo.  “Neo. Do you know which room in the Third Ward they’re keeping Utsurigi’s body in?”

“It’s likely in the Seventh Examination Room on the third floor. They said as much. But what are you planning on doing?” Neo tilted his head a little. “You… or rather, you and Kouta have no means of entering the Third Ward, do you? Just like you had no means of entering the Seventh Ward. I can shelter you here like this, I can offer suggestions as you deliberate, I can offer information, heck, I can even offer you coffee. However, any further collusion would be far too risky. I’m not in the best of positions either at the moment. You understand that, right?”

“…Sure, I get that, but…”

How would we? The first thing that came to mind was seeking my teacher’s help. However, even if we ignore the obvious risks, I couldn’t say the chance of success was all that high to begin with. It was the worst type of gamble. There’s no one in heaven or on Earth more self-centred than my teacher, Miyoshi Kokoromi; it’s not like her loyalty to Professor Kyouichirou ran especially deep, but in the same breath, I couldn’t see her betraying him either. There’s no way someone as keen and attentive as my teacher was just another hire. She had to be here for some personal reason. For that instructor, who couldn’t even conceive of a life not lived in pursuit of her own goals, the ability to put something ahead of her own aims didn’t have even a whit of existence. So the thought of her valuing something as trite as a former pupil over herself was beyond optimistic.

“…In that case, we only have one option.”

Kouta addressed me while I was still lost in thought. Without waiting for my response, she turned back to Neo. “In the meantime,” she said, “please run interference on the professor. Create as many distractions and feed them as much false information as possible. Stir up some wanton chaos and send them scrambling. That is your specialty, is it not?”

“……Ha-ha-ha,” Neo responded with a fake laugh. “I read you loud and clear, Ishimaru Kouta. I don’t know what it is, but I’m sure you have your reasons for being so buddy-buddy with the lad. What kind of information could you possibly want that bad, I wonder? Don’t worry, I won’t ask. I’m dying to know, but it’s best if I don’t. Alright. Leave it to me, Ishimaru. Your humble servant, Neo Furuara, will do what little he can to help.”

“Consummate. Then let us be off, dear friend.” Neo’s words elicited an uncharacteristically wide smile from Kouta, then she took my hand and helped me off the sofa.

“‘Tis time to set out on your adventure.”

“…You’re awfully carefree.”

“Because I’m not the one in peril. For the moment, at least.”

“Lad,” as I was being forcefully dragged away, Neo called out to me in a somewhat serious tone. “Take care not to run into anyone. If anyone spots you, you’re finished. If you think Miyoshi would let it slide because you’re old friends, or that you’ll be able to trick someone like Ougaki into working with you, you’re being far too naïve.”

“Trust me, I’m well aware.”

“It’s not just the professor. All the folks here are hopelessly depraved. Myself included, of course. Speaking of, be especially wary of Kasugai.”

“…Kasugai?” I hadn’t expected that. “How come? I would’ve thought the ones to watch out for would be Shito or Misachi…”

If the two of them could maintain their faith in the professor even after being subject to such unjust violence, then that makes them extremely dangerous individuals.

“In this case, it’s those without conviction who are more trouble. Just think about it. Why did Professor Kyouichirou entrust you— or rather Kunagisa— to Kasugai instead of keeping her in his own ward? Part of it is clearly so he can shirk responsibility if it ever comes down to it. However, there’s another reason that’s far more important: the objective fact that Kasugai would never betray him. As a professional backstabber, and as someone who always aims to betray, I can assure you— I can say this wholeheartedly— Kasugai will not betray him. They were never allies to begin with. Ougaki and Uze have their own reasons for looking up to the professor. Be it respect, or gratitude, or what have you. That’s why, so long as you can offer them something greater, you’re golden. You could strike while they’re still reeling from the shock of their beating at the professor’s hands, for instance. There’s a myriad of ways to get someone to turn coat. But Kasugai is different. She’s here just because.”

“Just because…?”

When I fed his line back to him, Neo sneered.

“That’s right. Could you imagine anything scarier, anything more frightening, than someone who acts without reason or conviction? She doesn’t have a single reason to obey the professor. Not one. She’s here just because. And that’s why there’s no way to shake her. She has no reason to cooperate with the professor, so there’s no logic that could move her. Multiply anything with zero, and you wind up with zero, but dividing by zero is outright impossible. What would you call that, if not blind fanaticism?”

“…………”

Kasugai Kasuga.

I recalled the conversation we had the night before.

The woman who chose not to choose.

The woman who had neither likes, dislikes, or indifference, who found nothing pleasant, unpleasant, or disinteresting.

The woman who had nothing.

The woman who was nothing, just because.

That said, in the moment, I didn’t truly grasp what Neo was trying to say. I was well aware that Kasugai was twisted in some way, but I couldn’t imagine her being as dangerous as Neo claimed. If anyone was to be labelled a fanatic, then Shito or Misachi still seemed far more fitting. What’s more, whatever sense of fear I was supposed to feel regarding a phrase as dubious as ‘just because’ was lost on me.

Kasugai Kasuga, just because.

That didn’t sound like much of a problem, right?

——However, a few hours later, I would come to understand. There exists those without a shred of conviction, who inspire terror through their presence alone. I would be made painfully aware that there is no solution for someone who isn’t a problem.
