And so, Kouta and I returned to the Fourth Ward’s roof once more.

“……What now?”

“That’s obvious. You wish to go to the Third Ward, do you not? If so, your route is right there. Your one-and-only, second-to-none route.”

I looked in the direction Kouta was pointing, but I found nothing but thin air. The space between the fourth and third wards. At a glance, the gap was around four metres… three and a half at best. Nearly a metre… no, over a metre wider than the distance between the fourth and fifth wards.

“…You’re asking me to jump? Again?”

“‘Tis consummate should you find it objectionable. If this is where you wish your game to end, then I shan't force you.”

“………”

I peered over the edge and looked down. Yup, no matter how many times I check, the drop’s still over ten metres. Both my eyes have 20/20 vision, so I’m confident in my assessment. It’s only in moments like these that I curse my healthy body.

“That’s three and a half metres, you know…?”

“Even middle school girls can jump that far nowadays,” Kouta said lightly. “‘Tis said that any elementary schooler with even a moderately competent upbringing should be able to jump four. Incidentally, the current long jump world record for men is eight metres and ninety-five centimetres, and for women, ‘tis seven metres and fifty centimetres. ‘Tis not even half of the woman’s record. Surely you can manage that much, can’t you?”

She could at least spare me the comparison to the world record holders. And even in their case, while they may have spent their lives long jumping, they surely never risked their lives long jumping. The risk of certain death should I fail, or at least very least, the risk of grievous bodily injury, weighed heavier than you might think.

“I don’t think it’s wise to linger in one spot. Utsurigi’s corpse shan’t remain in the Third Ward forever. Once they gather enough evidence— enough evidence to suit the professor’s purposes, that is— I wouldn’t think it unlikely that they dispose of the corpse by burning it. Should that happen, you’d be finished. No, I suppose the one who’d be finished would be Kunagisa, would it not? A Dead End, so to speak.”

Hearing that name spoken left me with no choice. “Good grief,” I muttered under my breath as I took my starting position facing the roof’s edge. This time, out of an abundance of caution, I gave myself nearly double the distance for my run-up. That said, if the run-up was too long, it’s possible that my stamina might flag before I even made the jump, so I had to be careful.

“—forget me, can you make this jump, Kouta?”

“Piece of cake.”

Bursting with confidence, Kouta laughed and pushed up her glasses. Her attitude suggested that it was likely just as easy for her as she made it sound. In that case, the only one I should be worrying about is myself. It’d be alright– so long as I built up enough momentum, there’s no reason I shouldn’t be able to leap three and a half metres. As long as I was careful not getting my foot snagged on the eavestrough——

I steadied my breathing and stepped forward. My seventh step took me right to the ledge, and my eighth launched me forwards. I arched my body like a bow— and with a view of the sky— for but a moment, I soared through the air, and then, I landed. I had made it across.

“—phew,”

I turned to look behind me at the roof of the Fourth Ward where I had been standing just a moment ago, but by the time I’d turned around, Kouta was already in the air. Before I could recognise what I was looking at, she had already touched down on the roof of the Third Ward; her excess momentum carried her forward as she skid on the heels of her high-laced boots, bringing herself to a halt.

“Oh-ho,” still leaning back somewhat, Kouta smiled at me. “We might make a better couple than once thought, you and I. ‘Tis likely we are the only pair in the whole wide world enjoying such acrobatics together.”

“I wouldn’t exactly say I’m enjoying this…”

I said, noticing that I had landed closer to the roof’s edge than Kouta had. She wasn’t as tall as Suzunashi, but Kouta was still tall for a woman, and, with her legs being longer than mine, she likely had an advantage when it came to long jumping, but still, rather than her stature, the difference in our performance likely boiled down to a simple difference in athleticism.

“What’s the matter? We ought to hurry. We’ve not much time, now do we?”

“Ah, right…” At that moment, I realized something else which stopped me in my tracks. “Kouta. Forgive me if I’m wrong, but… if someone were to use this method… leaping from roof to roof like this… wouldn’t they be able to infiltrate the Seventh Ward?”

Kouta looked surprised for just a moment, but she quickly brushed it off. “I don’t think that would be possible.” While it might not have been an instant rejection, I didn’t understand how Kouta could dismiss my suggestion so off-handedly, so I may have been overly demanding when I asked, “and why is that?”

“Try not to get so worked up, it’s unsightly. Were you like this when you snapped at Professor Kyouichirou?”

“That’s… No, you’re right. That was rude of me, I apologize.”

I bowed my head.

Right. What good does getting worked up do me? Even if every passing moment we wasted like this further endangered Kunagisa and Suzunashi, it’s not like getting hot-headed about it would solve anything. If anything, it was the opposite. It’s moments like this, situations like this, where I had to forcefully compose myself. Like always, I’d smother all emotion and think like a machine. A tin-man without a heart.

“Still, how could you just brush it aside…”

“You think I haven’t considered it? We’re currently leaping from roof to roof like Lupin the Third, do you think I’ve lived the kind of life where such an idea is in any way novel?” As she spoke, she turned her back to me and headed towards the door. “Regardless, I don’t think you’d be able to pull it off. I’ll explain my reasoning later. For the moment, we ought to be focused on examining Utsurigi’s corpse, should we not?”

“……Understood,” I nodded reluctantly and followed after Kouta. “Still, if that method’s impossible, then…”

At long last, I felt like I had glimpsed a crack in this confounding case, but I guess it had just been my imagination. An imaginary route into the impenetrable locked-room that was the Seventh ward.

As Kouta unlocked the door, she said, “‘Tis not as if that locked room is your only concern, now is it? There’s still the reason Utsurigi was so horrifically slaughtered. Or the matter of the curious bloody message scrawled on the wall. If you let your reasoning get tied up on a single issue, you’ll miss what’s right under your nose.”

“…Is that right? I suppose you have a point.”

I checked my watch. Roughly three and a half hours remained. While you could hardly call that a surplus of time, the problems weighing on my mind were in overwhelming abundance. To be blunt, I can’t say I had much hope. But so long as even a sliver remained, I had no choice but to push onwards. It was pointless to even think about.

As I continued descending the stairs after Kouta, once again, I noticed something. It had nothing to do with the case, but rather to do with the gamble I’d made with Kouta a little while ago. Heads or tails. It had ended with my victory, but had I truly won? Kouta’s left hand had been unmistakably empty. However, whether the coin had actually been in her right hand was something I never confirmed. One could hazard a guess that— just maybe— both hands had been empty. The idea that, out of concern for my lack of time, Kouta had willingly surrendered her advantage to me was so implausibly sentimental, that I couldn’t bring myself to broach the subject. Instead, I called out to Kouta as she walked ahead of me and asked something completely unrelated. “So, what does Neo actually do?”

“Did he not tell you himself?”

“I caught the gist, but he does a remarkable job at being evasive. No, I suppose it was more like he was meandering… He called himself an expert informant, a professional backstabber, a specialist in secrecy, and an immoral copycat— just a bunch of bullshit sounding titles.”

“And, what would you say he is?”

“…Well, I figured he was just a spy for a rival organization.”

“That's hardly a consummate answer. ‘Tis the same as declaring ‘everything that swims in the ocean is a fish.’ Let’s see, your answer scores three or four tenths of a consummate at most.”

“Is that right?” I didn’t quite understand her rubric. “Then what is he?”

“Keep this between the two of us, alright?” Kouta halted her descent for a moment, brought her index finger to her lips, and winked. “Neo’s not something so frivolous as a spy. In fact, far from being fabrications, his self-proclaimed monikers suit him to a T. He’s far more like an ambassador dispatched by a certain substantial organization… no, a substantial circuit, and that places him several ranks higher than a mere spy.”

“…This circuit sounds like a big deal.”

“That just goes to show how much attention it’s garnered. The research Professor Kyouichirou’s performing, that is… Or I suppose, given Utsurigi’s passing, I should say ‘the research he was performing.’ But then again, if they continue their research with Kunagisa as their lab rat, then I needn’t have bothered with the correction. But that all depends on your efforts, now doesn't it? You know, even your former compatriots, the ER3 System, must be itching to get their hands on the results of Professor Kyouichirou’s experiments. Of course they would.”

“…And the same goes for you, I take it?”

Kouta’s gentle smile seemed to say, ‘precisely,’ then she resumed walking. I decided to put off any further questioning for now and followed after her. I passed by the entrance to the fourth floor and made my way down to the third. Kouta was waiting for me in front of the door, and then, careful not to make any noise, she used her knife to pick the lock.

“Which room did they say it was again?”

“The Seventh Examination Room,”

As Kouta spoke, she gripped the knob to the metal iron door, carefully pushed it open a crack, and peered inside. However, no sooner had she done so than she pulled the door shut again. Despite being a spontaneous reflex, to her credit, the only noise that was made was the sound of the automatic locking mechanism.

“What’s the matter?”

“This is far from consummate. I’m afraid two women just stepped out of the examination room in question.”

“Two women? What do they look like?”

“The two of them are both wearing lab coats. One is donning a pair of round spectacles, and the other appears to me like the aloof type.”

In that case, we were most definitely talking about Miss Kokoromi and Kasugai. When it came to women, there was also Misachi, but given the intel we got from Neo and the fact that they were wearing lab coats, it’s probably safe to count her out.

Kouta crouched where she was standing and pressed her ear up against the door. I didn’t think it’d accomplish much, but I followed suit.

“…    …………Y’see    ………    ”

“…    …………Just the worst   ……   …   ”

“…is………hard work……ain’t it”

“The usual    ……    ……    a pain in the…   ”

I couldn’t hear too well, the two of them must’ve been quite far away. However, their voices gradually grew clearer, which meant they were probably getting closer.

“Still, whatever the case, what’s the professor fixin’ on doing with the three of ‘em?”

Miss Kokoromi’s voice.

“I should think the answer would be obvious by now.”

Kasugai’s voice.

In other words, I’d been right about who Kouta spotted. Kouta and I, still crouching facing each other, exchanged a brief look. Kouta gave a small nod before turning her ear back to their conversation.

“He’s as boorish as ever. Don’t you think? It hardly feels like the actions of a learned man. It’s wretched enough to lock children up underground like this but to frame them for murder? He must be out of his mind.”

“That’s a mighty sensible opinion. Well, I reckon that’s why they call him The Mad Daemon. Still, it ain’t as if I don’t get where he’s comin’ from. After all, shit hit the fan immediately after the three of ‘em showed up, right? Even without all that theorizing, ya can’t help but be suspicious, now can ya?”

“It’s unlike you to be so unreasonable. Your former pupil’s among the things locked up in my underground kennel you know?”

Kasugai spoke about people as if they were objects.

“I should think you would want to stand up for him would you not? After all when he blew his top you were the first to rush to stop him.”

“Ahh, y’see, that was just ‘cause I saw it comin’. That kid used to lose his temper all the time abroad as well. He’s usually mild-mannered, but if ya so much as touch a sore spot, he throws a hissy fit. Folk who dedicate themselves to academia— or just smart folk in general— are all kinda like that, but that kid’s a tad different. At any rate, he’s always had a short fuse. ‘Specially in his first year. I was always the one who had to come and break it up. He was a real handful, I tell you what.”

I had plenty I wanted to say, but I held my tongue.

“Still, I reckon that’s what made him so gosh darn cute.”

“Really? I'm somewhat put off by it.”

“Is that right? What’s the matter, Kasugai, are hot-blooded men no good?”

“No good at all.”

“You’ve got some mighty strict standards, don’tcha, Kasugai. Still, I gotta agree with ya, that kid is absolutely no good.” Miss Kokoromi had no issues saying terrible things about someone when she thought she was doing so behind their back. She continued. “That said, he’s not no good in your usual way. Sure, he’s fundamentally no good, but he’s no good in practice either; even his prospects ain’t no good— that kid sure don’t half-ass it when it comes to being no good. He’s the first-and-last, unprecedented, undefeated, trailblazer when it comes to being a no-good bastard. Not that I’m trying to sing his praises or anything.”

Don’t worry, no one’s going to get that impression.

“So you’re saying there’s nothing to worry about, Miyoshi?”

“Well, I’m certainly not worried. If anything, I’m giddy with anticipation. All we gotta do is sit tight. The professor, Shito, and Uze will spend the next couple hours tryna come up with some way to fix this mess, but by then, I dare say the kid’ll have this whole thing figured out.”

“He’ll figure it out? Him?”

“Damn straight. When it comes to situations like this, there’s no one better suited for the job. No, I s'ppose it’s better to say these kindsa situations are best suited for him. To put it another way, situations like these are his natural enemy. He’ll get himself all riled up and put this whole thing to rest.”

“He is your pupil after all.”

“Sure is tempting to think about it that way, but I’m ‘fraid that don’t got much to do with it.”

Miss Kokoromi dismissed the idea with a laugh.

…Come to think of it, the voices were neither approaching nor getting further away. The two of them must have stopped. Just what were they doing? I couldn’t think of a suitable reason for the two of them to stop and chat right in front of the emergency exit, so could it be that they realized we were here? No, if they had, they would’ve immediately swung the door open instead of wasting time on pointless chit-chat. The fact that they hadn’t proved we still remained unnoticed.

That’s when I remembered. When we went to visit the still-living Utsurigi in the Seventh ward yesterday, the elevator (that Shito claimed Utsurigi had torn apart) was right next to the stairwell. If the Third Ward had the same layout, then the elevator shaft should be located right next to this door. In other words, Miss Kokoromi and Kasugai weren’t posted up outside, but simply waiting for the elevator nearby.

If so, this was our chance. The two of them would soon leave the floor. Suddenly, sneaking into the examination room that housed Utsurigi’s corpse was looking a lot easier.

Huh, things were starting to look up. This might just be my year— if it weren’t for the fact it was already early July. That, and the countless times I’d nearly been murdered these past six months.

“Even with that said he’s currently locked away in a cage back at my place. Whether he’s perfectly suited or a natural enemy or what have you there’s nothing he can do. Or are you saying he’s the kind of armchair detective who could solve it without budging an inch?”

“If anything, he’s more of a backwards thinker. When he’s in the thick of it, he’s the kind of dunce who’s all, ‘I don’t get it. I don’t get it. I have no clue what’s going on. I have so little clue what’s happening that if even one more thing pops up that I don’t get, I’ll drop dead. This case is killing me,’ but then the most trivial of clues will have him saying, ‘that’s it! I solved it! How did I not realize something so simple sooner!? Am I an idiot or what? I’m so dumb that it’s killing me!’”

“So it kills him either way?”

It seems like it killed me either way.

“So no, he ain’t the armchair type. He ain’t the remote operation type or a close-range powerhouse either, so now that I think about it, I s’ppose you’re right. So long as he’s locked up there ain’t nothing he can do.”

“In that case he’s more of the electric chair type. I suppose all your anticipation was for naught then.” Kasugai’s words were frigid, blunt, and without a hint of tenderness. “Still that’s not something for us to be worrying about. We ought to leave everything to the professor.”

“That again? It’s like your catchphrase or something. ‘Leave everything to the professor.’… Not that I hate that side of ya, or anything.”

“Exactly which side of me are you referring to Miyoshi?”

“The side of ya that can’t stomach thinkin’ ‘bout stuff on your own, so ya pawn it off on others. The side that can never come to a decision.”

I heard Miss Kokoromi laugh, but Kasugai didn’t say a word.

I remembered Neo’s words of advice, so I strained my ears to listen even closer, but in the end, they never said anything particularly important. It was all idle and worthless conversation. Such as:

“Ya know the game Kokkuri? I get that the ‘ko’ is written with the character for ‘fox’, and ‘ri’ is written as ‘tanuki’, but what’s the ‘ku’ s’pposta be?”

“Dog if I’m not mistaken.”

“Howd’ya read ‘dog’ as ‘ku’?”

“Different kanji. Just like how ‘snake’ is written differently when part of the Chinese zodiac.”

“I see… still, a dog feels like an odd choice compared to a fox or a tanuki, don’tcha think?”

“They’re all animals that live in the mountains.”

“Then it could just as well’ve been a monkey…”

Or:

“Y’know how you often hear people say, ‘I could care less’? If ya think about it, ain’t it s’pposta be ‘I couldn’t care less’?”

“Indeed it would be quite strange to admit that you could care less. I suppose it’s one of those eggcorn things where people misremember or mishear a saying.”

“Hmph, in other words it’s just like how we got ‘A Catcher in the Rye’.”

“Speaking of which when I was still an intern I had a friend who’d studied abroad and they insisted ‘the Japanese translation is all wrong! This isn’t what Sallinger meant at all! I’m the only one who understands him! I’ll retranslate the whole thing from scratch for Sallinger’s sake.’ Then he penned a book titled ‘Catch them in the Rye!’.”

“Was it any good?”

“It was awful.”

And so their conversation went. Come to think of it, the two of them sounded far more passionate during their idle chatter than they had while discussing the case.

The elevator arrived, and I faintly heard the sound of the doors opening.

“Well then I’ll be off Miyoshi.”

“Yeah. What’s Neo want with you anyhow?”

“He insists that there’s some urgent problem with the model skeleton he’s working on but that sounds like a bald-faced lie. Still it’s not as though I can outright reject a request from a senior. Even though I’d much rather head back to my research ward as soon as possible.”

“I see. Neo, huh? …I’m sure it’s fine. Catch ya later.”

I heard the sound of the elevator door closing followed by the hum of an electric motor.

Taking that as our cue, I stood up, but Kouta didn't follow. She remained frozen with her ear pressed up against the door and a serious expression on her face, as if still listening to Miss Kokoromi and Kasugai’s conversation.

“…Kouta? What are you doing?” I asked quietly. “Neo’s risking a lot to buy us this window… do you hear something?”

“I don’t hear anything?”

“…Then what’re you doing?”

“I don’t hear anything, dear friend,” Kouta repeated in a whisper. “Why do you suppose that is? Going off that conversation just now, Kasugai boarded that elevator alone. Miyoshi should still be on this floor. And yet, I don’t hear a thing. Do you not find that strange?”

After having it explained to me, I finally understood. She heard nothing. It’s not that she simply couldn’t hear their conversation anymore, she heard absolutely nothing, not even a single footstep. In other words, despite Kasugai leaving, Miss Kokoromi hadn’t taken a single step from where she stood. She had no reason to still be here, so why was she lingering?

Why?

“It’s high time you came on out, don’tcha think?”

Miss Kokoromi called out in a voice loud enough that even I, with my face no longer pressed against the door, could hear her clearly. Even Kouta seemed shocked by the sudden exclamation and naturally recoiled away from the door.

“It’s not very manly to scamper around and hide, kiddo!”

“I feel like I’ve heard that line somewhere before,”

Kouta narrowed her eyes and shot me a sarcastic glance. Having who I’d stolen that line from exposed like this was so embarrassing that I couldn’t meet her gaze.

Does this mean… she noticed us? Had she seen right through us from the beginning? Had she carried on that conversation with Kasugai knowing that this single door was all that separated us? —No, that couldn’t be. After all, Miss Kokoromi wasn’t superhuman enough to pull a stunt like that through an insulated iron door. She wasn’t three years ago, at least.

“Not gonna show yourself? Fine, no skin off my nose. I’ll just report this to the professor, then. If I ring him up, he’s sure to come runnin’, don’tcha think? He’ll race on over like a bat out of hell. If that happened, even a pupil of mine would find themselves in quite the pickle.”

Kouta gave me a look that said, ‘what should we do?’ Unable to avoid her gaze forever, I reluctantly said, “We don’t have a choice.” Damnit, even if it was just for a moment, I was stupid for believing anything like ‘good luck’ would ever come into my life.

“You should head on back to Neo’s place.”

“Are you going out there?” Kouta’s brow slightly furrowed. “It shan’t end well for you.”

“Things could hardly get much worse.”

This was the second time I said that exact line to Kouta. The rate at which things had been getting worse was accelerating exponentially.

“Teeeenn! Niiiiiiine! Eeiiiight! Seeeevvennn!”

Miss Kokoromi began loudly counting down. It was like she was excitedly welcoming in the turn of the millennium. It was something I thought about a lot during my time abroad, but Miss Kokoromi had some crazy pipes. She really ought to dissect her own throat.

“Siiiiiiiix! Fiiiiiiiive! Foouuuuur! Threeeeee!”

“Kouta, if I’m not back in the next half-an-hour—”

“I understand.” Kouta nodded before I could finish. “Although, in that case, our contract would be void, so I shan’t guarantee anything. I wouldn’t be against making another contract with Miss Kunagisa, however. Still, for the time being, you have my word.”

“I see. The wonderful thing about giving your word is that it doesn't matter when you break it.”

“You say some outrageous things.”

With that, Kouta held her knife out to me and asked, “you know how to use it?”

“Yeah, I’ve used one before actually.”

“How consummate. With that, I bid you adieu.”

When I took the knife, Kouta quickly made her way up the staircase. Once I was sure I could no longer see her, I inserted the blade into the key-hole and jimmied it two or three times. Before long, I heard the door unlock.

I gripped the knob, pulled the door open, and stepped through.

“Twooo! Ooone!  Zerooo! Negative O—”

“Why’re you still counting?”

“Oh-ho?”

When Miss Kokoromi spotted me, she stopped shouting.

“—Wouldya look at that. You were really here after all. Well, I’ll be damned.”

“……” So this bastard really was bluffing. “Hello, Miss.”

“Why hello. …Say, that reminds me, the last time the two of us were alone like this was back in that hospital room, ain’t that right, kiddo?”

Miss Kokoromi adjusted the frame of her glasses before treating me to a mischievous smile. Mischievous might not be the right word; the word I was likely looking for was cruel. I got the distinct impression that this was the kind of expression a cat might make as it torments a mouse— that kind of smile.

It was probably an expression that only a prepubescent girl could get away with.

Like Kunagisa Tomo, for example.

“…Haha” Seemingly unable to hold it in anymore, Miss Kokoromi burst into laughter. “Hahaha! Hahahaha………hahaha! Fantastic, Kiddo! Simply, fantastic! You’re one fascinatin’ character, I tell ya what! If only ya were just a touch smarter, things woulda turned out much better for ya… that, or a touch stupider, I s’ppose.”

“Miss, I have a request.”

“Hmm?” Miss Kokoromi made a show of tilting her head. “…Look at you, being all honest. That’s twice now you've surprised me.”

“Can you keep the fact you saw me to yourself?”

“Sure thing,” she nodded readily. “Don’t go askin’ something so cold. We’re pals, ain’t we, kiddo?”

“…………”

I had no choice but to be cautious. Normally, this would be the moment when I could let down my guard. The moment where I’d let out a sigh of relief and give my earnest thanks. Even I can manage that much courtesy. I might even be moved by her warm words of affection. However, this was none other than the infamous Miss Miyoshi Kokoromi I was dealing with.

I wasn’t fool enough to think things would play out that way.

“One—”

Making no attempt at consideration towards how I was feeling, Kokoromi began almost monologuing to herself. She folded her arms as if deep in thought, occasionally glancing my way.

“…No, two. There's at least two.”

“……?”

“Three would be perfect… but that don’t seem like the case. If it were, ya wouldn’t be meandering around a place like this. Then again, I s’ppose too many would be a problem as well.”

“What are you talking about, Miss.”

“What’s that? Why, how many collaborators ya have in the facility, of course.” Miss Kokoromi brought her hands up and made the shape of a fox as if she were making shadow puppets. “Ya’d need at least one to spring ya from your cage. It sure ain’t Kasugai… so who is it, I wonder? But that alone wouldn’t cut it… that’s why there’s gotta be two.”

“…I’d like to compliment you on your perceptiveness, but, as usual, you’re dead wrong, Miss.” I put up a bold front. “I did everything on my own. I actually have superpowers.”

“First I’m hearing of it.”

“You’re the first person I’ve told, Miss. I assume you can keep that a secret, too?”

“Fine then. Since ya clearly don’t wanna talk about it, I won’t pry. For now, at least.”

With a swish of her lab coat, Miss Kokoromi turned her back to me and began walking. Looks like I hadn’t fooled her. Roughly five steps ahead of me, she stopped. “Come along then,” she said. “You’re here to pay your respects to Utsurigi, ain’tcha, Kiddo?”

“……”

“No need to be so cautious. It ain’t like we’re strangers, or nothin’”

“I’d be less cautious if we were…”

“As witty as ever, haha!”

Seemingly unbothered by my sarcastic response, she just kept on walking. That said, Miss Kokoromi is quite short which left her with a narrow stride, so even my trepidatious footsteps managed to keep adequate pace. Miss Kokoromi’s stature could give Kunagisa a run for her money, so compared to Suzunashi, she’d look less like a kid next to an adult, and more like a dwarf next to a giant. But this wasn’t the time to be thinking such things.

Miss Kokoromi stopped in front of a door marked with a plate that read ‘SEVENTH EXAMINATION ROOM’ in all-caps for some reason (although the writing was so messy that it was almost indecipherable. This plate was clearly either the result of a first-grade arts and crafts class, or Miss Kokoromi), and turned to face me. “By the way,” she said,

“What is genius in the first place?”

“……A difficult question. Let’s see, to answer that, we’d first need to think about what that word even means.”

"Who are ya? Descartes?” Miss Kokoromi answered with a philosophy-based quip. “Besides, there ain’t no such thing as a difficult question. Only difficult answers, don’tcha agree?”

“I’ve heard that saying a lot.”

“I bet ya have! Then again, that’s probably got to do with the law of large numbers. ‘Talent isn’t something you nurture, but something you’re born with’— that’s a quote from Fraulein Love, but don’tcha find it fitting? As Kunagisa Tomo’s lover, can’tcha see where she’s comin’ from?” Then Miss Kokoromi narrowed her eyes at me. “—Haha, so the girl you kept yapping about back in Houston was her, wasn’t it? Ah well, it’s not like you matter anyhow. So, what’s your answer?”

“I wouldn’t know.” Unable to understand why she was asking, I responded to Miss Kokoromi’s question with a resounding non-answer. “A genius is essentially just someone really smart or skilled, isn’t it? I think that’s probably good enough.”

“Probably?”

“If you’re not happy with my answer, then fine, ‘it is good enough’. I’m not a genius in the first place, so it’s not my place to try and define it.”

“Or so you think, but for geniuses— whether it be Kunagisa, the professor, Utsurigi, or whoever— genius is normal. To them, a definition ain’t worth squat.”

“What’re you even trying to say?”

“Nonsense, your favourite.” Turning the knob, Miss Kokoromi pushed open the door. “Now then, welcome to my castle.”

The room’s interior was dimly lit— scratch that, it was pitch black. There weren’t any windows, so not even a ray of light entered the room. Miss Kokoromi stepped inside without even turning on the lights. I had no idea where the light switch was, so I just followed after her, careful to mind my feet. The dim glow from out in the hall was of some help, but for some reason or other (perhaps the result of a simple loose hinge) the door swung shut on its own, plunging the room into complete darkness. Everything disappeared from view, even my own hands.

“Hang on— Miss? Miss? Where are you?”

No response. But I could still sense her. Not too far from where I was standing, I heard her stifled breathing. I didn’t know what she had planned, but— if this was the same Miss Kokoromi I knew, then it was certainly nothing good. It seemed like she truly had no intention of replying.

I tried inching forwards, relying solely on intuition. However, since my intuition was exceptionally dull when it came to anything except sensing ill-omens, I bumped into something before I even managed my third step. Based on its height, I guessed it was some kind of table, except, instead of being supported by table legs, it stood on some sort of stand. Which means this was likely some kind of operating table, or—. Something compelled me to feel around on top of the table; I brushed against something soft yet rigid. It had no elasticity; instead, it felt almost jelly-like. What on earth was this? This faint, tepid, warmth… Ah, I have a feeling I know exactly what this is.

It likely had nothing to do with my sudden realization, but at that exact moment the fluorescent light came on overhead. It seems Miss Kokoromi had thrown the switch. And so, almost exactly as I had predicted, right in front of me was a large dissection table, and enshrined on it– at the end of my outstretched fingers– was the naked body of Utsurigi Gaisuke. No, it was just laying on its back, so ‘enshrined’ was an odd choice of words, but now wasn’t the time to fuss over word choice.

“…………”

Utsurigi’s body was patched up to some extent; most likely Miss Kokoromi’s handiwork. The mutilated chest and stomach had been sutured up, and his slack jaw had been forcefully shut so you could no longer see the wound inside. Of course, there was no fixing his eyes or eyelids, so the hollow pits that they had been scooped out of unsettled me. Compared to his expressionless expression, even the stumps where his arms used to be were easier to look at.

Oh man. I couldn’t imagine this as the same easygoing Utsurigi that I met yesterday. There wasn’t a trace of him left.

“Like I thought, not even a yelp.” Before I knew it, Miss Kokoromi was right behind me. “How should I put it, as always, ya manage to be cute and repulsive at the same time.”

“And as always, you’ve got sick tastes, Miss.” I removed my hand from Utsurigi’s body and turned to face her. “What was the reason for all that?”

“There was no reason. It just was. Same with everythin’ else.”

“Don’t try and dodge the question. I’ve got no clue what you’re even saying.”

“It’s ‘A clockwork Orange’.”

“Now I’m even more lost.”

“It’s called an analogy, Kiddo.” Miss Kokoromi walked the perimeter of the dissection table until she stood directly in front of me, with Utsurigi’s body sitting in between us. “I guess it’s less of an analogy and more of a metaphor.”

“They’re the same thing aren’t they?”

“Hehe, the difference has to do with belief.” She said something utterly incomprehensible. “Essentially, it’s a matter of conviction. More importantly, it’s time for your extracurricular lesson. Let’s begin Miss Kokoromi’s Vivisection Crash Course. Now then, Kiddo, why don’tcha start by telling me your impression of this here corpse.”

“Hmm, let’s see, just going off what I can see, it’s just like I thought, he’s dead.”

“You fail.” Her evaluation was as strict as you would expect from an anatomy instructor. “How ‘bout I rephrase the question for the slower kids in the class? Whaddya reckon the cause o’ death was?”

“He bled to death, didn’t he? You said so yourself, right?”

“Nevertheless, that’s the wrong answer.” Miss Kokoromi said as she prodded Utsurigi’s cheek with her finger. “The cause o’ death was the destruction of his brain.”

“…The destruction of his brain? What do you mean? Like a cerebral contusion?”

“Wrong. A cerebral contusion is when external trauma results in significant injury to the brain. But think about it, he had scissors stabbed into his eyes, didn’t he?”

She said as she made a peace sign and stuck a finger into each of Utsurigi’s hollow eye sockets. Did respect for the dead or sympathy for the departed mean anything to this woman? I suppose it didn’t.

“They went pretty deep. If ya remember, they were buried to the handles. The blades woulda pierced straight through the cerebrum and lodged themselves in his thalamus.”

“Well yeah, I could tell the blades reached his brain just by looking at him, but does that mean… there’s a chance he was stabbed through the eyes, not after he was dead, but while he was still alive?”

“It ain’t just a chance. The very first wound inflicted woulda been the rupturing of his eyeballs and the destruction of his brain. The scissors were plunged into his grey matter and wrenched about, scrambling it. I reckon it took five to ten seconds.”

It hurt just thinking about it.

“His stomach being sliced open, his legs being mangled, and his arms getting lopped off were all done posthumously. Ya can tell by the body’s physiological reaction, can’tcha?”

“——You know human anatomy was never a strong subject for me,” I said, taking care not to look at Miss Kokoromi or Utsurigi. “Besides, examining a body that’s so horribly disfigured… is meaningless in every sense of the word.”

“Then why'd ya come?”

“I was looking for a flash of inspiration. I’m a backwards thinker after all. Or was I the electric chair type? I can’t remember.”

“I did say that, didn’t I? In that case, your good ol’ teacher will explain everything. I’ll stop pesterin’ ya with questions for now, and answer a few of yours.”

I couldn’t help but feel hesitant. What on earth was she scheming? What on earth was she after? The only thing I knew for certain was that she was definitely up to something, but either way, I couldn’t remain hesitant forever. Time felt like it had come to a halt in this artificially lit room, but every moment I spent here was another moment lost.

Three hours and ten minutes remained.

“——When was he killed?”

“At precisely one o’clock this morning?” she answered immediately.

“And there’s no chance you’re mistaken.”

“My instincts are never mistaken.”

She’s going off instinct?

“I’m just yankin’ your chain. Still, it shoulda been around one a.m. Right around when you met with Kasugai.”

In other words, Kasugai couldn’t be the culprit. The one who corroborated that was none other than myself. Kasugai, the only person to leave their research ward last night (no matter how briefly), establishing an alibi was not an especially welcome development.

“You’re telling the truth, right? You’re not just trying to mess with me?”

“Do I look like someone who’d do something like that?”

“Do you really want me to answer? Besides, Miss, even if you’re not just messing with me— there’s always the possibility you’re just saying what the professor ordered you to say.”

“The professor, huh? …You’re mighty suspicious, aren’tcha, kiddo? Oh well, I suppose it’s fine.” Miss Kokoromi acknowledged my doubts, but neither confirmed nor denied anything. “Either way, there ain’t anything strange ‘bout the time of death… The odd part comes next.”

“The odd part?”

“The stomach and legs were mutilated right after the brain was destroyed. That’s why there was such a garish amount of blood… but the arms.”

Thwack, she slapped one of the stumps. She did some unbelievable things.

“These arms were lopped off several hours after death. The crucifixion— in other words, the skewering of the throat and legs was done even after that.”

“…? But why?”

“Strange, ain’t it? There was no real reason for them to wait to cut his arms off and string him up; they coulda done it right after killin’ him. And yet, there’s a time lag between time o’ death and time o’ crucifixion. What I’m gettin’ at is our culprit hung around the scene of the crime for hours for no real reason. Why do you reckon that is?”

“‘Why?’”

How should I know? Besides, I didn’t even understand what the problem was? Sure, the time of death didn’t match the time his arms were chopped off, but was it necessary to attach such importance to a difference of a couple hours?

“Couldn’t it just be that it took too long to mutilate the rest of the body? I’m much more interested in the reason they cut his stomach open, chopped his arms off, and crucified him in the first place. Isn’t that a more important question than ‘when?’”

“There was no reason. It just was.” Miss Kokoromi repeated her earlier line. “If there was a reason, then we’d have to grapple with whether it was justified or not. Not that you could excuse any sin with the right reason. A sin committed for no good reason warrants a larger punishment, is all I’m sayin’. If you’re gonna fuss over that, then the real question is why they killed him at all.”

“The reason people kill each other, huh? …but I can’t imagine there being a reason to kill Utsurigi…”

“I’m sure I taught ya that sort of thing before. People kill out of simple self-interest or base impulses. I’m talkin’ about whether those feelings are justified.”

“Ah, you mean Thanatoast?”

“It’s Thanatos, ya dunce. What kind of toast would that even be?”

“It’s hard to remember foreign words, you know…”

If I were to give a rough explanation of the ‘Thanatos’ that Miss Kokoromi was talking about, it would be something like the shared instinct of all animals, not just humans, that says, ‘I want to experience death, but since I don’t want to die, I’ll kill someone else instead.’ (but that’s a really rough explanation) Although I don’t think that has anything to do with this case.

For example, the typical reason a killer might dismember a body is primarily as a means to feel control over their victim. That’s how it was for last month’s case. To hurt, mutilate, and disfigure a helpless subject to their heart’s content. There likely wasn’t a single situation where you could possibly exert more control over someone. And speaking for Utsurigi’s crucifixion, if the killer was the kind of person who desperately craved the limelight, then that might be a possible reason his body was maimed to such an extent.

“……Even if that were true, there’s still something off about it.”

“Oh yeah? What’s that?”

“Let’s forget about the mutilation. The arms too. We can even set aside the time lag for the time being. I won’t pretend to understand any of that, but there’s something I understand even less. The severed arms— where on earth did they take them?”

“—Well, I’ll be.”

Her uncharacteristic smile seemed to say, ‘well spotted.’

“That’s right. Utsurigi’s arms weren’t at the crime scene— and by ‘crime scene’ I’m talkin’ bout the whole entire Seventh Ward. Neither of ‘em. It ain’t the same as his eyes or stomach where they were just mutilated. They were taken. That’s the one thing that makes it hard to say ‘there was no reason. It just was.’”

“…………”

As I listened to her speak, I gazed at the stumps where Utsurigi’s arms used to be. The exposed flesh had already started to blacken. Miss Kokoromi must’ve treated the area; the blood had been washed away and the flesh cleaned, but there’s nothing that could be done to make the sight any less grotesque.

“Why did they take something heavy like his arms…?”

“Are ya open to a romantic interpretation?” Miss Kokoromi held up her index finger. “Utsurigi was a top-notch computer systems engineer. The culprit must’ve murdered him ‘cause they were jealous of his talents. Nothin’ motivates a criminal like jealousy, y’know? The desire to harm others comes from the fear of others surpassing ya… or maybe it’s a sense of inferiority over other’s convictions. Either way, jealousy is just the other side of envy. Our culprit admired Utsurigi; that’s why they snatched his arms out of respect. So they-”

“So they took his arms as a souvenir? He isn’t the Venus de Milo.” I cut Miss Kokoromi’s rambling short. “Take this a little seriously, Miss.”

“I ain’t the one who’s gotta take it seriously, that’d be you, kiddo. This ain’t got nothin’ to do with me.”

It was like I was speaking to a child, but she was right.

I had no choice but to do as I was told and give it some serious thought. The reason… the reason the killer felt the need to chop off the arms and carry them away…

“The first thing that comes to mind is some kind of fetish.”

“That’s hardly any different from what I said.”

She was right again.

I really was the one who needed to take this more seriously.

The theft of his arms could be explained in an endless number of ways— nearly endless, anyhow. If Kunagisa were here, she could likely go through them all, but to me, it was an impossible task. And as I’ve said over and over again, I just don’t have the time. Which means I had no choice but to accept a little arbitrary thinking. In other words, just like a mystery novel rich with heroic rationalism, I had to assume the arms were some sort of clue. If I presupposed the necessity of a reason for the arms being stolen— or at least not being left at the crime scene— then…

“Based on how he died— It must’ve been a cadaveric spasm.”

A cadaveric spasm— in other words, instantaneous rigor mortis. It primarily occurs in cases of an especially violent death. There’s a saying that goes: ‘a drowning man will clutch at straw,’ but this was a real-world example of that phenomenon. Moments before death, if accompanied by horrific violence or intense pain, the dead will grip onto whatever they’re holding with unbelievable strength. Because whatever physical limiters they once had are no longer functioning, their grip strength is often strong enough to warp the shape of a coin so long as the metal is soft enough.

The reason this is important is because, even after their deaths, the victim’s grip is ridiculously hard to wrench open. Even if you used a bench or some kind of bar, it would still be an extraordinarily difficult procedure to pry open even an otherwise-weak person’s fingers.

Take strangulation for example.

Let’s say a victim unwittingly grabs onto a button on their assailant’s jacket as they’re being strangled (In other words, as they met their violent end). Let’s say the button gets torn off, and winds up clenched in the victim’s fist. This would serve as unshakeable evidence. Because unlike typical rigor mortis, a cadaveric spasm can’t be staged. You can be, not just one-hundred percent, but two-hundred percent certain that whatever is clenched in the victim’s fist was there at the moment the crime occurred.

From the point of view of the investigators, this acts as invaluable concrete evidence, but for the perpetrator, it serves as an insufferably concrete obstacle. One they must avoid at all costs.

Even if that meant cutting the arms clean off, for example.

“There was a case like that before, wasn’t there… The ‘La Bansing Case’ or somethin’. I ain’t too sure.”

“I can’t remember the name either…but in that case, instead of going through all the trouble to open the hand, it was quicker to just dispose of it all together.”

“Then just cut the hand off at the wrist. There ain’t no need to cut it off at the shoulder.”

“It’s misdirection, isn't it? If they just cut off the hands it’d be too conspicuous. After all, the cause of death was having his brain obliterated by a blade jammed through his eyes. There’s hardly a more violent death out there. That more than meets the conditions for a cadaveric spasm. Who’s to say he didn’t snatch a button from someone’s lab coat…”

That would be motive enough to take his arms. Even if it had nothing to do with a cadaveric spasm, the arms might’ve provided some other vital clue. That’s why it was necessary for the culprit to remove them from the crime scene.

Unexpectedly, the whole eye-catching crucifixion and mutilation farce might’ve been done merely to obfuscate how bizarre the theft of his arms was, even if only a little. The best place to hide a tree is the forest, and the best place to hide a forest is the Amazon. Isn’t that all this is?

“I see. That bloody ritualistic message would also make sense thinkin’ like that. There ain’t no meaning, it’s just a bluff.《You just watch,『DEAD BLUE』!!》, was it? Honestly, it don’t make a lick of sense.”

“…………”

Huh? Could it be that Miss Kokoromi didn’t know that the Dead Blue in question was actually Kunagisa Tomo? I see, Utsurigi himself had claimed he only called her that when he was speaking to her directly, so I suppose it’s not too odd for her not to know. Even if the word Cluster had already become common parlance.

“Hold your horses, Kiddo,” Miss Kokoromi said, changing topics, “ya mentioned lab coats just now, didn’tcha? Does that mean what I think it does? Are ya suggesting the culprit who killed Utsurigi is a faculty member?”

“……I suppose I am.”

“Ya haven’t changed one bit. Listen ‘ere, Kiddo. Do you really think there’s no chance Kunagisa or Suzunashi coulda done it? ……Whoa now, stop glarin’ at me like that. Talk about scary. Miss Koko’s shakin’ in her boots.”

Miss Koko? Who’s that? I know no such person.

“Are you saying I’m soft on my friends?”

“Are ya sayin’ y’ain’t? After all the horrible things you’ve been through abroad, have ya still not learnt your lesson? Don’tcha know better by now, Kiddo?”

“It’s not that— it’s just that this is easier for me. The only reason I’m doing all this is to save Kunagisa, so doubting her is a non-starter.”

“It ain’t just a non-starter, it’d be the end. And it’s always easier to just end it, ain’t it?” Her voice dripped with sarcasm. “Hypothetically, what if Kunagisa is the culprit— what if the professor’s theory is spot on?— What wouldya do?”

“I don’t want to think about it.”

“There might come a time when ya have to.” Miss Kokoromi didn’t let up. “You might think such a vague relationship will last forever, but ya couldn’t be more wrong.”

“I’m truly touched by your concern, Miss. I guess you haven’t changed either.”

“Oh? What makes you say that?”

“You still run your mouth like you know the first thing about me.”

“That’s still miles better than a certain someone who clams up and pretends not to know the first damn thing about himself.”

Suddenly, Miss Kokoromi and I found ourselves glaring at each other. Invisible sparks flew over Utsurigi’s corpse sandwiched between us. The first one to break eye contact was me, although that likely goes without saying. I looked away and said in a small voice, “Sorry. I went too far. I’ll take your advice seriously. Even I don’t think Kunagisa and I can carry on like this forever.”

“Is that so? I s’ppose that’s just how ya are. Ya see failure coming, but don’t lift a finger to get out of the way.”

“It’s nothing as cool as that. There’s just something wrong with my brain— No, my heart.”

“Your heart, huh— Hehe, y’sure it ain’t got somethin’ to do with Magokoro?”

“………”

“I see. So that’s how it is. I don’t think ya need to feel that way, but what can ya do… Well then, I’m off. The professor wanted to see me. Feel free to stay as long as ya like. And don’t worry, I won’t snitch on ya. Bye-byee.”

Miss Kokoromi turned away, made her way around the dissection table, and went to walk by me. As she did, I took hold of one of the oversized sleeves of her lab coat, stopping her from leaving.

“What is it? Ya want somethin’?”

“……………”

“If ya don’t want anythin’, let go so I can have my cool exit.”

“Miss… What’re you after?” I said in a low voice without turning around, our backs still facing one another. “Why are you helping me? No… more importantly, why would you leave the ER3 System just to work in a facility like this?”

“Ya don’t trust me?”

“Honestly, no. I don’t trust you one bit,” I continued flatly. “There’s no reason for you to put yourself at risk by helping me, no reason to risk being ousted from the facility you left the ER3 System for— no reason at all.”

“Glad ya think so highly of me,” Miss Kokoromi let out a small laugh. “But don’t go ‘round thinkin’ people are so cold-blooded.”

“At the very least, I’ve always thought you were a pragmatist.”

“Is that right?” Once again, Miss Kokoromi laughed lightly. “That’s somewhat disappointing to hear. Hate to break it to ya, it’s simpler than you think. I’ve already lost my reason to stay here. It died along with Utsurigi Gaisuke.”

“…? What do you mean?”

“…Just that. You heard the professor, didn’tcha? With Utsurigi dead, it’s all over. He was spot on. And Miyoshi Kokoromi ain’t got time to stick around a place that’s already finished.”

“But the professor doesn’t seem like he’s ready to give up yet. He’ll start over again— or I guess it’s more like he plans to continue where he left off.”

“That’s right, using Kunagisa Tomo,” she said. “But I’m sure you’ve got thoughts about that too, don’tcha, kiddo? Don’tcha think it’s absurd? Don’tcha think it’s a desperate last resort? Don’tcha think it’s just a temporary solution? Sure, there ain’t no argument that Kunagisa’d make for a better sample than Utsurigi.”

“…………”

“But if he ain’t careful, the professor could wind up turning the Kunagisa Syndicate, his very own backers, into his enemies. It’s a stupid plan. I’ve no clue what he’s thinkin’. Perhaps he thinks he can bargain with the Kunagisa Syndicate, but they ain’t the kinda organization to let that sorta thing fly. Ain’t that right, kiddo. They ain’t the kind to take orders, just give them. The professor should know that already. He should know that better than anyone. Or maybe his memory’s finally gotten that bad… I ain’t nice enough to hang around while he hangs my ass out to dry. So you’re damn right, I’m a pragmatist.”

“So by helping me, you’re just hoping to curry some favour with Kunagisa Tomo.”

Miss Kokoromi didn’t reply. I took her silence as her answer and let go of her sleeve. Even then, she said nothing. Neither did I. No one said a word.

I heard the door creak open, followed by the sound of it closing a few moments later.

Then silence.

The only ones left in the examination room were me and Utsurigi’s corpse.

“……What a bunch of nonsense, huh, Utsurigi?”

I asked.

Surprisingly enough, there was no answer.

Kouta was sitting on the stairs.

I used the anti-lock blade to access the emergency stairwell in Miyoshi Kokoromi’s Third Ward, but when I swung the door open, I froze. It was ten seconds later when I finally managed to ask, “what are you doing here?”

“I’ve been waiting ages for a certain someone to arrive,” Kouta replied calmly. “‘Tis not consummate.”

“……Then your wait is over. But weren’t you supposed to head back to Neo’s ward?”

“Give it some thought. At present, Kasugai is paying Neo a visit. ‘Tis hardly a consummate time to return.”

Kouta stood up and dusted off the seat of her jacket. Then she stretched, making a show of cracking her neck.

Did she stay behind out of concern for me? I wondered, but I wasn’t sure. Who could say? It was surely possible she had, but it was equally likely that she hadn’t. I was uncertain. The odds were much the same as that coin we tossed earlier. I said nothing and returned the knife she had lent me.

“So, do you come bearing good news, my dear friend?”

“Somewhat,” I closed the door behind me as I answered. “I’ve made some progress, but that’s it. I’ve got even more information now, but I’m not any closer to piecing it together.”

“Excessive information will only get in the way… but so be it. If you would be so kind as to tell me what you learned.”

I didn’t have any particular reason to hide anything, so I told her everything I’d gathered from Utsurigi’s corpse as well as everything Miss Kokoromi taught me. Afterwards, I told Kouta all the details of our conversation. I have a poor memory, so my explanation wasn’t very cohesive, but it looked like Kouta understood everything without me having to repeat myself.

“…The reason his arms were severed, you say?”

“The only reasons I can think of to dismember a body are to make transport and disposal easier, some kind of grudge, or for fetishistic reasons. But if it was just about the arms, then I think it’s safe to assume there was some other reason for it.”

“…You shot down Miyoshi’s interpretation earlier, saying, ‘he isn’t the Venus de Milo.’ or what have you, but what did you mean by that?”

I struggled to wrap my head around Kouta’s question at first, so, unsure why she was asking, I answered, “I didn’t really mean anything. I was just talking about one of the many explanations for what happened to Venus' arms. Miss Kokoromi’s theory reminded me of it, so I brought it up. Simple.”

“My preferred interpretation is rather pedestrian, but I believe there were never any arms to begin with.”

“Huh. Is that important?”

“Oh, it isn’t. I’m just making conversation. It just goes to show that no matter the result, one is always left with a finished product. No matter the result— whatever that may be. Now then,” Kouta narrowed her eyes at me, “What shall we do next?”

“Next…” I thought for a second, “For now, let’s head to the roof. There’s no point sitting around.”

“As you command.”

With a swoosh of her coattails Kouta began climbing the stairs. I followed after her. Somewhere around the tenth step, “while we’re still on the subject,” Kouta prefaced before saying, “I still haven’t got your student-teacher relationship pinned down.”

“Pinned down? What’s that supposed to mean?”

“It means I’m not certain whether it’s a relationship founded on trust. This is just my perspective– that is, my own opinion– but, despite all you said earlier, you seemed assured of your safety. It’s as if, deep down, you had faith that your teacher would not only keep your meeting a secret from the professor, but actually lend a hand.”

“You’ve got the wrong idea, Kouta. I simply had no other option. There was always a chance that things would play out well for me, but make no mistake, I took one hell of a gamble.”

“That may be. Nonetheless, I can’t shake the illusion.”

“Illusion, huh… There’s a marked difference between trusting each other, and knowing each other’s true nature,” I replied bluntly. “There was no one abroad who I got along with worse.”

“No one abroad, you say? The implication being?”

“There’s a certain fortune teller here in Japan who I can’t stand even more… Compared to her, Miss Kokoromi almost seems cute. Either way, that’s just how it is. The connection between Miss Kokoromi and I is weaker than gravity on the moon.”

“Perhaps,” as if she were truly just making conversation, she readily conceded. “Now then, your time limit’s down to precisely three hours. How do you fancy your chances?”

“They’re not looking good. It’s like: ‘tune in next time to see how he gets himself out of this bind.’”

“What on earth are you saying?”

“Nonsense.”

Come to think of it, a long time ago, I read a book that had tune in next time written smack dab in the middle of the prologue. While I let my mind escape reality, Kouta and I arrived at the roof of the Third Ward. Kouta continued walking until she was standing in the centre of the roof. There, she raised her arms as if doing a banzai pose. Supposing she wasn’t trying to call down a UFO, she was most likely just stretching.

“Everything considered, this place still has a really nice view,” I found myself saying. “I wonder if it’s because of the ocean of cedar. It almost helps me forget what I have to do. I wonder if this is what people mean when they say the scenery steals their heart.”

“I don’t mean to spoil your poetry,” Kouta said plainly, “but ‘tis not cedar. ‘Tis primarily oak.”

“Huh? Really?”

“That, and chestnut. Also some pine. There are a fair few others mixed in as well, but no cedar.”

“Is that right? Wow… I thought all mountains had cedar.”

“You couldn’t be more wrong. Is your head alright? Well, talk of trees aside,” Kouta turned to face me, “do you know what I’m thinking right now, dear friend?”

“……No. Can’t say I do.” probably something to do with my lack of forestry knowledge. On second thought, probably not. “What is it?”

“I’m still a little astonished. With how quickly Miyoshi gave up, that is.”

“Ahh…” I nodded. “She did, didn’t she? Still, you can’t argue she was wrong, can you? She only acts in her own interest, so she was never going to stick around without a good reason.”

“Unlike Professor Kyouichirou, you mean?” Kouta said. “In your heart, he’s taken on quite the villainous role, hasn’t he? Although, who can blame you after how you’ve been treated. I suppose there’s no helping it. Decency is a luxury afforded only to the fortunate, after all.”

“What do you mean?”

“Only those with excess can start worrying about being good people. Heartwarming thought, ‘tis it not? And yet, we’re all merely scraping by,” she said cynically. “Of course, if one were a true genius like Kunagisa or Utsurigi, then they ought to be capable of kindness. There’s a saying that goes, were I Thomas Edison, it’s possible I, too, would be called the father of invention, or something to that effect. Someone with ten-billion yen, wouldn’t feel the pain of giving a billion away. Because when all is said and done, they would still be nine-billion yen richer.”

“Why are you covering for him? You’re the one who called this place a graveyard last night.”

“And? Grave robbing is one of the highest paying professions, don’t you know?” Kouta boasted casually. “Regardless, what’s most important is the ‘excess’.”

“Kunagisa aside— Utsurigi was plenty excessive, but he certainly wasn’t kind. If anything, it just made him excessively unpleasant.”

“Whether he showed kindness or not was a matter of his own discretion. How fortunate he was to have a choice. After all, wouldn’t it be tragic to lack such leeway and have the decision thrust upon you?”

“Not tragic. Just sad,” I replied indifferently before changing the subject. “Miss Kokoromi’s already decided to leave, but what about Neo? If things play out like Miss Kokoromi said, then there’s no real point in continuing to spy, is there? And… what about you? What’ll you do, Kouta?”

“You needn’t worry. Miyoshi, Neo, and I– our objectives are all separate, so we needn’t walk the same path. Besides, while Miyoshi may have been quick to give up— and you can even argue she was smart to do so— from my perspective, the professor’s proposal doesn’t seem too bad. His chances of success aren’t all that high, but you can’t say they’re especially low either. And supposing he does succeed, the merits— namely, Kunagisa Tomo— would be monumental. It’s a risk bearing a consummate reward.”

“It’s been a pain in the ass for us though,” naturally, my displeasure began seeping into my voice. “Every single one of them… they’re nothing but vultures. Using other people as specimens, as guinea pigs, as lab rats… honestly, are they even human?”

“They used to be. Before they became academics.”

Kouta’s cynical reply sent shivers through my entire body. When it came to being inhuman, this woman stood head and shoulders above the rest, didn’t she?

“Then again, when you said, ‘every single one of them,’ I’m sure you meant me as well. Still, that, too, is consummate. Now then. Shall we return to Neo’s place for the time being and revise our strategy? Perhaps Neo’s got his mits on some new information. Besides, ‘twould be wise to inquire about what the professor’s been up to.”

“………”

As Kouta spoke, I gazed off in the opposite direction of Neo’s Fifth Ward. In other words, towards the Second Ward. More specifically, I was trying to eyeball how wide the gap was between here and there. Seemingly catching on to what I was doing, Kouta asked, “what’s on your mind?” and twirled around to face me.

“I’m thinking about whether it would be possible to get to the Seventh Ward from here.”

“……I believe I told you ‘twas impossible.”

“But I’ve yet to hear the reason. Look, from what I can tell, the distance to the Second Ward is two metres. That’s about the same distance as the one between the Fifth and Fourth Wards… No, if anything, this one looks a bit shorter. Next, we’d go from the Second Ward to the Primary Ward… the central research ward where the professor is. I think I remember the gap between those two not being too wide either.”

“You’re awfully fixated on this, aren’t you…? Perhaps the obsessive one was you all along?” Kouta sounded somewhat exasperated. “‘Tis not consummate in the slightest.”

“Then tell me why. Why is it impossible?”

I didn’t have the right angle to gauge the distance between the Primary Ward and the Sixth Ward from here, nor the distance between the Sixth Ward and the all-important Seventh Ward. Was that the issue that Kouta was alluding to? I didn’t know. However, Kouta has spent far more time in this facility than I had. When it came to infiltration or breaking in, Kouta’s opinion held far more weight than mine. I knew that. And yet-

“I still can’t come up with any other way someone could break into the Seventh Ward while bypassing the security system.”

“If that’s all you can think of, then you’re better off not thinking at all,” Kouta said bluntly. “…You wouldn’t understand even if I explained it to you, so why not see it for yourself? For a backwards thinker, there’s no such thing as a waste of time, so ‘tis actually more wasteful to stand here and argue about it,”

Kouta said and began walking towards the Second Ward. Then, as casually as if hopping over one of the puddles, she found herself on the roof of the Second Ward. No matter how many times I assure myself it’s only two metres, her bravery despite the fact that a simple slip could cost her her life astonished me.

I followed after her, making my way to the Second Ward. Kouta moved quickly, reaching the opposite ledge of the roof in no time at all. Once there, she waited for me. I caught up, and when I looked, the gap between the Second and Primary wards was around three metres… No, not even. Compared to the gap between the Third and Fourth Wards, it may as well have been nothing.

With only a brief run-up, Kouta leapt to the Primary Ward. It was readily apparent that she was not giving it her all, as her light jump saw her safely on the roof of the other ward. As soon as she landed, she turned around and waited for me in silence. Given that this was already my fifth jump, I had naturally grown somewhat accustomed to it. That said, I hear it’s acrobats who’ve grown complacent who are in the most danger. I braced myself and jumped.

“…I guess this is some kind of helipad,” I muttered, standing at the edge of a giant circle (with a large ‘H’ drawn in the middle) painted on the roof of the Primary Ward. “This antenna’s pretty massive too… despite how remote we are, I guess this means we’re not entirely cut off from outside communication…”

“Changing your mind about asking for help from Kunagisa’s brother or that contractor you’re acquainted with?” Kouta prodded at me. “Go right ahead. I’m sure they’ll come to your rescue straight away.”

Kouta didn’t seem especially conscious of it, but the way she spoke– it almost sounded like she actually knew Nao and Aikawa. Despite my suspicions, I didn’t press the matter. In hindsight, I probably should have, but I’m neither clever enough nor psychic enough to regret things before they happened. “I don’t have to resort to that quite yet,” I dismissed her before looking eastward. Wards one through five had been arranged in a straight line, but likely due to being an architectural afterthought, the Sixth and Seventh Wards were built to the side. So when I turned, the Sixth Ward was directly ahead of me, with the Seventh Ward just beyond it.

Kouta gazed down at the rooftop as if she could peer straight though it. “What sort of scheme do you think Professor Kyouichirou is concocting at this very instant to implicate you… or rather, Miss Kunagisa as the culprit? Ha, even supposing we succeed at infiltrating the Seventh Ward, who’s to say we won’t run headfirst into someone already tampering with evidence?”

“We have no choice but to take that chance.”

“I suppose we don’t. We shall just have to trust Neo on that front. Even if putting trust in others isn’t your cup of tea.”

Kouta grinned inappropriately and began walking towards the Sixth Ward.

“I guess— wait, hang on?”

The roof of Sixth Ward didn’t have anything resembling an entrance. Right, according to Shito, the Sixth Ward was a power generator— what type was it again? A carbon generator? Silicone, maybe? Or was it nitrogen? I felt like it was one of those three, but then again, I wasn’t really listening so I can’t be too sure— and as such, there was no way in or out, let alone a line for hanging laundry. I suppose that was to be expected; however, looking across to the roof of the Seventh Ward, I couldn’t make out any doors either. On the eastern edge, there was a large water tank accompanied by a number of wide pipes, but aside from that, the roof was completely flat and empty.

“Is that what you meant, Kouta?” I asked, in a daze. “The Seventh ward never had a rooftop entrance to begin with—”

“It most certainly does,” Kouta replied immediately. “Can you not see it? How’s your eyesight?”

“I haven’t had it checked lately, but I haven’t noticed it getting any worse, so it’s probably still 20/20.”

“Then you should be able to see it. ‘Tis roughly three metres in front of the water tank. Do you see that round iron cover that resembles a manhole? ‘Tis more of an emergency exit than an entrance, but it should grant rooftop access.”

Exactly as Kouta said… once she pointed it out to me, I noticed the door (if I could even call it that). However, given the distance and the fact that the Sixth Ward still lay in between us, it was still barely visible. How powerful was Kouta’s eyesight for her to make out something like that? The glasses she wore must’ve just been for show after all.

“The reason we can’t use this path is something else entirely. Now then, shall we head to the Sixth Ward? You’ll understand once you get a closer look.”

Kouta said before leaping the gap between the Primary and Sixth Wards. The gap in question being roughly one and a half metres. It was so narrow that if we laid Kunagisa on her back with her arms outstretched, we could’ve used her as a bridge (as horrible as that was to imagine). I cleared the gap without even taking a running start. It was remarkably easy, but when I looked down, I felt a slight shiver run through me. You might be tempted to say, ‘well don’t look down then,’ but human psychology is a curious thing.

“Now. Do you finally understand,” before I’d even had a chance to catch up, Kouta called out to me from the far side of the Sixth Ward, “the reason why this route to Seventh Ward is impossible?”

“…………”

As I approached her, the meaning behind Kouta’s words grew more and more clear. By the time I made it halfway across the roof, I had no choice but to agree with her– no matter how much it pained me to.

“…what on earth?”

Without a doubt, this was… impossible.

The distance between the Sixth and Seventh Wards. Compared to the distances we’d already crossed— The two metres between the Fifth and Fourth Wards, the three and a half metres between the Fourth and Third Wards, the nearly two metres between the Third and Second Wards, the almost three metres between the Second and Primary Wards, and the metre and a half between the Primary and Sixth Wards— the difference was an order of magnitude. No, it wasn’t that great, but the gap was so distressingly large, that if you were to insist it was, I doubt anyone would correct you.

Five metres.

Five metres…

“Impossible, is it not?” Kouta repeated. “Now do you understand why I claimed this route was hopeless, dear friend?”

“I see…”

Five metres. Risking your life on a jump like this was beyond reckless. You wouldn’t be risking your life so much as throwing it away. I don’t know all that much about athletic records, but going off what Kouta said earlier, the world record’s eight metres and ninety-five centimetres. Let’s call it nine metres even. The gap between these two wards was a full four metres shorter. But just like when Kouta explained it to me the first time, I didn’t appreciate the comparison to the world record holders. I was Japanese, and not an especially well trained one at that. And while I may not be at Kunagisa’s level, I was most certainly the indoor type.

Five metres.

Surely, this was too much to ask of me.

“…Now then, no sense dawdling. Let’s return to Neo’s for the time being. Who’s to say there isn’t another route out there—?”

As I listened to Kouta’s empty placations— No, I wasn’t listening— I tormented myself over and over. I couldn’t shake the thought. ‘This was too much’. An unshakeable, immaculate impossibility.

“ ————————”

And yet,

For that very reason.

The crucified Utsurigi ‘Malignant Green’ Gaisuke. His arms severed, his eyes and brain devastated, his throat gouged out, dissected like a frog and gutted like a fish, and his shattered legs run through. That empty, inhuman, hollow room, stained an unsettling reddish-brown, and that bloody message— in the truest sense.

The research ward and its unflinching security system melded into one massive locked room. There was no record of anyone having entered. And apart from one exception, no record of anyone stepping foot outside. A crime only physically or logically possible to the security system’s former administrator, Kunagisa ‘Dead Blue’ Tomo, the leader and iron-fisted ruler of the TEAM responsible for rewriting Japan’s cyber law fifty-five times over. Her, and her alone.

The Mad Daemon Shadou Kyouichirou’s research facility.

It was absurd. This was no ordinary case. A crime so impossible, it left no room for argument. A murder so unusual, it defied explanation. A situation so anomalous, it was beyond reproach.

That’s why. That’s why.

The solution to this case had to be psycho logical. It had to be. It can’t just be the killer. I, too, had to be mad. That’s the logic here.

I breathed deep. Once. Twice. Three times.

“…Hold on. What are you planning, dear friend,” Kouta said suspiciously. “I suddenly had a terrible premonition.”

“It’s about to come true.”

I said, and from where I was standing—roughly ten metres away from the edge of the Seventh Ward— I took off. I had no room for error. None whatsoever. I couldn’t waste a single centimetre that was given to me. I thought nothing, I felt nothing, I even forgot I was still alive; every muscle was working at maximum capacity. My brain had long since ceased its function. Like a tin-man without a heart, it did as I commanded.

Not yet. Don’t jump yet. One more step.

“Wait—you idiot!”

For the first time since I’d met her, Kouta’s refined mannerisms gave way to a genuine outburst of emotion— the instant after her jeers washed over me, I planted my left foot. It felt like subatomic particles were coursing through me, like all my blood was gushing out, like my head was being bathed in liquid nitrogen. While I’ve never been showered with subatomic particles, bled out, or doused in liquid nitrogen, if I had, I imagine this is what it’d feel like.

In other words.

I was set free from everything.

Liberated from everything.

Unfettered.

This is dying.

This is what it means to die.

To fade away.

To disappear.

To end.

Death.

With this. I can die. I will die. I have died. I am dying. I was dying. I had been dying. I will be dying. I will have died. I’m dead.

“And that’s why—”

As my life flashed before my eyes, I was suddenly reminded of something someone once told me.

“You should just die.”

Yeah.

You’re right.

“Kusanagi? Kuginasa? What was it again?”

“I’d be fine with a pig, or a cow, or even a monkey. Hell, I’d settle for a worm. Just so long as I never run into Kunagisa Tomo…”

I’d probably only lost consciousness for a moment— less time than it would take you to blink. I was lying on the bare concrete roof of the Seventh Ward. I suppose it’s more accurate to say I was splayed out. I’d likely fumbled the landing. My legs hurt a little. However, that was clearly just due to the impact. If so, then the instant I landed, out of relief— or perhaps despondency— my senses must’ve briefly abandoned me. It seems I had unconsciously braced myself, so none of my injuries were especially injurious. Compared to the beating I took from Suzunashi and Miss Kokoromi this morning, it may as well have been just some minor bruising.

“Good grief— I must have done something terrible in a past life…”

I had survived.

I made the jump.

As I came to terms with that fact, I slowly picked myself up. At least I tried to.

“——I am beyond exasperated with you right now.”

A voice came from right beside me, causing me to abandon the attempt halfway through. There, with her denim coat flapping in the breeze, stood Ishimaru Kouta, glaring down at me.

“……Huh? Wait, wha-…”

I turned my head in the direction I had just come from, in other words, towards the Sixth Ward. Kouta wasn’t there. That meant, supposing I hadn’t failed the jump after all and this was all some sort of hallucination as I teetered between life and death, Kouta had successfully made the jump as well. While the former didn’t seem out of the realm of possibility (better odds than a coin toss at least), the pain I felt surging through my body was undoubtedly real. That said, phantom pain is a real phenomenon. Since I couldn’t be sure, I figured I’d ask.

“I’m alive, right?”

“You’re not dead, I’ll grant you that much,” Kouta replied coldly, “but I wouldn’t call anyone who would senselessly rush to their own death truly alive.”

“I see…”

This time I succeeded in picking myself up, and I rose to my feet. My muscles, bones, and sinew all appeared to be in working order. I did something resembling stretches before turning to Kouta and saying, “So you made the jump too, huh?” Kouta didn’t answer; she just let out a huge sigh.

“I may have made a mistake in choosing you as my compatriot,” she said. “I never expected I’d be party to such recklessness. This is not consummate. Not consummate in the slightest.”

In other words, the researchers were no longer above suspicion. By moving from rooftop to rooftop, I had proven with my very body that the researchers could've infiltrated the Seventh Ward without ever needing to bother with what was previously thought to be the only entrance. That way, the security wouldn’t have logged their comings and goings from their own wards, let alone the Seventh Ward.

Of course, all I’d done is prove that anyone could be the culprit; I still had no clue who it might be. At the very least, there was no longer any reason—any good reason, that is— for all suspicion to rest on Kunagisa. None at all.

“You don’t even stop to consider the consequences of your actions, do you?” Kouta’s voice was still as cold as ever.
