As expected of something belonging to Humanity’s Strongest Contractor, despite causing so much destruction, the blade wasn’t so much as nicked. It might be easier than I thought-

To tear open my own throat.

I looked at Kunagisa.

She looked like she was about to cry. Clutching the bars, she looked like she was on the verge of tears. Except, no tears came. She wore a sorrowful expression as if she were trying to laugh and cry at the same time. That’s right. Just as I couldn’t laugh, she couldn’t cry. Just like me, she couldn’t cry. She didn’t know how to be sad. That’s what resulted in such an ugly expression. What a damn shame. I had hoped the last thing I saw would be Kunagisa’s innocent, pure smile.

Ahh, then again,

That would be,

Asking for the moon, wouldn’t it?

I noticed my left arm felt heavy.

The black dog- The black dog whose lifeblood had already seeped out- still had its jaws clamped tight around my arm. It reminded me of Utsurigi. It reminded me of his corpse. The scissors that were plunged through his eyes, destroying his brain, his throat and chest, his mutilated stomach, his skewered legs, and his severed arms. It seemed, unconsciously, I had taken a page from the culprit’s playbook. What an awful joke. Perhaps I really was the culprit after all.

Not like it mattered anymore. What actually happened was no longer the issue. All that mattered was what was perceived to have happened. That’s all. The footsteps drew closer. As they did, my vision grew hazy, so I couldn’t tell how far away they were. One thing's for sure: my time was well-and-truly up. I brought my right hand, still holding the knife, to the dog's mouth. It was somewhat difficult to move like this. And besides, it felt cruel to leave this thing hanging on. How pitiful, let’s cut you loose. Odd, it must’ve been snagged or something, because I couldn’t pry it off. No this wasn’t about it being snagged or stuck or anything. It was rock solid. That’s right, a so-called cadaveric spasm. The phenomenon where, after meeting a violent end, the body stiffens. I’d talked about it with Miss Kokoromi only a couple hours ago, but I never thought I’d get to see it with my own two eyes.

“—huh—?”

Just as I was about to use the blade to start carving away at the dog's mouth, I stiffened as well. I completely froze.

A— Cadaveric Spasm? Did I say that?

“—You bastard! What are you doing!?”

Shito’s voice echoed through the basement. However, his words meant nothing to me. Frozen as I was, nothing meant anything at all. My eardrums didn’t so much as oscillate. Wait a second. Think. Think! Calm down. No, don’t. Get fired up. I’m right there. All I need to do is grasp it. Just grasp it. A little more. Reach. Reach a little further.

Are you telling me… that’s how it was?

I didn’t even notice that I’d let go of the knife as it clattered to the ground.

Utsurigi Gaisuke. Suppose- suppose he’s the kind of man I thought he was. Given yesterday’s conversation and all. Malignant Green. The Bacteria. Cluster. Cracker. The fact that a man who would never surrender himself to death was murdered. For Kunagisa’s sake. For Kunagisa’s sake that man did anything Professor Kyouichirou asked of him. The former comrade of Kunagisa Tomo.

His crucifixion.

Suppose that was just the impetus.

Not an illusion, but an impetus.

“Hey, asshole! Are you even listening!?”

Thump, somebody shoved me. It was probably Shito. I had only made it halfway up before my body became intimately familiar with the ground again. It hurt. My sense of pain was returning. My nerves, springing back to life. My body hurt all over. Especially my arm. Naturally. It felt like half my flesh had been gouged out. But I couldn’t complain. Not when I had taken my opponent's life.

Only now did I consider how wrong I was.

But it wasn’t wrong, was it?

You weren’t wrong.

Even though you're not wrong, you still died.

Even though you’re not wrong.

Even though you’re not wrong.

“Oi, Kasugai— what the hell—” “Ahh— I told him but—” “Kiddo, what in tarnation–          — hey, kiddo—” “            hang on——” “——Explain yourself, bastard–      –” “…dog…” “      —       ” “     blood—fangs       ” “      first         aid         ” “

I spoke quietly,

“For the first time since I was born, I actually feel like praising myself. Sure, I know it’s delusion talking- I know that- but I couldn’t care less anymore. So please, even if only a little, let me bask in this feeling just a little while longer–”

But even that was out of reach. They couldn’t even allow me that much. I slowly began to lose consciousness. This time, out of relief. Only, I thought I might never wake up.

I might never wake up…?

Well, I guess that’s fine too.

I’m just- so happy right now.

“………………”

The last thing my fading sight glimpsed was Kunagisa Tomo. Everything was hazy, so I couldn’t make anything out, but my vision was blue.

Pure,

Clear,

Beautiful,

And comfortable.

How — blue.

“………………”

Can I say something selfish?

I love you.

Psycho Logical (Part Two)

2

Let me recount an old tale.

Once upon a time, there was a lone boy– utterly hopeless and beyond saving. A boy who spewed nonsense just to go on living, relying on nothing but his horribly twisted personality and hideously fractured set of values.

Once upon a time, there was a lone girl– utterly hopeless and beyond saving. A girl who smiled innocently just to go on living, relying on nothing but her horribly straight-forward personality and hideously right set of values.

Normally, that’s where the tale would end. The boy would live out his short, relatively miserable, relatively tragic life, and the girl would live out her short, relatively happy, relatively comfortable life. The world the boy lived in and the world the girl lived in were entirely separate, after all.

Only, against all reason, the boy met the girl, and the girl met the boy. In the end, how did it happen? Who made it so? By whose whim did these two meet? Whose interest? It would be far too cruel to the two of them to chalk it up to mere coincidence, fate, or miracle.

Many people died.

Lots of other things died as well.

The boy died a lot.

The girl died a lot as well.

The boy killed a lot.

The girl killed no one.

And so, the boy, unable to bear the weight of sin, unable to bear the weight of punishment, fled on his own.

Leaving the girl behind, he fled on his own.

“—just a commonplace tale…”

I made it sound like a tragedy where I was the only victim.

Like I carried the weight of the world’s sadness on my shoulders.

Like I had sole rights to all the world’s misfortune.

Always the poor, pitiable victim.

Even though I was the wrongdoer. Even though I was the wrongdoer. Even though I was the wrongdoer.

Even though I wasn’t pitiable at all.

“There’s people like me everywhere…”

Alone, I mumbled to myself.

My left arm, wrapped and swaddled in a needlessly large bandage. Although, maybe it wasn’t so needless after all. If anything, Miss Kokoromi had said this was merely a stopgap measure. Even though the dog’s fangs never did end up reaching my bone, because of its fearsome bite strength, it seemed like the radius in my left arm had experienced an avulsion fracture. Of course, that’s not where my list of injuries ends. Given how many times I tumbled down that stairwell, I suppose this should come as no surprise, but apparently my body was injured all over. ‘Apparently,’ makes it sound like I am talking about someone else, but in truth, I hadn’t really noticed. My sense of pain had mostly returned, but since Miss Kokoromi had loaded me up with so many pain killers, my nerves were numb all over again.

“Still, wounds like this would normally have ya writhin’ in pain,”

Miss Kokoromi said. And if a renowned anatomy professor thought so, then who was I to argue? But if that were true, then maybe something was wrong with my body after all. Honestly, it was to the point where I was tempted to ask Miss Kokoromi to crack me open and take a look.

Those were the kinds of thoughts I had as I stood alone on the roof of Neo’s research ward— the Fifth Ward.

Even still, it was all too nonsensical. What on earth happens now? You could claim this farce of an ending was predictable; you could also claim the opposite. And by farce, I mean everything that led up to this point— all the developments that I’d brought about in my half-day in the leading role.

Which is to say, the very instant I understood everything— everything in its entirety— the farce had come to a close. There was no need for a curtain call. There was no need to lower the curtains in the first place. Everything had ended in that very moment.

If so, this scene that was about to play out– what would you even call it?

“If anything, this is more like a footnote…”

No, that’s not it-

If anything, this was foreshadowing. This was foreshadowing the start of something- something big. An inevitable rite of passage. Thinking of it that way, even a nonsensical scene like this had some meaning to it, or so I came to believe. That said, meaning or not, I had no intention of complaining either way.

Now then, here we go.

Time for the Nonsense User’s once-in-a-lifetime puppet show.

First, the two metres between the Fifth and Fourth Wards. I had long since learned that such a jump was child’s play. With only a slight run-up, I cleared the gap. The impact on my legs was noticeable, but not enough to worry about. Fortunately, the painkillers still seemed to be working.

The Fourth Ward. The place Kunagisa, Suzunashi, and I were confined. All-in-all, I couldn’t help feeling like we’d done Suzunashi wrong. Something like this happening to Kunagisa and I was almost a forgone conclusion, but she truly had nothing to do with this. It wasn’t fair to drag her into it like this. Suzunashi wasn’t as forgiving as Miiko, so in all likelihood, I was in for a lecture once all of this was over. Well, whatever. It’s not like I hated being lectured. Especially when it was by Suzunashi.

Next, the leap from the Fourth Ward to the Third. This one was three and a half metres so I had to be careful. Conversely, this was the kind of jump anyone could manage so long as they were careful.

The Third Ward. Miss Miyoshi Kokoromi’s turf. I couldn’t tell you how she felt about it, but I can assure you, honestly and truly, that being reunited with her was something I never wished for. Not because I hated her. I think. I just didn’t want to see her. Honestly, never again. Still, had she never been here… Perhaps our reunion had been worth something after all.

Continuing from the Third Ward to the Second. Not even two metres. Much like the distance between the Fifth and Fourth Wards, this one was a cakewalk.

The Second Ward was— Koutari’s Ward. Koutari Hinayoshi. I thought back on all he did. And on the conversation between him and the ‘scoundrel’, Neo that we heard over the transceiver. ‘Utsurigi’s death was a suicide.’

“Even for a suicide, it’s rare to see one that’s so suicidal…”

I muttered, but I didn’t really buy it. Maybe it was, maybe it wasn’t. You’d be right either way. You’d be wrong either way. In the end, that too, was all a matter of perception.

From the Second Ward to the Primary Ward was a little under three metres.

What came to mind next was Hime. My ‘self-proclaimed’ disciple, who I’d left in charge of things once I was gone.

If it was Hime, she’d certainly understand what I was going through. That girl had faintly reminded me of Tomo, but inside, she was far more similar to me. Our chance meeting last month had led to her just recently moving into the first floor of the same antique apartment where I lived. She enlisted me as her in-home tutor, but progress was slow going. It turns out teaching someone who hates learning was no easy task. And yet, that’s what I was about to do. What I had to do for Professor Shadou Kyouichirou, I thought as I stood on the roof of the professor’s presiding Primary Ward.

I turned to face the Sixth Ward. One and a half metres. This was even less than child’s play.

Once I’d made my way over, I could see across to the Seventh Ward’s rooftop. There, I could make out the shapes of several figures. They were both the audience, and the players in my puppet show. Put another way, they were the subjects I aimed to tame with my nonsense. Supposing that was even possible. As I thought about it, I was reminded of the woman in the denim coat. If we’re counting all the people ‘I would have failed without’ she would, without a doubt, wear the crown, even though it had ultimately ended with us falling out. That was my responsibility and my responsibility alone. As such, it was likely my responsibility to do what little I could to pay her back.

On the subject of the woman known as ‘Ishimaru Kouta’, I decided to feign complete ignorance. Since Shito and Misachi had seen her, there was no way to conceal her presence at the facility entirely, but if I confessed to being associated with her, that would also necessitate confessing everything about Neo as well. Realizing how bad that would be, I luckily had an out by making it seem like ‘I had freed myself from the cage using the lockpicking knife’ and ‘got around the facility by wandering around on the rooftops.’ Of course, that explanation was rather clumsy, but since they were so off-put by the presence of an intruder, they seemed to buy the story wholesale, inconsistencies and all.

“Even for someone who enjoys inconsistency as much as I do, this is pushing it, isn’t it—?” I muttered self-deprecatingly. “—No, in this case, it’s more inconvenience than inconsistency.”

From the Sixth Ward to the Seventh was five metres. However, factoring in the Seventh Ward’s height, you’d be better off thinking of it as four and a half.

After talking to Kunagisa, it seems that the national average for high school boys’ long jump was a similar distance. Knowing that, I felt a little more at ease about it. Say what you will about my lack of exercise lately, but I don’t recall letting my body deteriorate to the point where I’d ever lose to a seventeen-year-old. Now, just because I don’t recall it happening doesn’t mean it didn’t happen, but regardless, I’d made the jump once already. I may have completely lost myself in the moment, but there’s no denying that I made the jump. No matter how you look at it, having already succeeded once was certainly encouraging. Out of caution, I took a generous approach.

Success in long jump wasn’t solely the result of good leg strength, Kunagisa had said. The momentum from my run-up would become the force required to propel me through the air. Apparently, it all came down to technique. The technique in question involved reaching top speed halfway through your approach before slowly transitioning your centre of gravity to your upper half— or at least that’s what Kunagisa’s long-jump lecture taught me, but even if you could conceptualize it in your head, it was hard to put into practice. To someone experienced, they would view it as a plain old jump, but there was no way an amateur like me would be able to replicate it quite so simply. And so, I decided to go with my version of a plain old jump as well.

I took off running— then planted a foot.

My body- floated.

A slight commotion could be heard. Someone must have cried out. Others were silent. I had plenty of time to consider such trivial things. The time I spent in the air seemed to stretch on and on. They often say, when people feel like their life is in danger, they see the world in slow motion; at that moment, I was likely experiencing exactly that. Either that, or I simply hadn’t jumped far enough and was plummeting head-over-heels towards the ground below. Either was fine by me, although it really shouldn’t have been.

Finally, and perhaps fortunately, I landed on the roof of the Seventh Ward. To be precise, I didn’t so much as land as clumsily tumble over myself. My injured left arm took the brunt of the collision with the roof’s surface, and while I didn’t lose consciousness, I did bang my head a little and spent a short while writhing there in pain. I had made a horrifically uncool entrance.

“What in the Sam Hill are ya doin’, Kiddo?” Miss Kokoromi sounded utterly amazed as she made her way to my side. “Y’alright? What’re ya thinkin’, landin’ on your bad side like that?”

“I’m fine— more importantly,”

I said, taking Miss Kokoromi’s hand as she helped me up. Propping myself up on her shoulder, I turned to face everyone else. The professor, Shadou Kyouichirou. The secretary, Uze Misachi. The assistant, Ougaki Shito. The researchers, Neo Furuara, Koutari Hinayoshi, and Kasugai Kasuga. And, a little bit off to the side, Suzunashi Neon– and Kunagisa Tomo. Nine people all together- ten, if you include me- were gathered on the roof of the Seventh Ward. Naturally, the one who had gathered them here was none other than myself.

“—Well, as I’m sure you saw for yourself,” I said as I stood up straight, spreading my arms wide in a grand gesture as if surveying the whole group. I had largely done so to give the appearance that I was unharmed. “By sticking to the rooftops like this, it’s possible to access the Seventh Ward from any of the others. Are we all following?”

“–Hmph,” I shouldn’t need to tell you that the interjection came from Professor Kyouichirou. He looked and sounded annoyed as he scowled at me. “Preposterous. How utterly preposterous, you whelp.”

“A whelp, am I? Harsh,” I took the insult in stride; I had to do whatever I could to bypass my emotional circuits, “but if we don’t acknowledge reality, then we can’t move on, professor.”

“Do you really think I’d fall for a trick that would barely work on children— No, that’s being too generous, even children would see through it. From where I’m standing, it’s blindingly obvious. The Seventh Ward was built ever-so-slightly shorter than the Sixth. You may have proved it possible to leap from there to here, but you’ve done nothing to prove the opposite.”

Leave it to the professor. Unlike me, he noticed the difference immediately. It would be easiest if I could wrap this up with a Q.E.D. right now, but it didn’t look like things were going to be that convenient.

“Or do you intend to demonstrate that jump right now?”

“No, no… That would be impossible. You're correct.”

‘I told you so,’ the professor’s sneer said.

“What a complete waste of time. To think, I humoured you thus far- I must have gone soft.”

Soft— you’re completely right.

Even if it was just the result of underestimating his opponent and the misplaced sense of ease that came with it, Shadou Kyouichirou’s softness was undeniable. To let me— his enemy— move about freely like this? If that’s not soft, I don’t know what is. So, forgive me if I take full advantage of it.

“Now, now, I wouldn’t be so quick to jump to conclusions,” I said. “Still— you have a point, professor. It’s not possible to return to the Sixth Ward from the Seventh. Not unless one of us has world-class leg strength, that is. However, I believe what I did does prove something. Namely, even if you can’t return, there is a route into the Seventh Ward.”

“And what of it?” the professor interrupted. “What use is there in a one-way-trip? It goes without saying, but to even exit the building, one would have to bypass numerous locks. And even supposing they did, it would have left behind a log. We have a log for every entrance and exit. And yet, there’s nothing of the sort.”

“There isn’t, is there. I suppose you’re right,” I agreed disinterestedly. “The logs and the lock acts as a kind of double-bind. So, let’s go with that for now.”

“Oh? What are you implying? Are you suggesting that I, Shadou Kyouichirou, tampered with the logs? That I deleted them?”

“I’m suggesting nothing of the sort. Besides, you wouldn’t have been able to, would you? While Kunagisa could’ve pulled it off, you couldn’t. Right? Even though Kunagisa would’ve found it easy. You said as much yourself, professor.”

That line may have been a little cruel, because the professor’s face hardened into an intense glare. However, rather than anger, his expression was closer to one of frustration over not being able to predict what cards I would play next.

“You, wretch—”

“What’s more—” I spoke over him, “It’s still too early to conclude they ‘couldn’t return’. After all, there’s no rule that says we have to make the jump relying on physical strength alone. If they used a rope, for example, the route to the Sixth Ward would be more than possible.”

“It most certainly would not. If you’re implying they had a rope that could bear their whole weight, then where is it?”

“Admittedly, you wouldn’t find any at the facility… but when I say rope, it’s more of a metaphor. For instance, they could’ve tied their clothes together to use as a rope, or twisted a handful of computer cables together.”

“And you think that would bear someone’s weight?”

“No,” I said, taking my eyes off the professor— and turning to face Koutari. “However, if we’re talking about a candidate for a rope that could bear someone’s weight– as the professor so elegantly put it– then how about human hair?”

All at once, everyone’s gaze landed on Koutari. However, Koutari just adjusted his sunglasses and remained silent. He was as untalkative as ever. Somewhat taken aback by his excessive commitment to silence, I continued.

“Koutari’s hair was just long enough. If you were to tie it together, you could create a bridge between here and the Sixth Ward— don’t you agree? What do you think, Suzunashi?”

“…Hm?” She seemed somewhat surprised. “You’re asking me? Then, sure… hair is certainly strong enough. Although that depends on the person, I guess. Speaking of, I’ve seen Miiko choke someone out with that samurai ponytail of hers.”

“Exactly. Although, that’s definitely a situation I’m glad not to have been witness to… According to records, a woman once did an experiment to find out how much weight her hair could withstand if she gathered it all together. Apparently, it held up to one tonne before tearing.” This was also second-hand information I got from Kunagisa. “That’s an extreme case, not the norm, but regardless, using a rope made of human hair would be entirely feasible. Although…”

This time I set my sights on Kasugai. The rest followed suit.

“If they weren’t a human, but rather an animal, jumping this gap may have been possible. Just look at this…” I said, raising my bandage-wrapped arm for everyone to see. “You can’t honestly claim a massive dog, like the one that nearly killed me, wouldn’t at least have a chance of being able to jump a gap like this, can you, Kasugai?”

“Who knows? I’ve never tried but I suppose it might be possible,” Kasugai tilted her head as she replied. “If that were true would that make me your suspect?”

“No, I wouldn’t go that far quite yet. All I’m trying to say is that the Seventh Ward was never a locked room– it was never completely closed off. Those were just some specific examples. If so, what now? At the very least, there’s no more reason for Kunagisa— no, all three of us, to be the only ones who are—”

“That’s the oldest trick in the book,” none of what I’d said so far seemed to surprise him as he interrupted derisively. “You fabricate some miraculous-sounding hypothesis, and convince people the shock they feel is merely the astonishment of finally understanding the truth. All that showboating by jumping to the Seventh Ward was part of it, was it not? This is a typical con-artist’s tactic. Well, I’m not biting, whelp.”

“Fabricated— you say?”

“Exactly. It’s obvious if you try thinking about it. Both of your hypotheses fall apart with only a little thought. Koutari’s hair may have been long, but it was still only a metre at most. Even if you divided it up to make a rope while still leaving it strong enough to hold someone, the limit would only be around four metres. That doesn’t quite cut it. And your animal-culprit theory is even more laughable. Care to enlighten us on how a dog would be capable of butchering someone, crucifying them to the wall, then writing a message in the victim’s blood?”

“Well then— what if someone was riding on the dog’s back?”

“I don’t think that would be possible.” Kasugai took my joke seriously. Maybe she was kinder than I thought. “It couldn’t jump that far while carrying someone else.”

“…Thank you for telling me,” I bowed my head. “I’ll take that into consideration.”

“So? What’s next, whelp? Don’t tell me you’re out of cards already.”

“In that case— how about something like this? Let’s try and understand the reason why the killer found it necessary to mutilate Utsurigi Gaisuke so savagely. Why did they carve open his stomach? What if it was so they could tear out his organs?”

I said, making a series of theatric gestures for those present. I was almost chewing the scenery as bad as Neo, but then again, you can never go too far with these kinds of things.

“Tear out his organs—?” Miss Kokoromi asked doubtfully. “What are ya goin’ on about, Kiddo?”

“The human digestive tract is like one long tube, is it not? One long tube that stretches from the esophagus to the rectum. What’s more, being made of flesh, this tube is suitably elastic– and that elasticity gives it considerable strength. Suppose, instead of a rope, the killer used—”

“Huh? Hold your horses,” Miss Kokoromi cut me short. “Utsurigi’s organs were all accounted for. I dissected his stomach and intestines m’self.”

“Precisely. This was all just another theory.” I said, raising my hands. “Using intestines as a rope isn’t all that practical, let alone possible… It was a bad joke, okay? What you would call lip service. Still, trying to understand why the killer tore up his body isn’t a bad idea on its own. I have no intention of having you all stand here listening to a lecture on criminal psychology from a whelp like me, but… don’t you think there’s something to the fact that Utsurigi’s murder seemed almost obsessive?”

“Something to it?” Professor Kyouichirou sounded a little irritated. “What’s with you and never getting to the point? You’re just beating around the bush. Do you have something to say? If so, then be a man and spit it out already.”

“Be a man? Naturally, I can’t say I’m all too offended, but…” I languidly shrugged my shoulders. Beating around the bush, huh? Unfortunately, there were topics I had to avoid, so there was no helping it. “Come to think of it, I can’t say the professor’s hypothesis is all that manly either. The whole ‘it wouldn’t have been impossible for Kunagisa’ thing… it’s a bit of a stretch. And even if she could have done it, that’s not reason enough to conclude that you— the lot of you— couldn’t have done it as well. All you’ve done is insist it can’t be done.”

“…And that’s your solution?”

“No, that was just me nitpicking. No deeper meaning than that. Not yet, at least.”

My constant proposal of half-assed theories only to immediately retract them caused the professor to gaze at me with a look of mild bewilderment, but he held his tongue. Ultimately, that was my true goal all along. I sought to hide my true intent behind a smokescreen until the very last second. To muster as much false bravado as I could and utterly baffle the professor– as well as everyone else. To confuse them. To disorient them. To ensure we didn’t stand on equal footing.

“Miss,” I called out to Miss Kokoromi, “why don’t you take this opportunity to share the results of Utsurigi’s autopsy?”

“Hm? Ah- let’s see– The time o’ death was around one in the mornin’. Cause o’ death was the scissors that were jabbed through his eyes and into his brain. The whole business with his stomach came later. The arms getting lopped off took place after that, and the crucifixion was done last. That’s pretty much the short of it.”

It was information I’d already heard back in the Third Ward. However, that had to remain a secret. Miss Kokoromi understood and gave an impromptu explanation, not for my sake, but for the sake of everyone else. It was never my intention, nor was it necessarily true, but it somehow felt like Miss Kokoromi and I had wound up accomplices in all this. And that relationship, too, likely had nothing to do with trust.

“If y’ask me, the part I’m most curious about is the time lag before chopping off his arms. They were severed three or four hours after death. It don’t take nearly that long to do the deed, so why the hold up—?”

“Alright, that’s more than enough, Miyoshi,” the professor chided, “I don’t know what kind of relationship you two had, but I won’t have you taking his side.”

“I ain’t,” she grinned sardonically, “but have it your way. I won’t speak out of turn. Now then, havin’ heard Utsurigi’s autopsy report, whatcha fixin’ on doing with it, kiddo?”

“I’m fixin’ to do whatever I can— Speaking of, wouldn’t mangling a body that badly and crucifying it take a considerable amount of strength?”

“Are you trying to suggest that Lady Kunagisa’s scrawny arms exonerate her?” The one to answer my question was professor Kyouichirou, possibly in an attempt to keep Miss Kokoromi from saying anything further. “Hah. I’ve had enough of you splitting hairs. There’s no need for Lady Kunagisa to have carried out the act herself. So long as she could bypass the door, then anyone could have done it. Like you for example.”

“Exactly. I don’t intend to fight you on that,” I didn’t fall for his bait. Earlier—this morning, when I let him provoke me and lost my temper– that was my first big mistake. I wouldn’t be making it again. Not so long as I could help it. “Still, the question why Utsurigi was so viciously mutilated remains.”

“Are you saying you know the answer?”

“Let’s save that for later. Now then, no point spending too much more time on this— it’ll start getting tedious— how about we finally get to the solution. It’s a fact— an unshakeable fact that not only the Seventh Ward, but every building in the facility has next to no means of entry. You could even call them virtually impregnable. Given the lack of windows— by their very nature, they have only one entrance. An entrance locked by a security system of Kunagisa Tomo’s design no less. Now, set aside the lock for the time being; you’ll find that the only ways in or out of the building would be this roof and the entrance. Like one big tunnel to heaven. Professor Kyouichirou’s theory is that whoever killed Utsurigi came and went through the entrance.” I glanced over at him. He said nothing, so I continued. “If that were true, then it would be impossible for the culprits to be anyone other than Kunagisa Tomo and her companions, but well, as one of her companions, I reject that outright. I’m sure the professor will claim this is just collusion, but I can vouch for her innocence. No, I know of her innocence. That means that the entrance is out of the question.”

“So, you reckon they must’ve taken the rooftop route?”

“Miyoshi!” the professor hollered. “That’s quite enough! You’re completely out of line!”

“My bad, I s’ppose no one asked for my opinion.”

Miss Kokoromi, half-heartedly bowed her head. As someone who’d already decided to cut ties with the professor, it was probably more convenient for her if my little puppet show succeeded. In that sense, the two of us might actually be accomplices after all, I thought.

“Yes, that’s right. That said— it’s not like that route doesn’t come with its own strict limitations.” I muttered, turning to face the Sixth Ward that I had just come from. “I’m sure I don’t need to explain what those limitations are, now do I?”

The question wasn’t addressed to anyone in particular, so it went unanswered. Still, I let it sit for a little while before the professor finally spoke up. “Like I said, this route is a one-way-trip,” he sounded irritated. “Even if you could make it here, there would be no going back, that’s—”

“No. Well, I suppose that’s also an issue. You’re right, there would be no going back— But, if you’d just think about it, you’d realize making it here is no easy feat either.”

“—What?”

“Going from the Fifth Ward to the Primary Ward, and finally to the Sixth Ward– the furthest you’d have to jump is around three and a half metres. Anybody here could pull that off— however, the same can’t be said for the last jump—”

Five metres—Four and a half if we factor in the angle. Far enough to give the high school boy’s average a run for its money— That said, an average is only an average when there’s deviation. We’re not talking about the minimum distance anyone could clear. In fact, it was the opposite; it meant that around half of them couldn’t.

In other words, when it came to this four-and-a-half-metre jump, there were those who could clear it, and those who could not—

“As you all saw, I was able to make the jump. Despite how I look now, back in the day— I guess you all know already, so I’ll just come out and say it— I studied abroad as part of the ER3 System’s adolescent cultivation project, the ER Program, for five years. As part of that program, I had to keep myself reasonably fit, and as a result— I’ve managed to maintain a moderate level of fitness even now.”

I did pick up a bit of an accent though, I added jokingly.

“Let’s see. Excuse me, Suzunashi,” I turned my questioning on her once again. “If you wanted to, do you think you could jump this distance?”

“I probably could,” as if she were expecting the question this time, she answered immediately. “I haven’t actually tested it or anything, but I could probably do up to five metres easily. If it were six metres— that’s where I’d draw the line. I’m pretty sure, anyway.”

“I see.”

Even as an amateur when it came to long-jumping, Suzunashi was unusually tall, she had long legs, and was in good shape, so her answer came as no surprise. She could probably jump even further than me, I thought. I nodded my head and turned to face Kunagisa.

“Tomo, what about you?”

“Uhhh– not a chance,” Kunagisa pursed her lips and answered, sounding a little miffed. It was as if she were saying, ‘why make me admit it?’ “I probably couldn’t even jump one metre.”

This was also to be expected. Kunagisa was tiny on top of being a shut-in and a fussy eater who often skipped meals; she never had much in the way of muscles or leg strength. “You see,” I turned back to face the professor.

“Even amongst the three of us, we all have different levels of ability. That said, if we assume they took the rooftop route, then our innocence is proven. After all, you can’t take this route unless you start in one of the wards. And since every research ward was locked tight, we couldn’t have gotten inside.”

“Are you saying one of us is the culprit?”

The professor said, scowling at me.

“I’ve been saying that this whole time, haven’t I?”

I replied indifferently.

“Then who? Spit it out.”

“I’m getting there. Don’t rush me. This is the end, so we might as well enjoy it. —Now then, who do you think we should count out? Professor Shadou Kyouichirou, his secretary, Uze Misachi, his assistant, Ougaki Shito, Miss Miyoshi Kokoromi, or the other researchers, Neo Furuara, Koutari Hinayoshi, or Kasugai Kasuga—?” I narrowed my eyes at them as I said their names one by one. “—Let’s start by removing the three women. In other words, Miss Kokoromi, Kasugai, and Misachi.”

“——”  “ ………”  “………”

All three of them were silent.

“It’s simply a matter of physique… the three of them are all quite petite. And I don’t mean to sound sexist, but there’s also the matter of innate strength to consider. It would be far too risky for a woman to try and pull off this level of acrobatics.”

Somehow, I felt as though I could feel Suzunashi’s glare coming from my right, but I ignored it. It wouldn’t do me any good to lose my nerve by thinking about the repercussions I would face later. Nonetheless, I was very clearly being glared at. Bear with it, this is a vital situation. I shook my head gently before saying, “let’s continue,”

“Neo’s out too. This is also a matter of physique,” let’s see. What’s the best way to put this? “Neo’s a bit larger than most, you see…”

“You can say that again,” Neo responded to my hesitance by slapping his belly and letting out an exaggerated laugh. “It’d be like doing long-jump with an extra twenty kilos on your back. I never would’ve made it. I guess that means you can scratch me off your list of suspects as well.”

“…In that case, we’re left with three. Professor Shadou Kyouichirou, the assistant, Ougaki Shito, and the researcher, Koutari Hinayoshi. …Of the three of them, the one we can most easily rule out would be you, professor.”

“…And why is that?”

“If you mean to tell me you could make that jump, then by all means go ahead, but you’re no spring chicken, professor. Sixty-three years old… you’ve got to admit it would be difficult.”

The professor was silent. However, there was no need to wait on an answer. After all, anybody could tell the professor wouldn’t have been able to make this jump just by looking at him.”

“That leaves us with two—”

Koutari and Shito.

All eyes were on them.

“It’s possible for these two to have taken the rooftop route— to be specific, Shito would’ve crossed over from the Primary Ward to the Sixth Ward, and finally to the Seventh Ward. Koutari’s route would’ve gone: Second Ward, Primary Ward, Sixth Ward and then Seventh Ward, but he still could have made it here—”

As I spoke, I made note of their condition. Koutari looked the exact same as he had a little while ago. He seemed completely unshaken as he carefully readjusted the position of his sunglasses. He looked like composure itself. Shito, on the other hand, did not. His face had gone beet-red with anger and he cut me off with a shout,

“Oi, asshole! Don’t think I’ll just shut-up and take it while you say whatever you want about me—!”

“Sorry, now's not the time for our back-and-forth comedy routine. Can you just keep quiet and listen for a second?”

“The fuck did you just say? Listen here, asshole—”

“Relax. You couldn’t have taken this route either.” I held up one hand to appease the furious Shito, still speaking calmly all the while.  “You have a vision problem.”

“Wha-” at that single word, ‘vision’, Shito deflated. “—What?”

“Your vision… you can’t see very well, can you?” I answered, trying my best to sound as if it were simply common knowledge. “I doubt it’s an issue with the lenses of your glasses or your eyes… so I’d guess it's likely a neurological problem. I was never the best at anatomy, so I couldn’t tell you the specifics.”

A slight murmur arose amongst all who were present. Those in the know were glancing at me, and those who were out of the loop had their eyes set on Shito. Among those from the facility, it seems Misachi and Kasugai were the only ones who hadn’t known. As for the outsiders, Suzunashi didn’t seem to have noticed, but Kunagisa seemed like she had already figured it out. Given Kunagisa’s insightfulness, it was certainly possible.

“Bastard… how did you—”

“It just came to me, that’s all there was to it.”

Consider how close he had to get to confirm who I was during our first meeting, or how he had to prod at Kunagisa to check, or how he wasn’t able to tell whether Suzunashi was a man or a woman just because she was tall. And then there’s also the fact that noticing Kouta and I hiding in the blind spot behind the water tank wouldn’t have been possible for anyone who relied on their eyesight day in and day out. Or how despite that, he couldn’t discern Kouta’s gender either just because she happened to be tall like Suzunashi. Perhaps that was the reason Kouta had focused her attacks on Shito’s abdomen and had avoided his head. Taking all that together, it really ‘just came to me’.

“Am I wrong?”

“—No, but…”

An optic nerve abnormality resulting in loss of vision. Whether it was congenital or something acquired was more than I could determine. That said, even if it ended up being the result of the professor’s human experimentation, it wasn’t for me to know. It was none of my business. Essentially, Shito could only faintly make out people or his surroundings. Given the way I saw him navigate the facility, he couldn’t be completely blind… still, with his condition…

“Then we should assume you wouldn’t have been able to make the jump.”

“H-hey, I’ll admit that you’re right about me, but… but that would mean,” the anger in Shito’s voice had somewhat subsided, but it was replaced with a confused panic. “That would mean the only one left is—”

“That’s right. Only one left. Koutari,” I pointed in his direction. “—Now then— what about him? If we were to try and search for issues of gender, physique, age, senses, or any other suitably compelling reason why he wouldn’t be able to make this jump, I think you’ll find—”

Koutari. He didn’t move a muscle. He didn’t scowl. He didn’t get angry. He didn’t show any reaction whatsoever.

“—none.”

The sudden remark didn’t come from me.

But from Koutari himself.

“That’s right, I don’t have an excuse.”

“—Koutari!” the professor barked. “What are you saying!? You—”

“Please calm yourself, professor,” Koutari said in a tone dispassionate enough to rival my own. “He’s simply shown that I would have been able to make it across. That’s all. Isn’t that right, Loverboy?”

Loverboy. At a time like this, those deeply cynical words cut deeper than ever, making me shiver. After all. He was bringing up Kunagisa.

The distance between the two of us was roughly five metres, or maybe six. It might be better if I got a little closer. With that in mind, I took one step towards him. Standing directly across from him.

From here on out— my opponent wasn’t the professor.

From here on out, my opponent was Koutari Hinayoshi.

“Or is it that you’re accusing me of being the culprit?”

Spoken like a true culprit.

“That’s right. I’m saying you did it, Koutari.”

Spoken like a true detective.

I could hear the professor shouting, but I paid him no mind. I took one more step towards Koutari. There was no point getting any closer. Four and a half metres lay between us— how fitting.

“—Amusing. If you’re so insistent that I’m the culprit, then go ahead, try and prove it, Loverboy,” Koutari said, his facial expression unchanging. “I admit I was the only one who could’ve taken this route. After all, my name means ‘the feet of god’. However, as the professor already said— and as you yourself admitted— there would be no way back.”

“No way back, huh…” I repeated his words. “—That’s assuming you would even need to return in the first place.”

“…………”

Koutari didn’t respond.

“…No, of course you would have had to. Otherwise, the logs left on the central computer wouldn’t add up. Suppose, after you murdered Utsurigi, you waited around until Shito discovered the body and then snuck out the entrance… but that wouldn’t work either. Since the doors lock automatically, you would have had to leave immediately after they opened, and it’d be difficult to slip out without Shito noticing. Even if you made use of a blind spot, Shito would’ve noticed anyway.” Just like he had discovered Kouta and I. “Even if fortune was on your side and you managed to make it out of the Seventh Ward, you wouldn’t have been able to get back into the Second Ward. Not because you couldn’t open the door, but because it would have been recorded in the logs.”

“I’m already sick and tired of listening to your impossible theories,” the professor wasn’t simply trying to shut me up, he genuinely sounded exhausted. “Give it up already. I don’t have time to play along with any more of your nonsense—”

“That’s a shame, but unfortunately, just as you are The Mad Daemon, I am the Nonsense User. Still, there’s no need to worry, we’re nearly there. We’ll be arriving at our last stop shortly,” that’s all I had to say to the professor before turning my attention back on Koutari. “Let’s back up a bit— why did the killer mutilate Utsurigi Gaisuke’s body so badly? Was it out of malice? For a sense of control? Some kind of ritual? Whatever the case, I don’t really care. However, there’s one thing I’m curious about— that being the reason why the culprit stole his arms.”

His face unmoving, Koutari didn’t answer.

“Perhaps they wanted the hands of a once-great cyber terrorist— in the literal sense. However, such a romantic interpretation seems a bit too far-fetched… My first thought was that it was done to hide evidence of a cadaveric spasm. A cadaveric spasm being—” my eyes flitted over to Miss Kokoromi. “—a phenomenon where a violent death causes a body to undergo instantaneous rigor mortis. If the victim is firmly griping onto something as they’re murdered, then that’s how they would stay. So, if that something happened to be a button from the culprit’s lab coat or a name tag, then that would serve as unshakeable evidence that the culprit would have to dispose of at all costs.”

“So, you’re saying Utsurigi’s was clutching onto some kind of vital clue?” Suzunashi asked. “Then wouldn’t it be easier to just cut the hands off at the wrist? Or you could get back what’s inside by cutting off the fingers. Listen, Inoji, I’m getting close to my limit here too. Could you dumb it down a bit?”

“Sorry,” I apologized. How lame. “Let’s see, the reason why they couldn’t cut off the arms or fingers would be that that would be the exact kind of thing to raise suspicion about there being a cadaveric spasm. By cutting the arms off at the shoulders, they had somewhat covered up–…or rather, misled everyone about its true purpose— or so I thought.”

“Or so you thought?”

“Just think about it, Suzunashi… Utsurigi’s cause of death– it was the scissors jammed through his eyes. That makes the whole theory fall apart.”

“Why? Sounds pretty violent to me.”

“I thought so too, that’s not the issue… the problem is this: there isn’t a person alive who, in a life-or-death situation like having a pair of blades thrust towards their eyeballs,” I made a scissors hand-gesture and pointed them towards my own eyes, “would think to reach for a button or lapel…”

“Ahh… you’re right,” Suzunashi nodded. “The first thing you’d do is grab your attacker’s arms to try and defend yourself. Hmm… now that it’s been said out loud, it seems obvious. But in that case, why were the arms cut off?”

“That’s not the only question either. Like Miss Kokoromi said earlier, why was there a time lag before they did it? Allow me to clear up that question right away. They were simply waiting for the rain to stop.”

“—the rain?”

“Yes, the rain. If they took the rooftop route, the return trip would’ve been dangerous enough as is, but last night it rained quite heavily.” Kouta had said that the fact the arms were cut off all that time later meant that it must have been raining by the time they left, but the opposite interpretation was possible as well. In other words, because it was already raining, they chose to wait before cutting off the arms. “But the rain had already stopped by the time the sun came out— That’s right, the killer really shouldn’t have picked such a rainy night to commit a murder. Don’t you agree, Koutari?”

“Who knows?” he kept his replies brief. “I can’t say I follow.”

“—Still, there was a reason they had to kill him that night. That was because they couldn’t be sure when the three of us would be going home. If they had missed their chance last night and we decided to leave today— then they wouldn’t have had a scapegoat to pin the blame on.”

“……………”

“Fortunately, the rain stopped. All you had to do then was head back.”

“But how! That’s what we’ve been asking this whole time!”

The professor finally exploded and hurled his cane at me. It seems he had finally reached his wits end. The wooden cane directly struck the bandaged portion of my left arm. The painkillers were still doing their job so it didn’t hurt, but the force of impact made me stumble two or three steps back. There’s a chance that my arm was now well and truly broken.

Like Suzunashi had done this morning, I just glared at him without saying a word.

“—What? Those eyes. Why do you— who do you think you are?” I didn’t throw anything in return, but nonetheless, the professor took a few steps back. As he did, he bumped into Misachi and stopped. “How dare a whelp like you have their eyes?”

Their eyes? Who was he talking about? Surely not Suzunashi. Perhaps Utsurigi. Or maybe Kunagisa Tomo or Nao when they were younger. I didn’t know. I didn’t care to know. I didn’t care who it was.

“—Looking at it from the Sixth Ward,” I said. “It’s surprisingly easy to miss. The fact that it’s a one-way trip, that is. What if Koutari— no, that hasn’t been decided yet— What if our culprit didn’t realize they couldn’t get back until they’d already made it across? What would they do then? Simple. They’d use a rope.”

“……How! I told you there’s no such thi—!”

“As I pointed out earlier, Koutari could have used his hair.”

“And as I pointed out earlier, it wouldn’t be long enou—!”

“If it’s not long enough, just make it longer. For example—

—using Utsurigi’s arms.”

As expected— no one had anything to say. In all likelihood, not a one of them could have ever predicted that was what I was going to say— no. I suppose it’s possible one of them had. Just one. I turned to face them-

-to face Koutari Hinayoshi.

“You fashioned a rope out of your hair then fastened one of his arms on each end. I can’t tell you the average arm span of a grown man— However, if we use my arms as a benchmark, then they should have been sixty to seventy centimetres each. Together they would have been around one metre and thirty centimetres— correct? Add that to the length of the hair and it would have been more than enough to reach the Sixth Ward. And don’t tell me part of a human body wouldn’t be able to support a human’s weight. Right, Koutari?” Without answering, Koutari readjusted his sunglasses. I continued. “Using a rope or some kind of substitute comes with its own problems— namely, since the Sixth Ward has no railing, you’d need a hook in order to snag it on the roof. Except, if Utsurigi’s arm was attached to the end of the rope— then you’d be in the clear. If Utsurigi had a cadaveric spasm while gripping your arms, then his hands would’ve been frozen in a perfect hook-shape. You would’ve been more than capable of using that to hook onto the lip of the eavestrough that runs along the edge—”

“—Even nonsense has its limits!”

The professor– Mad Daemon Shadou Kyouichirou stomped his foot as hard as he could and shouted breathlessly. Misachi made an attempt to hold him back, but was thrown aside. “You don’t honestly expect us to believe something so impractical— contrived— absurd— and far-fetched— do you!?”

“Impractical? Contrived? Absurd? Far-fetched? That’s exactly what it is!” I replied emphatically. “And yet, professor, there is no way the solution to a case involving none other than Shadou Kyouichirou, Utsurigi Gaisuke, and Kunagisa Tomo could be anything but impractical, contrived, absurd, far-fetched, and psycho logical! That is the one and only truth of this facility!”

“Preposterous…what a load of rubbish! Or are you honestly suggesting that’s what happened!?”

“It’s not a matter of what happened. It’s not a matter of what didn’t happen either. It’s not even a matter of the act itself. It’s all a matter of perception. Isn’t that right, Koutari!?”

“B-be quiet!” the professor’s face contorted in anger. He turned red, and then pale. “Ko…Koutari! Say something! Tell this laughable brat he’s wrong—”

“……………”

Koutari didn’t respond to his words either. Then, he raised his head only slightly and spoke to me.

“…and your proof? Any evidence I did what you claim?”

“Proof, huh… Sure, something as minor as you cutting your hair doesn’t prove anything, but—” I pointed at him. “If my thinking is correct, then one of your arms should still bear Utsurigi’s hand print. One left by the tight grip caused by his cadaveric spasm.”

“………………”

“Koutari!”

The professor yelled once more.

“Tell him he’s wrong! Hurry, roll up your sleeves and show him you’re innocent! Once you do, we’ll make sure this brat never leaves his cage again! We’ll lock him deep, deep, underground and thoroughly, and I do mean thoroughly—”

“—well, I’d say you score a sixty.”

All at once, the deep voice Koutari had been using until now was replaced with something lighter.

“Koutar—”

“Sixty points. You should be grateful for that much. You were far too clumsy and took way too long.”

“—Then you have my gratitude.” I shrugged my shoulders. “—Even then, that’s still a passing grade…right?”

I said lowering my voice.

Koutari laughed.

An easygoing, laid-back laugh.

As if laughing at my foolish antics.

A fool.

In reality, that’s exactly what I was. This whole time, this man had been leading me around by the nose. This whole time— from start to finish. From beginning to pre-determined end. Every last second.

“W-Why!?” The one to shout was Shito. “Why on earth did you— What reason did you have for killing Utsurigi!?”

“Reason? I see… a reason, huh?”

Koutari seemed to be thinking as he reached into his lab coat.

“Then again, the reason doesn’t really matter, now does it?”

“—What are you—” There was a slight tremor in Shito’s voice. “To kill without reason— to kill without motive is…”

That sort of thing-

It shouldn’t exist.

A senseless killer.

A convictionless killer.

It couldn’t exist.

In which case–

“Then is killing fine so long as you have a reason?”

“…Koutari.”

“Just kidding.”

Koutari wore a thin smile. It was chilling.

The kind of scornful smile one would have for a clueless child.

A patronizing sympathy.

A tender disdain.

That’s the impression I got as Koutari gazed at Shito.

“Isn’t that obvious?”

The hand in his lab coat grasped hold of something.

“That’s right. A murder is no good without a motive— isn’t it!?”

Suddenly, he pulled his hand free from his lab coat— hurling the knives held between his fingers. All three of the flying blades burrowed themselves into the bandages wrapped around my left arm. The impact caused me to topple over. I fell flat on my back. The harsh impact, driving the air out of my lungs. My head collided with the floor a second later.

For a second, all eyes were on me sprawled out on the floor. A second later, all eyes darted back to Koutari.

All in all, two seconds.

And that was enough.

Thunk, the sound of the door closing.

When everyone looked back, neither hide nor hair of Koutari Hinayoshi could be found.

He had disappeared. Just like that.

Almost as if-

Almost as if such a character had never existed to begin with.

“—That bastard! Don’t fuck with me! Shit! Shit!” Shito took off towards the door in an effort to chase after him. “—I won’t let you get away!”

“Give it up, Shito,” Still sprawled out on the floor, even I was surprised by how listless I sounded. “There’s no point going after him.”

“—Huh?” Shito turned to face me, his brows furrowed. “What’s that supposed to mean—?”

“Exactly what it sounds like. It’s too late to catch him now.”

That’s right. He was probably far beyond our reach. The confidence he exuded as we worked out the solution was more than enough for me to reach that conclusion. He had some sort of escape route already secured— and a foolproof one at that. One that would allow him to evade not only us, but the police as well. Not that I could have said what kind of route that was.

This is fine.

I never really cared to catch him in the first place. All that mattered was proving Kunagisa’s innocence. And that had already been accomplished. This was good enough. What came next was a job for someone else. Not for me.

“Besides— Shito. Doesn’t your job lie elsewhere?”

I sat up and began plucking the knives out of bandages one by one. Seeing as I didn’t start bleeding, it must not have been too serious an injury– probably just some superficial cuts. It seems like the bandage had served as some kind of barrier. The cuts didn’t even hurt thanks to the pain killers, but I was seriously starting to dread the moment they wore off. Would I ever be able to use my left arm again?

Still— these knives. If I hadn’t shielded myself with my arm, they certainly would have pierced my heart. Had he known that I would defend myself? Or had he simply not cared whether he ended up killing me. There was no need to even consider the answer, it was almost certainly the latter.

He had a good reason to kill me after all.

And I had my reasons to let him.

After I was done removing all the knives from it, I took my left arm–

–and pointed it at Professor Shadou Kyouichirou.

“Shito. Your job is to be his assistant, isn’t it?” I did my best not to sound too cold, but as expected, my voice was still as emotionless as ever. “If so, then you ought to see it through to the end.”

“—Professor.”

Shito sounded surprised.

There, was an old man. Dazed– and slumped to the floor. His unblinking eyes fixed on the door Koutari had closed behind him, his mouth hanging open.

Like he would topple at the slightest push.

Like he would crumble at the slightest nudge.

A small, old man.

An aging scholar who lost Utsurigi Gaisuke, who let Kunagisa Tomo slip through his fingers.

Having lost his sole purpose.

Having lost his one and only hope.

This is what’s left of someone who’s lost everything, huh?

A Mad Daemon.

In the truest sense.

“What pure unadulterated nonsense.”

I let out an exaggerated sigh.

I see— this bacteria truly was malignant. Spreading and spreading, with no hope to ever contain it. Professor Kyouichirou had tried to pull the strings of Cluster’s very own cracker, Utsurigi Gaisuke, and this was the result— and if a genius like Shadou Kyouichirou couldn’t handle him— what hope did someone as small and insignificant as me have?

“Iichan,”

Something took hold of my right hand.

It was Kunagisa.

The blue-coloured-

Girl I know so well.

“Now that everything’s over and done, wanna go home?”

Over. Done.

What exactly is over, and what on earth had we done?

I didn’t know.

I didn’t know.

There’s only one thing I did know.

And that was Kunagisa Tomo.

“Hm? What’s the matter Iichan? You don’t wanna go?”

Just past Kunagisa, I could see Suzunashi. She was in the middle of lighting a cigarette. Our eyes met for just a moment, but she paid me no mind, instead turning her gaze to the sky above.

“…That’s right.”

That’s right.

It was over and done.

There was nothing left to do.

There was nowhere left to be.

There was nothing left behind.

From here on out, I was free to float along.

And so,

And so, let’s go home.

“Let’s go home, Tomo.”

But,

Where on earth were we supposed to go home to?

Psycho Logical (Part Two)

Psycho Logical (Part Two)

Utsurigi Gaisuke, “Criminal Judge,” Malignant Green

Hinemosu Suzu, “Consigned Stillness,” Double Flick

Gotodoroki Seigo, “Scornful Compatriot,” Reverse Cross

Munefuyu Mutsuki, “Clamoring Bloodshot,” Cubic Loop

Nadekiri Hakuraku, “Despondent Momento,” Dancing with Madness

Ayaminami Hyou, “Spinning Suzuki,” Cheetah

Shikigishi Kishiki, “Squirming Ruination,” Bad Kind

Shigai Touno, “Resurrected Abasement,” Trigger-happy End

Kunagisa Tomo, “Walking Wrath,” Dead Blue

And now for the Epilogue— or rather, a peak behind the curtains that would be best left unspoken.

Where were we supposed to go home to? For now, the only place for me to return to was my antique apartment in Kyoto. That night— the night everything had come to a close— without even waiting for it to get dark, we got back in Miiko’s Fiat, which we had Shito refuel, and put Shadou Kyouichirou’s research facility behind us. While we drove, Suzunashi booked us a hotel room, and we spent a single night in Nagoya. Despite the last-minute booking, the rooms were spacious, and the service was top-notch— Is what I wish I could say, but even then, it was still much better than the facility’s Haunted Manor. Lined up like sardines in the same bed (Me → Kunagisa → Suzunashi), the three of us slept like corpses. Even though it wasn’t exactly true, it still felt as if it had been ages since I last slept.

At daybreak, Suzunashi’s lecture began. For the next few hours, I made no rebuttal as I knelt silently in front of her; Suzunashi’s relentless scolding was only interrupted by the occasional smack on the head. Before long, Kunagisa woke up and we spent the rest of the day sightseeing around Nagoya. Keeping watch over Kunagisa out of the corner of my eye as she frolicked like a child, I managed to pick up the uirō-mochi Hime asked me for (luckily, they were selling them in five-colour sets, so it was an instant purchase) as well as some extras for Miiko and the others at the apartment for a total of ten blocks.

That evening, we dropped Suzunashi off back on Hie Mountain in Shiga prefecture.

“Say hi to Miiko for me. We’ll finish the rest of your lecture some other time,”

She said. Apparently, she still wasn’t through with me. Part of me was apprehensive, but the other part of me was looking forward to it.

Next, we arrived at Kyoto’s pride and joy (or perhaps deepest shame), the high-end residential neighborhood, Shirosaki. I parked the car outside Kunagisa’s strikingly conspicuous apartment building and walked her to her room.

“Next time, then.” “Yeah, next time.”

I didn’t know exactly what ‘next time’ entailed, but nonetheless, I said my goodbyes, got back in the Fiat, and finally headed back to my own apartment. I parked the car in the lot, and from there it was less than a minute’s walk. Rather than return to my own room, I knocked on the door to the room right next to it.

“Oh, welcome back.” Luckily Miiko was home and she came to greet me wearing one of her usual jinbei. She seemed a little– no, a lot drunk, and her face was glowing slightly. “That was quick. Only spent two nights, huh?”

“Two nights…”

That’s right. In fact, the three of us hadn’t even spent two whole days at the facility. And yet, despite that, it somehow felt as though we were imprisoned there for over a month.

“Something like that. Thanks for the car. Here’s your keys back. And some money for gas… and some uirō-mochi as a souvenir.”

“Thanks…hm?” Miiko noticed my left arm. Miss Kokoromi had taken another look at it, so it wasn’t bandaged anymore, instead sporting a full-on cast. “…Inoji, you drove all the way back from Nagoya like that?”

“Huh? No, look, I can still move my fingers just fine. And besides, you can operate the gearshift with your right hand anyways.”

“I see… I guess that’s fine then.”

That’s where the questions stopped. She never asked how I got hurt.

“Come on in. Let’s eat some uirō-mochi together. These kinds of things always taste better when you share them with someone else.”

“Normally, I wouldn’t take you up on that, but…”

But after being shown genuine human warmth for the first time in a long while, even I had trouble turning her down.

“I’ll let you spoil me today, Miiko.”

“Good. C’mon then, don’t be a stranger.”

And that’s how I ended up in Miiko’s room being treated to uirō-mochi and tea— although dealing with a plastered Miiko was an ordeal of its own. After that, I returned to my own room. It was empty.

“…Huh?”

Hang on, the lack of furniture may have been normal, but the lack of clothing and books certainly wasn’t. My cellphone and charger were missing. Oh man, so were my health insurance card and bank book. I was worried I’d been robbed for a second, but the truth hit me a second later, and I made my way towards Hime’s room on the first floor.

“But you said I could have everything, master.”

The culprit was Hime.

“I cleaned your room. I even took out the garbage for you.”

The ‘garbage’ in question no doubt included my personal belongings.

“…Hime. You were only supposed to do that if I didn’t make it back okay…”

“Really? But- but, master, just look at your arm– you don’t seem very okay to me.”

“…I guess not.”

Man… if only all cases were this easy to solve.

I only managed to recover my bank book and health insurance card by trading them for the uirō-mochi before I returned to my room once more.

“Ah—…how should I put it?”

It was like waking up from nothingness. Like waking up from a nightmare. Of course, that was nothing more than a fantasy bordering on delusion. After all, The Mad Daemon, Shadou Kyouichirou’s research facility had been undeniably real.

“Real, huh? —but how is that any different from illusion?”

What would happen to that lab now? I thought about it for quite some time. With the facility’s head, Professor Shadou Kyouichirou, in such a sorry state, they wouldn’t be able to continue to function as a laboratory; as such, they would likely be absorbed by a nearby research institute, or so Kunagisa said. Indeed, with The Mad Daemon becoming worthless— in the literal sense— I can’t imagine the Kunagisa House being willing to continue pouring money into him forever. If that happened, what would become of the other researchers?

It probably wouldn’t be much of a problem for Neo. That man was a scoundrel from the very start. He’d made betrayal his job— a rogue who ultimately belonged nowhere. He would likely just chalk it up as a loss, compensate his client for duties unfulfilled, and as the professional lowlife that he is, begin searching for his next job.

“—I gotta say, I wouldn’t be against teaming up again some time. If anything, I’m half-tempted to scout you and bring you back with me.”

“That’s not funny… Don’t go around telling people they’ve got the makings of a backstabber.”

“Don’t be silly, you don’t strike me as a backstabber at all. If anything, you’re the type to look someone in the eyes as they betray them.”

“…………”

“Hm? That one actually was supposed to be funny.”

—Though I’ll likely never have anything to do with the man again, looking back on it now, I can’t help finding him a strangely amusing character. It’s rare to find anyone so straightforward about their betrayal.

Miyoshi Kokoromi— Miss Kokoromi, said something about returning to the ER3 System. There’s no reason they would turn down someone as talented as her, so everything would likely work out just fine.

“This is goodbye forever then, Miss.”

“Y’think? I reckon we’ll be meeting again soon.”

“…………”

“What’s more, next time things’ll be far, far worse. Nothin’ would suit you better— Frankly, it ain’t even funny. Well then, bye-byee.”

Once again, Miss Kokoromi left me with a dreadful premonition. Man, why did she have to be so terrible at goodbyes? Cut me some slack already.

Kasugai Kasuga. Kasugai will– well, she’ll probably do just about anything. She’d make it work somehow, so there was likely no need for me to worry. In the most literal sense, she would do anything. Of all people, I could never imagine her in a hopeless situation. She never had any convictions to speak of— a person composed of nothing but talent. Without goals, nothing is off limits. Without desires, nothing is unnecessary. Without satisfaction, there is no disappointment. Without happiness, there is no sadness. Without something to protect, there is no urge to destroy. If you’re not alive, you can’t die. To have value, but not values. There is no solution to something that isn’t a problem— That’s the kind of person she was.

If I had to guess, she will likely get swept up by some branch of the Kunagisa Syndicate. She was far too talented to be left to her own devices. I would likely never meet her again, but— No. When it came to her, there were no ‘but’s.

Ougaki Shito— Uze Misachi. Apparently the two of them planned to go wherever the professor went. They would follow him now and forever. I have nothing to say to that. It isn’t my place. Those with strong convictions had nothing to be gained from listening to those with no conviction at all.

And then.

Koutari Hinayoshi.

Koutari Hinayoshi— escaped.

Not even the security guards at the mountain-pass gate caught sight of him. Just like a puff of smoke, he had vanished into thin air.

“Vanished?— people can’t just vanish…”

But people can be made to disappear.

That’s all there was to it.

“…Wait, I’m forgetting someone.”

That’s right, there was someone else. Someone I mustn't forget. Someone I must never forget…

With those thoughts in mind, I drifted off to sleep.

The next day arrived. As easy as it is to forget, I am a university student, and as such, I had to be on campus on weekdays. To tell the truth, I would have liked to spend another day recuperating, but thanks to this little trip of ours, I had already missed three days of class, and that’s not even counting all the days I missed last month while in the hospital. I had already missed too much, and exams were right around the corner, so regardless of how beat up my body was, I had no choice but to drag myself to class. I got ready to leave (I couldn’t use my left arm, so I had to get Miiko to help me dress) then stepped out of my apartment. Houko, the little girl who lived on the floor above me, was crouched in the alley doing something. The straw hat she wore to protect her from the early-morning sun looked oddly fitting on her and made for a cute scene.

“Yo, good morning, Houko”

“Good morning, big brother.” Without looking up at me, she quickly bowed her head. “Are you going to school?”

“Yeah. What are you doing, Houko?”

“Killing bugs.”

“…I see. Do your best then.”

“Yup, I will.”

As I walked past her, she reached out and grabbed the hem of my pantleg without looking up.

“Big brother, if you go to school today, you’ll probably die.”

She said casually.

“I know,” I replied casually.

“You know and you’re still going?”

“It’s a worthless life anyway,” I shrugged. “Besides, I have exams coming up.”

“Okay then,” Houko let go. Houko still didn’t look up at me, but I gave her a small wave and continued on my way to school.

Class was as boring as ever. Whether something is boring or not has more to do with the person feeling bored than anything, so I had no right to complain. That’s just how university is. And whether it’s exam season or not, whether I attend class or not, that will never change. And so, I spent the boring (through no fault of its own) lecture reading a book I borrowed from Nanananami, The Yacht of Death. Both the cover and prose were ridiculously antiquated, so it was somewhat difficult to read. It was a boxed hardcover and was so bulky that even when I put it in my bag, it stuck out a little. I just can’t wrap my head around Nanananami’s tastes. That said, if we’re just talking about the book’s contents, I personally found them quite interesting and enjoyable.

After lunch break, I had a review seminar. For lunch itself, I bought some sweet bread and took the stairs to my classroom on the fourth floor. This was the kind of situation where you’d usually take an elevator, but for some reason I wasn’t in the elevator kind of mood.

“…an elevator kind of mood? What would that even be?”

Speaking of— Utsurigi despised elevators. I suppose it doesn’t matter, but I can’t help wondering what his reasons were.

Was it because they made him feel trapped…?

I was still considering the answer when I arrived at the classroom where I was greeted with a rather odd sight. A number of my classmates were huddled around the door as if trying to peer into the room. They were free to enter and take a seat, but for some reason all of them wore serious expressions as they tried to catch a glimpse through the crack of the door.

“…What’s everyone doing?”

“Oh, Ikkun.” Yoshige (wears coats even in the summer. Hobby: bead collecting) turned to face me. “Long time no see. Ah, did you get hurt again?”

“Hm? You’re right, it really is Ikkun.” Minayama (wears a jersey and high heels. Personal Scripture: Dogra Magra) also noticed me and waved me over. “C’mere a sec. Don’t just stand there, come take a look.”

“Look at what? Just hurry up and go insi—”

“No way!” Yoshimasa (combs back his blonde hair. Wears shorts. Dream job: Astronaut) panicked, swatting away my hand as I reached for the doorknob. “What’re you doing? Don’t throw away this precious gift.”

“Gift?”

“Y’see, right now there’s this strange woman in the classroom,” Märchen (keeps a hamster on her right shoulder. Gothic Lolita) explained, “so how should I put it? —Going inside’s a little awkward.”

“A strange woman? And she’s not one of our classmates?”

“That’s right! But she’s sooo cool!” “Yeah! She’s amazing!” “A complete bombshell!” “She’s so tall— and her hair is gorgeous—!” “Look how long her legs are—” “She seems kinda wild—” “She looks crazy strong!” “I bet she just does whatever she wants, don’t you think!?” “ —red—” “She’s got this unapproachable aura or something—” “She’s, like, super imposing, or, like, heroic or something—”

“Hang on.”

I stopped them.

“Did someone just say red?”

“Yeah, I did? Why?”

“—I think I’ve got an idea who it is. Can everyone step aside, I’m coming through.”

Instantly, everyone’s eyes sparkled. Then, as if this is the moment they’d all been waiting for, they happily cried out in unison,

“That’s our, Ikkun! He’s got way more guts than we do! He’s my idol! I want to be him!”

I hate them.

I ignored them and opened the door.

There, as promised–

“—Yo,”

–in an excessively arrogant manner, with her legs kicked up on one of the desks, sat Humanity’s Strongest Contractor, Aikawa Jun. As usual, she was dressed in a maddeningly crimson suit with her entire being radiating an intimidating aura. Her mere presence, already a work of art.

“What are the chances I’d meet you here, Iitan?”

“—If this counts as chance, then no one would ever need dice…”

“Ha-ha, true that,” Aikawa laughed cynically. Then, without shifting her posture, she leapt out of her chair, over the desk, and landed directly in front of me. “That’s right, Iitan, I came here to see you.”

“Right… that’s fine and all, but please refrain from jumping from a seated position.”

“No need to be so tense- not after all we’ve been through,” she said, slinging her arm around my shoulder in an overly-friendly manner. Face to face, cheek to cheek, she brought me unnaturally close. Then, she turned towards my classmates and said, “Now then, all you extras. I’m gonna snatch this bride-to-be for a sec.”

“By all means,”

They all said in perfect unison.

I hate them so much.

The powerless nineteen-year-old bride let himself be dragged out of the classroom. Aikawa never removed her arm from around my shoulders, instead she locked it even tighter, pressing our bodies together. You could almost call it an embrace. I wondered how the two of us looked to those around us.

Definitely not like lovers.

…even though I came to that conclusion myself, I found the speed at which I arrived there a little disappointing.

“Hmm? What’s the matter, Iitan? You’re even quieter than usual? You depressed or something?”

“No… and more importantly, can you let go of me, it’s way too hot.”

“What’s with you? How cruel—” Aikawa replied in a playful tone. “If you keep talkin’ like that, you’ll hurt big sis’ feelings— You’re so cold, Iitan– You’re a cold-blooded monster. A real meanie–”

“It’s hot. It’s summer. And it’s hard to walk.”

“Just admit you’re embarrassed. You’re such a boy,” Aikawa snickered, finally letting go of me. “Well, I can’t pretend like that part of you ain’t cute. There’s plenty of freaks out there who go wild for that sort of thing. So? How’ve ya been?”

“…What do you want? Why’d you come all the way to my university? Don’t tell me you’re here just to kill time.”

“Hmm– It’s more like I put in the effort to make time. I just finished a job, y’see.”

“Is that right? A job, huh?”

“You really are cold, arent’cha, Iitan?” Aikawa said with a wry smile. “Alright, I get it, I get it… if I want you to be honest, I gotta do the same. I admit it, I came here to see you.”

“Yeah, obviously. You already said as much.”

We left the school building. It was still technically lunch break, so the campus grounds were packed with people still milling about. Aikawa and I carefully threaded our way through the crowd. Judging by Aikawa’s deliberate stride, it seems like she had a destination in mind. Even though I felt a touch of unease about where she was leading me, I followed behind her.

“Y’see, I figured maybe I ought to try and patch things up between us,”

Aikawa said. I was so utterly shocked by Aikawa’s genuine humility that I was left momentarily speechless. However, that was quickly followed by a happiness akin to walking on air— and yet, it still felt like something was missing.

That’s right. Something’s wrong. That’s not how this goes. Our Aikawa Jun is a little more—

“So, I’m gonna make you apologize.”

Aikawa continued with no trace of hesitation. YES! I balled my right fist and did a fist pump. That’s the stuff. That’s exactly what I’m looking for. Now that’s Aikawa Jun.

“Sure— no problem whatsoever, Ishimaru Kouta.” I nodded. “That whole mess was my fault to begin with, so I apologize.”

Aikawa pursed her lips slightly before responding, “Alright. You’re forgiven. Frankly, I ought to sock you one for all that, but since I’m trying to make amends here, I’ll be the bigger person.”

Oh? Grandstanding over not hitting someone?

I knew it. This kind of Aikawa is the best.

“I wouldn’t mind. I don’t want to fight with Aikawa ei–”

“It’s Jun.” Even at times like this, she was still as unforgiving as ever. “How many times have I told you not to call me by my last name? Get it through your thick skull already.”

“—I don’t want to fight with Jun either…” I could not be more serious about that. “…So, does that mean the braids were a wig or something?”

“Yep. All a part of the disguise. Same with the hat and glasses. It’s all laughably cliché, really,” Aikawa replied, running a hand through her actual hair. “Still, it sure took you long enough. I thought you knew all about my love of disguises. Honestly, I was starting to think you never picked up on it at all, but I guess I wasn’t giving you enough credit.”

“I guess not… it didn’t occur to me at the time, but if anyone could pull of such a perfect Lupin the Third impression, it’d have to be you, wouldn’t it?”

“Ha-ha, maybe so. Still, I don’t remember dropping any hints this time. What gave it away?”

“No, there were plenty of hints… Like when you used vocal mimicry to trick the security system and break us out of the Seventh Ward… “Kouta” made it sound like child’s play, but in actuality it was no small feat. This was a defense system built by Kunagisa Tomo after all, so there’s no way any run-of-the-mill vocal trickery would have cut it. You also gave me the lockpicking knife. That was strange too. How would “Kouta” have been able to get past any of the locked doors without it? That said, if she had the lockpicking and vocal mimicry skills of Humanity’s Strongest, then I’m sure she would have found a way somehow. That sort of thing…”

“So, you brute-forced it using the same strained reasoning as Shadou Kyouichirou?”

I shrugged my shoulders at Aikawa’s needling.

“Still, you’ve got a point. Anybody could change their voice enough to trick the people around them– but changing your voiceprint? I might be the only one capable of pulling that off. I get where you’re comin’ from. Still, given the situation there was no way around it.”

“You also told me that no one would ever think to use “Zerozaki” as an alias.”

“I did? I don’t remember saying that.”

“Really now? Still, that’s all just hindsight… What really made me realize, or rather, the first moment I remember doubting Kouta came right at the end. When Kouta gave me the lockpicking knife, she said something about me not being content with just the knife in my right-breast pocket.”

“Hmm, I did, didn’t I?”

“Except, at that moment, I was concealing the knife in my left-breast pocket,” I said. “I thought it would be easier to wield that way, so I switched it around earlier that very morning.
