Psycho Logical (Part Two)

0

A strong person is far less dangerous than one without weakness.

1

Kouta was sitting on the stairs.

I used the anti-lock blade to access the emergency stairwell in Miyoshi Kokoromi’s Third Ward, but when I swung the door open, I froze. It was ten seconds later when I finally managed to ask, “what are you doing here?”

“I’ve been waiting ages for a certain someone to arrive,” Kouta replied calmly. “‘Tis not consummate.”

“……Then your wait is over. But weren’t you supposed to head back to Neo’s ward?”

“Give it some thought. At present, Kasugai is paying Neo a visit. ‘Tis hardly a consummate time to return.”

Kouta stood up and dusted off the seat of her jacket. Then she stretched, making a show of cracking her neck.

Did she stay behind out of concern for me? I wondered, but I wasn’t sure. Who could say? It was surely possible she had, but it was equally likely that she hadn’t. I was uncertain. The odds were much the same as that coin we tossed earlier. I said nothing and returned the knife she had lent me.

“So, do you come bearing good news, my dear friend?”

“Somewhat,” I closed the door behind me as I answered. “I’ve made some progress, but that’s it. I’ve got even more information now, but I’m not any closer to piecing it together.”

“Excessive information will only get in the way… but so be it. If you would be so kind as to tell me what you learned.”

I didn’t have any particular reason to hide anything, so I told her everything I’d gathered from Utsurigi’s corpse as well as everything Miss Kokoromi taught me. Afterwards, I told Kouta all the details of our conversation. I have a poor memory, so my explanation wasn’t very cohesive, but it looked like Kouta understood everything without me having to repeat myself.

“…The reason his arms were severed, you say?”

“The only reasons I can think of to dismember a body are to make transport and disposal easier, some kind of grudge, or for fetishistic reasons. But if it was just about the arms, then I think it’s safe to assume there was some other reason for it.”

“…You shot down Miyoshi’s interpretation earlier, saying, ‘he isn’t the Venus de Milo.’ or what have you, but what did you mean by that?”

I struggled to wrap my head around Kouta’s question at first, so, unsure why she was asking, I answered, “I didn’t really mean anything. I was just talking about one of the many explanations for what happened to Venus' arms. Miss Kokoromi’s theory reminded me of it, so I brought it up. Simple.”

“My preferred interpretation is rather pedestrian, but I believe there were never any arms to begin with.”

“Huh. Is that important?”

“Oh, it isn’t. I’m just making conversation. It just goes to show that no matter the result, one is always left with a finished product. No matter the result— whatever that may be. Now then,” Kouta narrowed her eyes at me, “What shall we do next?”

“Next…” I thought for a second, “For now, let’s head to the roof. There’s no point sitting around.”

“As you command.”

With a swoosh of her coattails Kouta began climbing the stairs. I followed after her. Somewhere around the tenth step, “while we’re still on the subject,” Kouta prefaced before saying, “I still haven’t got your student-teacher relationship pinned down.”

“Pinned down? What’s that supposed to mean?”

“It means I’m not certain whether it’s a relationship founded on trust. This is just my perspective– that is, my own opinion– but, despite all you said earlier, you seemed assured of your safety. It’s as if, deep down, you had faith that your teacher would not only keep your meeting a secret from the professor, but actually lend a hand.”

“You’ve got the wrong idea, Kouta. I simply had no other option. There was always a chance that things would play out well for me, but make no mistake, I took one hell of a gamble.”

“That may be. Nonetheless, I can’t shake the illusion.”

“Illusion, huh… There’s a marked difference between trusting each other, and knowing each other’s true nature,” I replied bluntly. “There was no one abroad who I got along with worse.”

“No one abroad, you say? The implication being?”

“There’s a certain fortune teller here in Japan who I can’t stand even more… Compared to her, Miss Kokoromi almost seems cute. Either way, that’s just how it is. The connection between Miss Kokoromi and I is weaker than gravity on the moon.”

“Perhaps,” as if she were truly just making conversation, she readily conceded. “Now then, your time limit’s down to precisely three hours. How do you fancy your chances?”

“They’re not looking good. It’s like: ‘tune in next time to see how he gets himself out of this bind.’”

“What on earth are you saying?”

“Nonsense.”

Come to think of it, a long time ago, I read a book that had tune in next time written smack dab in the middle of the prologue. While I let my mind escape reality, Kouta and I arrived at the roof of the Third Ward. Kouta continued walking until she was standing in the centre of the roof. There, she raised her arms as if doing a banzai pose. Supposing she wasn’t trying to call down a UFO, she was most likely just stretching.

“Everything considered, this place still has a really nice view,” I found myself saying. “I wonder if it’s because of the ocean of cedar. It almost helps me forget what I have to do. I wonder if this is what people mean when they say the scenery steals their heart.”

“I don’t mean to spoil your poetry,” Kouta said plainly, “but ‘tis not cedar. ‘Tis primarily oak.”

“Huh? Really?”

“That, and chestnut. Also some pine. There are a fair few others mixed in as well, but no cedar.”

“Is that right? Wow… I thought all mountains had cedar.”

“You couldn’t be more wrong. Is your head alright? Well, talk of trees aside,” Kouta turned to face me, “do you know what I’m thinking right now, dear friend?”

“……No. Can’t say I do.” probably something to do with my lack of forestry knowledge. On second thought, probably not. “What is it?”

“I’m still a little astonished. With how quickly Miyoshi gave up, that is.”

“Ahh…” I nodded. “She did, didn’t she? Still, you can’t argue she was wrong, can you? She only acts in her own interest, so she was never going to stick around without a good reason.”

“Unlike Professor Kyouichirou, you mean?” Kouta said. “In your heart, he’s taken on quite the villainous role, hasn’t he? Although, who can blame you after how you’ve been treated. I suppose there’s no helping it. Decency is a luxury afforded only to the fortunate, after all.”

“What do you mean?”

“Only those with excess can start worrying about being good people. Heartwarming thought, ‘tis it not? And yet, we’re all merely scraping by,” she said cynically. “Of course, if one were a true genius like Kunagisa or Utsurigi, then they ought to be capable of kindness. There’s a saying that goes, were I Thomas Edison, it’s possible I, too, would be called the father of invention, or something to that effect. Someone with ten-billion yen, wouldn’t feel the pain of giving a billion away. Because when all is said and done, they would still be nine-billion yen richer.”

“Why are you covering for him? You’re the one who called this place a graveyard last night.”

“And? Grave robbing is one of the highest paying professions, don’t you know?” Kouta boasted casually. “Regardless, what’s most important is the ‘excess’.”

“Kunagisa aside— Utsurigi was plenty excessive, but he certainly wasn’t kind. If anything, it just made him excessively unpleasant.”

“Whether he showed kindness or not was a matter of his own discretion. How fortunate he was to have a choice. After all, wouldn’t it be tragic to lack such leeway and have the decision thrust upon you?”

“Not tragic. Just sad,” I replied indifferently before changing the subject. “Miss Kokoromi’s already decided to leave, but what about Neo? If things play out like Miss Kokoromi said, then there’s no real point in continuing to spy, is there? And… what about you? What’ll you do, Kouta?”

“You needn’t worry. Miyoshi, Neo, and I– our objectives are all separate, so we needn’t walk the same path. Besides, while Miyoshi may have been quick to give up— and you can even argue she was smart to do so— from my perspective, the professor’s proposal doesn’t seem too bad. His chances of success aren’t all that high, but you can’t say they’re especially low either. And supposing he does succeed, the merits— namely, Kunagisa Tomo— would be monumental. It’s a risk bearing a consummate reward.”

“It’s been a pain in the ass for us though,” naturally, my displeasure began seeping into my voice. “Every single one of them… they’re nothing but vultures. Using other people as specimens, as guinea pigs, as lab rats… honestly, are they even human?”

“They used to be. Before they became academics.”

Kouta’s cynical reply sent shivers through my entire body. When it came to being inhuman, this woman stood head and shoulders above the rest, didn’t she?

“Then again, when you said, ‘every single one of them,’ I’m sure you meant me as well. Still, that, too, is consummate. Now then. Shall we return to Neo’s place for the time being and revise our strategy? Perhaps Neo’s got his mits on some new information. Besides, ‘twould be wise to inquire about what the professor’s been up to.”

“………”

As Kouta spoke, I gazed off in the opposite direction of Neo’s Fifth Ward. In other words, towards the Second Ward. More specifically, I was trying to eyeball how wide the gap was between here and there. Seemingly catching on to what I was doing, Kouta asked, “what’s on your mind?” and twirled around to face me.

“I’m thinking about whether it would be possible to get to the Seventh Ward from here.”

“……I believe I told you ‘twas impossible.”

“But I’ve yet to hear the reason. Look, from what I can tell, the distance to the Second Ward is two metres. That’s about the same distance as the one between the Fifth and Fourth Wards… No, if anything, this one looks a bit shorter. Next, we’d go from the Second Ward to the Primary Ward… the central research ward where the professor is. I think I remember the gap between those two not being too wide either.”

“You’re awfully fixated on this, aren’t you…? Perhaps the obsessive one was you all along?” Kouta sounded somewhat exasperated. “‘Tis not consummate in the slightest.”

“Then tell me why. Why is it impossible?”

I didn’t have the right angle to gauge the distance between the Primary Ward and the Sixth Ward from here, nor the distance between the Sixth Ward and the all-important Seventh Ward. Was that the issue that Kouta was alluding to? I didn’t know. However, Kouta has spent far more time in this facility than I had. When it came to infiltration or breaking in, Kouta’s opinion held far more weight than mine. I knew that. And yet-

“I still can’t come up with any other way someone could break into the Seventh Ward while bypassing the security system.”

“If that’s all you can think of, then you’re better off not thinking at all,” Kouta said bluntly. “…You wouldn’t understand even if I explained it to you, so why not see it for yourself? For a backwards thinker, there’s no such thing as a waste of time, so ‘tis actually more wasteful to stand here and argue about it,”

Kouta said and began walking towards the Second Ward. Then, as casually as if hopping over one of the puddles, she found herself on the roof of the Second Ward. No matter how many times I assure myself it’s only two metres, her bravery despite the fact that a simple slip could cost her her life astonished me.

I followed after her, making my way to the Second Ward. Kouta moved quickly, reaching the opposite ledge of the roof in no time at all. Once there, she waited for me. I caught up, and when I looked, the gap between the Second and Primary wards was around three metres… No, not even. Compared to the gap between the Third and Fourth Wards, it may as well have been nothing.

With only a brief run-up, Kouta leapt to the Primary Ward. It was readily apparent that she was not giving it her all, as her light jump saw her safely on the roof of the other ward. As soon as she landed, she turned around and waited for me in silence. Given that this was already my fifth jump, I had naturally grown somewhat accustomed to it. That said, I hear it’s acrobats who’ve grown complacent who are in the most danger. I braced myself and jumped.

“…I guess this is some kind of helipad,” I muttered, standing at the edge of a giant circle (with a large ‘H’ drawn in the middle) painted on the roof of the Primary Ward. “This antenna’s pretty massive too… despite how remote we are, I guess this means we’re not entirely cut off from outside communication…”

“Changing your mind about asking for help from Kunagisa’s brother or that contractor you’re acquainted with?” Kouta prodded at me. “Go right ahead. I’m sure they’ll come to your rescue straight away.”

Kouta didn’t seem especially conscious of it, but the way she spoke– it almost sounded like she actually knew Nao and Aikawa. Despite my suspicions, I didn’t press the matter. In hindsight, I probably should have, but I’m neither clever enough nor psychic enough to regret things before they happened. “I don’t have to resort to that quite yet,” I dismissed her before looking eastward. Wards one through five had been arranged in a straight line, but likely due to being an architectural afterthought, the Sixth and Seventh Wards were built to the side. So when I turned, the Sixth Ward was directly ahead of me, with the Seventh Ward just beyond it.

Kouta gazed down at the rooftop as if she could peer straight though it. “What sort of scheme do you think Professor Kyouichirou is concocting at this very instant to implicate you… or rather, Miss Kunagisa as the culprit? Ha, even supposing we succeed at infiltrating the Seventh Ward, who’s to say we won’t run headfirst into someone already tampering with evidence?”

“We have no choice but to take that chance.”

“I suppose we don’t. We shall just have to trust Neo on that front. Even if putting trust in others isn’t your cup of tea.”

Kouta grinned inappropriately and began walking towards the Sixth Ward.

“I guess— wait, hang on?”

The roof of Sixth Ward didn’t have anything resembling an entrance. Right, according to Shito, the Sixth Ward was a power generator— what type was it again? A carbon generator? Silicone, maybe? Or was it nitrogen? I felt like it was one of those three, but then again, I wasn’t really listening so I can’t be too sure— and as such, there was no way in or out, let alone a line for hanging laundry. I suppose that was to be expected; however, looking across to the roof of the Seventh Ward, I couldn’t make out any doors either. On the eastern edge, there was a large water tank accompanied by a number of wide pipes, but aside from that, the roof was completely flat and empty.

“Is that what you meant, Kouta?” I asked, in a daze. “The Seventh ward never had a rooftop entrance to begin with—”

“It most certainly does,” Kouta replied immediately. “Can you not see it? How’s your eyesight?”

“I haven’t had it checked lately, but I haven’t noticed it getting any worse, so it’s probably still 20/20.”

“Then you should be able to see it. ‘Tis roughly three metres in front of the water tank. Do you see that round iron cover that resembles a manhole? ‘Tis more of an emergency exit than an entrance, but it should grant rooftop access.”

Exactly as Kouta said… once she pointed it out to me, I noticed the door (if I could even call it that). However, given the distance and the fact that the Sixth Ward still lay in between us, it was still barely visible. How powerful was Kouta’s eyesight for her to make out something like that? The glasses she wore must’ve just been for show after all.

“The reason we can’t use this path is something else entirely. Now then, shall we head to the Sixth Ward? You’ll understand once you get a closer look.”

Kouta said before leaping the gap between the Primary and Sixth Wards. The gap in question being roughly one and a half metres. It was so narrow that if we laid Kunagisa on her back with her arms outstretched, we could’ve used her as a bridge (as horrible as that was to imagine). I cleared the gap without even taking a running start. It was remarkably easy, but when I looked down, I felt a slight shiver run through me. You might be tempted to say, ‘well don’t look down then,’ but human psychology is a curious thing.

“Now. Do you finally understand,” before I’d even had a chance to catch up, Kouta called out to me from the far side of the Sixth Ward, “the reason why this route to Seventh Ward is impossible?”

“…………”

As I approached her, the meaning behind Kouta’s words grew more and more clear. By the time I made it halfway across the roof, I had no choice but to agree with her– no matter how much it pained me to.

“…what on earth?”

Without a doubt, this was… impossible.

The distance between the Sixth and Seventh Wards. Compared to the distances we’d already crossed— The two metres between the Fifth and Fourth Wards, the three and a half metres between the Fourth and Third Wards, the nearly two metres between the Third and Second Wards, the almost three metres between the Second and Primary Wards, and the metre and a half between the Primary and Sixth Wards— the difference was an order of magnitude. No, it wasn’t that great, but the gap was so distressingly large, that if you were to insist it was, I doubt anyone would correct you.

Five metres.

Five metres…

“Impossible, is it not?” Kouta repeated. “Now do you understand why I claimed this route was hopeless, dear friend?”

“I see…”

Five metres. Risking your life on a jump like this was beyond reckless. You wouldn’t be risking your life so much as throwing it away. I don’t know all that much about athletic records, but going off what Kouta said earlier, the world record’s eight metres and ninety-five centimetres. Let’s call it nine metres even. The gap between these two wards was a full four metres shorter. But just like when Kouta explained it to me the first time, I didn’t appreciate the comparison to the world record holders. I was Japanese, and not an especially well trained one at that. And while I may not be at Kunagisa’s level, I was most certainly the indoor type.

Five metres.

Surely, this was too much to ask of me.

“…Now then, no sense dawdling. Let’s return to Neo’s for the time being. Who’s to say there isn’t another route out there—?”

As I listened to Kouta’s empty placations— No, I wasn’t listening— I tormented myself over and over. I couldn’t shake the thought. ‘This was too much’. An unshakeable, immaculate impossibility.

“ ————————”

And yet,

For that very reason.

The crucified Utsurigi ‘Malignant Green’ Gaisuke. His arms severed, his eyes and brain devastated, his throat gouged out, dissected like a frog and gutted like a fish, and his shattered legs run through. That empty, inhuman, hollow room, stained an unsettling reddish-brown, and that bloody message— in the truest sense.

The research ward and its unflinching security system melded into one massive locked room. There was no record of anyone having entered. And apart from one exception, no record of anyone stepping foot outside. A crime only physically or logically possible to the security system’s former administrator, Kunagisa ‘Dead Blue’ Tomo, the leader and iron-fisted ruler of the TEAM responsible for rewriting Japan’s cyber law fifty-five times over. Her, and her alone.

The Mad Daemon Shadou Kyouichirou’s research facility.

It was absurd. This was no ordinary case. A crime so impossible, it left no room for argument. A murder so unusual, it defied explanation. A situation so anomalous, it was beyond reproach.

That’s why. That’s why.

The solution to this case had to be psycho logical. It had to be. It can’t just be the killer. I, too, had to be mad. That’s the logic here.

I breathed deep. Once. Twice. Three times.

“…Hold on. What are you planning, dear friend,” Kouta said suspiciously. “I suddenly had a terrible premonition.”

“It’s about to come true.”

I said, and from where I was standing—roughly ten metres away from the edge of the Seventh Ward— I took off. I had no room for error. None whatsoever. I couldn’t waste a single centimetre that was given to me. I thought nothing, I felt nothing, I even forgot I was still alive; every muscle was working at maximum capacity. My brain had long since ceased its function. Like a tin-man without a heart, it did as I commanded.

Not yet. Don’t jump yet. One more step.

“Wait—you idiot!”

For the first time since I’d met her, Kouta’s refined mannerisms gave way to a genuine outburst of emotion— the instant after her jeers washed over me, I planted my left foot. It felt like subatomic particles were coursing through me, like all my blood was gushing out, like my head was being bathed in liquid nitrogen. While I’ve never been showered with subatomic particles, bled out, or doused in liquid nitrogen, if I had, I imagine this is what it’d feel like.

In other words.

I was set free from everything.

Liberated from everything.

Unfettered.

This is dying.

This is what it means to die.

To fade away.

To disappear.

To end.

Death.

With this. I can die. I will die. I have died. I am dying. I was dying. I had been dying. I will be dying. I will have died. I’m dead.

“And that’s why—”

As my life flashed before my eyes, I was suddenly reminded of something someone once told me.

“You should just die.”

Yeah.

You’re right.

chapters.title: Psycho Logical (Part Two)
chapters.text:
Psycho Logical (Part Two)

2

…………………

“Kusanagi? Kuginasa? What was it again?”

“Kunagisa, it’s Kunagisa. K-U-N-A-G-I-S-A, Kunagisa. Then Tomo, for friend. Kunagisa Tomo.”

“Hm, I see. Kunagisa, huh? Your hair’s pretty cool.”

“You can call me Tomo.”

“Is that right? Then you can call me Tomo, too.”

“That’s confusing. I’m gonna call you Iichan.”

“Then I’ll call you Iichan, too.”

“That’s confusing.”

…………………

……………………………………

“That one’s like a baby bird.”

“A baby bird? What do you mean?”

“Do you know what imprinting is? They say when baby birds are born, the first living thing they see, no matter what it is, they love it like a parent… Although that’s nothing more than superstition.”

“You think your sister sees me that way?”

“I do. As of now, you’ve become her one and only compass. You’ve become something completely irreplaceable. A fact I find utterly unpleasant.”

“It’s no fun for me either.”

“You’ve been given a privilege. The privilege to demand obedience from Tomo as you see fit, as if you were her parent. You’ve gained complete ownership over Kunagisa Tomo.”

“Some parents are killed by their children, Nao.”

…………………………………

…………………………………

“Wanna die? Wanna die and make amends? Wanna be forgiven?”

“………………”

“Then pray. Just pray. Cry, and beg for forgiveness. Clasp your hands in prayer.”

“………………”

“Like I once prayed to Kunagisa Nao, call upon god or even the devil.”

“………………”

“When I’m born again, please make me a dog or a cat.”

“………………”

“I’d be fine with a pig, or a cow, or even a monkey. Hell, I’d settle for a worm. Just so long as I never run into Kunagisa Tomo…”

…………………………………

…………………………………

……………………………………

I’d probably only lost consciousness for a moment— less time than it would take you to blink. I was lying on the bare concrete roof of the Seventh Ward. I suppose it’s more accurate to say I was splayed out. I’d likely fumbled the landing. My legs hurt a little. However, that was clearly just due to the impact. If so, then the instant I landed, out of relief— or perhaps despondency— my senses must’ve briefly abandoned me. It seems I had unconsciously braced myself, so none of my injuries were especially injurious. Compared to the beating I took from Suzunashi and Miss Kokoromi this morning, it may as well have been just some minor bruising.

“Good grief— I must have done something terrible in a past life…”

I had survived.

I made the jump.

As I came to terms with that fact, I slowly picked myself up. At least I tried to.

“——I am beyond exasperated with you right now.”

A voice came from right beside me, causing me to abandon the attempt halfway through. There, with her denim coat flapping in the breeze, stood Ishimaru Kouta, glaring down at me.

“……Huh? Wait, wha-…”

I turned my head in the direction I had just come from, in other words, towards the Sixth Ward. Kouta wasn’t there. That meant, supposing I hadn’t failed the jump after all and this was all some sort of hallucination as I teetered between life and death, Kouta had successfully made the jump as well. While the former didn’t seem out of the realm of possibility (better odds than a coin toss at least), the pain I felt surging through my body was undoubtedly real. That said, phantom pain is a real phenomenon. Since I couldn’t be sure, I figured I’d ask.

“I’m alive, right?”

“You’re not dead, I’ll grant you that much,” Kouta replied coldly, “but I wouldn’t call anyone who would senselessly rush to their own death truly alive.”

“I see…”

This time I succeeded in picking myself up, and I rose to my feet. My muscles, bones, and sinew all appeared to be in working order. I did something resembling stretches before turning to Kouta and saying, “So you made the jump too, huh?” Kouta didn’t answer; she just let out a huge sigh.

“I may have made a mistake in choosing you as my compatriot,” she said. “I never expected I’d be party to such recklessness. This is not consummate. Not consummate in the slightest.”

“But, with this, we just proved it’s possible to jump from the Sixth Ward to the Seventh— in other words, we found a way in. Everything turned out alright, Kouta. We’ve established a route into the Seventh Ward. This case is no longer a locked room—”

In other words, the researchers were no longer above suspicion. By moving from rooftop to rooftop, I had proven with my very body that the researchers could've infiltrated the Seventh Ward without ever needing to bother with what was previously thought to be the only entrance. That way, the security wouldn’t have logged their comings and goings from their own wards, let alone the Seventh Ward.

Of course, all I’d done is prove that anyone could be the culprit; I still had no clue who it might be. At the very least, there was no longer any reason—any good reason, that is— for all suspicion to rest on Kunagisa. None at all.

“You don’t even stop to consider the consequences of your actions, do you?” Kouta’s voice was still as cold as ever. She seemed extraordinarily upset by my unilateral decision making. “‘Everything turned out alright’? Hilarious. Don’t make me laugh. Perhaps you should have Miss Miyoshi cut open that brain of yours. I’m sure she’ll find all your wires crossed.”

“That’s a bit harsh… Look, I’m sorry for running ahead, but wasn’t it worth it to prove that this gap isn’t as uncrossable as it looks?”

“I assumed you had the common sense to listen until I was done explaining. In what way have I ever, even once, claimed, ‘you can’t jump from the Sixth Ward to the Seventh’?”

“…………?”

Kouta’s words naturally raised some questions— or should I say, they evoked a feeling not all too dissimilar to unease. That’s right. When it came to outrageousness, there was no one more outrageous than Kouta. Whether it be casually infiltrating the facility under the name Zerozaki, cooperating with someone as shady as Neo, or, regardless of her own reasons for doing so, rescuing Kunagisa, Suzunashi, and me. The risks she took dwarfed any potential reward. So there’s no way Kouta would be this upset simply over me taking a risk— that, while life threatening, didn’t actually cost me my life—would she?

In other words… there was some other reason, wasn’t there?

Once I’d figured that much out— I began thinking. Then, I realized. I figured it out. That’s right. Given my lack of training, I never should have been able to clear five metres. So, despite knowing my odds of success, how come I still attempted it? Why? I must have noticed it subconsciously.

I turned back to the Sixth Ward once more.

And then,

“……Oh man………”

I see.

That’s how it is.

That’s what you were getting at, weren’t you, Kouta?

Acceptance. From the bottom of my heart. Then despair. From the bottom of my heart. Both for my own idiocy, and the truth behind Kouta’s insistence that ‘this route was impossible.’

“I’m not in the habit of complaining about what’s already said and done, nor do I find any pleasure in it,” Kouta’s frigid voice called out from behind me. “But please recognize that you’ve put us both in a far more precarious position than we already were, dear friend. Should you run off on your own again, I shall have no choice but to rethink our alliance.”

“…I understand…”

I nodded before once again confirming the reality of our situation. I wanted to confirm whether it was possible I had been mistaken, only to confirm beyond a shadow of a doubt that I wasn’t.

When compared to the Seventh Ward, the Sixth Ward was just a little bit taller. Which is to say, the Seventh Ward was constructed a little shorter than all the rest. It was hard to tell from the Sixth Ward, but from this side—from the shorter side— it was strikingly obvious. The roof of the Sixth Ward sat somewhat higher—by a couple dozen centimetres or so— than the Seventh Ward’s. Now then, as for what that means-

It meant the jump from that side to this side was easier. Even if the horizontal distance was five metres, gravity and the angle of the jump gave you an additional couple dozen centimetres of wiggle room. That was likely the reason I made it. It would’ve been nice to attribute it to my fiery resolve allowing me surpass my own limits, but the realistic explanation was far more convincing.

But so what if the jump had been easier? The fact that this ward was the only one that sat lower than the other wards could only mean one thing,

“……We can’t go back,”

I muttered.

I hadn’t meant to mutter, but I did regardless.

“Precisely, dear friend,” Kouta twisted the knife. “The reason this route is ineffective is precisely so. It seems that since this ward was built later, it is the only ward that is not a uniform height. The Sixth Ward is taller. So yes, unless you intend to leap around seven metres, I don’t suspect you will be making it back.”

“…………”

“If you wish to see for yourself, then by all means, don’t hold back on my account.”

“I’ll pass…” I took a step back- an act that was already more than I could bear and I crumbled to my knees. “……Oh man……I’m such an idiot.”

“‘Tis consummate so long as you understand. Most things can be smoothed over with an apology, after all.” Kouta shrugged, her icy tone regaining its warmth at long last. “Besides, I won’t deny I’m somewhat to blame for not being as forthcoming as I could have been.”

She had a point. If she hadn’t beaten around the bush, insisting, ‘you’ll know it when you see it,’ and had told me straightforwardly, ‘the Seventh Ward is a different height, so even if you can cross over, you wouldn’t be able to make it back,’ this all could have been avoided. That said, I really should have known it when I saw it, so I suppose it’s still my responsibility. The only explanation I could come up with was that the blood had rushed to my head.

“I guess the locked room remains locked after all…” I mumbled dejectedly. “…but maybe one of the faculty members is actually extraordinarily athletic.”

“Even supposing they are, ‘tis still not consummate, dear friend. There is yet another reason I consider this route impossible. Do you remember what it is?” Kouta asked. “Last night, when you and I met– It was just starting to rain, was it not?”

“Rain…?”

“My eyes fell on the roof beneath my feet. They had mostly dried by now, but there were still traces of the puddles left behind by the night before.

That’s right. Rain. It was raining all night.

“…I-” Why had I only realized that now? “Uh…”

“Miyoshi claimed the time of death to be some time around one o’clock in the morning… For our purposes, let’s say that’s when they crossed from the Sixth Ward to the Seventh Ward. However, that’s not all she said, is it? For whatever reason, the arms were severed several hours later. In other words, on their return trip—once they were done with Utsurigi’s murder and the redecoration that ensued— would it not have been raining?”

It was clear what that meant. It couldn’t have been simpler. A record you set under perfect conditions would be impossible in the rain. And you definitely weren’t about to surpass it.

I had been careless. Far too careless. If I had just remembered that it had been raining last night, I might even have been able to realize this route was impossible on my own. I had been hopelessly stupid. I always panic and rush headlong into things, only for them to blow up in my face. Even death couldn’t cure my idiocy.

“What do we do…?”

Far from dispelling the locked room, it had only sealed even tighter. What’s more, we found ourselves sealed inside. Naturally, since Kouta and I didn’t possess a key-card or ID, didn’t know the password, weren’t registered in the vocal or retinal scan system, and didn’t have administrator access like Kunagisa, we couldn’t use the front door. And even though this research ward was shorter than the others, I wasn’t about to leap off like a flying squirrel. And while I couldn’t say for certain, as far as I could tell, Kouta didn’t have wings. What’s more, the building was windowless. We were boxed in– in the truest sense of the word.

“You’re down to two hours and forty minutes. ‘Tis not much time to think,” Kouta said after a moment’s pause. “For now, shall we get to work? We managed to infiltrate the Seventh Ward at great pains— for better or worse— so why don’t we investigate, and think about what comes next later, dear friend?”

“…You’re awfully optimistic.”

“Because I’m not the one in peril,”

Kouta said as she began to open the manhole-like cover next to the water tanks. Either due to rust, or because it was designed to be unwieldy, it didn’t open easily. I lent a hand, and the two of us finally managed to pry open the iron cover.

“No need to be so crestfallen, dear friend. Perhaps we’ll find a sturdy rope somewhere in the ward. Who’s to say we won’t find something strong enough to hold our weight? If we do, then we’ll be able to escape.”

“Do you actually think we’ll find one?”

“Not a chance,” Kouta’s consolation left something to be desired. “Shall we be off, dear friend?”

Regardless, that’s the only option we had left. Using the iron ladder, the two of us made our way into the Seventh Ward.

chapters.title: Psycho Logical (Part Two)
chapters.text:
Psycho Logical (Part Two)

3

Thirty minutes later.

The gruesome smell still lingered at the scene of Utsurigi’s murder; Kouta and I stood idly, without a word spoken between us, as if we were merely there out of a grim sense of obligation.

Kouta leaned her tall frame against the wall by the door, her arms crossed and eyes closed as if deep in thought about something. Looking at her now, you could even mistake her for some sort of philosopher. That’s how dreadfully serene and detached she was. In direct contrast, like a shaved cat, I had been walking frantic circles around this hideous, reddish brown, unfurnished room for quite some time now. It was as if I had forgotten how to walk.

Shit. I never thought a time limit would be this painful. The remaining time— two hours and fifteen minutes. And that was a generous estimate.

Now that Utsurigi’s body had been removed from his private quarters and from the Seventh Ward altogether, it was like the air itself had shifted. It was like it left nothing but emptiness in its wake. I visited this place last night, and then again this morning. This was my third total visit, and yet the atmosphere was different each time. I never liked that man, nor did I believe I ever could have, but the first time I’d entered this room, despite how vehemently we argued, was still the least objectionable of the three. As for the most objectionable, that would have to be right now.

“—Have you not discovered anything?” It was the first time in the last twenty-five minutes that Kouta opened either her eyes or her mouth. “I can’t say the remaining time is looking all that consummate, my dear friend.”

“I haven’t found anything,” I spoke for the first time in twenty-eight minutes. “Not only have I not figured out the trick, I’ve completely lost the plot by this point… I sincerely have no clue.”

“Is that whining, I hear?”

“It’s the truth. I’ve been wracking my brain this entire time. Anybody else would have come up with something by now, but I’ve got nothing. I don’t have the slightest idea what thought process could’ve led the culprit to do this.”

“Thought process, you say? …There’s always the chance they weren’t thinking at all.”

“…Yeah. That’s always possible.”

If so, then my hands were tied. As an uninvolved bystander, even if I were able to predict someone’s thought process, I couldn’t read their thoughts themselves. Of course I couldn’t.

“It appears ritualistic… you could almost call it religious. No offence to religious people. This case isn’t just bizarre, it’s downright uncanny. You can always explain away the bizarre, but there’s nothing to be done about the uncanny. It doesn’t get more gruesome than that.”

“Is that so?” Kouta sounded surprised. “I’ve seen plenty of bodies far more gruesome than that. Dead or otherwise. I try not to rank them, but if I had to pick the worst of the bunch, it would have to be a certain severed head I came across two years back.”

“You mean a headless corpse?” My train of thought wasn’t going anywhere, so I humoured her. “If that’s all, then I’ve seen one too.”

“No, it wasn’t a corpse. The head managed to survive on its own.”

“That’s impossible. If you were just a head, you would die.”

“Not if you receive the proper medical care. After all, the heart is nothing more than a pump. The lungs serve only to provide oxygen, and you wouldn’t be wrong to say the other organs exist to create nutrients. So long as the brain still receives blood, oxygen, and nutrients, it’s entirely possible to live on as just a head. Of course, since they had no throat or any other organs, they weren’t able to speak, but we still managed to communicate.”

“……What’s the point of all that?”

“There was no point. Just curiosity. You can’t say you weren’t a little curious just now, can you? About whether someone could truly live as just a head. I understand that feeling well. Compared to something like that—” Kouta set her eyes on the far wall. The traces of where Utsurigi had been pinned still remained. “—the manner in which Utsurigi was killed doesn’t seem all that illogical. The opposite, even.”

Kouta gently picked herself up off the wall, and opened the door.

“Where are you going?”

“You’re lucky I’m so considerate. ‘Tis easier to think when you’re alone, is it not?”

“Well, sure… but where are you headed?”

“Have you forgotten my occupation?” Kouta flashed a daring smile. “We finally managed to infiltrate the impregnable Seventh Ward. I might as well pick up a few things. On the off chance they haven’t already disposed of them, that is… regardless, I’ll be back soon.”

With that, Kouta stepped out of the room.

“Occupation, huh? … but I’m just a student…” I muttered, as I made my way over to where Kouta once stood, before similarly propping myself up against the wall. “……why did things turn out this way…? Why do things always turn out like this, every goddamn time?”

I complained. To no one.

“I can’t take it anymore. I– really can’t. I’m sick of it. I’m sick of it. I’m sick of it. It’s too much.”

Damnit. God fucking damnit. You subhuman bastard. You may as well die right here and now. Let your blood muddle together with Utsurigi’s. Take that knife out of your breast pocket, plunge it into your stomach, and wrench it upwards. Drag your guts out and scatter them across the room. Liven things up by chewing your own liver, and then plunge the blade into your worthless eyes. Once you pierce your own brain, it may finally start to work properly. Drag the knife down your skull, across your throat, and through your collarbone; carve through your sternum and sever your aorta, and if you still have the strength and presence of mind, finish with your heart. That way, you’re certain to create a splendid fountain of blood. The only question is whether the knife would hold out that long. Even if it doesn’t, you’re sure to die anyway. And if you’re born again, study, study, study, so you can become a researcher. Open up a research facility in the heart of the mountains, and even if it all falls apart, don’t go insane; continue your thankless work day and night for the sake of the world and all the people who live there. Toil away in obscurity in the name of the needy and the disadvantaged. Don’t buy into the cheap stereotype that ‘all scientists are mad.’ Always think of other people. Become the kind of person who can put others first.

“…Oh man…what am I even thinking?”

Your life’s basically over once you start fantasizing about your next. I’m just so tired. With my back still pressed to the wall, I slowly sank to the floor. My heart felt too heavy. Even though I had fully crumpled to the ground, I couldn’t shake the feeling that I was still falling. I gripped my head and sighed deeply.

“I’ve finally snapped…”

Kunagisa’s words ran through my mind. If I ever felt like I wasn’t enough, I could always call Nao. Or perhaps Humanity’s Strongest, the Red Contractor. If I just ask for her help, I wouldn’t have to bear this agony anymore. I could borrow a phone from Neo…… or maybe connect to the network and send out a message. It’d take a bit of effort, but it wouldn’t be all too difficult in the long run. Despite having an out like that, my contradictory nature meant I couldn’t take it. But am I really tolerant enough… righteous enough to forgive that contradiction?

Haven’t I done enough?

“……Of course I haven’t.”

There’s no point in putting in effort unless you see it all the way through.

Even if you could hardly call this ‘putting in an effort.’

“How pathetic…”

There’s a difference between scarcity and value. I mumbled and stood up, not even trying to hide my frustration with myself over how dangerously close I came to blaming my own powerlessness on the world— No, over how dangerously close I came to revealing that I already did, and for trying to run away.

As I thought about how much time I wasted on pointless wallowing, I gazed at the far wall.

《You just watch,『DEAD BLUE』!!》

“《Shut up and watch,》huh…? Could this be some kind of code?”

It’s not impossible that the culprit had left some kind of clue on purpose. Ignoring any potential inconsistencies, I took the twenty letters written on the wall and tried rearranging them. I tried removing letters, adding letters, writing it in other languages, and a number of other tests, but it never amounted to anything conclusive. Halfway through, I managed to forcefully come up with ‘DARAKU ZANMAI’, the Japanese reading of the characters used to spell ‘Mad Daemon’, but that felt like too much of a stretch. I might have to take the message at face value after all.

By the time I came to that conclusion, I only had two hours left.

“Honestly, Kunagisa, what am I supposed to do?”

I called out for Kunagisa just like I had long ago, back before I knew she was a girl. Naturally, the Kunagisa Tomo from six years ago wasn’t here, and the current Kunagisa Tomo was still below the Fourth Ward. Obviously, there was no answer.

However, in that answer’s stead– Suddenly, out of nowhere— an ear-piercing alarm rang out from the hallway. No— this was no mere alarm. It was a shockwave. The air pressure alone was enough to batter my eardrums. The alarm was so harsh, that even someone with perfect pitch would be hopeless to place it. It carried in through the open door.

“What the- Did I do something!?”

I yelled as I rushed outside. There was no real reason for me to be shouting, it’s just that the alarm was so loud that if I didn’t, I wouldn’t have been able to hear myself speak. As I stepped out into the hallway, the sound got even louder. It’s like someone was crashing a symbol directly inside my skull.

“—————!”

I could no longer hear myself, even when I shouted. My own voice could do nothing to resist the oncoming tsunami of sound. There had to be a speaker around here somewhere. As that thought occurred to me, I clasped both hands over my ears and desperately scanned the ceiling. Unless I find and destroy the speaker soon, my already unstable brain would go completely insane.

But before I could even find the speaker, the alarm abruptly stopped. I cautiously removed my hands from my ears, but I quickly thought better of it. What if this was merely the eye of the storm? It was naïve to be comforted by a momentary reprieve when a second wave might be just around the corner. Hang on a second, I’m indoors, not about to be swept up in a typhoon. Oh man, I was completely disoriented. What was I even talking about? Am I stupid?

“Still feeling consummate, I hope.” The stairwell door opened as Kouta returned from downstairs. “Greetings, I hope you haven’t missed me.”

“Missed you? You’ve only been gone fifteen minutes—”

“Is that so? How consummate.”

Kouta grinned and pulled the brim of her cap down. Almost as if she were trying to avoid my gaze. No doubt about it. Kouta was unbelievably suspicious.

“Kouta… what did you do?”

“I got my hands on these,” Kouta reached into her coat and pulled out what I believed to be four MO disks which she fanned out for me to see. “They don’t pertain to my objective, but Utsurigi’s research data is too good a find to pass up.”

“I see you found the alarm as well…” even I was surprised by the exasperation in my voice. “I know this is rich coming from me, but… did you ever stop to consider the consequences?”

“How rude, of course I did. I’m in the middle of thinking about them as we speak.”

It’s a bit late for that.

“What a perfect pair we make…” I muttered. A joke that felt all too real. “What should we do? That sound just now likely carried all the way to the Primary Ward. Then again, the place is sealed tight, so maybe not. Either way, the Professor should have gotten some sort of security alert.”

“How splendid it would be if they mistook it for a false alarm, but life is hardly ever that consummate.” She still talked as if it had nothing to do with her, despite the fact that she was directly responsible this time. “How bothersome.”

How bothersome indeed.

I was used to Kouta dragging me along, but I can’t say I expected her to drag me down like this. In all sincerity, what nonsense.

“…Let’s escape to the roof. They might not find us there.”

“Agreed. ‘Tis certainly favourable to staying inside at least.” Kouta answered urgently before taking off towards the stairwell. We opened the door with the lock picking blade, went up the stairs, climbed the ladder, threw open the iron cover, and stepped out onto the roof. After a brief stretch, Kouta began crawling her way towards the roof’s western edge. I didn’t know what she was up to, but I found myself following suit. From there, I could see two figures jogging down the cedar pathway— or was it oak? I can’t quite remember— at a half jog (the contradictory nature of that last sentence should illustrate just how shaken I was). I see, we were lying down so that they wouldn’t spot us. And here I was, certain that Kouta was just an eccentric like Samuel Beckett. Okay, maybe not.

“—...Let’s see.” If I strained my eyes, I could just make out their silhouettes. “…That’s Shito……, ……and Misachi……isn’t it?”

“It would appear so.” Still crawling, Kouta made her way back to where she could no longer be seen from the ground before kipping up to a standing position. “They must have been ordered by the professor to come and take a look…or so it would seem.”

The two of them rounded the corner and faded out of sight. They were headed towards the Seventh Ward’s entrance, the insulated steel door. After confirming that was the case, I crawled back just like Kouta had. However, now that I think about it, they wouldn’t have been able to see me anyway because of the angle, so there was no real point in doing so.

“While I wouldn’t call this consummate, I suppose we should still count ourselves fortunate,” Kouta said. “I was concerned a whole squadron of guards would descend on us……but we should have no issues handling a couple of youngsters. The professor must have deemed it a false alarm after all.”

“That’d be nice… still, that doesn’t change the fact that getting caught would be really bad.”

“Then come this way,” Kouta gripped my hand and forcefully pulled me along. I didn’t know where she was taking me, but it turned out to be behind the water tank. Once we stepped over the numerous pipes, she guided me to a small spot that couldn’t be seen from the roof’s entrance. “As long as we remain here, we should evade detection.”

“Sure, they might not be able to spot us at a glance…but…”

I wouldn’t call our hiding place spacious. By any estimate, it was only large enough to hide one person. Kouta was quite tall, and while I wasn’t exactly on the larger side, I was still a grown man; there’s no way the two of us could hide here together.

“Of course we can.”

Kouta laughed mischievously— that’s when I knew exactly what was about to happen— with an abrupt tug, she pulled me in tight. From a third-party-perspective, it might appear as if she were giving me a hug, no, that’s exactly what this was. She pressed our bodies together, wrapped her long arms around my back, and placed my chin on her right shoulder. Naturally, I could feel Kouta’s breathing, her heartbeat, and her body heat. Naturally, she could also feel mine.

“This way we’ll only take up one person’s worth of space.”

“—this might prove to be a problem.” My arms had already been pinned, so I couldn’t put up any resistance. “A very big problem.”

“Do you dislike problems?”

“I tend to also hate solutions…”

“My-my, how innocent,” Kouta chuckled. It was a decidedly suggestive laugh. “By the way, I have something to discuss with you. As I was searching for those MO disks, I tried looking around for anything we could use as a rope.”

“And did you?” I asked, as I tried to stop my heart from pounding. Since the heart is an involuntary muscle, I obviously had no success. “Find a rope, that is?”

“I did not. There were plenty of computer cables and things of that nature, we weren’t lacking in that department, but even if we strung them together, we’d never reach the Sixth Ward…Besides, if all the cables went missing, they’d surely know something was up.”

“Fair point…”

Conveniently finding a rope capable of holding a person’s weight in a place like this was likely a pipe dream to begin with. If we couldn’t find a rope, then what about something rope-adjacent…? I tried to concentrate, but the scent of Kouta’s hair distracted me. No, if anything these thoughts were what was distracting me from the scent of her hair. Calm down. Calm down. Think about something else.

“…Hair, huh… Kouta, what about hair?”

“I beg your pardon? What about hair?” Kouta said, pulling me in even tighter. Since Kouta was taller than me, this whole affair felt horribly infantilizing. Suzunashi also treated me like a child, but how should I put it, it felt completely different when she did it. “You’re not talking about my hair, are you?”

“Not at all…I’m talking about whether you could use hair as a makeshift rope?”

I’ve heard that hair is surprisingly sturdy. Of course, a single strand wouldn’t amount to much, but a couple thousand bundled together might make a good substitute. There’s also no shortage of incidents where hair has been used to strangle someone, so if I had to say whether it was possible or not—

“Ah, are you talking about Koutari then, dear friend?” Kouta spoke into my ear, almost like a whisper. I shivered. “I admit, he went full skinhead after a few mere words from you; there was no need for all that—”

Exactly. There’s no world in which my words should’ve held that much weight. Didn’t that suggest the reason he cut– no, shaved his long hair must’ve been something else. My mind wandered back to that blunt, taciturn researcher.

“‘For example— let’s say Koutari managed to successfully infiltrate the Seventh Ward using the same route we took. Then he murdered Utsurigi. After crucifying him to the wall, he tried to return only to realize the jump was impossible. What’s more, it was raining, so it was twice as impossible. Even so, he absolutely couldn’t afford to hang around the scene of the crime. That’s why he needed a rope–”

“And you’re saying he used his own hair?” Kouta said. “‘Tis reasonably consummate, but there’s a slight problem.”

“And that problem is?” Was it a larger problem than the fact you were currently stroking my thigh? “Tell me, Kouta.”

“First of all, none of the wards have any kind of fence or railings. Even if you were able to throw a rope across, there’d be nothing to snag it on. In order to snag it on the eavestrough, you would require some sort of hook. Secondly, there still remains the problem of distance.”

“The distance— you mean five metres? If he used a rope, I don’t think we’d need to take the angle into account.”

“Let’s suppose Koutari’s hair was a metre long. When I saw him from a distance, he did seem rather bushy, but even if you used all of it, once you divide it into five equal parts, it wouldn’t have been able to hold a person’s weight. No matter how skillfully he tied them, he would have only been able to cross four metres at most.”

Five equal parts— four metres. That’s right, in order to fashion it into a strong enough rope, you’d need to twist the strands together; there was also the issue of tying the knots. Of course it wouldn’t reach five metres. Kouta was right, four metres looked like the limit. Even if we gave every benefit of the doubt imaginable— like Koutari’s hair suddenly growing— and it managed to reach, there was still the first problem to contend with: there was no hook. Just when I’d come up with a suitably psycho logical deduction— even as I was at dire risk of losing my chastity!— it seemed like Koutari had simply chopped his hair off after all. How misleading could you get? If this were a mystery novel, I’d be tempted to call it unfair.

“And what about Jumping the distance…are we sure it’s not possible somehow?”

“If you were amongst the world’s best, I suppose it wouldn’t be impossible. However, I don’t think we shall find any average human capable of such a feat.”

“Human…” That word stuck out to me. “…Then it might be possible for something inhuman, wouldn’t it?”

“Huh?” Kouta replied incredulously. “What are you saying? It can’t be. You aren’t seriously suggesting our culprit is some kind of youkai, are you? Goodness… I don’t particularly mind, but I wonder what the others would think if they heard you say that. Be careful who you share that with.”

“Don’t just immediately jump to youkai. It’s not like people and youkai are the only two things that exist. There are plenty of other animals… like dogs for instance.” I continued, my mind still racing. If I didn’t keep up the momentum my concentration would start to waver. “It’s not impossible that a large dog might be able to leap seven metres, right?”

“Are you talking about the three dogs in Kasugai’s care?”

“I suppose I am. A so-called animal culprit theory.” I nodded. When I did, my face was brought even closer to Kouta’s body. Oh man. “…and even if that’s wrong, I think I remember someone saying something about boars on this mountain… and if the boars can’t make the jump…then…birds or something…”

“Are you sane? How can you rattle off so many preposterous ideas one after the other? I’m impressed.” Kouta didn’t sound impressed in the slightest. “So tell me, how would a dog murder Utsurigi? Or are you saying the dog managed to chop him up with a knife? ‘Tis a remarkably fantastical theory, but don’t you think it’s a little far-fetched?”

“Maybe if you trained them, then… No, you’re right. It’s not possible after all.” There was no chance I could win that argument, so I abandoned it all together. “…Shit. Are we still no closer to deciding the culprit…?”

“‘Deciding’? Don’t you mean ‘deducing’?”

“We can’t just come up empty handed, so we’ve got to decide on one eventually, don’t we? …More importantly, isn’t this enough? Shito and Misachi must be long gone by now. They’ve gotta be.”

I tried to un-contort myself from around Kouta, but she refused to let me go, saying, “We can’t relax quite yet.” But even if we couldn’t relax, it had been ten or fifteen minutes since Shito and Misachi had entered the Seventh Ward—meaning I had spent the last ten or fifteen minutes in Kouta’s arms— so it was likely safe to assume they had concluded it was a false alarm after all.

“Kouta, I-” “Shh”

Kouta forcefully silenced my protest. To be specific, she grabbed the back of my head and pressed my face into her shoulder so I couldn’t speak. When I looked out past the water tank to see what was going on, the manhole cover that led to the roof had already begun to move slightly. Naturally, there was no reason an inorganic, non-mechanical, iron lid should be moving on its own—

“Shit! What’s with this cover!? It’s heavy as hell! Damnit! Who does he think I am, an Olympic weightlifter?!”

It was Shito’s voice. I could hear it coming from the other side of the entrance. He seemed to be having trouble lifting the cover.

“—I never expected them to go out of their way to check the roof…” I lamented. “I guess they’re being cautious…given the circumstances, I can’t say I blame them…”

“‘Tis only natural given the sudden disappearance of numerous MO disks,”

The thief said. That’s right. The reason the alarm rang in the first place was because of Kouta’s sticky fingers. In that case, the room she took them from was likely the first place they looked. If they noticed the disks were missing, then there’s no way they’d chalk this up as a false alarm. Of course they’d perform a thorough sweep of the whole ward.

“You should have just put them back…”

“You can’t exactly call yourself a first-rate thief if you give something back once you’ve stolen it, now can you? Come, squeeze in a little tighter. We shall be spotted.”

Squeeze, Kouta’s grip on me tightened as she attempted to force our bodies ever closer together. Naturally, we couldn’t possibly get any closer, so all she effectively did was smush us together harder. If Shito spotted us like this, I’d be hard pressed to come up with an excuse. With that in mind, I wrapped my arms around Kouta’s back as well. If I was to be found eating poison, I might as well finish the plate. I’d scarf down the table and chairs while I’m at it.

“My-my, how risqué, dear friend,” Kouta smiled delightedly. “I must say, I don’t find the thought utterly without appeal.”

“Well, I do… so I’m begging you, please keep quiet…”

Apparently getting the hang of it, Shito finally managed to lift up the cover. He slowly dragged his small frame out of the hole and onto the roof.

“Ah– Shit, what a pain in the ass… Why am I stuck doing this when I’m so damn busy with everything else… It’s ridiculous… it’s not like we’re actually gonna find an intruder… how would they even get in in the first place… there’s a limit to how cautious you can be, Misachi…”

He grumbled to himself the entire time. It seems like Shito’s the type who always talks to himself. This sparked a newfound sense of kinship within me. Especially the part where most of the things he said were complaints.

Shito sealed the manhole cover, and looked around where he stood.

“Not a soul…” Shito muttered. “Right side’s clear. Left side too…God, I feel like an idiot…”

It didn’t appear like Shito was planning on doing any kind of extensive search. In which case, we really had found the perfect hiding spot. Our hiding posture was still somewhat problematic, however. Oh man. I was nearing my limit. Ahh. I was starting to get light-headed.

“And I haven’t managed to get a hold of the Kunagisa Syndicate either… Honestly…” Shito continued his monologuing as he once again gripped the manhole cover. “What’s gonna happen… I mean, why use such a cute girl as a lab rat? It’s insane. Are you tryna make another one like me, professor? —What’s craziest is tryna do that to one of the Kunagisa Syndicate’s own.”

The Kunagisa Syndicate… Hearing that, all the reason I lost came flooding back. While it sounds like things hadn’t been smooth sailing, it seems like Professor Kyouichirou was proceeding exactly as Suzunashi, Neo, and Miss Kokoromi had predicted. However, that wasn’t what caught my attention; Shito’s tone was that of someone who still had some reservations. Shito was supposed to be someone unwaveringly sympathetic to the professor, so what happened?

That’s when I remembered Neo’s words. ‘Ougaki and Uze have their reasons for looking up to the professor. Be it respect, or gratitude, or what have you. That’s why, so long as you can offer them something greater, you’re golden.’ It likely all came down to simple arithmetic. Add, subtract, multiply, and divide. At this very moment, Shito was probably wavering. Then– If that were true—

Suddenly, Shito paused as he was about to open the cover. Not only did he pause, but he was staring in our direction. Doubtfully, as if suspicious of something, Shito stared intensely at the water tank Kouta and I were hiding behind. Did he notice us? No, there’s no way. In just a moment, he’ll be on his way. There’s no way he could have seen us. There’s no way he could have seen us, and yet—

“Oi, is someone there?” Shito finally asked. “Is someone behind that tank?”

I almost let out an audible gasp, but Kouta muffled that too.

“If someone’s there, then come on out!” Shito let go of the manhole cover and stood back up. “Jig’s up, it’s obvious someone’s there! You hear me?! If you’re not gonna come out, then I’m gonna come to you!”

“—I suppose there’s no other option,” Kouta said, reluctantly letting go of me. “Wait here, won’t you?”

“Huh? Wait, hang o–”

“I’m coming out!”

Kouta yelled out to Shito. Then, in a whisper, she said, “until everything’s over, don’t come out no matter what.” No sooner had she said that than she pushed me down, made her way around the tank, and stood out in the open where Shito could see her.

I didn’t even have time to stop her.

Even if I did, I wouldn’t have been able to find the words. After all, despite the horrible predicament we found ourselves in, the instant I saw her confident expression– an expression that seemed to say,‘‘tis nothing to worry about’– I knew there were no words that could have stopped her to begin with.

“—Eh? I was right?” Shito’s voice was dripping with confusion. “Wait… Hang on… Who the hell are you?”

“Shall I introduce myself?” Kouta smiled at him. “The name is Ishimaru Kouta. However, perhaps you know me better as Zerozaki Itoshiki.”

“…The intruder from three days ago,” Shito replied. “…What’s this? That voice… you’re a woman? You’re massive… not as massive as the other one, though.”

“Interested in women, are you, boy?” Kouta nonchalantly approached him. “How consummate.”

“Don’t move! I won’t let you get away with this!”

“With what?” Kouta played dumb. “We can’t converse without getting closer, now can we? That is the reason you called me out, is it not?”

“Shit- I said, don’t move! —I’m warning you!”

Shito backpedaled as he spoke. There was no reason for him to retreat– it’s just that– he was probably horrified. Kouta’s presence felt utterly unknowable. It reminded me of our first meeting. It was overwhelming. Dreadfully overwhelming. Faced with that, it was all you could do not to crumble. That’s why Shito was doing whatever he could to escape. It wasn’t so much unconscious as it was instinctual.

“Oh-ho—” Kouta stopped her approach. Right next to the entrance. “If you don’t care for conversation, then this is where I bid you farewell.”

“! Oh no you don’t!”

Shito launched himself at Kouta. His sense of duty must have won out over his sense of fear. However, while that may have been the right thing to do, I certainly wouldn’t call it wise. Because it should have been obvious to Shito that Kouta, an intruder who’d already made herself known to him, never had any intention of fleeing. Her words were nothing more than a blatant provocation.

And having fallen for that provocation, Shito had already lost.

Kouta spun backwards, evading Shito’s fist. Then, following through with her rotation, Kouta planted a long leg deep in Shito’s gut. The spinning kick appeared more akin to taekwondo than something out of karate. There are numerous martial arts out there, but only taekwondo would have a move that involved turning your back on your opponent.

Despite Shito already having doubled over, Kouta showed no mercy. With her other leg— utilising yet another taekwondo move— she buried her heel in Shito’s chest, forcefully righting his posture as he arched backwards. Then, utilising the momentum of yet another rotation, Kouta drove her fist into his right lung— A judo move this time.

“Gugh…gah!”

Unable to scream or even cry, he choked out more of a gasp. The instant that sound left his mouth, the battle was already decided. And yet Kouta wasn’t done. She still didn’t let up. An elbow strike to the stomach, a backhand to the heart, a knee strike to the solar plexus consummating in a leg sweep that brought Shito to the ground.

It was over before he could utter another cry. Shito seemed to have fainted. Although I suppose it’s more accurate to say Kouta had simply beat him unconscious. The targeted strikes to his vital organs must have been for that very purpose. Of course, while I couldn’t deny it had bought us a window to escape, I also couldn’t deny how excessive it all felt.

“Kouta—”

I was about to step out from behind the tank when–

“Freeeeeeeeeze!!!!”

The sudden explosion of anger, once again nailed me to the spot. I looked to see what was going on. There, aiming a handgun at Kouta, was Uze Misachi. Still crouched beside Shito’s collapsed body, Kouta looked somewhat surprised by Misachi’s sudden appearance.

“Oh my- Then again, there were two of you, weren’t there? — It completely slipped my mind.”

“—Stay where you are, please— I won’t hesitate to shoot.”

The pistol gripped in her hands… It was a Jericho 941. Just as I thought. An Israeli clone of the CZ-75. A multi-caliber pistol capable of using both 9mm and 41AE bullets. If I remember correctly, the same company went on to reuse the design in manufacturing the much more famous Desert Eagle. I can’t be positive because of my crummy memory, but one thing’s for certain, the issue at hand had nothing to do with the make and model.

Given the classified nature of the facility’s research, it wouldn’t be strange for security to be armed— but this was way out there. Completely beyond the pale. Even if Kouta was capable of easily dispatching someone like Shito, if she had to go up against an armed opponent, then—

“—Pfft- Ahahahahah!”

And yet, Kouta’s response was to burst out laughing. Then she leisurely rose as if she hadn’t even noticed the gun. Her laughter was filled with scorn. She was mocking her.

“Ahaha-hahaha!”

“Is something funny!? Why are you laughing!? I’m telling you not to move!”

“That’s exactly why I’m laughing, young lady.” Kouta gazed down her nose at Misachi, who was roughly three heads shorter than her. “Look around, your partner’s already down for the count. Yet despite threatening to shoot if I move, when I move anyway, you can’t pull the trigger. How lukewarm. It’s one thing to be cold, another to be hot-headed, but you’re truly lukewarm. Even for minor characters who only exist to lose, to think you’d even try, it’s just too funny—”

“Shut up! Stop talking!”

Misachi pointed the barrel at the sky and pulled the trigger. It served as both a means of intimidation, and as concrete proof that the gun really was loaded. Given how ear-splitting the gunshot was, it was safe to say the gun wasn’t loaded with 9mm, but with 41AE. In other words, even in the best-case scenario, there were still nine more bullets in the magazine. That was five less than if it were a 9mm, but that’s hardly a worthwhile comparison. Nine shots were more than enough to kill one person— or even two.

“The next time you open that insolent mouth of yours, I’ll shoot for real, intruder! Step away from Shito!”

“You tell me not to move, and then in the very same breath, you tell me to step away? Which is it, young lady?” Kouta smirked– continuing to make light of her opponent. “‘Tis not consummate in the least. A young lady such as yourself for a secretary, and a simple-minded fool for an assistant, Professor Shadou Kyouichirou mustn’t be all he’s chalked up to be. Perhaps I needn’t have bothered with the roundabout approach and should have merely waltzed straight in.”

“Who are you calling young lady? Do you understand the situation you’re in!? Don’t think I won’t do it—!”

“You think everyone will yield just because you have a gun? You think everyone will fall in line after a little show of strength? If so, then I was right to call you a young lady,” Kouta said calmly, staring down Misachi— staring down the barrel of the gun. “If you think a toy like that is capable of killing someone, you’re woefully mistaken. You don’t also happen to believe you could take down a battleship with a spear, do you?”

“That’s enough— Do you really think I’d miss at this distance?” Misachi tightened her grip on the pistol. “Things won’t have to get ugly if you just comply.”

“And wind up as one of the professor’s human experiments? —Like this simple-minded fool over here?”

“Shut up!” Those words must have hit a nerve. “—What are you after? Why did you break in here!? Did another facility send you!?”

“—Let’s talk possibilities.” Kouta lowered her voice slightly, “Let’s say the initial velocity of a bullet is nine hundred kilometres an hour. If so, how long would it take for that bullet to travel the two metres betwixt us?”

“…? …What are you talking about?”

“Possibilities, like I said. Now then, young lady, what’s your answer?”

“… 0.08 seconds,” Misachi answered dubiously. “…but what’s your point? That humans can’t dodge bullets?”

“If those were the only numbers you had to contend with, then certainly. However—” Kouta pointed at Misachi. No, that’s wrong. She was pointing at the gun in her hands. “—The Jericho 941. The trigger is 7.7 millimetres, which makes it a double action, does it not?”

“…? ……? Like I said, what’s your point!?”

“Leave it to a young lady to immediately resort to hysterics. You’re no different than those vapid airheads you find downtown, are you? ‘Tis a double action, meaning pulling the trigger would require five kilograms of force. ‘Twere it a single action, it would only require half as much. For a woman such as yourself, pulling the trigger would take a full half-second. And that’s being generous.”

“—? …!”

“And that’s not all. It would take yet another 0.02 seconds for the hammer to fall. All in all, 0.6 seconds. Now then, everything thus far has merely been a measurement of how long it would take for the bullet to reach its target; however, we must also take into consideration the time it would take you to target it in the first place. In other words, how long it would take for you to line up your sights. Whether you’re aiming at my head or my heart, it doesn’t matter, the action required to ensure that 41 Action Express hits home would take a professional 0.1 seconds, but for an amateur such as yourself, the least you’re looking at is 0.4 seconds… which brings us to a grand total of one second. A full second. That may as well be an eternity. At the very least, ‘tis more than consummate enough to close a mere two metre gap.”

“Don’t mess with me! Even if I miss my first shot, I won’t miss the second or third—”

“What’s the point if each shot takes over a second, young lady? ‘Twould be more expedient to just use your fists. ‘Tis not everyday you have this kind of opportunity, so allow me to enlighten you: guns are weapons best used at range. Five metres would be the bare minimum, but what you really want is at least ten metres between you and your opponent. That way, no matter how quickly I move, all you would have to do is shift your aim a little and fire away. It might even be consummate to assert that, supposing you don’t catch them by surprise, firearms are weapons that can only be used at range. Novices tend to be suckered in by the allure of power. However, a one-hit-kill weapon is pointless if you never manage to hit anything with it.”

“Sh-Shut Up!”

Misachi pulled the trigger. This time, aiming at Kouta.

A loud shot rang out— and that was it. Just like with Shito, Kouta spun out of the trajectory of the bullet, and then, in the same motion, she closed the gap between them, thrusting the heel of her palm up into Misachi’s jaw. Misachi was lifted off the ground. The instant Misachi’s body was liberated from gravity, the entirety of Kouta’s considerable strength, concentrated into an elbow strike, crashed down on her.

The chain of events was hard to describe. It felt entirely different than when she had faced off against Shito. That’s right, it was more like a terribly efficient, beautiful—wave.

Misachi’s body slid and tumbled across the rooftop— it reminded me a little of a curling stone— stopping just before it tumbled over the ledge. She didn’t make any attempt to stand up, nor did she groan in pain. Kouta approached, confirmed she was unconscious, and then picked up the handgun.

“—‘Tis safe to come out now, dear friend.”

“……………” I stepped out from behind the water tank. “…………Well done.”

“Hehe…” Kouta playfully pointed the Jericho in my direction. “Bang! Ahahah-!”

“…………”

“Oh my, you seem displeased.”

“No, not really… It’s just, did you have to take it so far…?” I said, glancing at the two people collapsed on the floor. “Also, you were way too reckless. I can’t believe you provoked someone holding a gun…”

“Had I not provoked her, I would have been shot.”

“I guess. …does that mean everything you said was a lie?”

“I’d prefer you think of it as a means to an end,”

Kouta said with a smile, tossing me the Jericho. I caught it, wondering why she couldn’t have at least switched the safety on first. It weighed heavy in my hands. It was only natural. The Jericho weighed over a kilogram. Holding this thing at arm’s length for any considerable amount of time would be difficult even for a man like myself. That’s why—that’s why, for Misachi it must’ve been–

Essentially, that’s what it came down to. Kouta’s harsh diatribe had merely been a ploy to buy time. She had actually been waiting for Misachi’s arms to tire. To tire to the point where she could no longer aim properly. Her loss of fine motor skill was obvious, even from the sidelines.

“Novices tend to be suckered in by the allure of numbers and logic— I suppose.”

If you let yourself get fooled by numbers, you’re in for a rough time— was how Kunagisa had put it.

“Indeed. I don’t actually know the Jericho’s bullet velocity,” Kouta nodded. “Hold onto that for me, will you? I’m sure you already know how to use it. I could carry it as well, but guns are not to my liking. They feel a little unfair.”

“…Unfair, huh…?” As she spoke, I switched the safety on and hung the Jericho from my belt. It felt a little uneven, but I couldn’t think of any other way to carry it. “But what will you do now? Now they know you’re here.”

“That is consummate in its own right. After all… if there’s an ‘outsider’, that lessens the suspicion in Kunagisa, does it not?

“Sure, that’s good for me, but what about you…”

“I don’t concern myself with such things. In fact, there is nothing that could cause me concern. Besides…” Kouta made her way towards where Shito was lying. “It appears we’ve just found our means of escape.”
