chapters.text:
Psycho Logical (Part Two)

0

It’s easy to trick a genius.

It’s hard to trick an idiot.

It’s impossible to trick a pig.

1

By the time I returned to Neo’s private quarters, roughly an hour and a half remained. Neo and Kouta were in a separate room discussing what came next— In all likelihood, what came next would have nothing to do with Kunagisa and I— so I was all alone. Surrounded by paintings, I didn’t utter a word; I just sat on the sofa.

The ticking of my watch was deafening. If I had known this was going to happen, I would have worn my digital one. That said, Kunagisa’s tinkering had turned my other watch into something unthinkable. Besides, this analogue watch was a gift from Hime, which brought with it a sense of obligation, so I suppose I never really had a choice to begin with.

“A choice, huh— Wouldn’t that be nice?”

To choose.

The act of choosing.

I pulled Misachi’s Jericho from out of my belt and tried aiming down its sights. My form was that of a complete amateur. However— so long as I didn’t lose my cool like Misachi did— handling it didn’t seem all that difficult. There was no need for any formal training, I could get used to aiming it with just a little practice.

“This country sure is peaceful, isn’t it…”

The ‘means of escape’ Kouta mentioned should be blindingly obvious. First, she dragged Misachi and Shito inside and tied the still-unconscious Misachi up with a computer cable. Even if she hadn’t, it likely would have taken her half the day to wake up, but it didn’t hurt to be cautious, or so she insisted. If you’re wondering what we did with Shito, Kouta tossed him to me (literally) and I slung him over my shoulder.

“Why should a woman have to do all the heavy lifting, did they not teach you morals?”

“I’m a feminist. I believe men and women should be treated equally.”

“Then ‘tis only right you should carry him, dear friend.” Kouta smirked. “Men and women being equal, ‘tis abundantly clear which of us is in charge.”

It was.

The reason Kouta had me carry Shito obviously wasn’t out of consideration for him. Essentially, Ougaki Shito's role was to act as a key. We used his unconscious body to pass the retina scanner. He also had his key card on him, and I’d heard his ID number many times by this point, so I was able to memorize it. I couldn’t quite remember if it was ikwe9f2ma444 and ikwe9mada423, but when Kouta pressed me for an answer, I somehow managed to come up with something. The same went with the password. There was still some level of uncertainty (if only Kunagisa were here), but it seems like I had gotten it right. That said, the ID number and password felt almost incidental when it came to a security system like this. What really mattered was the key card, the retina scan— and the voice recognition. Essentially, everything that proved you were who you said you were. We were in the clear when it came to the card and the retina scan, but none of that mattered without his voice. And there was no way we could coax him to speak while he was still unconscious—

“Ougaki Shito. ID: ikwe9f2ma444.”

Kouta said, completely changing her voice.

“Voice and retina scan confirmed. Please wait,”

The synthesized voice responded, and the door slid open.

“What’s with the surprised look? ‘Tis not as if Aikawa Jun has a monopoly on vocal mimicry, now does she?” Kouta gloated. “Even I’m capable of tricking machinery. Especially when that machinery is as consummately rudimentary as this.”

“You know Aikawa?”

Kouta looked a little bothered by my question, but she quickly shook it off and said, “I’ve only heard the rumours. When you mentioned that contractor back in the stairwell, I pretty much surmised that it was the infamous Aikawa Jun— ‘Twere it her, she wouldn’t just be able to deceive machines, but the gods themselves. Now then, if we don’t hurry up, the door will close. Ah, you can just leave Shito where he is. With his arms and legs bound, he won’t be getting up to much.”

This time, it was Shito and Misachi who were the ones locked up. If they weren't, they would report everything about Kouta to the professor, and while that was bound to happen eventually, I wanted to delay it for the time being. When the two of them don’t return, the professor will undoubtedly grow suspicious and be forced to take action. Still, the reprieve should last at least until the time limit is up. Perhaps that’s just wishful thinking, but either way, that’s how Kouta and I managed to escape the Seventh Ward.

“………”

—but I had some doubts.

After meticulously infiltrating the facility, going so far as to deceive them into thinking she had already left, why would Kouta— a crafty, conniving, and cunning veteran such as Kouta— lose sight of her goal over a few MO disks (regardless of how vital the data they contained was!) and trip the alarm? And while I’m at it, setting aside Misachi and her pistol, Kouta had also launched into a long-winded speech with the unarmed (and clearly outmatched) Shito as well. Suppose that was just to keep Shito talking so she could accurately mimic his voice—

How terrifying. What was even more terrifying was not the act itself (—If that’s all it was, then Aikawa Jun would’ve been able to pull it off too; likewise, Kunagisa would’ve been able to devise a way out as well), but the audacity to pull it off with such nonchalance. Even her most ardent defender would have to admit her chances of success weren't all that high. If Misachi had simply run away, we’d have been finished. And that’s assuming more people didn’t show up in the first place. Countless other faults with her plan kept popping up one after the other. The most fatal of which was relying on my (MY!) memory. If it was a plan I’d come up with, it would, without a doubt, put the ‘fool’ in ‘fool’s errand’. In hindsight, this kind of heroic bravado often appears like the one viable means, but this time around, I just couldn’t bring myself to think that way. It was nearly as bad as risking– no, throwing away my life by jumping to the Seventh Ward; there was no doubt in anyone’s mind that it was a terrible idea.

“………”

But Kouta’s scheme had been a great success, and so, here I was.

Once we got outside, Kouta contacted Neo via wireless transceiver, so he feigned hospitality, stepping outside to seeing off his visitor, Kasugai (whom he had invited in the first place), so he could let the two of us in on his way back inside.

In the end, Kouta was convinced of her success, and I was not. It wasn’t even a matter of weighing the risks; I couldn’t have come up with such an extreme plan in the first place.

“—I suppose that’s the difference between completion and perfection…”

The difference between what can be seen, and what can’t. Utsurigi’s crucifixion must’ve also been something of that nature. The killer had seen something that was invisible to an ordinary person like me, and the dissection and mutilation of his body, the theft of his arms, and the scrawled bloody message, all of it had to have meant something.

“…One hour and twenty-five minutes left…”

Or as Dead Blue would say, One hour twenty-four minutes forty-six seconds and seventy-seven milliseconds. But if I hadn’t come up with anything after thinking about it for the last two and a half hours, another hour and a half wasn’t likely to make any difference. Being pessimistic wouldn’t resolve anything either, but my thoughts had taken an unavoidable turn for the worse.

“Shiogi— if you were in my place, even in the worst situation, even under the worst conditions, I wonder if you could still come up with some brilliant tactic.”

Well, since it’s you we’re talking about, I’m sure you’d make it work somehow.

But there’s no hope for me.

I could never be a tactician like you.

Let's give it a shot- let’s try to force ourselves to come up with something– Something enticing enough to get one over on Professor Kyouichirou. That’s right, for instance— what about the one helping me with all this, Ishimaru Kouta? Couldn’t she be the culprit?

You’ve got to admit that it’s possible. After all, the professor didn’t know about her existence, and the only person on the inside who knew was the unscrupulous Neo (I suppose we can add Shito and Misachi to that list as well now). Besides, unlike the faculty members, she wasn’t locked up inside one of the wards. In other words, she only had one obstacle, which was one less than the other suspects. And with the cunning, knowledge, and judgement she just displayed, she could’ve pulled off Utsurigi’s murder and arranged it to appear like an impossible crime all before her morning tea—

“…What dreadful nonsense.”

My forced hypothesis was met with forced rejection. You could only go so far off the rails. I didn’t want to hand it to him, but compared to my theory just now, Professor Kyouichirou’s Kunagisa culprit theory seemed far more credible. Jesus, what a strange thing to praise him for.

“Then, assuming the same goes for Neo as well… that only leaves me with one more bizarre theory…”

That being the possibility that I was the culprit. As Kunagisa’s attendant, I followed her here just so I could murder Utsurigi– wouldn’t that be a neat twist? But while it might’ve been neat, it was utterly meaningless. I knew I wasn’t the killer, and despite harboring no small amount of ill will for the man, I never had any intention of killing him.

However,

In this case, what actually happened didn’t matter. All that was important was what was perceived to have happened. As long as it was suitably logical, then—

“Stop being so stupid,”

I muttered, setting my sights on the room’s phone. I owned a cell phone, but I had left it back at the antique apartment. The satellite phone that Kunagisa used (the one taken by Professor Kyouichirou) might’ve worked, but there was no way mine would’ve gotten a signal this deep in the mountains. However, phone companies were bound by law; no matter where you were, so long as you were in Japan (be it an isolated island, or the heart of an undeveloped mountain range), if you make a request, they are required to set up a telephone line. As such, even Shadou Kyouichirou’s research facility was connected to an outside network, which is why Neo had a telephone in his room.

Then it hit me. Normally, these kinds of organizations had a phone operator to connect calls, or some kind of internal network, so you couldn’t directly contact outside, but this facility only hired a select few, so it was entirely unlikely they would hire any superfluous staff. Meaning this phone likely connected directly to the outside. By the time I reached that conclusion, I was already standing in front of the phone with the receiver in my hand.

Halfway through dialing the first number, I stopped and placed the receiver down again. Thinking about it carefully, it was likely unreasonable to expect to be able to talk with her over the phone. When she doesn’t want to speak, she doesn’t, and even when she does want to speak, she still doesn’t; even if she were to listen to everything I have to say, she doesn’t follow any orders besides her mistress’, and even then, she had a remarkable talent for not listening to those either. Thinking again, who's to say she would even be the one to pick up the phone. Worst case scenario, it’s even possible that it could be that nutty fortune-teller. What the hell would that clairvoyant even have to say about all this? Just the thought of it made me want to vomit blood.

“On the other hand, Miiko’s probably not home… and she doesn’t own a cellphone.”

Besides, Miiko’s instincts were as sharp as the legendary blade, Onimaru Kunitsuna, so it’s not impossible she already sensed that Suzunashi and Kunagisa were locked up. Given Miiko’s impulsive personality, that wouldn’t be a welcome development. Once I was done agonizing over who to call, I finally decided to dial Hime’s cellphone number.

“Hello hello?” Before the dial tone even rang for the second time, Hime’s listless, yet perceptibly nervous, voice came through the receiver. “Who am I speaking to?”

“A man hellbent on world domination.”

“Ahh, master, hiya!” Hime sounded relieved, the nervousness in her voice dissipating. “You spooked me with the call from an unknown number, master. Whazzup? Aren’tcha in the middle of a vacation in Nagoya prefecture?”

“Yeah, something like that,” I answered, but Nagoya wasn’t a prefecture, was it? And if it were, had I ever been? I don’t think so, but Nagoya prefecture did ring a bell. “Right now, I’m, well…I’m calling from my room.”

“Hmm, that explains the unknown number then. Ahh, that’s right! This is perfect! There’s something I forgot to tell you, master!”

“What?”

“Souvenirs! I want you to buy me five blocks of uirō-mochi!”

“Huh? Did you always have such a sweet tooth?” I said, trying to remember if uirō-mochi was even sweet to begin with. Ah, that’s right. This was Aichi prefecture. Nagoya was a city here. Nagoya prefecture must’ve just been a slip of the tongue. “…Uirō-mochi is that soft desert made of red bean paste, agar, and sugar, isn’t it? Do you really like that stuff, Hime?”

“Nope, but my friends do. Don’t you remember? I introduced you, didn’t I? Usagi and the others. Uirō-mochi came up when I mentioned you were going to Nagoya, but I completely forgot. I don’t need any, but five should be enough for my pals. If you can, get a bunch of different colours. You’ve been leaching tons of money off me, so you should be able to afford it, right?”

“Don’t start spouting stuff that’ll ruin my image… but sure, if I manage to make it back alive, forget five, I’ll buy you five hundred.”

“I’ll pass. This isn’t Dazai’s Yam Gruel.”

“Yam Gruel was by Akutagawa,”

I gave a suitably master-like answer.

“Was it? Wait, hang on, master? ‘If I make it back alive’? You make it sound like you might not.”

“Who knows. Where you find people, you find graves; if you flip that around, then it shouldn’t be too surprising to think that people could die just about anywhere.” That’s right, it’s not surprising at all. Especially in the case of someone like me. “Well, in the case I don’t come back, you can do whatever you want with my things.”

“Really?” Hime’s voice lit up. Then I can keep your weird T-shirts, your weird jeans, your weird jackets, and your weird socks!?”

“Don’t call people’s clothes weird…” and what are you planning to do with my socks? “But sure. In exchange, you’ll be responsible for clearing out my apartment. That includes moving the furniture and all the other bulky stuff.”

“Whaaat?” Hime deflated immediately. She was far too self-serving. “Wait, are you for real, master? You’re not in trouble, are you? Are you under attack by terrorists? Did they crash a plane into your building, or maybe a submarine?”

“Nah, not this time… but I guess it’s something similar.”

“Hmm,” Hime didn’t seem happy with my explanation.

“For someone so smart, master’s kinda stupid, huh?” Despite her age, Hime spoke like she knew everything. “I may be dumb, but I’m not stupid. That’s why I can tell just how troubled you are right now, master.”

“Really? That’s reassuring. Does that mean you’ll help me?”

“Nope. Class is about to start.”

What a banal reason.

“Ah, that’s right…you’re at school right now.” I said, checking the time on the watch she gave me. “You shouldn’t be bringing your cellphone to class, you know.”

“Yeah, yeah. I know, master.” Along with Hime’s voice, a distant chime could be heard through the phone. “Oh, looks like that’s the bell. I’ve gotta hang up now, master.”

“Yeah, see you.”

As the person who called, it was only polite that I hung up first. Now that some of the weight was lifted off my shoulders, I felt exhausted. I sighed so deeply that I may have emptied my lungs in their entirety before returning to the sofa.

This is fine.

Isn’t it?

I, an individual who had honestly and sincerely never once had faith in himself, had no self-confidence to speak of. That hadn’t meant I lied to Kouta a couple hours ago, it’s just that my life had been nothing but a litany of failures, decidedly stained by regret and remorse. And that’s why. When I fail, when regret and remorse are all I've got left, it’s best not to have any unfinished business.

Now that the loose ends were tied up.

I was free to do as I liked.

“…It might be smart to head back to the cage and talk to Kunagisa…”

No one fits the term ‘remote-operation type’ better. Shut up in her mansion, unable to even take the stairs on her own. And yet, whether it be world affairs or academic pursuits, Kunagisa’s knowledge was all encompassing (not as all encompassing as Chee-kun’s, mind you). If I were to input the data I collected over the past two and a half hours, she should be able to spit out some unforeseen solution.

That said, given that Kasugai had already returned to the Fourth Ward, going back would carry its own risks. I don’t think Kasugai would use the stairwell, so I would be in the clear at first, but given the fact that any slip-up would be my last, I had no choice but to be cautious.

“Is it even worth worrying over…?”

“At least Hime’s in class,” I muttered something anyone else would find utterly incoherent as I made to leave the room. For now, I should talk things over with Kouta. However, before I even had a grip on the doorknob, the door swung open. Huh? Was this another automatic door? I haven’t had the pleasure of laying eyes on one, but I’ve heard tales of automatic doors that didn’t just slide open sideways— but no, I don’t remember this door being anything that high-tech. All this to say, someone must be trying to enter the room. That someone being Kouta, standing in the hallway with her eyes wide in surprise at finding me directly in front of her.

“—My, what seems to be the matter, dear friend? ‘Tis an odd place to stand.”

“No, I just figured I’d go back and check on the cage… I wanted to hear Kunagisa and Suzunashi’s opinions on all this. I can't pretend it's not risky though, so I was waffling about what to do.”

“Well, ‘tisn’t a bad idea,” Kouta said. “In fact, it may be ideal.”

“Ideal how? By the way, Kouta, are you done talking with Neo?”

“Our talk isn't concluded so much as on hold,” she said ambiguously. “We’re taking a short recess. It appears we’ll be having an unexpected guest. Neo received a call from Koutari just now about some business they need to attend to, and ‘tis not as if I’m about to let him see me. They intend to use this room, so I’ve been sent to retrieve you.”

“Huh.”

……Koutari, eh?

The Koutari-culprit theory I conjured up out of pure desperation (desperate in more ways than one), once again sprang to mind. Kouta had flatly rejected my suggestion that he had fashioned his hair into some kind of rope, but that didn’t necessarily clear him of all suspicion. It was still possible that he had murdered Utsurigi by some other means– as possible as it was for any other researcher at least. Regardless, it didn’t seem like Koutari and Gaisuke were on good terms— now that I mention it, Utsurigi didn’t seem to be on good terms with anyone.

“Not a soul— ……but why?” The doubt captured my attention. “I figured he would’ve got on perfectly fine with Miss Kokoromi…”

“Utsurigi may have distanced himself from others deliberately,” Kouta said. “You would know for certain if you just asked Kunagisa about it, would you not? But then again, Kunagisa hardly seems keen on talking about him.”

“Can’t be helped. She’s completely tactless after all. She’s loose-lipped, but it’s either all or nothing, nothing in-between. She seems to have a tough time judging how much she can get away with sharing. The criteria are too fuzzy for her.”

“How Boolean. Or perhaps I should say, how blue.”

“She’s definitely both.”

I stepped out of the room and into the hallway where Kouta stood. There, the first half-decent idea I had popped into my head. Naturally, we couldn’t let ourselves get spotted by Koutari, but thinking about it another way, didn’t that mean we could do whatever we wanted so long as that wasn’t the case? From an information-gathering perspective, I certainly had plenty I wanted to ask him. And since I couldn’t ask him directly, then I might as well—

“Kouta,”

“Understood.”

Without me even having to say anything, Kouta reached into her coat and pulled out a wireless transceiver. It was even smaller than a cell phone with an exceptionally slim design. Rather than any buttons, it had four-or-so dials that Kouta began readjusting. She had used the same device to contact Neo earlier, but still, as expected of a thief, she had all kinds of secret gadgets.

“Yes— Precisely, Neo. If you would be so kind.”

It only took two or three sentences for Neo and Kouta to come to an understanding— or rather, to come to an agreement.

“Well then, let us bide our time on the roof. Another room might be adequate as well, but should the worst come to pass and Koutari opens the door on some whim, it shall be over for us in one fell-swoop.”

“Right…” the roof again? “But how will we eavesdrop from the roof?”

“That’s what this transceiver is for. If we set it to receive only, then they shan't be able to hear us on their end. That said, ‘tis not as if there’s no cause for concern; there always remains the possibility of someone somewhere picking up on the radio waves and exposing us… although the chances of that happening are so slim ‘tis not worth fretting over.”

Kouta said as she began making her way towards the stairwell that connected to the roof.

“If there’s anything to fret over, it would have to be those two.”

“You mean Shito and Misachi?” I asked, following up the stairs behind her. “It’d take them half the day just to wake up, wouldn’t it? Given all the needless pummeling you did, I mean.”

“Dear-o-dear. ‘Tis not consummate at all to deliberately paint others as sadists. I never use any more force than is absolutely necessary.”

“Misachi’s one thing, but I still think you went a little too hard on Shito. You deliberately aimed for his organs. If you just went for the head, you could have knocked him out in one blow, couldn’t you? It’s gonna hurt a hell of a lot when he wakes up.”

“Keep on talking and you shall find out just how kind I was being,”

Kouta threatened vaguely. Reaching the top of the stairs, Kouta opened the door, stepped out onto the roof, laid down her jacket and took a seat. I followed suit and sat grasping my knees facing her. Kouta began to fiddle with the transceiver’s frequency.

“…Now that I think about it, despite all the alarms, this place doesn’t have any security cameras, does it?” I said off-handedly. “That’s awfully convenient for the two of us, but from a security perspective, isn’t that a problem?”

“Perhaps. However, from a management perspective, ‘tis far more consummate,” Kouta answered without looking up from the transceiver. “Besides, I’m sure there are things they would rather not have recorded as well. Take those MO disks from earlier, while they may have been fairly valuable in their own right, twasn’t any of the good stuff. That sort of thing.”

“So, any and all records were kept in their heads…?”

Wasn’t the strict security more than enough?

Kouta appeared to have finished tuning the receiver, and placed it on the roof between us. I could hear the rustling of clothes. Neo must’ve had his receiver in a pocket or something.

“Hmm– The signal’s a tad weak.”

Kouta tilted her head as she adjusted a dial ever so slightly. When she did, something resembling a human voice leaked out of the transceiver.

“Not at…ll…outari.”

“I don’t care.”

“Be that as it may, you’re a little late. That's unusual for someone who’s usually so punctual, Koutari.”

“It’s because the elevator’s busted for some reason.”

It was Neo and Koutari’s voices. Since the two of them didn’t sound like they were walking and talking, it seemed that they were in Neo’s painting-adorned private quarters after all.

“…So, what did you want to see me for, Koutari?”

“A research matter, of course.”

Then the two of them launched into a conversation full of technical lingo (such-and-such efficiency, and the what-have-you circuits— that kind of jargon). At first, I tried to listen carefully, but there’s nothing more boring than hearing people ramble on about things you don’t even understand. While it might be rude to admit, I was slowly losing all interest in what they had to say.

“…this feels like a complete waste of effort,” Kouta muttered disinterestedly. She must’ve been feeling the same way. “Not that it was much effort at all, mind you. How can they prattle on about something so dull? Do they really find it that interesting?"

“At least you can understand them somewhat, can’t you? To me, it may as well be another language.”

“‘Tis because I can understand it that I find it so boring,” Kouta said. “How dreadful does it have to be for it to be boring both when you understand it and when you don’t?”

“I can’t shake the feeling we’re wasting our time… just get to the incident already, Neo.”

“It would seem far too unnatural to bring that up so suddenly. He has his own affairs to be concerned about as well, you know. At the very least, he can’t go blowing his cover over something like this.”

“Yeah, I get that but…… then can I leave this to you, Kouta?” I stood up. “While you handle things here, I’m gonna head back to the cage and check on Kunagisa.”

“Splitting up, are we? ‘Tis hardly consummate to saddle me with such a menial task, but I suppose it can’t be helped this time. There’s still the matter of the deadline after all.”

I glanced at my watch. Only an hour and fifteen minutes left.

“Ah… but if taking Shito and Misachi out of the equation distracts them, …the professor’s confusion might buy us a little more time.”

“And it might just as well do the opposite,” Kouta said, glancing at me as she righted her crooked cap. “The two they sent to check on the Seventh ward never returned. ‘Twould clearly invite suspicion. Still, supposing the professor trusts them, ‘tis far more likely he assumes they can handle whatever happens, and that they are only performing an extra thorough sweep given the situation.”

“Not so sure about trust… but conviction, maybe,” I said, remembering something. Namely, what it was that Kouta had mentioned as she faced off against Misachi. “By the way Kouta, what was that all about?”

“That, being?” Kouta deliberately avoided giving an answer. “I don’t recall us being close enough to pick up on what the other’s saying without any context. Or could it be that you desire such intimacy, dear friend.”

“Don’t dodge the question. You mentioned something about Shito when you were talking to Misachi. About how you didn’t want to ‘wind up as one of the professor’s human experiments’ like that ‘simple-minded fool,’”

I said, trying to mimic Kouta’s cynical delivery. I thought I hadn’t done a half-bad job of it, but Kouta looked exceptionally uncomfortable for some reason. I cleared my throat before continuing, “what did you mean by that?” forcefully righting the conversation.

“I meant nothing by it at all. ‘Twould be consummate to take it at face value,” Kouta gave a brusque answer, her spirits seemed to have fallen considerably. “In short, just like Utsurigi Gaisuke, Ougaki Shito is one of his lab rats. Although, in his case, there are plenty of replacements lined up, so ‘tisn’t quite right to imply they are the same. However, one thing’s for certain, that boy is something extraordinary.”

“Something extraordinary…?”

She was probably right. Since arriving, Shito hadn’t shown me anything too brilliant, but it wasn’t impossible that that was only because he hadn’t had the chance to. The fact that he could make a life for himself in a facility like this was more than enough proof that he was capable.

However, if the human experiments Kouta mentioned were as I thought they were, then wouldn’t that take on a somewhat different connotation. To wind up the professor’s guinea pig, nothing more than a research subject. In other words,

“He’s manufacturing geniuses— don’t you agree?” With her ear still lent to the transceiver, Kouta spoke in a somewhat playful tone. “But why don’t we leave that conversation ‘till everything’s concluded. How Ougaki Shito came to live here and what kind of role he plays has nothing at all to do with Kunagisa Tomo or Utsurigi Gaisuke. Even you can see that, can you not?”

I wonder. I didn’t get it. It was yet another thing I didn’t get. Just like everything else. I didn’t understand it at all.

Then, at that moment.

The sound of Koutari’s voice coming through the transceiver seized my thoughts.

“Neo. About this incident.”

chapters.title: Psycho Logical (Part Two)
chapters.text:
Psycho Logical (Part Two)

2

“Neo. About this incident. What do you think?”

“It hardly matters what I think— Besides, I have next to no opinion on it to begin with. Other than the fact that it’s landed us in some hot water, that is. With Utsurigi dead, it may as well be curtains for us. Then again, the professor seems to have something up his sleeve.”

“That blue-haired girl, you mean?”

“Exactly, that is precisely what I mean. Say what you will, but she’s the former leader of Cluster. As far as raw materials go, she’s even better than Utsurigi. And she’s not even twenty. She would be far more pliable and easier to work with as well, don’t you think?”

“She doesn’t look easy to work with to me.”

“Perhaps. If she were all alone, then you’d be right. However, it seems you’re forgetting the two acquaintances of hers we have hostage, Koutari.”

“Hostage? Is that what they are?”

“It is. The lady in black aside— the two of them don’t appear to be all that close— the lad is always a handy card to have at our disposal. And it seems we got our hands on an ultra rare card at that— the lover of a direct descendent of the Kunagisa house. It may not be too valuable, but it’s rare all the same.”

“You’re right. I don’t get it myself, but it seems like the blue-haired girl is head over heels for the brat.”

“Certainly. That said, according to the professor she has no emotions to speak of. He said her genius was like interfacing directly with a machine. Still, from an outsider’s perspective— or at the very least, from mine— she doesn’t look all that special. She doesn’t even seem all that smart. If anything, the lady in black seems far brighter.”

“Smart people always look dumber than they are… You shouldn’t judge a book by the cover.”

“You’ve got a point, Koutari. And trust me, I’m aware; I’ve heard more than enough about Lady Kunagisa’s skills through the grapevine, after all. That’s why I can’t say I don’t understand why the professor’s willing to go through all this effort to frame her.”

“It’s not framing if she actually ends up being the culprit.”

“You’re still on about that? Still, I suppose you’re right. The professor’s version of events isn’t wholly unbelievable. That said, it won’t be easy to prove it, now will it?”

“There’s no need.”

“You may be right. There’s no need to go through the grueling process of establishing guilt if you just assert it hard enough. But then the problem becomes how to deal with the Kunagisa Syndicate. Or perhaps I should say ‘how to strike a deal with the Kunagisa Syndicate’— it’s more or less the same either way. When they hear that one of their own is being used as a prototype, I’m sure they won’t stay quiet.”

“If we get her to claim she consented to it, we should be fine.”

“So just like Utsurigi then, huh? That wouldn’t be a bad idea, but how would we get her to do it?”

“Did you forget what we just talked about? You were the one who brought it up in the first place."

“Ah yes, the hostages. I see. Hmm— not a bad plan. Not bad at all.”

“It’s the same strategy we used on the pervert, so you can’t exactly call it inspired.”

“The pervert? Ah, you mean Utsurigi? I suppose you’re right. But, it’s not as if creativity is high on the docket when it comes to these things. We’re academics, not artists. Still, unlike with Utsurigi, the solutions already laid out for us— that being taking the lad hostage. In other words, locking up Lady Kunagisa means locking up the lad as well. Am I wrong?”

“You aren’t. But we should consider that a blessing.”

“Oh-ho? And how do you figure that, exactly?”

“That blue-haired girl isn’t able to see reality. It doesn’t matter where she is, it’s all the same. In other words, she’s everywhere and nowhere at the same time.”

“I never had you pegged for a poet, Koutari. Ah, pardon me, I didn’t mean to interrupt. As you were.”

“Essentially, whether she’s at home or here at the facility, it doesn’t matter. So long as that brat is by her side.”

“Aha- Now I get it. I see what you mean. In that case, the Seventh Ward would become their little love-nest. Then again, they’d be under 24/7 surveillance, so I doubt it’d be all that pleasant. Still, it’s not half-bad.”

“For her, at least.”

“Ah, right. I doubt Lady Kunagisa is all it’d take to keep the ER Program drop-out complacent. Then again, he’s hard to get a grasp on, so I can’t say anything too insightful about him.”

“You can grasp him just fine. You just wind up grasping so much it’s hard to make heads-or-tails of it.”

“Alright, I concede. You’re exactly right. Leave it to Koutari, the depths of your insight know no bounds! —Hmph, even with Lady Kunagisa madly in love with him, the problem is the lad himself. I wonder what the professor plans to do about that. He’s completely unaffiliated with the Kunagisa Syndicate, so if he were to disappear, surely his friends and family would kick up a fuss.”

“He doesn’t look like the type with many friends to me.”

“You could say that. He seems talkative and charming enough, but maybe it’s his fear of human contact that made him that way— or at least that might be a psychologist’s perspective, but I fear it probably has to do with something far deeper in the lad’s case. There’s something elusive about him. In that sense, you could say he’s similar to Lady Kunagisa and Utsurigi. The only thing scarier than those who’re capable of anything, are those you can’t predict. All the more so since he’s so young. In any case, modern society hasn’t grown so apathetic that someone up and vanishing wouldn’t draw any attention.”

“Is that right? I wouldn’t be so sure.”

“Well, I suppose you have a point. After all, that Prowler case in Kyoto– Lady Kunagisa’s home town– still hasn’t been solved, and the world may be rife with danger, but that alone doesn’t mean—”

“Neo. Rather than that brat, I’m more worried about the woman you call the ‘lady in black’.”

“Oh? And why is that? Let’s see– If I remember correctly— her name was Suzunashi. Suzunashi Neon.”

“Exactly. What do you suppose he’ll do with her? Professor Kyouichirou, that is.”

“Ah– One hostage is more than enough, isn’t it? That said, if he wants to keep everything under wraps, he can’t just send her on her merry way. But if he keeps her here, then he’ll run into the same problem he will with the lad. Namely, her friends and family causing a stink.”

“Didn’t the professor do an investigation? He should’ve already performed a background check.”

“Now that you mention it, he told me he did. Although, since he didn’t have a lot of time, the data he pulled wasn’t exactly thorough. In fact, we didn’t know the lad was an ER Program participant until Miyoshi was kind enough to tell us. We’re not the ones with access to Cluster’s monstrously talented seeker, after all. Besides, given how confidential the ER3 System is, that should have been obvious even without me having to tell you. And— there was one more thing. I can’t quite remember what it was though.”

“—Well I looked into it. It’s unbelievable.”

“Unbelievable? What is? The lad’s history?”

“No. Suzunashi Neon’s.”

“Oh? And why is that? Now I’m curious.”

“That’s actually what I came here to discuss. I’ll tell you the specifics later, but continuing to keep that woman locked up is an extraordinarily bad idea.”

“A worse idea than locking up the lad and Lady Kunagisa, you mean? If so, that doesn’t sound like a pleasant conversation.”

“It’s to the point where I’m hesitating over whether to even bring it up to the professor. After all, the only thing on The Mad Daemon’s mind is how to get his hands on that blue-haired girl. If things go badly, we might get dragged down with him.”

“Dragged down, eh? That’s it, Koutari! I just had a brilliant idea for if that happens! Tell me what you think about this: Essentially, the two of us would work together to find Utsurigi’s real killer. It could be just like a shounen manga, the two of us could both point them out and cry, ‘The culprit was you, all along!’ After all, you and I have always made a pretty good team.”

“We have not.”

“Is that so? A shame, then. Still, as a matter of practicality, what do you think? Do you think Lady Kunagisa’s actually the culprit?”

“Who knows. At this point it doesn’t really matter who the culprit is.”

“Is that right— I suppose it is. It might not make a difference. Still, murder is unthinkable. To think that a monster like that could be walking around this facility, what can I say, it makes me shudder.”

“‘Kill one man, and you are a murderer. Kill millions of men, and you are a conqueror. Kill them all, and you are a god.’ — The words of Jean Rostand.”

“Darn. You beat me to it. Still, he might be right. If you think about it, killing Utsurigi may as well be the same as killing millions. They killed the countless people who were meant to follow in his footsteps. Then again, they also say ‘one death is a tragedy, a million deaths is a statistic.’”

“And they’d be right.”

“Without question.”

“However, I suppose there’s one more thing to be said about all this.”

“Oh? And what might that be? Don’t leave me hanging, Koutari. We’re pals, aren’t we? If you keep teasing me like this, I’m gonna lose weight from all the stress. Tell what else there is to say already.”

“Just that the incident involving Utsurigi Gaisuke, was a suicide.”

chapters.title: Psycho Logical (Part Two)
chapters.text:
Psycho Logical (Part Two)

3

“Just that the incident involving Utsurigi Gaisuke, was a suicide. And I don’t mean metaphorically.”

When I heard those words pour from the transceiver, my body stiffened even further. I unconsciously huddled over the device, accidentally resulting in me awkwardly bumping into Kouta’s nose. “Ow!” Kouta cried and pulled away.

“—You needn’t get so close to hear, dear friend. That stung.”

“Sorry…”

I gave an absentminded apology as I backed off the transceiver a little. Even then, I was still aware of how (pointlessly) close I was. I was aware, but I couldn’t bring myself to back up any further.

“………”

“A suicide? What ever could you mean, Koutari?” Neo said in his characteristically theatric tone. “No matter how you look at it, he was killed by someone else. I’ll admit, any locked room murder really ought to be considered a suicide, but that’s most certainly not the case this time around. After all, the one responsible for locking the locked room was the auto-lock security system.”

“When I say suicide, I mean suicide,” came Koutari’s low mutter. “After all, Neo, the Utsurigi Gaisuke we know wasn't the type to go out without a fight, was he?”

“Huh. I guess. I haven’t actually met the man face-to-face myself, so I can’t really say. Then again, based on the phone calls and mail I’ve read, not to mention all the rumors I’ve heard about his past, I suppose you could have a point. He didn’t seem like one to lay down and take it.”

He was exactly right. I hadn’t even talked to Utsurigi for an hour, but that was enough to tell me all I needed about his strong sense of will— just like how the way Kunagisa talked about him was enough to tell me about his obstinance. For better or worse, he had the air of a prodigal genius who fundamentally viewed others as beneath him— self-righteousness wrapped in pride. Would a man like that willingly let himself be killed? Not a chance. So long as it wasn’t by Dead Blue, there wasn’t a chance.

“But who’s to say he really did just roll over and die?” came Neo’s rebuttal. “After all, his corpse was violated beyond belief. How should I put it, it’s like killing him wasn’t satisfying enough. In other words, it’s because of his personality, because he wasn’t the kind of person who would let himself be killed, that he wound up like that. Isn’t that how we should view this? Being scholars, and all.”

“That’s merely a matter of opinion. Let’s take a look at it from the beginning,” Koutari continued dispassionately. “Why was Utsurigi Gaisuke confined here to begin with?”

“The reason behind his confinement, huh? On the surface, that would be to serve as a research fellow, and behind the scenes he was the professor’s personal think-tank, but if we peel back yet another layer, he was the professor’s specimen, was he not?”

“That’s not what I meant. I meant why he allowed himself to be confined.”

“Ahh– I see what you’re getting at.”

Neo seemed to agree with where this was heading. I found myself nodding along as well.

That’s right— the reason Gaisuke was here. That was another thing I was curious about. During yesterday’s session, he had done a remarkable job dodging not just my questions, but Kunagisa’s as well. Still, it appeared like something was up with him— like some kind of weakness was being used against him (although he had burst out laughing when I’d suggested as much), and that was the reason why he remained here.

“Let’s see… I wonder what it was. I was never actually informed, so I don’t know for certain, but it’s something to do with his criminal past, no doubt— in other words, he threatened to expose some of his evil doings from his Cluster days or something, don’t you think?”

“Wrong. That, too, is just the surface.”

“Ahh. I see, a false rumour spread to conceal the truth, eh? I’m not sure if I should be calling him underhanded or just well-prepared, but at least the professor’s consistent. So? Does that mean you know the truth then, Koutari?”

“I heard it from the man himself,” Koutari said surprisingly. “I’m sure it was just a slip of the tongue, but— it had something to do with Kunagisa Tomo’s birth.”

Those words were met with silence from Neo. I was silent too. How could I not be? Kunagisa’s…birth? Did I hear him right?

I couldn’t have.

“……What on earth– what do you mean?” Neo replied, straining to maintain his jovial tone. “I’m not sure I follow.”

“I don’t either,” Koutari answered. “All I know was that it was a rather sore spot for Utsurigi. Until the end, it seems like that blue-haired girl took up no small part of his thoughts. After all, she was his leader from back in his Cluster days. If he refused to meet the professor’s demands, or worse, run away, that secret would be exposed to the light of day— or something, I don’t know. I know that he’s The Mad Daemon and all, but I can’t imagine there was any possible profit worth risking the ire of the Kunagisa Syndicate over. However—”

However, those kinds of threats–

“Those kinds of threats only hold power so long as they’re not acted on. But ‘what if’ is a hard thought to shake— and that’s why Utsurigi Gaisuke was trapped here.”

“Hmm, I see— but all this to say…what exactly, Koutari? Whether Utsurigi had a reason to be here, or whether the professor’s reason for confining him was what we thought it was doesn’t change the outcome, now does it? On the surface or behind the scenes, it doesn’t matter. Utsurigi was forced to be here.”

“Except, then, Kunagisa Tomo arrived,” Koutari said. “That birthed a contradiction. He stayed here for the blue-haired girl’s sake, but that could no longer be said to be true.”

“So, you’re saying— he killed himself?”

“It’s only logical. By dying, the professor could no longer touch him. What point is there in blackmailing a corpse?”

Something about Koutari’s opinion— struck a chord with me. At the very least, I got where he was coming from emotionally. This is the Utsurigi who had boldly claimed Kunagisa as his Kaiser. If the contents of the threat levied against him pertained to Kunagisa— it wouldn’t be strange for him to pick death. If so, then was yesterday’s session meant to be some kind of final words. His last will and testament for his former leader, and for me, the man who would watch over her after his passing. If that’s what this meant, then I can’t say I’m not starting to understand what Kunagisa meant when she said he wanted to restore his wicked name.

Not restore his good name. Not clear his name, either.

But restore his wicked name.

To sully it further.

That said, if I were to add my two-cents, there still remained one more contradiction.

“Still, Koutari,” as expected, that contradiction wasn’t lost on Neo. “That’s quite odd. Quite odd indeed. Utsurigi’s murder— or suicide, as you so suggest, only put Lady Kunagisa in even more danger. I mean right now she’s confined to a cage, a brand new semi-permanent fixture of this fine establishment.”

“You’re right,” Koutari readily conceded as if this contradiction wasn’t news to him. “Regardless—”

Just as Koutari was about to say something, his voice was overtaken by white noise. A sharp piercing screech caused me to unconsciously crank down the volume. Neither Koutari or Neo were still audible.

“—Is it broken?”

“No, it must have been a sudden phone call,” Kouta said coolly. “You did notice the phone in the room, yes? There must have been some outside correspondence. Just because the phone is corded, doesn’t mean there aren’t any radio waves. ‘Tis similar to how it becomes difficult to use a cellphone when working at the computer. The radio waves clashed, and it seems our feeble signal didn’t stand a chance, or so I think.”

“You think? These machines are awfully finicky.” Let down by the sudden anti-climax, I stopped hovering over the transceiver and planted myself back down on the rooftop. “…Neo was doing his best to get Koutari to spill anything he could, but… it doesn’t feel like we made any real progress.”

“Is that so? That seemed like quite a telling conversation to me.”

“Sure, I guess,” I said, acquiescing. “On a conceptual level, I’m fine with the idea of Utsurigi’s death being a suicide. I am, really, but now isn’t the time for conceptualizing. I wouldn’t mind chit-chatting about it when we’ve got a little more time… but in reality, Utsurigi was murdered. There’s no question. A suicide like that isn’t possible. Whether he went quietly or kicking and screaming is one thing, but he was murdered.”

“Hmm… that may be.” Kouta folded her arms.  “By the by, what was all that about Kunagisa Tomo’s birth? You wouldn’t happen to know, would you?”

“No, I wouldn’t.”

An instant reply. A little too instant. Kouta looked as suspicious as could be. I didn’t care. No matter how blatant the lie, once you’ve told it, you have to see it through. You have to.

“Fine then. ‘Tis not as if digging into Miss Kunagisa’s affairs would help me any…” after a moment or two glaring at each other, the one to break the silence was Kouta. “…More importantly, ‘tis a long call, is it not? They should be wrapping it up soon. Then again, perhaps ‘tis broken after all.”

Kouta began fiddling with the transceiver. As I watched her out of the corner of my eye, I heaved another sigh. It seems like ever since I arrived here, discounting the time I spent sleeping, sighs like this had been an hourly occurrence. I hate letting my emotions run wild, but these waves were especially harsh. Three more days here would likely drive me mad. Or maybe it already had. As I thought about all I’d done to get this far, I couldn’t help feeling that way.

I looked at my watch. There was precisely one hour left.

“Ah. We’re back,”

Kouta said, placing the transceiver back down on the roof. I abandoned my relaxed position and leaned forward, once again hovering over the device.

“ ………           …………—— what did he say?”

“Well, you see,” Neo said with an odd sort of clarity. “Listen carefully, Koutari. This is an extremely delicate matter.”

“? What is?”

“The professor’s call just now— it appears there’s been an incident. And not just any run-of-the mill incident either, it’s a big one— the incident to end all incidents.”

Neo’s old-fashioned tone was, once again, strangely articulate. That’s right. It’s almost as if. As if the voice that trailed from the transceiver on the ground was doing its best to reach Kouta and I at all costs. As if there was something it needed to tell us.

Suddenly, he cleared his throat.

Kouta also huddled closer to make out what he was about to say.

“The lad that came here with Lady Kunagisa— he’s disappeared.”

I hesitated for just a moment. But the very next-

I was up. And running. Without thinking. I cleared the two-metre gap between the Fifth and Fourth Wards, and touched down on the roof. From there, I ran towards the rooftop entrance. I could hear a voice call out behind me. It was Kouta’s voice. She was saying something. I couldn’t make it out. I didn’t have the time. I gripped the knob to throw the door open, but it was locked and didn’t budge. Like that would stop me. I summoned all my strength and repeatedly kicked the area around the doorknob. The door itself was sturdy, but if met with a concentrated and continuous force at the fulcrum, the point of stress, a lock like this was easily broken. Who was it that told me that? I can’t recall. Someone from when I lived abroad. It left signs of forced entry, but I was past the point of caring about leaving evidence. Everything was already out in the open.

A number of kicks later, the door was open. I had broken it down.

“—damn!”

The hour that remained. It had blown away like paper in the wind. How did they notice I was gone? How? Had Kasugai gone downstairs on a whim to check on things? Had Shito and Misachi woken up sooner than expected? No, come to think of it, even before that, Misachi had a chance to fire off that shot. Had the sound reached someone? Miss Kokoromi couldn’t have ratted me out to the professor, could she? Or perhaps the phone call I made to Hime just now left some kind of record and someone had found it suspicious? Any of which seemed possible, but none of them left me satisfied. Then again, nothing in this life is perfectly satisfying. This was reality. Goddamnit, what use are words and reason? In the end they lead to nothing but misunderstandings and false assumptions.

Since I’d already been found out, there was no reason not to use the elevator. However, since the elevator shaft didn’t reach the roof, using the stairs was unavoidable. I’d climb down to the fourth floor and take the elevator from there. Having made up my mind, I headed to the top of the stairs and was about to take the first step when-

–something gripped my shoulder from behind.

It was Kouta.

“—Where do you think you’re going?”

Kouta’s voice was the slightest bit haggard. Given my head start, it seemed like catching up to me was no simple task, even for Kouta. Ahh, that’s right. Kicking down the door had cost me some time. Damnit. I don’t have time to deal with you right now.

“—Even if you return to the cage, nothing will come of it.”

Nothing? Is that right? I suppose it was. She was spot on. Kouta was telling the truth. Even if I went back, there was nothing I could do. Make no mistake. But that’s precisely why I needed to go back. I tried to shake off her hand, but Kouta’s fingers dug into me; her grip was unshakeable.

“…I’m grateful to you, Ishimaru Kouta,” I said perfunctorily. “I really am. It’s because of you that I was able to hold on to hope for these past few hours. You let me keep dreaming that there was still some way out. Thank you.”

“What are you blabbering about? You make it sound like you’re about to die.” Kouta forcefully turned me to face her. “All hope is not lost quite yet. In fact, now that you’ve been found out, you are the only hope remaining, don’t you see? For Kunagisa, for Suzunashi, and for yourself. And you aim to throw that hope away?”

“I’m not throwing it away. I’m giving it back,” I answered robotically. “From here on out, this has nothing to do with you. So, you should just—”

A dry sound rang out. It took me three seconds to realize Kouta had slapped me. It didn’t hurt. It seems all the excitement had dulled my nerves. Still, it burned.

“It ‘has nothing to do with me’? We have been a team for hours, and now, all of sudden, you say it has nothing to do with me? You—” Kouta seemed somewhat agitated, but she managed to forcefully keep her voice down. “…You are completely off the rails.”

“I get that a lot,” I nodded, meekly. “More than you can imagine.”

“Do you recall? What I said to you on the roof of the Seventh Ward? ‘Should you run off on your own again, I shall have no choice but to rethink our alliance’.”

“Please do, it doesn’t matter.” I bowed my head. “Thank you for all you’ve done for m-”

I never got to finish before Kouta shoved me. I tumbled backwards, with no time to take a defensive posture, I landed in a heap on the landing, having bashed myself across all thirteen stairs. My momentum was halted when I crashed into the opposing wall. “That hurts,” I eked out. That said, it didn’t hurt at all. If anything, it felt like a weight off my shoulders. This was the first time I’d felt so relieved since stepping foot in this facility.

Then, something clattered down from above, coming to rest at my feet. It was the lockpicking knife, the anti-lock blade. The instant I laid eyes on it I glanced once again to the top of the stairs. There, in the same pose she took when she tossed the knife, stood Kouta.

“A parting gift, dear friend.” in a dispassionate, utterly disinterested tone, Kouta said her final remarks. “Try not to kick down any more doors. You shall hurt yourself. Moreover, ‘twill also make a decent weapon if it ever comes down to it. Surely you aren’t content with just that knife in your right-breast pocket, now are you? And a word of advice, don’t use the gun. Although perhaps this is naught but unwelcome meddling.”

“——”

I opened my mouth to speak, but as I watched Kouta turn back and walk away, I couldn’t say anything. When Kouta’s figure had finally faded from view, I picked up the knife and brought myself to my feet. Nothing seemed broken or swollen. You even shove people with finesse, Ishimaru Kouta, I thought, as I gazed at the knife. I thought, as I recalled the woman who called me her friend until the very end. When all was said and done, I had simply used her, unable to give anything back. I regretted it. That said, perhaps that wasn’t solely unique to her. They say human relationships are give and take, but I have always leant on others, I have always been a burden. If even one of the people I’d met hadn’t been there for me, I likely wouldn’t even be alive.

And so,

“There comes a time to put an end to everything, even nonsense…”

So. Let’s give back. Give it all back.

Just a bit, all of it. Half of it, in its entirety.

Like when I first met that blue boy.

Like before we met.

I hated deciding. I hated choosing. I was unable to take interest in others. I was unable take interest in myself. I hated conflict. I hated competition. I hated being laughed at. Me, who could not laugh. Me, who could not cry. I could feel neither joy nor anger. I couldn’t do anything. I couldn’t feel anything. I couldn’t grasp anything. And since I couldn’t have it, I broke it. I wanted it, so I destroyed it. I desired it, so I threw it away. I wanted to trust them, so I betrayed them. I liked them, so I rejected them. I wanted to protect them, so I hurt them. I felt comfortable, so I escaped. We were friends, so I was alone. I was jealous, so I crushed them. Necessary things became unnecessary. Love became hate. I pretended to be cold. I pretended to be detached. I pretended to be enlightened. I pretended to be a wise. I pretended to be a fool. I pretended to be human. I tried to be someone else. I was unable to be anyone but myself. I admired others. I hated myself. I tried to like myself. I tried to like others. I tried to love others. I could not love anyone other than myself. I could not love myself. I didn’t understand how to love or be loved, equally. So, I ran. But there was no escape. From anywhere. From anyone.

Life was cruel.

“…Now then, let’s have a masterpiece.”

I’ll kill them, slice them to bits, line them all up, trim them down to size – and set them out for all the world to see.

I felt dreadfully quiet.

I confirmed the knife in my breast pocket was still there, and then, with the lockpicking knife still gripped in my left hand, I began to descend the stairs.

I began to fall.

chapters.text:
Psycho Logical (Part Two)

0

Your value is determined by others.

Others’ value is also determined by others.

1

In the end I took the stairs all the way down. I had no trouble getting to the fourth-floor hallway, but when I arrived, the elevator was still stopped at the basement. Even in my excited state, I would have found it obvious that running down the steps would get me there faster. But by that point I wasn’t excited at all. My head was so cool my body temperature may have been below zero.

Halfway down I stumbled, tumbling two– three times before slamming into the staircase landing. Still, I was up again in no time. It’s not that I got off without a scratch, it’s just that it didn’t hurt. By now, it had spread all throughout me. While it’s impossible for living things to control their own nervous system, something very similar was happening to me. Speaking of which, I heard when living things receive a fatal injury— like having half their head crushed, or getting cut clean in half— their nervous system shuts down completely. When your body realizes that, no matter how desperately it struggles, it won’t last longer than a few minutes, the natural signals that denote danger become pointless– unnecessary. I found the thought comforting. As unseemly a story it was, I found it extraordinarily comforting. When one doesn’t fear death, pain loses its purpose. Who knew living things could become this strong with just that one conviction. Or perhaps by abandoning that conviction, they could become this weak. Whichever it was, I thought it was wonderful. As I propped myself up on the wall after falling for the fourth time, I truly thought so.

The fact that it didn’t so much as itch let alone hurt when I fell was something to be grateful for– although, in truth, there was a sensation somewhat resembling itching– but the fact I could no longer walk straight was becoming a problem. My feet never seemed to reach the floor. Each step was extraordinarily uneasy. It was like swimming around in zero-gravity. On the topic, once upon a time— when I was still thirteen-years-old, back before I’d participated in the ER Program, Kunagisa and I talked about something similar. By the time we’re adults, do you think anyone could take a trip to space? It’s possible. Would you wanna go? Nah, I don’t really care. What about you, Kunagisa? I’d go! Hmph, a shut-in who wants to go to space? How elitist can you get? What’s an ‘aleetist’? Something completely worthless. I’m not worthless. Perhaps, but space is worthless. After all, nothing on Earth’s worth anything either. There’s nothing of value anywhere at all. Nowhere? Nowhere. If you went to space and gazed at the Earth, the only thing you’d take away is that it’s ‘blue’. Is that really worth going to space for? If that’s all you’re after, you’re better off picking up some colour swatches. At least then it wouldn’t just be blue, you’d also have red, black, green and all the rest. Space exploration is nothing more than a way to prove your own insignificance. The result of unbridled romanticism and nothing else. If I wanted that, I’d be better off just looking at your hair. E-he-he. Don’t just laugh for no reason. It’s creepy. That’s exactly what I hate about you. And that’s exactly what I love about’cha! Oh, shut up.

“—stop trying to suck up to me…”

Honestly, what a worthless kid. I thought to myself. How conceited, how conceited, how conceited. How smug, how smug, how smug. I mistook that for self-awareness. I only looked at the world from the front, or perhaps the back— either way, my view was one-sided. And with that narrow view of things, I felt enlightened; I spoke as if I knew it all. Beyond terrified that my false veneer would crack. And when it inevitably did, it left me empty. The fabrication had become my reality. A tragedy that evoked neither tears nor laughter– a farce. What’s more, that farce wasn’t over. Continuing forever. Halted forever. In short, having gotten tangled up in Dead Blue, I haven’t grown at all. I don’t have any plans to either. Not when there were other things that needed doing.

The fifth tumble. This one landed me on the basement floor. I must have hit my head pretty badly this time. The pain was as vague and distant as ever, but I now experienced brief lapses in consciousness. They brought with them more memories of my past. First, my family. My younger sister. My older sister. My Father. My Mother. My grandparents. Memories of my childhood. But not once did I see the face of a friend. I knew no one. No one knew me. The accident. The collapse. The airplane. My little sister stopped appearing around then. Goodbye. Kasumioka. Nao. And Kunagisa Tomo. Everything else faded away. I wonder if this also counted as my life flashing before my eyes. Words lost their meaning. The ER3 System. My meeting with Miss Kokoromi. The classmates I never got to know. The rare few I had. Omokage Magokoro. My parting with my teacher. After that, all sorts of things happened. Most of which I didn’t remember. If I had, my head likely would have burst. Dropping-out. Japan. Kyoto. Reuniting with Kunagisa Tomo. Kunagisa Tomo, exactly the same as I had left her. And me, exactly the same as when I left. Asano Miiko. Suzunashi Neon. The Christian old man and the runaway siblings. I wonder what happened to the woman after she left for Tokyo. Wet Crow’s Feather Island. The painter without a style. The headless seventh fool. The nervous chef. The detestable fortune-teller. Him, the accomplice. The exiled lady and her triplet maids. How I wish I could see them again. Aikawa Jun. Humanity’s Strongest Contractor. May. Getting to know her and her friends. And my first contact with the Human Failure. Our self-indulgent conversations. Our self-loathing conversations. The wicked witch, Nananami Nanami. It wasn’t until the entrance of the young girl who called me master— Hime— that I managed to get a hold of myself again. Well look at that, I muttered to myself. I muttered consciously. I remembered an awful lot, didn’t I? Oh man, looks like my memory’s not completely worthless after all. Oh man, indeed. I picked myself up off the floor. Retrieving the lockpicking-knife that had clattered onto the ground, I thrust it into the keyhole on the door. I jimmied it around a couple of times, and just like that, it effortlessly came undone. I gripped the knob. I still felt no sensation. Judging by the way my body was moving, nothing seemed to be broken. That was nothing but hasty speculation, but I chose to believe it anyway as I pushed open the door.

The Fourth Ward’s basement corridor was dimly lit, with the only light source being fluorescent bulbs that hung from the ceiling looking like they might sputter out at any moment. I stepped inside. No sooner had I done so than I heard a voice. Relief. It seems my hearing wasn’t as muted as my sense of touch. After such a nasty fall down the stairs, it wouldn’t have been surprising if I had ruptured an eardrum, but it seems I needn’t have worried. I pricked my ears.

“—I          .    ——and so—”

This voice— who was it? It was horribly monotonous, leaving no space between each word— its cadence resembled synthesized speech. That’s when it hit me. Of course. It was Kasugai. Kasugai Kasuga. But where was she? Just ahead. At the cage just ahead of course.

“—If that boy were to run off somewhere then that would be my responsibility. If that were to happen I would be in quite the predicament. As such I have no choice but to question you. Understand?”

Kasugai’s voice. I wouldn’t call it calm per se— but it was far from agitated. Stepping quietly and stifling my breathing, I carefully crept down the hall one step at a time. Suddenly, I was hit with an awful headache. Perhaps one of those tumbles had done some damage to my brain. Not that it mattered. My brain was broken to begin with, so I didn’t much care what happened to it. I didn’t care so long as it could hold out just a little longer. Just a little longer. I just needed a little more time. There’s still something I had to do.

That was when I almost burst out laughing. I hadn’t laughed in so long. Something I had to do? Me? To think, me, of all people, winding up with something like that. Even a child who’d abandoned all sense of duty and privilege could wind up with something like that. If that were true, then perhaps I hadn’t been halted after all. Or perhaps it was always there, and I just pretended not to notice until now. Probably the latter. In other words, more than I had ever realized, more so than anyone had ever realized, I was a hopeless idiot.

But in the end, I did not laugh.

“Who’s to say, really?”

A nostalgic voice. Even though it had only been a couple hours since I’d heard it last, Suzunashi’s voice was music to my ears.

“Maybe he just went home? He couldn’t have been happy with his treatment. Inoji grew up quite spoiled it seems, so maybe he couldn’t bear another second in this dismal place.”

“—Take this seriously please.” Kouta’s voice was as unexpressive as ever. It conveyed neither anger, blame, nor confusion. “How do you suppose he got out exactly? If you’re saying that's what happened then surely you must have seen how he did it. How did that boy escape? Was it with the help of an insider perhaps?”

Odd. In addition to Kasugai’s voice, I also heard something resembling a low guttural sound. Like a wild animal. It surely couldn’t have been Kasugai. Not Suzunashi either. Then who? It couldn’t be Kunagisa, could it? Suddenly tingles ran through my legs as if they had fallen asleep. No, not my legs. My whole body. The pain I had sealed away seemed to be returning.

“Now that you mention it—”

Then-

“—I saw it! Iichan dislocated all his joints and slipped right through the bars! Classic Iichan, you never know what he’s gonna do next!”

The tingling ceased. A wave of relief washed over me. It seemed Kunagisa was still safe. However, overlapping Kunagisa’s words, the rumbling continued. What on earth was it? Was there someone else here as well? No, it didn’t feel that way. While my internal senses had been dulled, my external senses were amplified not two- but, two-hundred-fold. In that case. I had to do something while Kasugai was still alone.

I tried collecting my thoughts. Was there really no way to solve this? I’d only been thinking for two seconds when I shook my head in frustration. I’d been thinking for the past three hours and hadn’t come up with anything even resembling a solution. What good would come from thinking about it now? I didn’t need to think. After all, my brain was nothing more than a defective product. Like an expert relying on muscle memory, without a single thought, I just had to hope my body would move on its own. I just had to pray.

I made to round the corner so I could head in the direction of the voices. Right, once I round this corner, then the cage where Kunagisa and Suzunashi are should—

“—…”

Then- There was Kasugai. In her white lab coat. She turned her cold gaze in my direction. At her feet was a dog. One of the dogs that toyed with me last night. Ahh, so this was the source of the growling. The dog- massive, black, and vicious-looking. Just like last night, it wasn’t on a leash, it wasn’t even wearing a collar. Why did she bring the dog with her all the way to the basement? I didn’t understand what Kasugai was thinking. Naturally, I returned her gaze. Kasugai appeared a little taken aback, but she didn’t let it show on her face. “—Oh my,” she said calmly.

“Why are you—”

“Ah, it’s Iichan!” Kunagisa’s excitement was incredibly out-of-place as she clung to the bars. “Yoohoo, Iichan! Welcome back!”

I didn't respond. I just stood there, staring down Kasugai. That said, I couldn’t bring myself to ignore her completely either, and my gaze flitted over to the cage where Kunagisa was kept. She looked in good spirits. At a glance, she didn’t appear to be hurt or anything either. It seems like I had made it in time. At least, I think I did. Suzunashi was there too. She appeared calm and composed as she leaned against the wall. Except, at the sight of me, she let out a sigh of exasperation and said in a soft, somber voice, “…so, Inoji?”

“…from the looks of it, it doesn’t look good.”

“Ah! You’re right! Iichan’s all banged up. He’s all covered in scrapes. He’s even bleeding. You think he’s okay?”

Suzunashi’s comment was clearly about my progress on the case. However, Kunagisa didn’t seem to care about that at all; she was more worried about my body. Typical. Kunagisa never considered herself. Why? I didn’t understand.

I took out the lock-picking knife and took a couple unsteady steps towards the cage (…I had intended it to be a steady stride…). Huh? The cage was unlocked. Why? Kasugai must have opened it herself. I turned to face her.

“Hold on— I’d prefer it if you didn’t do anything hasty. Stay where you are.”

She was saying something. I couldn’t hear her. I must’ve ruptured an eardrum after all. I heard her, but I didn’t understand. I understood her, but the meaning was lost on me. It was like listening to beginner French for dummies. Well, whatever. Even if I could hear her, it wouldn’t have mattered. I opened the cell door.

“Let’s go home, Tomo.”

“Huh? Uh, sure—”

Kunagisa looked confused. That’s strange. Isn’t it? Did I say something weird? We’re just going home together. Like always. We go somewhere, then we come back. That’s all. That reminds me, I needed to pick up some uirō-mochi on the way home. For Hime’s friends. Miiko will probably want some too, so I’ll grab six or seven.

Something gripped my shoulder. It was Kasugai.

“—Why don’t you step inside for me. I promise not to be any harsher on you than I have to.”

“Shut up. I’ll kill you.”

I turned around and ripped her hand off me.

“Don’t get in our way. We’re leaving.”

“I can’t allow that.”

Showing no signs of intimidation, Kasugai pushed me away. Her shove caused me to stumble two or three steps away from the cage. Away from Kunagisa. Ahh, I had to get back to her. But my path was blocked. By Kasugai and her dog.

That’s when I finally realized. The black dog at Kasugai’s feet was not one I met last night. They looked nearly identical, but their aura couldn’t have been more different. It wasn’t just vicious-looking. It truly was vicious. Its two eyes glared at me as if I were its prey. Its front legs poised like it was about to pounce. Its weight settled onto its back legs, carefully preparing to attack. Compared to this, the two dogs last night may as well have been children's pets. They may have worn the same skin, but this was an entirely different animal.

“The final triplet—huh?”

“Precisely.”

Kasugai lowered her gaze slightly to rest on the dog.

“What’s more this one is far less docile and obedient than the two you saw last night. Remember my experiment? This is what you call a result.”

The result of her experiment? What kind of experiment could she have done to make this dog so different from its kin. I felt like she mentioned something about it yesterday. Or maybe she hadn’t. I couldn’t remember. I didn’t need to remember. The only thing that mattered was what Kasugai intended to use this dog for. What she intended to let it do to Kunagisa.

“—What were you thinking?” I asked. “Bringing such a mad dog with you— this isn’t funny anymore.”

“I had no choice since you escaped. All you had to do was wait quietly,” Kasugai answered coolly. Without hesitation or doubt. “So be a dear and get inside the cage won't you? If I had the choice I wouldn’t be doing this either. But I don’t. That’s all there is to it.”

Ordinary.

Kasugai’s tone was all too ordinary.

Despite this extraordinary place.

Despite the extraordinary circumstances.

She was still this ordinary.

“—I get it now. That’s how it is… That’s how it is, you’re like that too.”

I understood.

…At long last I’d come to understand what Neo had meant when he told me to be ‘wary of Kasugai.’

It all makes sense… that’s what he meant. This is what it meant to have no conviction. Ultimately, it meant you were capable of anything. You had no limitations. No creed. And thus, no obligation. That’s what Kasugai Kasuga was made of. Be it logic or debate– ethics or consensus– it all meant nothing to her.

By choosing nothing for herself, deciding nothing for herself, this was the outcome. She could bind others, imprison them, harm them, all without a care. And not even out of some strong sense of belief– for she had none to begin with.

Professor Kyouichirou had done what he did for the sake of his research. Miss Kokoromi had helped him out in service of her goals, and in service of her goals, she abandoned him. Shito and Misachi had assisted him because of their loyalty, and it was because of that loyalty that they crumbled so easily.

Kasugai was different.

She had no reason. She had no motive. She never followed any logic to begin with. And in the end, she was never meant to be understood. If I had to put it into words, it would be ‘psycho logical’- nothing more. Beyond saving. Beyond redemption. If I had arrived a moment later and Kasugai had set that dog loose inside the cell, she would likely be just as unmoved as she was now. Even if it had resulted in Kunagisa’s death, she would be just as calm. Without an end, there can be no means, and without guilt, there can be no remorse. There was no room for diplomacy. She could be neither persuaded, enticed, nor coerced.

A lack of conviction.

It was just as frightening as Neo insisted.

But in that case—

“In that case, you’re just like me—”

I reached into my breast pocket and retrieved the weapon. My left hand still gripped the lock-picking knife, and the thin blade I got from Aikawa was in my right. Each of them pointed directly at Kasugai. Not only did Kasugai not look particularly surprised, she didn’t look affected in the slightest.

“I wouldn’t put up any meaningless resistance if I were you.”

“Meaningless?”

“Utterly. The professor and the other researchers should be on their way any minute now. Even if you cut through me what do you think will happen next? It’s pointless.”

“I wouldn't say that,” I took a step closer. The distance between us wasn’t even two metres. There was no point using the gun this close. Even without Kouta’s warning, I wasn’t foolish enough to try something like that given my lack of training. No, what I had in mind was far more foolish. “After I cut through you, I’ll cut my way through the professor and anyone else who comes running. That’s what I planned to do in the first place.”

“You’re mad.”

I don’t want to hear that from you.

But before I could tell her as much, Kasugai clicked her fingers. When she did, the black dog moved swiftly. Snapping her fingers must’ve been some kind of signal. I should’ve expected as much from Kasugai, a zoologist. Although, it wasn’t completely unexpected— which meant her surprise attack had failed; I didn’t panic too much as I hopped onto my backfoot, retreating three or so feet. As if making clear its intent to protect her, the black dog stopped directly in front of Kasugai.

“As your senior let me give you some advice. Once it sinks its fangs into you you’re finished. If we stop now I can still keep a tight leash on it— metaphorically at least. Regardless it’s still under my control.”

I ignored Kasugai and focused my attention on the black dog. Kunagisa and Suzunashi said nothing. They weren’t within my field of view, so I couldn’t see the expressions on their faces either. Although, perhaps they were saying something and I just couldn’t hear it.

Oh man— I might’ve lost my mind.

To not even be able to hear Kunagisa’s voice–

“Honestly, how pleasant… honestly honestly honestly honestly honestly honestly honestly honestly honestly honestly honestly honestly honestly.”

I tossed the lock-picking knife to the ground.  Clatter, a dry sound echoed down the hallway. The dog reacted slightly, but it didn’t lunge. There was no chance I’d be able to fight a dog like this with both hands occupied. One blade was more than enough.

“I see— that’s how it is. I can tell you’re serious about this. I’ve got to say I’m somewhat disappointed.” Even if it was only a little bit, Kasugai truly did sound let down. “I always thought the two of us might be able to get along.”

“I’ve just felt that way for the first time, Kasugai Kasuga.”

“—break it.”

That was the signal. As if releasing all of its pent-up momentum, the black dog exploded into action- its massive jaws opened wide as it lunged for me. I see. Its intent was never to protect Kasugai. It was to tear me apart. That was one hell of a miscalculation. I had been unwittingly chatting with Kasugai, completely unaware that I was already dead. I was already dead, but my body moved anyway. Long before a single thought entered my head, my body moved swiftly.

What my body chose to do struck even me as odd. I thrust my left arm into the open jaws of the lunging dog. To be more precise, with all my weight behind it, I thrust my forearm in between the crowded rows of sharp fangs aimed directly at my throat, almost as if I was attempting to take its jaw clean off. After all, a dog’s legs served little purpose besides being a means of locomotion. When hunting prey, their sole weapon was their fangs— as Kasugai herself hinted at, it was the fangs to watch out for. With that in mind, it was easy to predict its trajectory, and once I’d done so, blocking was even easier. Unfortunately, as a simple fact of base animal instinct, once dogs bite on, removing them becomes no simple task. Especially once the fangs have sunk in.

That’s how I’d explain it logically at least, but I wasn’t thinking about such things. Simply put, when your opponent opens their mouth, you elbow them in the face.

Nonetheless, despite stealing the initiative, I was still knocked down. Even with all of my body weight focused into my elbow strike, holding my ground against such a massive dog was impossible. I was reminded of the fundamental difference in strength between man and beast. I landed hard on my back with the black dog pinning me down. It was a similar scene to last night. Only that time there were two of them, still, I found it much more preferable to now. Having succeeded in bringing me to the ground, the black dog planted its front paws on my chest. Then it sunk its fangs deeper into my left arm.

The black dog continued to bite down harder. It seemed to have no intention of letting go after all. Of course it didn’t, it had bitten through my jacket. What’s more, the fabric had bunched up. Removing its fangs wouldn’t be easy. Not like that was all too convenient for me. If it couldn’t let go, it would be easier to bite my arm clean off. Still, the arm is fairly muscular, even for someone like me, so despite being such a large dog, it wasn’t about to bite all the way through. That said, it was more than capable of crushing my bones. It was certainly strong enough for that. The strength of the legs that pinned me down made that abundantly clear. The pain made my nerves go haywire; I could do nothing to resist.
