chapters.text:
Psycho Logical (Part Two)

Utsurigi Gaisuke, “Criminal Judge,” Malignant Green

Hinemosu Suzu, “Consigned Stillness,” Double Flick

Gotodoroki Seigo, “Scornful Compatriot,” Reverse Cross

Munefuyu Mutsuki, “Clamoring Bloodshot,” Cubic Loop

Nadekiri Hakuraku, “Despondent Momento,” Dancing with Madness

Ayaminami Hyou, “Spinning Suzuki,” Cheetah

Shikigishi Kishiki, “Squirming Ruination,” Bad Kind

Shigai Touno, “Resurrected Abasement,” Trigger-happy End

Kunagisa Tomo, “Walking Wrath,” Dead Blue

And now for the Epilogue— or rather, a peak behind the curtains that would be best left unspoken.

Where were we supposed to go home to? For now, the only place for me to return to was my antique apartment in Kyoto. That night— the night everything had come to a close— without even waiting for it to get dark, we got back in Miiko’s Fiat, which we had Shito refuel, and put Shadou Kyouichirou’s research facility behind us. While we drove, Suzunashi booked us a hotel room, and we spent a single night in Nagoya. Despite the last-minute booking, the rooms were spacious, and the service was top-notch— Is what I wish I could say, but even then, it was still much better than the facility’s Haunted Manor. Lined up like sardines in the same bed (Me → Kunagisa → Suzunashi), the three of us slept like corpses. Even though it wasn’t exactly true, it still felt as if it had been ages since I last slept.

At daybreak, Suzunashi’s lecture began. For the next few hours, I made no rebuttal as I knelt silently in front of her; Suzunashi’s relentless scolding was only interrupted by the occasional smack on the head. Before long, Kunagisa woke up and we spent the rest of the day sightseeing around Nagoya. Keeping watch over Kunagisa out of the corner of my eye as she frolicked like a child, I managed to pick up the uirō-mochi Hime asked me for (luckily, they were selling them in five-colour sets, so it was an instant purchase) as well as some extras for Miiko and the others at the apartment for a total of ten blocks.

That evening, we dropped Suzunashi off back on Hie Mountain in Shiga prefecture.

“Say hi to Miiko for me. We’ll finish the rest of your lecture some other time,”

She said. Apparently, she still wasn’t through with me. Part of me was apprehensive, but the other part of me was looking forward to it.

Next, we arrived at Kyoto’s pride and joy (or perhaps deepest shame), the high-end residential neighborhood, Shirosaki. I parked the car outside Kunagisa’s strikingly conspicuous apartment building and walked her to her room.

“Next time, then.” “Yeah, next time.”

I didn’t know exactly what ‘next time’ entailed, but nonetheless, I said my goodbyes, got back in the Fiat, and finally headed back to my own apartment. I parked the car in the lot, and from there it was less than a minute’s walk. Rather than return to my own room, I knocked on the door to the room right next to it.

“Oh, welcome back.” Luckily Miiko was home and she came to greet me wearing one of her usual jinbei. She seemed a little– no, a lot drunk, and her face was glowing slightly. “That was quick. Only spent two nights, huh?”

“Two nights…”

That’s right. In fact, the three of us hadn’t even spent two whole days at the facility. And yet, despite that, it somehow felt as though we were imprisoned there for over a month.

“Something like that. Thanks for the car. Here’s your keys back. And some money for gas… and some uirō-mochi as a souvenir.”

“Thanks…hm?” Miiko noticed my left arm. Miss Kokoromi had taken another look at it, so it wasn’t bandaged anymore, instead sporting a full-on cast. “…Inoji, you drove all the way back from Nagoya like that?”

“Huh? No, look, I can still move my fingers just fine. And besides, you can operate the gearshift with your right hand anyways.”

“I see… I guess that’s fine then.”

That’s where the questions stopped. She never asked how I got hurt.

“Come on in. Let’s eat some uirō-mochi together. These kinds of things always taste better when you share them with someone else.”

“Normally, I wouldn’t take you up on that, but…”

But after being shown genuine human warmth for the first time in a long while, even I had trouble turning her down.

“I’ll let you spoil me today, Miiko.”

“Good. C’mon then, don’t be a stranger.”

And that’s how I ended up in Miiko’s room being treated to uirō-mochi and tea— although dealing with a plastered Miiko was an ordeal of its own. After that, I returned to my own room. It was empty.

“…Huh?”

Hang on, the lack of furniture may have been normal, but the lack of clothing and books certainly wasn’t. My cellphone and charger were missing. Oh man, so were my health insurance card and bank book. I was worried I’d been robbed for a second, but the truth hit me a second later, and I made my way towards Hime’s room on the first floor.

“But you said I could have everything, master.”

The culprit was Hime.

“I cleaned your room. I even took out the garbage for you.”

The ‘garbage’ in question no doubt included my personal belongings.

“…Hime. You were only supposed to do that if I didn’t make it back okay…”

“Really? But- but, master, just look at your arm– you don’t seem very okay to me.”

“…I guess not.”

Man… if only all cases were this easy to solve.

I only managed to recover my bank book and health insurance card by trading them for the uirō-mochi before I returned to my room once more.

“Ah—…how should I put it?”

It was like waking up from nothingness. Like waking up from a nightmare. Of course, that was nothing more than a fantasy bordering on delusion. After all, The Mad Daemon, Shadou Kyouichirou’s research facility had been undeniably real.

“Real, huh? —but how is that any different from illusion?”

What would happen to that lab now? I thought about it for quite some time. With the facility’s head, Professor Shadou Kyouichirou, in such a sorry state, they wouldn’t be able to continue to function as a laboratory; as such, they would likely be absorbed by a nearby research institute, or so Kunagisa said. Indeed, with The Mad Daemon becoming worthless— in the literal sense— I can’t imagine the Kunagisa House being willing to continue pouring money into him forever. If that happened, what would become of the other researchers?

It probably wouldn’t be much of a problem for Neo. That man was a scoundrel from the very start. He’d made betrayal his job— a rogue who ultimately belonged nowhere. He would likely just chalk it up as a loss, compensate his client for duties unfulfilled, and as the professional lowlife that he is, begin searching for his next job.

“—I gotta say, I wouldn’t be against teaming up again some time. If anything, I’m half-tempted to scout you and bring you back with me.”

“That’s not funny… Don’t go around telling people they’ve got the makings of a backstabber.”

“Don’t be silly, you don’t strike me as a backstabber at all. If anything, you’re the type to look someone in the eyes as they betray them.”

“…………”

“Hm? That one actually was supposed to be funny.”

—Though I’ll likely never have anything to do with the man again, looking back on it now, I can’t help finding him a strangely amusing character. It’s rare to find anyone so straightforward about their betrayal.

Miyoshi Kokoromi— Miss Kokoromi, said something about returning to the ER3 System. There’s no reason they would turn down someone as talented as her, so everything would likely work out just fine.

“This is goodbye forever then, Miss.”

“Y’think? I reckon we’ll be meeting again soon.”

“…………”

“What’s more, next time things’ll be far, far worse. Nothin’ would suit you better— Frankly, it ain’t even funny. Well then, bye-byee.”

Once again, Miss Kokoromi left me with a dreadful premonition. Man, why did she have to be so terrible at goodbyes? Cut me some slack already.

Kasugai Kasuga. Kasugai will– well, she’ll probably do just about anything. She’d make it work somehow, so there was likely no need for me to worry. In the most literal sense, she would do anything. Of all people, I could never imagine her in a hopeless situation. She never had any convictions to speak of— a person composed of nothing but talent. Without goals, nothing is off limits. Without desires, nothing is unnecessary. Without satisfaction, there is no disappointment. Without happiness, there is no sadness. Without something to protect, there is no urge to destroy. If you’re not alive, you can’t die. To have value, but not values. There is no solution to something that isn’t a problem— That’s the kind of person she was.

If I had to guess, she will likely get swept up by some branch of the Kunagisa Syndicate. She was far too talented to be left to her own devices. I would likely never meet her again, but— No. When it came to her, there were no ‘but’s.

Ougaki Shito— Uze Misachi. Apparently the two of them planned to go wherever the professor went. They would follow him now and forever. I have nothing to say to that. It isn’t my place. Those with strong convictions had nothing to be gained from listening to those with no conviction at all.

And then.

Koutari Hinayoshi.

Koutari Hinayoshi— escaped.

Not even the security guards at the mountain-pass gate caught sight of him. Just like a puff of smoke, he had vanished into thin air.

“Vanished?— people can’t just vanish…”

But people can be made to disappear.

That’s all there was to it.

“…Wait, I’m forgetting someone.”

That’s right, there was someone else. Someone I mustn't forget. Someone I must never forget…

With those thoughts in mind, I drifted off to sleep.

The next day arrived. As easy as it is to forget, I am a university student, and as such, I had to be on campus on weekdays. To tell the truth, I would have liked to spend another day recuperating, but thanks to this little trip of ours, I had already missed three days of class, and that’s not even counting all the days I missed last month while in the hospital. I had already missed too much, and exams were right around the corner, so regardless of how beat up my body was, I had no choice but to drag myself to class. I got ready to leave (I couldn’t use my left arm, so I had to get Miiko to help me dress) then stepped out of my apartment. Houko, the little girl who lived on the floor above me, was crouched in the alley doing something. The straw hat she wore to protect her from the early-morning sun looked oddly fitting on her and made for a cute scene.

“Yo, good morning, Houko”

“Good morning, big brother.” Without looking up at me, she quickly bowed her head. “Are you going to school?”

“Yeah. What are you doing, Houko?”

“Killing bugs.”

“…I see. Do your best then.”

“Yup, I will.”

As I walked past her, she reached out and grabbed the hem of my pantleg without looking up.

“Big brother, if you go to school today, you’ll probably die.”

She said casually.

“I know,” I replied casually.

“You know and you’re still going?”

“It’s a worthless life anyway,” I shrugged. “Besides, I have exams coming up.”

“Okay then,” Houko let go. Houko still didn’t look up at me, but I gave her a small wave and continued on my way to school.

Class was as boring as ever. Whether something is boring or not has more to do with the person feeling bored than anything, so I had no right to complain. That’s just how university is. And whether it’s exam season or not, whether I attend class or not, that will never change. And so, I spent the boring (through no fault of its own) lecture reading a book I borrowed from Nanananami, The Yacht of Death. Both the cover and prose were ridiculously antiquated, so it was somewhat difficult to read. It was a boxed hardcover and was so bulky that even when I put it in my bag, it stuck out a little. I just can’t wrap my head around Nanananami’s tastes. That said, if we’re just talking about the book’s contents, I personally found them quite interesting and enjoyable.

After lunch break, I had a review seminar. For lunch itself, I bought some sweet bread and took the stairs to my classroom on the fourth floor. This was the kind of situation where you’d usually take an elevator, but for some reason I wasn’t in the elevator kind of mood.

“…an elevator kind of mood? What would that even be?”

Speaking of— Utsurigi despised elevators. I suppose it doesn’t matter, but I can’t help wondering what his reasons were.

Was it because they made him feel trapped…?

I was still considering the answer when I arrived at the classroom where I was greeted with a rather odd sight. A number of my classmates were huddled around the door as if trying to peer into the room. They were free to enter and take a seat, but for some reason all of them wore serious expressions as they tried to catch a glimpse through the crack of the door.

“…What’s everyone doing?”

“Oh, Ikkun.” Yoshige (wears coats even in the summer. Hobby: bead collecting) turned to face me. “Long time no see. Ah, did you get hurt again?”

“Hm? You’re right, it really is Ikkun.” Minayama (wears a jersey and high heels. Personal Scripture: Dogra Magra) also noticed me and waved me over. “C’mere a sec. Don’t just stand there, come take a look.”

“Look at what? Just hurry up and go insi—”

“No way!” Yoshimasa (combs back his blonde hair. Wears shorts. Dream job: Astronaut) panicked, swatting away my hand as I reached for the doorknob. “What’re you doing? Don’t throw away this precious gift.”

“Gift?”

“Y’see, right now there’s this strange woman in the classroom,” Märchen (keeps a hamster on her right shoulder. Gothic Lolita) explained, “so how should I put it? —Going inside’s a little awkward.”

“A strange woman? And she’s not one of our classmates?”

“That’s right! But she’s sooo cool!” “Yeah! She’s amazing!” “A complete bombshell!” “She’s so tall— and her hair is gorgeous—!” “Look how long her legs are—” “She seems kinda wild—” “She looks crazy strong!” “I bet she just does whatever she wants, don’t you think!?” “ —red—” “She’s got this unapproachable aura or something—” “She’s, like, super imposing, or, like, heroic or something—”

“Hang on.”

I stopped them.

“Did someone just say red?”

“Yeah, I did? Why?”

“—I think I’ve got an idea who it is. Can everyone step aside, I’m coming through.”

Instantly, everyone’s eyes sparkled. Then, as if this is the moment they’d all been waiting for, they happily cried out in unison,

“That’s our, Ikkun! He’s got way more guts than we do! He’s my idol! I want to be him!”

I hate them.

I ignored them and opened the door.

There, as promised–

“—Yo,”

–in an excessively arrogant manner, with her legs kicked up on one of the desks, sat Humanity’s Strongest Contractor, Aikawa Jun. As usual, she was dressed in a maddeningly crimson suit with her entire being radiating an intimidating aura. Her mere presence, already a work of art.

“What are the chances I’d meet you here, Iitan?”

“—If this counts as chance, then no one would ever need dice…”

“Ha-ha, true that,” Aikawa laughed cynically. Then, without shifting her posture, she leapt out of her chair, over the desk, and landed directly in front of me. “That’s right, Iitan, I came here to see you.”

“Right… that’s fine and all, but please refrain from jumping from a seated position.”

“No need to be so tense- not after all we’ve been through,” she said, slinging her arm around my shoulder in an overly-friendly manner. Face to face, cheek to cheek, she brought me unnaturally close. Then, she turned towards my classmates and said, “Now then, all you extras. I’m gonna snatch this bride-to-be for a sec.”

“By all means,”

They all said in perfect unison.

I hate them so much.

The powerless nineteen-year-old bride let himself be dragged out of the classroom. Aikawa never removed her arm from around my shoulders, instead she locked it even tighter, pressing our bodies together. You could almost call it an embrace. I wondered how the two of us looked to those around us.

Definitely not like lovers.

…even though I came to that conclusion myself, I found the speed at which I arrived there a little disappointing.

“Hmm? What’s the matter, Iitan? You’re even quieter than usual? You depressed or something?”

“No… and more importantly, can you let go of me, it’s way too hot.”

“What’s with you? How cruel—” Aikawa replied in a playful tone. “If you keep talkin’ like that, you’ll hurt big sis’ feelings— You’re so cold, Iitan– You’re a cold-blooded monster. A real meanie–”

“It’s hot. It’s summer. And it’s hard to walk.”

“Just admit you’re embarrassed. You’re such a boy,” Aikawa snickered, finally letting go of me. “Well, I can’t pretend like that part of you ain’t cute. There’s plenty of freaks out there who go wild for that sort of thing. So? How’ve ya been?”

“…What do you want? Why’d you come all the way to my university? Don’t tell me you’re here just to kill time.”

“Hmm– It’s more like I put in the effort to make time. I just finished a job, y’see.”

“Is that right? A job, huh?”

“You really are cold, arent’cha, Iitan?” Aikawa said with a wry smile. “Alright, I get it, I get it… if I want you to be honest, I gotta do the same. I admit it, I came here to see you.”

“Yeah, obviously. You already said as much.”

We left the school building. It was still technically lunch break, so the campus grounds were packed with people still milling about. Aikawa and I carefully threaded our way through the crowd. Judging by Aikawa’s deliberate stride, it seems like she had a destination in mind. Even though I felt a touch of unease about where she was leading me, I followed behind her.

“Y’see, I figured maybe I ought to try and patch things up between us,”

Aikawa said. I was so utterly shocked by Aikawa’s genuine humility that I was left momentarily speechless. However, that was quickly followed by a happiness akin to walking on air— and yet, it still felt like something was missing.

That’s right. Something’s wrong. That’s not how this goes. Our Aikawa Jun is a little more—

“So, I’m gonna make you apologize.”

Aikawa continued with no trace of hesitation. YES! I balled my right fist and did a fist pump. That’s the stuff. That’s exactly what I’m looking for. Now that’s Aikawa Jun.

“Sure— no problem whatsoever, Ishimaru Kouta.” I nodded. “That whole mess was my fault to begin with, so I apologize.”

Aikawa pursed her lips slightly before responding, “Alright. You’re forgiven. Frankly, I ought to sock you one for all that, but since I’m trying to make amends here, I’ll be the bigger person.”

Oh? Grandstanding over not hitting someone?

I knew it. This kind of Aikawa is the best.

“I wouldn’t mind. I don’t want to fight with Aikawa ei–”

“It’s Jun.” Even at times like this, she was still as unforgiving as ever. “How many times have I told you not to call me by my last name? Get it through your thick skull already.”

“—I don’t want to fight with Jun either…” I could not be more serious about that. “…So, does that mean the braids were a wig or something?”

“Yep. All a part of the disguise. Same with the hat and glasses. It’s all laughably cliché, really,” Aikawa replied, running a hand through her actual hair. “Still, it sure took you long enough. I thought you knew all about my love of disguises. Honestly, I was starting to think you never picked up on it at all, but I guess I wasn’t giving you enough credit.”

“I guess not… it didn’t occur to me at the time, but if anyone could pull of such a perfect Lupin the Third impression, it’d have to be you, wouldn’t it?”

“Ha-ha, maybe so. Still, I don’t remember dropping any hints this time. What gave it away?”

“No, there were plenty of hints… Like when you used vocal mimicry to trick the security system and break us out of the Seventh Ward… “Kouta” made it sound like child’s play, but in actuality it was no small feat. This was a defense system built by Kunagisa Tomo after all, so there’s no way any run-of-the-mill vocal trickery would have cut it. You also gave me the lockpicking knife. That was strange too. How would “Kouta” have been able to get past any of the locked doors without it? That said, if she had the lockpicking and vocal mimicry skills of Humanity’s Strongest, then I’m sure she would have found a way somehow. That sort of thing…”

“So, you brute-forced it using the same strained reasoning as Shadou Kyouichirou?”

I shrugged my shoulders at Aikawa’s needling.

“Still, you’ve got a point. Anybody could change their voice enough to trick the people around them– but changing your voiceprint? I might be the only one capable of pulling that off. I get where you’re comin’ from. Still, given the situation there was no way around it.”

“You also told me that no one would ever think to use “Zerozaki” as an alias.”

“I did? I don’t remember saying that.”

“Really now? Still, that’s all just hindsight… What really made me realize, or rather, the first moment I remember doubting Kouta came right at the end. When Kouta gave me the lockpicking knife, she said something about me not being content with just the knife in my right-breast pocket.”

“Hmm, I did, didn’t I?”

“Except, at that moment, I was concealing the knife in my left-breast pocket,” I said. “I thought it would be easier to wield that way, so I switched it around earlier that very morning. And yet, “Kouta” said it was in my right pocket. If she had simply spotted the knife in my left pocket, then I could chalk that up to keen perception— but for her to claim the knife was in my right pocket, she would have to have prior information. And the only other person in possession of that prior information was none other than the person who gave me the knife in the first place, Jun.”

“—damn.”

Aikawa slapped her own forehead.

“Ah—… I see. What a stupid mistake.”

“I didn’t know you were capable of making mistakes. I was starting to wonder whether you said that on purpose.”

“Man, guess I let my guard down. Nah, that’s not it. Maybe I was just too pissed off at you.” Jun wore a cynical smile. “I’m still in need of training, it seems.”

“Training? That’s Ishikawa Goemon’s line, isn’t it—? Still, that was awfully mean of you, Jun. Why didn’t you just tell me? If I knew Ishimaru Kouta was actually Aikawa Jun, then it would have been much easier to trust her—”

“Trust, eh? Don’t give me that— I was on the job, you know. You’re not exactly tight lipped. And more importantly, it was fun to see your reactions.”

“That’s why you did it?”

“When I first called out to you, it was just so I could see you squirm a little. But then you had to go and get yourself captured the very next day. I couldn’t just leave you there to rot, could I?”

She spoke as if it were the obvious course of action.

“Then I figured, since I’m already going out of my way to help you, I might as well tease you a little more by keeping up the disguise—”

…She made that, too, sound like the obvious choice.

“Except, then you started goin’ on about how you didn’t need my help– As a contractor, I can’t just go around helping people who insist they can do it all themselves, so I wasn’t sure what to do– …Nah, that’s not quite right.” Aikawa shrugged. “I’ll just come out and say it– I was a little touched by your words back then. I’m talkin’ ‘bout the ‘I’m glad I was able to become their friend,’ part. I felt like I’d already missed my chance to come clean.”

Oh.

Ahh— all the way back then? Now that she mentions it, I did say that, didn’t I? How was I to know I was saying it right in front of the person in question? I’d only spoken my mind because I was certain I’d never see “Kouta” again.

“I’ve been glad we were friends for ages,” Aikawa teased, grinning. “I love ya, Iitan.”

“……”

Guah. How embarrassing. I’d made a complete fool of myself. I’ve really done it now. Let’s- let’s quickly change topics. How do I get out of this?

“A-anyway, why the false identity? That doesn’t seem like you at all. Even if Zerozaki Itoshiki was just a bad joke, what was Ishimaru Kouta all about?”

“The explanation’s a bit tricky… Like I already told you, I was on a job, so my hands were tied. There’s confidentiality to consider, so I can’t tell you everything— but I was contracted to pull a heist. Y’see, Ishimaru Kouta’s a real person.”

“Really? Then you were just taking over the job for her?”

“Exactly. Kouta and I are something like uneasy acquaintances. She may talk all fancy, but she’s a real piece of work. She’s closer to the Fiend with Twenty Faces than Lupin the Third. The real Kouta might’ve still asked for your help, but she never would have returned the favour. Honestly, working for her is a pain in the ass, so I was planning on turning her down, but then I found out you and Kunagisa were gonna be in the same place. I really only took the job because I was worried about you two.”

This woman always lets her feelings interfere with her work.

“But why did Kouta— the real one— not just do the job herself? Why ask you?”

“Right, the thing about Kouta is that she can’t stand Neo.”

So, she let personal feelings interfere with work too.

“I’m actually quite a fan. He’s a complete scumbag, but somehow, he’s hard to hate. A real scamp, I think they’re called— Ha-ha, you’re a bit of a scamp yourself, aren’tcha, Iitan?”

“Please don’t lump me together with someone like him… And hang on, Neo and the real Kouta are acquaintances, aren’t they? Are you telling me he never noticed you weren’t her?”

“That’s exactly what I’m telling you. Even if you ignore my top-notch disguise skills, it’s not like people ever really pay much attention to one another. It’s the same kind of deal as you not realizing it was me either. Ah, then again, Kunagisa probably noticed.”

“Probably.”

That’s right. Given Kunagisa’s perception and memory, it wouldn’t put it past her. However, whether she would have told anyone was a different matter altogether. Perhaps that was the reason Kunagisa looked so spaced out when Kouta appeared before us in the cage in the Fourth Ward’s basement. Since I never asked her— since I had no desire to ask her, I could never say for sure.

“Exactly. You could even say that I was Tuxedo Mask this time around.”

It seems Humanity’s Strongest Contractor had a soft spot for shoujo manga as well.

“So— he really just never noticed? I mean, it’s not like you changed your height or anything… or did you?”

“It’s not like I couldn’t have. There’s just no reason to bother. Once people get stuck in their preconceived notions, you can fool them just about any way you like.  —Ahh then again, there’s one thing I’ve gotta admit, the real Kouta doesn’t actually wear glasses. That was just a trick to stop you from seein’ through me.”

“Huh…? All it took was glasses…?”

“Pretty much. You know how they cover the eyes of juvenile suspects with black bars? It’s the same idea. It ain’t easy to recognize someone with their eyes covered, y’know. I guess what I’m tryna say is: no matter how well you disguise yourself— the only things you can’t fake are your eyes and your fingerprints,” Aikawa said. “That’s why gouging out the eyes, wearing sunglasses, or even growing out your hair to hide your face before suddenly shaving it all off might be good tricks to consider. Same with wearing gloves.”

“…huh. I see.” I tried to answer as calmly as possible. “That makes a lot of sense.”

“It’s as obvious as it gets. Still, that’s the gist of it. The only reason I pretended to be Kouta was to fool Neo. I did a hell of a job, didn’t I? They don’t call me Humanity’s Strongest Contractor for nothin’.”

That’s when Aikawa grinned fiercely.

Ahh, damnit. She’s just so cool.

I felt genuinely captivated.

“…So, in the end, how did your job turn out?”

“Hm? I told you, didn’t I? ‘I just finished a job.’ When you hear those words comin’ from me, it means the job was a success. Aikawa Jun has never once failed a job.”

“Is that right?”

“Of course… and I couldn’t have done it without your help, Iitan,” Aikawa clapped me on the back. “That’s what you were trying to do, right? Thanks to you gathering everyone in one place, I had free run of the facility. I’m especially grateful that you bought me some alone time in the Primary Ward.”

“……You’re welcome,” I nodded casually. “Well, that was sort of…paying you back. It was the least I could do.”

“How noble of you.”

“I may lie, but I never break a promise.”

“Hmph… now that sounds like a lie. It’s like, ‘never judge a book by the cover, unless they’re a wanted criminal’.”

“…come on now, that’s enough of that… you’ll make Mikoko mad.”

“Hehehe, her running gag is mine!”

“Isn’t that just plagiarism?”

“It sounds like a certain someone doesn’t know about the law of conservation of energy. It’s like ‘trying to move on while being stuck looking back, just do the moonwalk!’”

She had perfected it.

Then Aikawa stopped, turned to face me, and stuck out her right hand.

“Now then. How ‘bout a handshake to prove we’ve buried the hatchet. Or would you prefer a kiss?”

“Ah, umm” even though I hesitated, like the chicken I am, I ended up choosing the handshake. “Well then, I look forward to our continued relationship.”

“Likewise,” playing it up, she smiled seductively. “May it be a long one.”

Even after leaving the campus, Aikawa kept walking. Where on earth was she taking me? Judging by her stride, she seemed keen to get there, but would it kill her to at least tell me how long it would take?

“Hm? What’s this? This book looks ancient.”

Disregarding my feelings, Aikawa cried out almost joyfully when she spotted Nanananami’s book peeking out of my bag.

“It’s a book I borrowed from a witch. It’s apparently a mystery novel.”

“Hm, let’s have a gander.” Without asking, she plucked the book out of my bag, took it out of the box, and began flipping through the pages. She quickly lost interest and slid the book back into the box. “Hmph. Boring. You’re better off throwin’ it away.”

No sooner had she said so than she tore the book in half straight down the middle, box and all, before tossing it onto Nishioji street. Just then, several trucks passed by, and Nanananami’s book was gone from this world.

“………………………”

“It feels good takin' out the trash.”

“…Yeah, sure.”

The words of Goethe or Dazai were meaningless when faced with Aikawa Jun. Naturally, I levied no complaints against anyone who could rip a hardcover in half as easily as if it were calligraphy paper. Jeez, it wasn’t even mine… Oh well, it was just Nanananami’s. It was pretty beat-up anyways, so I’ll just buy her a new copy. I could probably pick one up at market price for three hundred yen.

“I can’t stand mystery novels.”

A bombshell confession.

“They constantly spout all this drivel about the sanctity of logic, and yet they all want unexpected solutions. Something about how that’s what makes a tantalizing mystery. Anyone with a brain knows the only solutions logic leads to are boring as hell, don’tcha agree? Now if they could manage to make one plus one equal three, then maybe they’d be worth my time.”

“Really…? Then what genre of books do you like?”

“A fine question. Something you gotta learn about me, Iitan, is that I hate when authors try to be overly clever or catch you off guard. I like hackneyed, cliché stories, like the ones where a man gives his life for a woman. Tried-and-true stories with predictable twists, protagonists you’ve seen before, and a villain that everyone knows. Stories with a worn-out moral about how good triumphs over evil, about hot-blooded idiots and cunning fools. Stories about the friendship between rivals that have a tear-jerking happy ending. I absolutely love that kinda thing.”

“…I see. Tried-and-true, huh?”

“Exactly. Who the hell needs unexpected twists or surprises? Cheap tricks are more than fine by me… Only the royal road befits a king, after all. Going off the beaten path is a job for the court jester, don’t you agree? Hm?”

“…I have no words.”

“That so?” Aikawa nodded contentedly.

“Speaking of tried-and-true— don’t you think the story of Shadou Kyouichirou’s research facility and the case on Wet Crow’s Feather Island have a lot in common?”

“A lot in common…?”

A gathering of geniuses. An isolated setting. A locked room murder involving someone under lock and key, and the body parts stolen from the scene of the crime, never to be found—

“Yeah. Now that you mention it, they’re almost eerily similar.”

“Come to think of it, if that incident never happened, the two of us never would’ve met—”

“What’s that about all of a sudden? Don’t go off on a heartfelt speech like this is the last time we’ll ever see each other.”

In response to my dig, Aikawa’s lips curled into a smile. “Do you believe some people are fated to meet, Iitan?” she asked. I thought for a second then shook my head.

“Fate, I can get behind— but I can’t bring myself to believe in meetings.”

“I see. Typical,” Aikawa said. “—still, for as similar as this case was to the one in April, there are a number of notable differences. For one, in terms of major incidents on the island, there were two or three– or was it four? The point is, there were a number of them, but this time you managed to put a stop to it at one. I guess we could chalk that up to you actually putting in a modicum of effort for once. That said, the biggest difference would have to be that, of all the geniuses gathered there, each and every one of them was your enemy. While they may not have thought very highly of you on that island— you certainly weren't adversaries, but this time you played a splendid villain.”

“…villain.”

“There wasn’t a single person on your side– even the victim turned out to be against you. Honestly, that kinda thing’s gotta be rare, right? Despite the situations looking almost identical at the outset, the outcome couldn’t have been more different. Doing the same thing, but getting different results? That logic just doesn’t add up. It just goes to show that what’s really important ain’t plot, but characters. That’s right, it’s like we took the incident on Wet Crow’s Feather Island, turned it over, and flipped it inside-out.”

“—Then it must have been awfully boring for you. I don’t remember much happening on that nonsensical island other than my love story with Akari.”

“Oh really? That’s really somethin’.”

Humanity’s Strongest spoke in a carefree manner, yawning as she strolled along. But I wasn’t about to let that easy-going attitude fool me.

That’s right, don’t forget.

The contractor’s role in the story.

The reason for her appearance here at the end.

Indeed— if this case truly was the inverse of the case that brought Aikawa and I together— if this truly was Wet Crow’s Feather Island turned inside-out— then what kind of tried-and-true twists did she have in store.

Tried-and-true.

Predictable.

—predictable, huh?

We passed by some high school students on a field trip, as we crossed Imadegawa street. After going a little further, Aikawa finally stopped and entered a nearby café. The FM radio was blaring. Perhaps it was because of the lunch rush, but the place was packed. Maybe Aikawa would even pay for my meal. If she did, what should I do with the sweet bread I went out of my way to buy? No, like I said, this was no time to be so easy-going.

Aikawa took a seat, gesturing for me to sit across from her. Then, after casually ordering some drinks, she said, “So, Iitan, if I told you I had another reason for coming to see you, what do you think it’d be?”

“—Likely something to do with the case.”

“Such a business-like answer. If you were the kinda guy who could say something witty at a time like this, your life would’ve turned out so much different,” Aikawa smiled. “Still, you’re not wrong— but before we get into that, let’s chat a little longer. We’ve still got some time,”

Aikawa said without even looking at the clock. This lady’s internal clock could give an atomic clock a run for its money, so she had no use for the digital or analogue variety. However, the word ‘still’ caught my interest. No— perhaps it’s better to say that word triggered an overdue realization. Just like the words ‘right-breast pocket’ had led to my realization about Aikawa’s disguise.

I understand it now. So that’s how they managed to escape the facility without being caught. Certainly, with this person’s help— nothing was impossible.

If so— then perhaps that was it. Maybe that had been the contractor’s job all along. If that were true, then the reason Aikawa never revealed her true identity to me— doesn’t it start to make a little more sense?

…I was almost certainly overthinking it, but— but I couldn’t shake the illusion. In that case, given what Neo was up to, by the time Humanity’s Strongest got involved— the research facility’s fate had long since been sealed, hadn’t it?

Suspicion clouded my mind, but with seemingly no consideration for my current mental state, Aikawa continued.

“So, what’s been going on between you and Kunagisa since then?”

She asked.

“What’s been going on…? Not much. It’s not like anything’s changed. We had some fun in Nagoya and then I dropped her off at home yesterday. We haven’t seen each other since.”

“I see,” Aikawa nodded. “Well, I suppose that’s to be expected.”

“And why is that?”

“No reason, I was just thinking– rather than hold someone, you’re the kinda guy who prefers to be held, aren’tcha?”

“I don’t get it.”

“That’s because I’m being vague on purpose. It’d be a pain in the ass if you actually understood. Regardless, I’ve gotta say, I’m honestly shocked by your loyalty to Kunagisa— your fealty. Almost like a mediaeval knight.”

“You’re giving me too much credit.”

“Really now? And here I thought I was being rather objective. That said, your clumsiness really stood out this time.”

“Was it that obvious?”

“It was,” Aikawa laughed.

“I mean– what was all that about? Singling out your culprit using the process of elimination? Were you trying to make me laugh?”

“You were listening?”

“Just at the start. It was so ridiculous I had to give up halfway. I heard the rest after the fact— besides, I was busy using the window your puppetshow bought me to sneak around the Primary Ward. That was more important.”

“………”

After the fact.

But who did she hear it from?

“The rooftop route. I gotta say, your naming sense leaves a lot to be desired—” Aikawa said. “You can’t use it because you’re a woman. You can’t use it because you’re fat. You can’t use it because you’re old. You can’t use it because you have bad eyesight— give me a break. You don’t seriously believe any of those reasons are good enough, do you?”

“You don’t?” I played dumb. “I don’t see why not.”

“Sure, the risk would be high, but that’s all the more reason to go through with it. Looking at it the other way, if you manage to pull it off despite the risk, then you can escape suspicion. —I mean, speaking frankly,” Aikawa pointed at herself with her thumb. “If it were me— Aikawa Jun. Even as a woman, even if I were a hundred-year-old granny, I could leap ten metres with my eyes closed and a two-hundred-and-fifty-kilogram dumbbell on my back— I wouldn’t even need a running start.”

“Well yeah, but you’re… an exception. You could probably run across walls.”

“I can run across ceilings, kid. So, if you know about outliers like me, why would your reasoning be so ordinary? Don’t tell me you forget how that turned out last month.”

“Last month…huh. You may have a point, but it’s not like any of them denied it and said they could’ve jumped it, right?”

“Like hell they would. That’s the same as begging to be put back on the list of suspects. In that sense, I’ve gotta give you props. That was a clever way to make the most out of the process of elimination. Anyone would be defensive if you suddenly insisted they were the culprit but there’s not a person alive who’d get defensive about being declared innocent. There’s no need to refute an argument that’s to your benefit after all.”

The process of elimination.

Looking at it from a psychological perspective— there was hardly be a more absurd technique. However, there are certain situations where absurdity makes for quite the weapon— and I’ve seen more than my fair share.

“—Still, you can’t deny that it is a difficult jump. It’s too far. If it weren’t for the situation I was in, I never would have considered jumping either.”

“If you’re gonna say that— then using the same logic as the process of elimination, couldn’t we question whether Koutari could have pulled it off too? It’d be one thing if he was a body-builder or something, but we’re talking about a middle-aged science geek. Do you still think he could have made that jump?”

“Who knows?”

I continued to play dumb. There was no real point to it, it’s just, having Aikawa back me into a corner like this was fun in its own right. Perhaps that pleasure was a little bit masochistic.

“Besides, if that’s not what happened, how do you explain everything else? Since it’s the only possible solution, we can’t just rule it out.”

“Hmph, I see. So that’s how you’re gonna be, Iitan. How cute– makes me want to pinch your cheeks.” In direct contrast, Aikawa’s broad grin was completely sadistic. “Then tell me… That whole story about how Koutari got back– how he used his hair to make a rope– how he used Utsurigi’s arms to make a hook and escape the Seventh ward— Do you really believe it?”

“Really really, and one more really for good measure.”

“Swear to god?”

“Swear to god.”

“Swear to Chiga Hikari?”

“That, I can’t do.”

“—You’re so friggin’ cute, you know that…?” Aikawa laughed in disbelief. “Well either way… suppose you’re right and you could suspend a rope between the Sixth and Seventh Wards,”

Aikawa continued,

“—what then?”

“…………”

“This isn’t about whether it could hold your weight. That part’s fine. But, what would you do next? You made a rope, and using momentum and centrifugal force, you’re able to launch the rope across so it spans the gap between the buildings. That part’s already batshit enough— but your next move would be… what exactly? Tightrope walking?”

“Is there something wrong with that?”

“You think scientists are that fit? And without a balance pole? Not even circus troupes have the guts to try that nowadays. Even if you took all the girls from that academy, Saijou Tamamo’s probably the only one who could’ve managed it. It’s not the sort of thing you can pull off with any ordinary sense of balance- much less when your life is on the line.”

“Who’s to say he couldn’t? Sure, the chances are slim, but they aren’t exactly zero either. You never know what people are capable of when their lives are at stake.”

“Ain’t that the exact opposite of what you were saying earlier, Mister Opportunist?” Aikawa laughed. “Then you won’t mind if I do the same— right? If you’re betting something as precious as your life, why on earth would you make such a risky gamble?”

“………”

“If they were prepared to go through something as stupid as tightrope walking, then they would’ve had a better shot at surviving if they just jumped down.”

“Come on now. That’s just nitpicking.” I tried deflecting like a mystery writer. “Whatever the final deduction is, it must be the truth. Besides, Utsurigi admitted to all of it—”

“He admitted it? Ha!” Aikawa forced a laugh.

“What was it again? The hand print on his arm—? That was your proof, right? Except, Utsurigi never actually showed us any hand prints, did he?”

“He must’ve given up.”

“He gave up— laughable,” Aikawa really did laugh. “Fine then, that’s enough. We’ve done more than enough talking, Iitan, so get over here.”

“What for?”

“I’m gonna punch you.”

You’d have to be an idiot to hear that sort of thing and willingly get closer. Rooted to the spot, I responded by simply spreading raising arms slightly. Seeing that, Aikawa said, “alright, alright, I won’t punch you, so come here.”

Relieved to hear that, I made my way over.

She kissed me.

“……………………………………………………………………………………………………………………………………………………”

“Hm? What’s that look for? It’s not like that was your first kiss, was it?”

“…well, no, but…”

I shrugged my shoulders again, trying to look unbothered. With a completely unfazed attitude, I slicked my hair back, lightly crossed my legs, took a sip of the coffee that had been placed in front of me, and spread my arms wide.

……It actually was.

“Anyway, here’s what I really wanted to say, Nonsense User. If you’re gonna put on a farce, at least come up with a more convincing lie.”

“………”

A farce— that’s right. What Professor Kyouichirou had called a ‘typical con-artist’s tactic’. Supplanting truth with amazement. In doing so, the latter half of my reasoning could be omitted. Purposefully spitting out vague half-finished answers that could be interpreted in any number of ways. Cementing confusion as truth.

There was no need for a correct solution.

It just needed to be unexpected.

That’s right, I never needed to uncover the truth.

I just needed to surprise them.

Entirely psychological.

Nothing to do with the act itself, but the logic of perception.

“Can you really blame me—?” I looked away evasively. Naturally, there was no escaping Aikawa’s gaze. It pierced right through me. “I ran out of time. I didn’t have a chance to iron out all the details. I only realized the truth of the matter at the very last second. Besides, it’s only natural that my reasoning had some holes in it given all the painkillers Miss Kokoromi put me on, isn’t it?”

And above all else, the biggest limiting factor was that I needed to manufacture an element of surprise. For instance, if my grand conclusion was something like there was a ladder hidden in one of the wards or they used a helicopter, no one would have bought it. If it didn’t shock and amaze, it was out of the question.

“Don’t make excuses, idiot.”

Wow, harsh.

“Still— with the detective, culprit, and victim all in cahoots, you could’ve gotten a confession no matter what theory you came up with. Surely you could've settled on something more elegant.”

“But Koutari himself gave me sixty points. That’s a passing grade.”

“He was being generous. I would’ve given you a one.”

“That’s awfully strict.”

That said, I can’t deny the conditions were in my favour. The one playing the role of the culprit had a solution prepared for me from the start— All that I had to do was decide how to spin it.

That’s not all, I had been blessed with an exceptional cast as well. The folks at that facility— the so-called scholarly researchers. They were used to wonders being wonders. To them, the secretive nature of this world was self-evident. With a gallery like that, orchestrating a puppetshow was remarkably easy.

All I had to do was take advantage of their blind spots— the things they unconsciously avoid, the things they don’t consider worth thinking about, the things once thought preposterous. Since the key culprit was actually an accomplice, the race was rigged from the start.

Besides— taking advantage of blind spots was a nonsense user’s specialty.

A makeshift bluff, a counterfeit philosophy.

So long as the goal was to bewilder, I was unmatched. The smarter they were, the sweeter the nonsense sounded.

“Well, since the test only had one question to begin with, one point may not be so bad.”

“For me, the hard part was realizing everything in the opposite order. Speaking of… when did you figure out the truth, Jun?”

“Don’t ask. It’s cooler to leave that kind of thing unsaid,” Aikawa struck a suitably cool pose. “Besides, the answer would just bum you out.”

“…………”

“……well, looks like it’s about time. So, Iitan,” Aikawa knocked back her glass of water then paused for a moment. Then she reached into her pocket, pulled out a pair of red sunglasses, and put them on. “This might be my last opportunity, so I’m just gonna go ahead and ask. Tell me, Iitan. Did you really never doubt Kunagisa? Not even once? Not even a little?”

A question posed as an afterthought.

For a second, I was at a loss for words.

“Kunagisa would barely have to lift a finger to bypass the lock on the Seventh Ward. She acknowledged that herself. I don’t think the professor was merely trying to pin it on her. I think he truly believed it to a certain extent. After all, it’s the only rational solution. …Actually, you know what? Forget all that. Whether the crime was possible or not, whether she had a motive or not– put all that boring shit aside, Iitan. Were you really convinced that Kunagisa Tomo wouldn’t kill Utsurigi Gaisuke?”

“…………”

Discarded or not, he was still hers.

She found it unpleasant having someone pick up after her.

“—I-”

“You don’t need to answer. I just wanted to ask.” Just as I was about to say something, Aikawa placed a finger to her lips. “You worked hard this time. So, keep it up just a little bit longer. I’m happy that I get to be friends with such a stellar guy,”

Aikawa said, taking the cheque in hand before excusing herself from the table. The sight was incredibly dashing, unbelievably bold, exceptionally cool, and splendidly red. She was so dazzling it was hard for someone like me to look straight at her. No, I’m sure someone like me could never truly see her at all.

And yet, despite that, my eyes stayed fixed on that blinding crimson, and I opened my mouth.

“Aikawa. If we meet again…”

“Yeah? What is it?”

“Would you hold me?”

A voice that feigned calm.

I knew it was just an act.

I knew it wasn’t a very good one.

Aikawa looked a little taken aback, wearing an uncharacteristically childlike and bewildered expression, but the very next instant I was treated to her usual wicked, nihilistic grin as she stuck out her flaming-red tongue.

“You’re a million years too early, virgin!”

She flipped me off.

“Now then, the next time a suitably consummate occasion arises let us meet again, dear friend.”

Her final remarks were delivered in Kouta’s voice, then without even waiting for my reply, Aikawa turned her back and made her way out of the café. Leaving me alone at our table-for-two. For a while, I didn’t think of anything. I didn’t want to. But— it doesn’t work that way. I’m always forced to think of something. Once I notice it, there’s no escape.

In the end— who was her employer?

Ishimaru Kouta?

Neo Furuara?

Utsurigi Gaisuke?

Or perhaps— Koutari Hinayoshi?

“…Still, next time, huh?”

For me-

The question of whether there’d even be a next time was a delicate one. That said, if it meant being able to stay Aikawa Jun’s friend, maybe putting in the effort to make sure there was wouldn’t be so bad. It might even be worth living another million years.

I thought.

I pondered.

“‘Never judge a book by its cover’— I suppose you’re right, Aikawa.”

I thought as I sipped the coffee in front of me. When it came to whether Kunagisa could’ve been the culprit or not, I could confidently declare she was innocent. Kunagisa has a strange condition where she can't make any vertical movements on her own— I suppose it’s more accurate to call it a compulsive disorder. In other words, whether it be the stairs or the elevator, all such modes of traversal were off limits for her. It wasn’t only logically impossible, but physically impossible as well.

However,

If we leave logical and physical reasoning by the wayside and narrow it down to the single question of whether or not Kunagisa would have killed Utsurigi, then–

Kunagisa probably wouldn’t have.

But the same couldn’t be said for Dead Blue.

I thought.

“——Nonsense.”

That’s right, such words were clearly nonsense.

However,

Even if the security system was meaningless before Kunagisa. Even if no one else could have bypassed it. All that meant was that Kunagisa was in possession of some kind of master key— In which case, even if Kunagisa herself couldn’t have committed the crime, if she were to pass that key off to someone else… just like Kouta— just like Aikawa had passed the anti-lock blade off to me, then-

It was possible.

“In the end, it all comes down to what Kunagisa and Utsurigi talked about that day— damnit,” I muttered bitterly to myself. “A conversation between two geniuses— I can’t even imagine it.”

I couldn’t even imagine it, but–

What if Kunagisa had taught him?

What if?

That would have meant Utsurigi would have had free reign of the facility. Bypassing the security and wiping the logs. He could have roamed about anywhere he pleased.

If you know the ultimate technique— then why bother with any others? Avoiding using it is nothing more than the last bastion of pride for petty cowards.

“…………”

Of course, even had Kunagisa taught me that ultimate technique, I couldn’t have made use of it. I didn’t have the skill to pull it off. But Utsurigi—that menace had the know-how. He possessed the brains to understand— and the arms to carry it out.

It would only be natural for Kunagisa to teach him. ‘If you do this, then you can escape.’ She would have spared no detail in her explanation.

But Utsurigi refused. He couldn’t accept her offer. He wasn’t trapped within the cramped locked-room that was the Seventh Ward— he was trapped in Shadou Kyouichirou’s palm.

If he truly wanted to escape— suicide was his only option.

And so, Utsurigi snuffed out his own existence.

“And so, he destroyed Professor Shadou Kyouichirou.”

Truly destructive, truly malignant.

Who was the real Mad Daemon? That's the kind of story this was. A story of nothing but destruction. Destruction and nothing else. No salvation, no forgiveness, no damnation, and no murder. Just destruction. Too laughable, too ironic, and all too tasteless. That’s the kind of made-up story this was.

In the end— even though it wasn’t necessary, even though he knew damn well that Utsurigi would never run away so long as he could use Kunagisa as leverage— The reason Professor Kyouichirou still chose to lock Utsurigi away in the Seventh Ward— the reason he had no choice but to lock Utsurigi away in the Seventh Ward was because-

He was scared of him.

He was terrified of Utsurigi Gaisuke.

Just as he was terrified of Kunagisa Tomo.

“The professor must’ve known that all along…”

Ah, is that how it was? I finally realized.

The professor realized I escaped the cage not for any of the reasons I anticipated, but simply because he had ratted me out. I see. Because I hadn’t solved the case— because I hadn’t reached the solution he prepared for me, that was his way of scolding me.

Indeed,

Like in his conversation with Neo, hints were scattered around so blatantly it was almost too obvious—

“And I still never noticed—” I placed the empty coffee cup back down on its saucer. “But how was I supposed to realize something like that? I was supposed to realize, right?”

Don’t ask the impossible from me.

Do I really have to put up with these unreasonable demands? Do I really have to obey? Aikawa had given my reasoning a single point— but even that was far too generous. Not even the truth deserves that high a score.

Ahh, Professor Kyouichirou.

In moments like these, I truly understand how you felt.

Meanwhile Kunagisa Tomo.

Utsurigi Gaisuke.

“As for your feelings, I can hardly stand to listen to and accept them, let alone understand them…”

Much less understand everything else.

However, whatever the final deduction is, it must be the truth.

That’s the rule.

The puppetshow rule.

There was no need for understanding. No need for acceptance.

No need for praise. No need for evaluation.

There was no coercion. There was no demand.

Simply obey.

Silent like a lamb, fed like a pig.

“—How’s that for logic, you bastards?”

Make hell the hell named hell.

Massacre the massacre named massacre.

Make sin the sin named sin.

Despair the despair named despair.

Make chaos the chaos named chaos.

Subdue the submission named submission.

Be proud, we, of this beautiful world.

This is the bedroom of the Verge of Death; rampage all you want, as the Verge of Death allows it.

“……Doing whatever you like, dying and coming back to like whenever you please— what are you Otokojuku?”

Truth… the truth?

How stupid. How stupid. How stupid.

What is truth? What is real?

Don’t make me laugh.

This is just— a result.

But,

As long as you get results— no one can complain.

“No matter the explanation, no matter the interpretation— it’s all nonsense.”

It’s not that I don’t understand.

I don’t know.

That’s why my explanation was not to explain.

Moving on while looking back.

The last line of defence.

—noticing my empty coffee cup, the waitress hurried over. She offered me a refill, but I turned her down. ‘Alright then,’ she parted with a smile. It was the fake kind of smile reserved for customers, but nonetheless, smiles were a good thing. Maybe the best of things. And no good thing— ever dies.

“—the nonsense ends here.”

—clack,

The echo of footsteps.

Among the clamor of the café and the ceaseless din of the FM radio, the footfalls rang clearly.

Clack—clackclack—clackclackclack—clackclackclackclackclack—clackclackclackclackclackclackclackclackclackclackclackclackclackclackclackclackclack——

The sound made my left arm throb with pain. I thought of the knife still hidden under my jacket and the Jericho still tucked into my belt. Not that they were ever very reliable, were they?

The footsteps passed me by— and took a seat directly in front of me. Without hesitation, they took the spot where Humanity’s Strongest had been sitting mere moments before.

Legs crossed and arms folded in a carefree manner.

Dressed in a stylish outfit. Wearing a white suit that, in all likelihood, bore the name of some famous brand. Gloves. Shoes. Wristwatch. When not wearing a lab coat, this must’ve been their standard fashion. But all of it seemed to go strangely well with his shaved head, giving him an almost comically intimidating presence.

Although he wore sunglasses just as he had inside the facility, the lenses were neither orange nor black, instead a clear, nearly transparent green.

From behind those green lenses, his eyes sneered gleefully at me. However, just behind those eyes, he wasn’t smiling at all.

And then he–

Sat there, not saying anything.

“—Ah, that’s right, it was my turn, wasn’t it?”

He was surprisingly conscientious.

Despite the situation, I felt somewhat pleased.

Pleased to see which face the die had landed on.

I didn’t dislike it, nor did I find it unpleasant.

“The arms were cut off simply to hide the fingerprints, weren’t they?”

Silently—

He confirmed my suspicions. As if grinning, he nodded.

It was a truly straightforward solution.

If only— if only every case could be solved so neatly, accepted so readily, and resolved so satisfactorily— wouldn’t that be wonderful?

“Come to think of it— you were the only one to call Kunagisa Dead Blue— no one else knew her by that name.”

Shut up and watch, Kunagisa Tomo.

Kunagisa— likely knew everything from the very start.

That Ishimaru Kouta was really Aikawa Jun.

The truth of the case and the reality behind the scenes.

And this conclusion.

And yet she remained silent.

She shut up and watched.

That’s fine, it’s not like she did anything wrong.

That was not betrayal.

There is no betrayal where there is no conviction.

There is no betrayal where there is trust.

Even I—

Had learned how to stay quiet.

“Now then—”

If I could have your attention, everyone.

If you could bear with me just a little while longer.

We can’t stop just yet— not when we’re having such fun.

Let us commence with the beginning of the end.

“You actually hate Kunagisa Tomo, don’t you?”

Abruptly, without any preface or preamble, instinctually and inevitably, without a drop of doubt or inkling of indecision, without a hint of hesitation or trace of tact, yet without being particularly forceful or especially arrogant, as if looking up at, as if gazing down upon, smoothly and slickly, as if it were clear as day, Utsurigi— Utsurigi Gaisuke spoke.

I answered.

“I don’t know.”

《MAD DAEMON & DEAD BLUE》is a Very Very DEAD END.

chapters.title: Psycho Logical (Part Two)
chapters.text:
Psycho Logical (Part Two)

Afterword—

Let’s see. I read it a long, long while ago, but there’s a passage in one of Dostoevsky’s novels that goes like this: ‘I agree that two times two makes four is an excellent thing; but if we are dispensing praise, then two times two makes five is sometimes a most charming little thing as well.’ You might be tempted to butt in and say, “What the hell is this guy saying!? That doesn’t even make any sense!” but if you manage to grit your teeth and bare it, you’ll find words like these have a way of resonating within your heart beyond any reason or argument. I’d much rather have my personal motto be a contradictory statement like that than some pretentious proverb. Beautiful logic is all well and good, but it would be boring if that’s all there was, so I wish more things would boldly exist as that kind of daring contradiction. Take Zeno’s paradox for instance— the sheer wonder of the paradox far outweighs the satisfaction of its solution, which, frankly, makes solutions come across as boorish and unrefined. There was a certain mathematician who took a fond liking to the phrase “the margins are too narrow,” and somehow, I find myself understanding why. After all, things rarely go to plan in this world, so why not let the unknown remain unknown and not force yourself to come up with an answer? I admit that’s rather indulgent, but it should be fine to indulge every once in a while, shouldn’t it? Life’s too short to break everything down into factors, and even if you come up with a solution, there’s no guarantee it will be a satisfying one, so why not forgo the idle reasoning, feel what you feel, and shut up about the rest? After all, if you don’t argue, you can’t lose the argument. Although, coming from the author of a book like this, I’m sure these words won’t amount to anything more than nonsense.

Following Kubikiri Cycle, Kubishime Romanticist, and Kubitsuri Highschool— or rather, in this fourth installment that doesn’t follow the rest, it’s hard to say exactly where our protagonist stands. The people around him aren’t the graceful sort like in Kubikiri, nor are they fine people like in Kubishime— they’re not even worthy rivals like in Kubitsuri. To call him the narrator implies too much insight into the story’s inner workings, to call him a tag-along makes him sound too inconsequential, and it’s undeniable that the term hero doesn’t quite fit. My hope is to distract from that question with this sour little song. An immature protagonist who nonetheless hasn’t experienced youth— that’s the kind of contradiction born by Psycho Logical (volume 2), Sour Little Song.

To my editor-in-chief, Outa Katsushi and my illustrator, Take, as usual, I extended my deepest gratitude. I would also like to thank all my readers whose reviews have begun trickling in one-by-one. After all, the written word is nothing without those who read it, so I’d like to express my sincere appreciation for all without exception. With that said, ‘till next time.

-Nisio Isin
